paragraphs.text: EXPOSITION OF PSALM 1

God set the delight of future blessedness before us as the highest incentive to virtue; the devil, for his part, contrived to make delight a sharp spur to error. Proof of both is given by Adam, the first of the human race. The Lord God placed him in the paradise of pleasure to enjoy eternal delight, so that his future offspring would be roused to virtue. God well knew that he would give way to error, and that the hope of salvation had to be set before the rest, so that they might strive to be restored to the dwelling that had been snatched from the human race. Yet this same Adam was deceived by his wife's persuasion, through the form of the serpent, which prefigured the allurements of delight.

So the adversary seized the occasion and worked death in me through delight. Thus what divine grace had granted for life became death for me. The enemy won man's consent to the fall all the more easily because he held out a semblance of nature. For the Lord took delight in his works, and the first beginnings of nature delighted him; seeing them, the Lord said: Very good.

The angels praise the Lord, the powers of heaven sing psalms to him, and before the very beginning of the world the Cherubim and Seraphim say, in the sweetness of their tuneful voices: Holy, holy, holy. Countless thousands of angels stand by, and the elders and a great multitude, like the sound of many waters, sing together: Alleluia. A fuller account even holds that the very axis of heaven turns with a certain

sweetness of perpetual harmony, so that its sound is heard in the farthest parts of the earth, where certain secrets of nature lie. Nor does this seem foreign to the way of nature, since a voice sent out comes back with more pleasing applause from woods or mountains, and they return what they have received with a sweeter sound. Even in crags and stones nature has found something to delight us: in some it is the lookout they give, in others their usefulness or their beauty. Wild beasts and birds are soothed by the delight of a pleasant spot or a melodious voice; and even for infants at the breast, sternness brings terror and caresses bring pleasure. Delight, then, is natural.

Holy David saw from what state man had fallen and by what deceit. Had man kept the grace of that eternal and heavenly delight which the Lord had poured into him, and not lost it through being captivated by worldly allurements, he would never have suffered the injuries of so wretched a hardship. And so David, eager to repair and restore that grace, established for us, through the service of psalm-singing, a likeness of the heavenly way of life.

For although all divine Scripture breathes the grace of God, the book of Psalms is sweet above all. Moses himself described the deeds of the forefathers in plain language. Yet when he had led the people of the fathers across the Red Sea, a wonder to be remembered, and saw King Pharaoh drowned with his forces, he raised his genius to greater heights,

because he had achieved things beyond his own powers, and he sang a triumphal song to the Lord. Miriam too took up a timbrel and urged the other women on, saying: Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea. Moses himself also, when he had read the law of the Lord, spoke in a song so as to fix its memory in the hearts of his hearers, saying: Hear, O heaven, and I will speak; let my speech be awaited like the rain, and let my words come down like dew, like a shower upon the grass and like snow upon the hay.

God, then, delights in song not only to be praised but also to be reconciled. That is why Moses made most use of song when he called heaven and earth to witness. He wanted the world to listen more eagerly to its salvation as it sounded in harmony with the music of heavenly grace, and he wanted the observance of the law to take root forever in human minds through the sweetness of a holy delight.

Indeed, before the tablets of the law were confirmed by a song, Moses broke and shattered them in his indignation; but once they had been consecrated by such a seal, human anger had no place, for the holiness of that sacred sweetness shut it out. So the song of the Lord came down from heaven like a gentle dew and soaked men's faith, as rain soaks the grass, with a shower of spiritual grace. These two songs in the books of Moses, then, are like the two eyes of the world and the lights of heaven, illuminating the whole body of his work.

But David was chosen by the Lord above all for this task. What is rare in others, and seems to stand out from the rest of their work, was to shine in him constantly and without interruption. We read one song in the book of Judges; the rest runs on in the manner of history, setting out the deeds of the forefathers. Isaiah wrote one song to soothe the hearts of his readers; in the rest he thundered with the terrible trumpet of rebuke.

His enemies persecuted him to death for his other sayings, but not even they could reproach him for his song. Daniel has one song, and Habakkuk one. Solomon himself, the son of David, is said to have sung countless songs, yet he left only one that the Church has received, the Song of Songs; he also wrote Proverbs. In the other writers, then, songs can be found only one at a time.

History instructs, the law teaches, prophecy announces, rebuke chastens, moral teaching persuades; in the book of Psalms there is the benefit of them all, and a kind of medicine for the salvation of humankind. Whoever reads it has a special remedy with which to heal the wounds of his own passions. Whoever cares to look into it will find, as in a common gymnasium for souls and a stadium of virtues, various kinds of contests

made ready, and he may choose the one he knows suits him best, so as to reach the crown more easily. If anyone is eager to review the deeds of the forefathers and wishes to imitate them, he will find the whole course of ancestral history contained within a single psalm, so that he gains a treasury of memory in a short reading. Things explained briefly also seem easier. And how profound it is that within a short space the psalm sets out the hardships that followed offenses and adds the blessings of reconciliation, so that

you learn at the same time what harm the offense of unbelief did and what ready faith brought! If anyone explores the force of the law, which consists entirely in the bond of love (for whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law), let him read in the Psalms with what loving devotion David exposed himself alone to grave dangers to drive away the reproach of the whole people. In this he will recognize a glory of love no less than the triumph of valor. If anyone dreads the harshness of rebuke, let him hear one who says: Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor in your anger

chasten me. Let him learn from this how he ought to soften the sentence of an angry judge. If anyone longs to know an example of patience, let him read in the Psalms: If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil. Let him notice that David foresaw the precept of the Gospel by the Spirit and anticipated it by his virtue. So you have that proverb: a meek man is a physician of the heart. And if anyone wishes to be armed against the attacks of spiritual wickedness, what better can he know than that he must sing psalms? David sang psalms as a youth and drove away the evil spirit that had previously gripped Saul.

And what shall I say of the power of prophecy? What others announced in riddles seems to have been promised to him alone, plainly and openly: that the Lord Jesus would be born of his seed, as the Lord said to him: Of the fruit of your body I will set upon your throne.

So in the Psalms Jesus is not only born for us. He also undergoes that saving passion of the body, rests, rises again, ascends into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. What no man would have dared to say, this prophet alone announced, and afterwards the Lord himself proclaimed it in the Gospel.

Moreover, all writers of psalms have put into their writings examples or sayings of those who came before them; the Psalms contain nothing but what is their own. What, then, is more pleasing than a psalm? Hence David himself says beautifully: Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good; let praise be pleasant and seemly to our God. And this is true. For a psalm is the blessing of the people, the praise of God, the tribute of the multitude, the applause of all, the speech of everyone, the voice of the Church, the tuneful confession of faith, devotion full of authority, the gladness of freedom, the cry of joy, the echo of gladness. It calms anger, releases from anxiety, lifts from sorrow;

it is armor by night and instruction by day, a shield in fear, a feast in holiness, an image of tranquillity, a pledge of peace and concord. Like a lyre, it draws a single song out of different and unequal voices. The rising of the day echoes with a psalm, and its setting resounds with a psalm.

The apostle bids women keep silent in church, yet they do well to cry out a psalm. It is sweet to every age and fitting for both sexes. Old men sing it, laying aside the stiffness of age; sorrowful veterans respond to it in the gladness of their hearts; young men sing it without reproach of wantonness; adolescents sing it together without the dangers of their slippery age or the temptation of pleasure. Young women sing psalms with no loss of womanly modesty, and little girls, without lapse

of modesty, sing a hymn to God with sober gravity in the sweetness of a modulated voice. Childhood is eager to grasp it, and infancy, which shies away from learning other things, delights to practice it. It is a kind of game of learning, and it profits more than discipline taught with severity. What effort it takes in church to get silence while the readings are being read! If one person speaks, everyone makes noise; but when a psalm is read, it creates its own silence: all speak and no one makes a disturbance.

Kings echo a psalm without the haughtiness of power; David rejoiced to be seen in this service. A psalm is sung by emperors and shouted with joy by the peoples. Each person vies to cry out what benefits all. A psalm is sung at home and repeated outside; it is learned without effort and kept with pleasure. A psalm joins those who are at odds, unites the quarrelsome, and reconciles the offended; for who will not forgive someone with whom he has raised a single voice to God? It is surely a great bond of unity for the whole number of the people to come together into one choir.

The strings of the lyre are unequal, but the harmony is one. On very few strings the fingers of a craftsman often go astray, but in the people the Spirit, who is the craftsman, cannot err. A psalm is the companion of work by night and the reward of rest by day, the training of beginners and the strengthening of the perfect, the ministry of angels, the warfare of heaven, a spiritual sacrifice. Even rocks answer a psalm; a psalm is sung and even stony hearts are softened. We see the hardest weep and the merciless bend.

In a psalm teaching vies with grace; it is sung for delight and at the same time learned for instruction. For harsh precepts do not last; but what you have taken in with sweetness, once it has been poured into the heart, does not usually slip away. What is there that does not meet you when you read the Psalms?

In them I read a song for the beloved and am set on fire with longing for holy love. In them I recognize the winepresses of the divine mystery and the grace of revelations; I review the testimonies of the resurrection and the gifts of the promise. In them I learn to avoid sin, and I unlearn being ashamed to repent of my offenses. So great a king, so great a prophet has challenged me by his example to strive either to lessen a sin I have committed or to guard against one I have not.

What, then, is a psalm but an instrument of the virtues? The venerable prophet played it with the plectrum of the Holy Spirit and made the sweetness of heavenly sound echo on earth. He played on strings and cords, that is, on the dead remains of animals, varying the distinctions of different notes, and directed his song of divine praise toward heaven. In doing so he taught us that we must first die to sin, and only then, in this body, bring out the various works of the virtues, each in its distinct place, so that the grace of our devotion might reach the Lord. In this way, for those intent on heavenly things, no desire for earthly vices would creep in, and at the same time the soul would shine with the sweetness of heavenly grace. Rightly, then, the Lord praised the minister of so great a gift, saying: I have found David, a man after my own heart.

They also say that the more skilled lyre players sing inwardly, as the stories tell of Aspendius the lyre player. They say, too, that the principles of melody and certain locks of the rhythms lie in the upper part of the psaltery. So David taught that we ought to sing inwardly and play psalms inwardly, just as Paul also sang when he said: I will pray with the spirit, I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, I will sing with the mind also. He also taught us to shape our life and conduct by looking to the things above, so that the delight of sweetness does not stir up the passions of the body. Those passions do not redeem our soul but weigh it down, while the holy prophet declared that he sang psalms for the redemption of his soul, saying: I will sing to you on the lyre, O God, the Holy One of Israel. My lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and so will my soul, which you have redeemed. But let us now enter on the opening of the psalm that is set before us.

Blessed, he says, is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly. How fitting, how timely a beginning! Those who have undertaken to put on a festival of games usually announce a prize and boast of how splendid the crown is, so that the contestants will gather with greater eagerness and compete with more strenuous effort. In the same way our Lord Jesus has set forth the glory of the heavenly kingdom, the grace of everlasting rest

and the blessedness of eternal life as incentives to human virtue. An emperor too, when he sets out for war, promises his soldiers a bounty and promotion in the ranks of the army, so that the hope of reward may steal away the hardships and hide the fear of danger. Like the herald of a great emperor, then, holy David encourages the soldiers, summons the athletes, and announces the prize, saying: Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly. He began with the prize to lighten the weight of the coming contest. He put the reward first so that each person, leaping over in his heart the anxieties and hardships of present things,

might strive with eager haste to earn the blessedness of the things to come. Blessed, he says, is the man. What more could be given to man than that beyond which nothing greater could be ascribed to God by apostolic authority? For God has been called blessed and the only Potentate, King of kings and Lord of lords. He alone is the Potentate, he is the King of kings, he is the Lord of lords; yet he does not go beyond the power of blessedness. He has given us a common share in that title, which has been judged worthy of divine honor.

Let us now consider why he said "blessed is the man" and not rather "blessed are human beings," since both sexes are called to grace. Did he exclude women from sharing in blessedness because he called only the man blessed? Far from it, just as God did not exclude women from a share in creation because he made the man first.

For God said: Let us make man according to our image and according to our likeness. And God made man, it says; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them. The word "human" signifies both; the word "man" specifies the sex. But just as both are included when "human" is said, so when "man" is named, the woman whose husband he is is also understood.

Indeed, it says, she shall be called woman, because she was taken from her husband. Add to this that beings who share the same nature certainly cannot have separate works, and those whose work is equal certainly receive an equal reward. So in saying "man," Scripture did not pass over his partner in marriage, just as in saying "human" it did not leave out his partner in nature.

There we read that a human being was made; and though the nature is one, we cannot deny that the principal sex was created first. In the same way, when we read "man" here, we recognize in the principal part the sex that is almost its equal as well. The pursuits of virtue, then, are equal, because the privilege of creation is equal. Why argue about sex when what is required of you are contests of the soul and not of the body, and the soul has no sex? So do not distinguish honor or divide the reward where sex makes no distinction.

Yet it is not without reason that the one who was later in falling should be called first to the training. She who began badly ought to follow, not lead; or at least, after that experience, let her be more modest. Eve did wrong in disregarding the order of nature; she ought to have waited for the one who went before her. The serpent cunningly began with the one who came second. That is why the prophet returns to the first, the one who would not have fallen had he not followed the one who came second.

So he called us back from the fall before he challenged us to the palm of victory. Blessed, he says, is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly. See where you are called blessed, O man. It is not in riches, not in power and honors, not in noble birth or in comeliness and beauty, not in bodily health, for in these there is nothing good by nature. Indeed, not only do they easily turn into their opposites, but they even become instruments of guilt for anyone who does not know how to use them. For who is made just by money, who humble by power, who merciful by noble birth, who chaste by good looks? These things are more enticements to sin than aids to progress in virtue.

Next, what does he mean by choosing to say "has not walked" and "has not stood," as if speaking of the past, when he could have said: "Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, and does not stand in the way of sinners, and does not sit in the seat of pestilence"? Note the teaching here. For a person is not

blessed at once merely because he is not ungodly or a sinner, since his end is uncertain. It is not written idly: Praise no one before his death. So as long as anyone is in this life, he cannot be praised with a final verdict, since he may still be open to error. But whoever has ended his life without offense is rightly counted worthy of the name of blessed, since he enjoys the fellowship of the blessed.

But perhaps you will say: "Why, then, did he say elsewhere: Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor? For he did not call blessed the one who has considered, but the one who considers." The reason is that those who do good find in the work itself the means by which they are approved, receiving their reward in the work itself, since a good deed is the fruit of a blessed conscience. But those who refrain from evil are not blessed at once if they have avoided guilt once or twice; they are blessed only if they have managed to escape the contagion of guilt for the whole span of their life.

Now this question arises: why did he choose to call blessed not the one who has performed some duty of godliness, but the one who has kept away from the counsel of the ungodly? For the one who has fulfilled the task of virtue seems more worthy of praise than the one who has avoided sin, since neither an ox nor a horse nor a stone is in the habit of sinning or of sitting in the seat of pestilence. But such things do not have

the fruit of blessedness, for they have no sense of virtue. How could things that have no desire to follow the law ever reach the reward of the law? I see, then, that the statement concerns rational beings, that is, us. And for us the beginning of good things is to abstain from sins, for we read: Turn away from evil and do good. This is the order of discipline: you should strive from lower things to more perfect ones, so that you are not daunted by the weight of greater things, since you ought to be drawn on by beginning with lighter ones.

For Scripture teaches us that the ascent of godliness is like the ladder on which holy Jacob, a man of spiritual training, saw the angels of the Lord ascending and descending. He is set before us so that through him we may learn that we ought to advance in virtue step by step, little by little. In this way we can strive from the lowest things to the highest, if we proceed by small steps toward things that seem beyond human nature. Always keep this ladder set before you.

Do not be afraid, O man, to climb these steps of discipline. The first step is close to the earth, and the next is like the first; so by equal steps one climbs to the top. Do not scorn that first step, O man, as though it were the lowest of all. That first ascent separates you from the earth: once you have lifted your foot from the ground, you are treading on air. Standing in virtue, you have left the earth by rising; you leave the earth if you turn away from guilt. The beginning of progress toward virtue, then, is to abstain from sin.

So that we may know that this is the proper order of teaching, listen to the law when it says: "You shall not commit adultery, you shall not commit murder"; for these commandments seemed suited to the imperfect. Indeed, the Lord Jesus himself, knowing that the man who asked him by what works he might come to eternal life was imperfect, answered him:

"You shall not commit adultery, you shall not commit murder, you shall not steal," and the rest. Then, when the man said that he had done all these things, he added more perfect commands, saying: "Sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven." And he showed that there is so great a distance between turning away from evil and imitating good that the man who judged the first easy for himself refused the second. But because he had not truly climbed even to the first, he could not fit himself for the second;

for if he had loved his neighbour, he could not have refused the poor the help of his inheritance. Climb, then, the first step of the law, so that you may reach the heavenly summit of the gospel. That is why I think that the holy prophet, as one placed under the law and following the law's manner, in the first psalm, speaking in his own person, warns us of what to avoid rather than setting out what to follow; whereas in the fortieth psalm, which is spoken in the person

of the Saviour, there is an exhortation to virtue rather than a rebuke of error; for it speaks of the Saviour's passion. And so the dispenser of the gospel too, as far as we can judge, since we have heard him say, "Blessed are the merciful," crowned mercy alike in the psalm of his own passion and in the gospel. But let us now set about explaining the psalm and look into the force of the prophecy.

"Blessed," it says, "is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence." We can say that there are three kinds of sin, which we think are expressed here: of thought, of deed, and of persistence; and that the one called blessed is he who has not even thought what is evil.

For how can anyone be blessed who is to be convicted on the day of judgment by his own thoughts accusing him? Even if he has deceived men, escaped a witness, and evaded an accuser, he still cannot escape himself as his own accuser—and him he ought to fear most of all, because he will have both an accuser and a defendant who confesses.

Blessed, therefore, is he who has neither thought what is evil, nor committed sin—for sometimes we offend even without forethought, since "in much speaking we do not escape sin"—nor persevered in sin. Or else: blessed is he who has not thought anything of error, or has not stood in such a thought, or at least has not persevered in those thoughts which he has noticed to be full of error.

But whether these interpretations fit properly, the reader will judge. For he who has once thought evil ought neither to stand in it nor to persevere in it. Yet even if he did not persevere, he could not be blessed, because he stood in what he wickedly thought; and even if he did not stand in it, still, from the very fact that he thought evil, whether he has the fruit of blessedness is a question that needs some lenient interpreter.

Finally, since no one can say that he has a clean heart, grant that thought may be pardonable: is the committing of sins also pardonable? And further, if standing in sin is pardonable, is it also full of blessedness simply because it does not persist in the crime? Again, how could one who has not thought what is wicked stand or persevere in sin? Granting that he is blessed who has rightly kept these three, the order is certainly different.

For the first thing is not to persevere in sin, the second not to have stood in it, the third not to have thought anything of error. For one who did not persevere might still have stood; one who did not stand might still have thought; but one who did not even think is truly blessed.

For this reason I thought that another interpretation should not be passed over either, by which we maintain that three steps are set out in their proper order: that whoever wishes to be blessed should not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, that is, should not walk in their

thoughts; next, should not stand in the way of sinners; third, should not sit in the seat of pestilence. You, then, who have become a Christian in the Church, or you who are making your way toward grace, keep away from the counsels of the ungodly, so that you can say: "Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, O God, nor my life with men of blood," and do not think things that are ungodly. And what are those, if not things devised to wrong God?

For piety is owed first to God, second to parents. The enemy, indeed, often sows various things in our minds, and so the prophet was careful to hold that deliberate thoughts, rather than sudden suggestions, should be counted as guilt. So you have kept away from the counsels of the ungodly; well done, but you are not yet blessed. Take care also not to stand in the way of sinners.

With what careful weighing the words of divine Scripture are set down! Since we are all under sin, it does not demand of you what is beyond nature—that you commit no sin, for not even an infant one day old is without sin—but that you do not remain in sin in a lasting standstill. Not all are ungodly; therefore you are called back from all the thoughts and conspiracies of the ungodly. But all are sinners; therefore you are admonished to stop sinning. If you have fallen in the slips of youth, the progress of maturity ought to correct you.

So do not go on into graver sins, and do not stand in lighter ones. You have this also said by the Lord in Isaiah: "Go out from Babylon, fleeing from the Chaldeans"; that is, even if you have entered into the confusion of vices, go out. You ought not to have entered, but you did enter, driven by the law of the flesh and taken captive by the law of sin. Go out, depart even late, strip off your heavy servitude. You could not avoid entering into sin through frailty; you are given the means to go out of sin through sobriety. Go out, then, from Babylon, fleeing from the Chaldeans. Babylon is confusion, which does not keep the order of the virtues; for it is with a mind confused by allurements that we go wrong.

The Chaldeans are those who search out the courses of the stars in the pursuit of empty superstition and sow the errors of ungodly paganism. Flee from them, so that they do not capture you or bind you in the heavy snare of captivity. Abraham was a Chaldean, but he fled from the Chaldeans, and that before the law; you have been born under the law already—flee from the ungodly. He rejected the inheritance of his fathers so as to possess the inheritance of faith; you, leave behind the succession of the body and acquire the inheritance of devotion.

But even if you have not stood in sin, you are not yet blessed; there is still something you must keep free of. Many are the allurements, many the turnings aside from virtue: heavy are the incitements of pleasure, heavy the tinder of avarice, the lust for power, the ambition for honour, which taint men's minds as with a kind of poison and their souls with a pestilent wasting of vices. This is the seat of pestilence, on which the scribes and Pharisees sat, who lay heavy burdens on men but will not move them with a finger themselves.

These seats the Saviour cast out of the temple: the seats of those who boasted of their honour and sought the first places of rank, of those who used the priesthood or preeminence of office for gain, of those who, indulging their gluttony, by no means kept the guard of self-restraint they owed. This is true pestilence; indeed, the sons of Eli were sons of pestilence. On this kind of seat of vices Scripture forbids us to lean back our neck and recline the strength of our whole body. Note, then, the precise force of the words.

"Blessed is he who has not stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence." That "way" means the course of this life is not in doubt, since Scripture itself says: "In this way where I walked they hid a snare for me," and: "Agree

quickly with your adversary while you are with him on the way." For as long as we run the course of this life, we have a path along which we walk every day until we reach the end; even if we do not seem to be moving bodily, we are advancing. For just as those asleep on ships are driven into port by the winds, and though as they rest they have no sense of sailing, the voyage still presses them on toward

the end and drives them along unawares, so as the span of our life flows away, each of us is carried by a hidden course to his own end. Therefore it is said: "Rise, you who sleep"—for you sleep, and your time walks on—and see that while you sleep long your time does not pass by. So, even if you sleep, let your heart keep watch, and your heart will not be idle; if your heart is not idle, your times are not idle. You are on the way, O man; walk, so that

you may arrive, lest night overtake you on the way, lest the day of your life be spent before you hasten your progress in virtue. You are a traveller through this life; all things pass, all things fall behind you; everything on this road you see and pass by. You saw the loveliness of trees, the greenness of grass, the clearness of springs, and whatever else of the kind delights the eyes; it pleased you to look; it delighted you to attend to it a little; while you attended, you passed on. Again, as you walk, you came upon a rocky and broken road, hollows in the cliffs, sheer mountainsides, dense forests:

you were wearied a little; again you passed on. Such is this life, whose prosperity does not last and whose adversity is not long. So, as one set on a road, let neither good fortune lift you up nor adversity break you; let neither pleasing things delay you nor sad things hold you back. Always hasten to the end, hasten so that you may arrive; but choose your road before you run.

There are two ways, one of the righteous and the other of sinners, one of equity and the other of iniquity, of which the prophet said: "And see if there is any way of iniquity in me." Not only is our life a way, but our life itself is either a way of virtue or a way of iniquity. Take care, then, that avarice does not set its steps in you so that you become a way of crime, nor wickedness, nor lust, so that you become a way of iniquity, worn down by the crimes travelling over it. You are free to choose whom you will follow, either the righteous or the unrighteous.

The way of the righteous is narrower, that of the unrighteous broader; the one, of sobriety, narrower; the other, of drunkenness, broader, so that it can hold those who stagger. This one has the allurements of this world, that one the rewards of the world to come. In the one the fruit is more immediate; in the other the hope is slower. For things that are pleasant do not put off their enjoyment through long waiting but offer it at once; whereas what is serious is sought with toil, is scarcely grasped even by blessed thought, "what eye has not seen nor ear heard, which God has prepared for those who love him."

We find it hard to believe what we do not see, and so the soul is tossed about and turns its thoughts this way and that, as though they were eyes. Then various forms of things meet it and pour themselves before it; if it looks to what is eternal, it chooses virtue; if to what is present, it prefers pleasure. Hard and unequal is the struggle against the delights of the present.

On this side is freedom for the desires; on that, the injury of servitude: to do what you do not want and to abstain from what you have longed for. Here a banquet, there a fast; here unrestrained joys, there unceasing tears; here dancing, there prayer; here sweet songs, there heavy groans. It is indeed written: "The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of fools in the house of feasting. It is better to hear the rebuke of a wise man than to be a man who listens to the song of fools." But few hear these things, and fewer follow them.

The sweetness of sin, which flows in at once and fattens the feelings of the one who hears it, attracts men more than the bitterness of virtue, which wraps the hope of faith as in a kind of rind of hard labour. Blessed, then, and admirable is he who, set to choose between such ways, has not been bent aside by the allurements of pleasure so as to plant his step on shallow and crooked ground; to him it is not said: "You who have forsaken the straight paths to walk in the ways of darkness."

We have learned, then, what the way of sinners is, on which the prophet warns us not to stand; and Ecclesiastes also teaches it, saying: "Do not stand in an evil word," that is, do not persist in evil words, and likewise in wicked deeds. How one should stand in good things the same holy prophet teaches, saying: "Our feet were standing in your courts, O Jerusalem."

In Jerusalem we must stand; from Babylon we must flee. To Moses too it is said, "But you, stand with me"—to him who fled from Egypt and persevered in standing with the Lord. And in the gospel, those who stood until the eleventh hour received a wage equal to those who had worked; and the virgins who had stood waiting until the coming of the bridegroom were found worthy to go in together to the wedding, while those who went away and came back later were shut out by the Lord's authoritative sentence. We have learned, then, not to stand in the way of sinners, but to stand in the duty of virtue, for it is written: "But you stand by faith."

Now let us consider what this means: "nor sat in the seat of pestilence." And first we say that it is not simply sitting on the kind of seat in common use that is being censured—for what would that have to bring it under blame?—but since the eyes of the Lord are always on the faithful of the earth, we ought to stand as men placed under the eye of the emperor and set, as it were, in some service.

A soldier under arms stands; he does not sit. A soldier in armour does not lean back, but rouses and holds himself erect. So it is said to the soldiers of Christ: "Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord." But iniquity, on the contrary, sits on a talent of lead, because, fixed fast in sin, it cannot separate itself from it. For those hardened in error and eagerly clinging to their crimes are said to sit; they refuse to rise or to listen to the one who says: "Rise, after you have sat."

Indeed, this same prophet says elsewhere: "Princes sat and spoke against me." Or do we not know that an ingrained habit of sinning has such power that it overrides nature, which, though curable unto salvation, is found incurable once the passions have been strengthened by time? Let us not, then, remain in our vices; but let each one, even if he has been in them, leap away from guilt, as it is written of the harlot: "Do not fix your eye upon her, but leap away, do not delay; leap away before the years of youth overtake you."

But, what is graver, many [?] have not blushed at the luxury of the body even with their hair turning white, and have dragged out a stained life even to old age; for the plague of guilt conceived in the inmost parts grows more bitter with the passing of time. Beware, then, of the counsels of the ungodly; let no such counsels penetrate your mind, lest it be said of you: "Will anyone bind fire in his bosom and not burn his clothes?" For whoever

has once kindled the flame of burning wickedness in the bosom of his mind will soon burn the clothes of his body. And as fire leaping into stubble clings and stays until it has consumed everything it has seized, so even a tiny spark of sin, if fanned by some tinder of vice, stirs up a great blaze. Do not, then, stand in sin. If you have set your foot above the abyss of guilt, quickly withdraw it, lest the filth rise above the sole of your foot and, deceived by an easier slip, you sink down into the mire.

The first vices, then, must be guarded against, so that they do not creep on into more and graver ones. For just as those who roll about in mud become the more soiled the more they wallow, so whoever has once spattered himself with the mud of wickedness, unless he leaps quickly out of it, coats himself more heavily, day by day, with the filth of his disgrace through a muddy way of life.

And so from the heavy stench of that foul and shameful abyss a kind of pestilence of souls is contracted, and when the breath of wholesome thoughts is corrupted, the wretched plague of seething passions spreads. From this a deadly poison pours into minds; from this sickness creeps into bodies and languor into souls.

For there is an evil languor: the languor of error, the languor of avarice, the languor of insatiable desire. These are riches, as Ecclesiastes says: "There is an evil languor which I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the harm of their owner." Tell me, Ecclesiastes, why is this languor evil? He will answer: because avaricious hope devours many. Greed is insatiable in its appetite; those who covet silver do not know how to be satisfied with silver.

Riches swell, they do not fill. Even if someone is glutted with riches, "there is no one," he says, "who lets him sleep." And indeed "all his days are in darkness and mourning and much anger and languor and wrath." For how can he sleep who keeps anxious watch over his gold, who dreads losses, who ponders profits, who reckons up interest, who counts his storehouses? It is an evil languor, then, that takes away the good repose of the mind.

Evil languor is luxury, lust, concupiscence, worldly delight, ambition, which quickly corrupts the health of sobriety. In short, all the corruption of this world is pestilence. Therefore "do not touch, do not defile" it: it is a plague, it contaminates; it is a disease, it pollutes. "Do not taste the things that all lead to corruption by their very use," as the Apostle said, who also cries elsewhere: "The root of all evils is avarice."

It stirs up diseases and implants pains; indeed, those who have craved it "have pierced themselves with many pains." This is the pestilence which often makes men neither hot nor cold, but—what is worse than either hot or cold—lukewarm, so that they are spat out of the mouth of the Lord Jesus, who rejects them for their grave sins. This is what stirs up sicknesses not in a few but in all. "Every head is in pain, every heart in sorrow.

From the feet to the head" are the sores of sinners. Every head is in pain when those who are reckoned wise are tormented by the pain of avarice. For "the wise man's understanding is in his head"; and this can also be applied to those who preside over the Church. Every heart is in sorrow when we savour the things of the flesh and bury the keen sight of our heart in bodily pleasures. Hence the Lord says of such people that he has given them a heart of flesh.

From the feet to the head the dreadful plague of diseases creeps, when men suffer by contagion, when they sympathize with others: if someone is cheated of the fulfilment of his lust, if he could not overcome a widow's chastity or seize a field; and all the sick pass their ailments on to one another. How often old men groan that they can no longer drink for long! How often they grieve that they have stopped whoring, though they still have the will to whore! How often, amid the talk of drunkards, virtues are a disgrace,

sins a matter of praise, decency a joke, self-restraint a laughing-stock, mercy folly! These are the diseases that pass their evils on to many; from a few the corruption reaches all. They sit in their gatherings disparaging the sober and belching up their surfeit; they sit in taverns competing in drunkenness; among them a harlot full of wine, smiling at one, scorching another, and inflaming them all with the heat of lust. If a modest man passes by, he blushes and is picked at by each of them; if a shameless one, he is praised by every mouth and passes like a disease into the souls of each.

For one who is renowned for his shameful deeds draws a great many to imitate his error. And so, while they imitate another's sin, they make the evil their own. Do not sit among those whom the holy prophet fled; imitate him, who fled and certainly did not sit, who says: "I have not sat in the council of the wicked, and with those who do iniquity I will not go in." Explain to us, David, why you fled from them; show

us these parties, so that we too may flee them and not be infected by their contagion. "They are corrupt," he says, "and have become abominable; there is none who does good, no, not one." This, then, applies generally to all the shameless, but can also be applied specifically to those who mock the good, whom Aquila called chleuastai, because these are truly diseases, who by mocking the good work a great deal of error in souls and corrupt minds. How many things he has named from which the blessed man must keep away! And he adds still others.

But his will was in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night. That is, blessed is the one who does these things by deliberate choice, by reason and with prudence. For even a little child can keep away from the things just mentioned, not by virtue but because he is unable to sin and does not know how. It could even apply to a brute beast, which has no power of deliberation and no sense of wrongdoing.

This, then, is the fourth point, or what follows: here the definition of the blessed man is set apart from the beast, because the wise man is subject to the law by will, not by necessity. This makes a very great difference, for what is done willingly bears the fruit of a reward, while what is done under necessity is only the obedience of a stewardship. So the apostle taught us when he said: If I do this willingly, I have a reward; if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me. The fitting order is first to love the law, and second to meditate on it. Whoever loves keeps the commandments of the law willingly; whoever fears keeps them unwillingly.

We have received this method of teaching from the justice of God himself in the law, for it is written: Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. And these words which I command you today shall be in your heart and in your soul; and you shall teach them to your children and speak of them when you sit, when you are on the road, when you are at rest and when you are awake; and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as jewels before your eyes; and you shall write them on the thresholds of your houses and on your gates.

And further on: And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you but that you love the Lord your God and walk in all his ways? Wisdom too says: Desire my words, therefore; love them, and you will have instruction. Wisdom is radiant and never fades, and she is easily seen by those who love her and found by those who seek her.

Rightly, then, the holy prophet teaches us to have our will in the law and our meditation according to the law. Will in the law lies not only in eagerness but also in deed: first the will, then the action. So too the Lord, when someone said to him, If you will, you can make me clean, answered: I will; be clean, to show that the will must go before our actions. Indeed the law seeks those who act willingly, because the law of the Lord is blameless, converting the soul, and no one is converted except one who is converted by his own will. And one who acts willingly hides the toil and steals away the sense of labor.

Therefore he meditates on the law day and night. What is required here is not so much a continual application to reading as a disposition to keep the law; for he meditates fully who is a law to himself, intent on the work of the law written in his heart. Aquila, however, put only "day" and not "night" as well. In doing so he was not so much disagreeing with the others as

referring it to something else, since whoever meditates on the law is always in the light and has no night. For one whose works shine cannot possibly walk in darkness, because his righteousness shines forth like the light. Let our life, then, meditate on the law; let our conduct meditate on it, our actions, our understanding of the heavenly mysteries. For the law is a copy and shadow of heavenly things, a shadow of the good things to come. Let whoever recognizes in the Gospel what he believes in the law meditate both in darkness and in daylight, that is, both when placed in adversity and in prosperity; for the law commands us to love the Lord. Whoever loves ought to keep the disposition of lasting love in every circumstance.

A father loves his son; he loves him even when he rebukes him, he loves him even when he beats him with a rod, for whoever spares his rod hates his son. The Lord too chastises us and loves us. So even when we commit offenses that deserve punishment, he still loves us, he who receives back even the one who has offended him; for the Lord chastises every son whom he receives. And you, when you are chastised, love him, for you are chastised precisely so that you may be received.

For what great thing is it to love the Lord your God when you have everything in abundance, when you enjoy what you wished for, when you delight in honors, wealth and children? We are accustomed to show gratitude even to a human being from whom we have received a kindness. So when Job was praised by the judgment of heaven, the devil replied that it was no wonder he was grateful to God, since he had such an abundance of prosperity; the test would come if he lost all of it and still performed the duty of a devout worshiper.

This, then, is the first virtue: not to be broken by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity. This is what the law teaches you: in affliction not to slacken your effort or put on despair, and, once victorious, not to say, My strength and my might have given me this, but to know that everything must be ascribed to divine mercy.

Isaiah cries out: He who is in distress will not be confounded for a time. Drink this first. What does "Drink this first" mean? Let us set aside the mystical sense for now and follow the moral sense that the letter teaches. He says that because of the gravity of their sins there would be grievous afflictions and troubles for the people, and these had to come first so that mercy might follow. Drink, then, first the tribulation; for through many tribulations we must

enter the kingdom of God. Drink, so that the sense of tribulation may be poured into the inmost parts of your heart; drink the pain of one who mourns with a patient spirit; for when you have turned back and groaned, then you will reconcile the offended Lord to yourself. Drink this first, then, that you may be in sorrow and distress; joy quickly pours error into us. The people grew fat and gross, rose up to play, and departed from the Lord.

It does you good to have a contrite heart; drink this first, so that your sacrifice may be accepted by the Lord. Let the apostle teach you what "Drink this first" means: it is the cup of tribulation, for tribulation produces patience. There can be no patience unless there has first been tribulation. Tribulation, he says, produces patience, and patience proof, and proof hope; and hope does not confound. Drink tribulation first, so that afterward so many cups of virtues may

be served to you. And so that you may know that tribulation is drunk, you heard the prophet say today: You have made us drink the wine of compunction; and later he says: And you will give them drink in tears, in measure. He asks for drink in measure, not beyond measure, lest they be unable to bear it. And he proved by his own example how good a disposition this prayer came from, for he mingled his drink with weeping, so as to incline the Lord's mercy toward himself.

Drink this first, then, so that you may drink the second as well (for now is the time to bring in the mystical sense): drink first the Old Testament, so that you may drink the New Testament too. Unless you have drunk the first, you will not be able to drink the second. Drink the first to soothe your thirst; drink the second to draw your fill of drinking. In the Old Testament there is compunction, in the New there is joy.

See how the Lord countered the devil's schemes on behalf of his servants. The devil deceived one man with the food of fraud, so as to ensnare all in that one; but Jesus redeemed all with the food of salvation, so as to restore in all of them the one who had been deceived as well. The devil devised the golden cup of Babylon, so that whoever drank more would thirst more, and since the drink itself could not please, he lured them to drink by the value of the gold.

He offered his own wine, but needed the help of metal to commend it. The Lord Jesus, on the other hand, poured out water from the rock, and all drank. Those who drank in figure were satisfied; those who drank in truth were made drunk. A good drunkenness, which pours in joy and brings no confusion; a good drunkenness, which steadies the gait of a sober mind; a good drunkenness, which waters the gift of eternal life. Drink this cup, then, of which the prophet said: And your cup that inebriates, how glorious it is!

And do not be troubled that the cup of Babylon is golden, for you too drink the cup of wisdom, which is more precious than gold and silver. Drink both cups, then, of the Old and of the New Testament, because in both you drink Christ. Drink Christ, because he is the vine; drink Christ, because he is the rock that poured forth water; drink Christ, because he is the fountain of life; drink Christ, because he is the river whose stream gladdens the city of God; drink Christ, because he is peace; drink Christ, because rivers of living water will flow from his belly; drink Christ, so that you may drink the blood by which you were redeemed; drink Christ, so that you may drink his words. His word is the Old Testament; his word is the New Testament.

Divine Scripture is drunk and divine Scripture is devoured when the juice of the eternal Word descends into the veins of the mind and the powers of the soul. Indeed, man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God. Drink this word, but drink it in its proper order: first in the Old Testament, then quickly see that you drink in the New Testament as well. And as if he himself were in haste, he says: Galilee of the Gentiles and regions of Judea, you people who walked in darkness, see a great light;

you who dwell in the land of death, a light will shine upon you. Drink quickly, then, so that a great light may shine on you: not the everyday light, not the light of day, of the sun or of the moon, but that light which shuts out the shadow of death. For those who are in the shadow of death certainly cannot see the light of the sun or of day. And as though you were asking where such splendor, such grace, comes from, he answers: For a child is born to us, a son is given

to us: a child, because he was born of a virgin; a son, because, born of God, he is the author of so great a light. A child is born to us: to us who believe, not to the Jews who did not believe; to us, not to heretics; to us, not to Manichaeans. He is born to us, because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; he is born to us who took flesh from the virgin, because he was born a man of Mary. The flesh is born to us, the Word is given; what is ours was born among us, what is above us was given to us.

We have digressed far enough, I think, but not to no purpose: our aim was to teach that we ought to love the Lord even in tribulations and not depart from him, since tribulation often follows joy, and joy follows tribulation. In short, whoever is not broken by tribulation and follows the law is blessed.

And he will be like a tree planted beside the streams of waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not fall; and whatever he does will prosper. What is this blessedness that is compared to a tree, unless we understand it of the tree of life, brought forth from the earth in paradise, that place of the blessed, in the midst of the other trees?

For among the many trees that were beautiful to look at and good for food, the earth brought forth this tree as well, and it was in the middle of paradise, so that the other trees might flourish by its greenness. What do we say this tree is, if not the one through which salvation came to us? And rightly the earth brought it forth, because a virgin gave him birth, and she was earth according to the Creator's sentence spoken against man: You are earth, and to earth you shall go.

Beautifully, too, we read that it was in the midst of the other trees, for he was in the midst of the apostles as they learned, or because he was in the midst of mind and heart, as he himself says: There stands in your midst one whom you do not know; and elsewhere he says: But I am in your midst. Indeed, Solomon also said of him: He is a tree of life to all who take hold of him.

Whoever is blessed, then, will be an imitator of the Lord Jesus, who is the tree of life, the tree of wisdom, planted in the womb of the virgin by the will of the Father, by whom he is planted to remain forever, so as to give his fruit in its season. For that planting could not wither, since it had within itself the abiding richness of spiritual grace.

Indeed, Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan. These are the streams of waters of which he speaks in the Gospel: Rivers of living water will flow from his belly. Now he said this of the Spirit, which those who were to believe in him were beginning to receive.

There is also another tradition, namely that there are waters from which Jeremiah forbids us to drink, saying: What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Gihon? There is also the river Tigris, which flows past the Assyrians, and the Euphrates, which runs toward Babylonia, and the Pishon, whose name in Latin translation means "change of mouth," which encircles the land

of Havilah, where there is gold, and the gold of that land is good, and the carbuncle and the green stone. Fittingly, the mouth is changed there, so that faith in promises is not kept and there is deceit in the mouth, where the good gold is; for avarice breaks faith and does not keep simplicity

of speech, and costly ornaments change the mind and spirit, so that one thing is in the heart and another in the words. So it was into the regions of these rivers that the Jews were led captive, into Egypt and to the Assyrians and to the Babylonians, where they sat by the rivers of Babylon and wept over the misery of their calamity, and, as this same prophet testifies,

there they hung up their instruments and laid aside all joy, there where they endured heavier sufferings. Indeed, the other ten tribes were led away to the Assyrians, but the two, Judah and Benjamin, as guilty of a graver crime, were carried off into Babylonia. For a priest's daughter who commits adultery is punished more severely than other women, because she has stained the grace of a priestly family with shameful disgrace.

Just as they, then, were in the most grievous trials, so our Savior exposed himself to many trials, so as to pass over none of the struggles of our temptation. He is therefore rightly said to be planted beside the streams of these rivers, not in the streams themselves, so that you may understand him as bordering on them, not submerged in them. His first encounter was with flesh and blood. Indeed, he said: Father, take this cup from me; yet not what I will, but what you will. There was the temptation of riches set before him, when the enemy offered him all the kingdoms of the earth if the Lord would fall down and worship him. There you have the streams of two rivers, Gihon and Pishon. He had a struggle against the princes of the world; in his very passion he had a contest against the tempters, whom the Hebrew interpretation calls Persians, who brought false testimony, and against those who said, Let him come down now from the cross and we will believe in him, which the devil was prompting. There you have the rivers Tigris and Euphrates.

The apostle, too, sums up our fourfold contest when he says that our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world and of darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. These are the rivers that go out from paradise.

Hence I think that whoever longs to return to paradise must cross these streams of waters. The same holy prophet expressed this not without purpose, showing that whoever has undergone all temptations may now hope that the rest of paradise is owed to him. So he says: My eyes have gone down streams of waters.

For just as there is a fiery sword at the entrance of paradise, so that whoever returns may come back through fire, burn away his sins and prove his gold, so whoever returns comes back through these streams; and rightly the saints say: We have passed through fire and water. Of these streams Isaiah also says: If you pass through water, the rivers will not shut you in. What rivers? Hear David speaking of those who were hastening toward paradise: Perhaps our soul would have passed through the unbearable water.

Some also take of these four temptations the verse: You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon, so that he walked upon them in the incarnation, trampled them in the passion, or will trample them in the handing over of the kingdom, which he will hand over to the Father when he has destroyed every principality. Aquila beautifully said to metapephyteumenon, that is, "transplanted," because he was first planted in the virgin and afterward transplanted into paradise, as he said to the thief: Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.

This tree, then, will give its fruit in its season. Earthly trees are said not to give fruit but to bear it; but the tree of life and wisdom gives fruit, that is, bestows and grants it. Again this question arises: "If it is the tree of wisdom, why will it give in its season and not always?" We would not want this thought about Christ to trouble us. But you have read that the Lord will set a faithful and prudent steward over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due season—

in due season, mark you, not always—so you certainly ought not to be disturbed. Wisdom can always give fruit, but because it is wisdom it must give wisely and dispense prudently, whenever we either deserve or are able to receive the full measure. Just as here [?] the last time [?] fruit, so there too it will give good fruit to those in need, so that we may be able to receive and keep a share in his resurrection. Now we cannot; in this corrupt age we cannot bear it, for here there is corruption.

And care had to be taken that we should not spoil the good fruits that the tree of life would give, because now we are corrupt, but there we shall be incorruptible, when, as he says, the dead will rise incorruptible and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. What good, then, would it have done one who was to die to receive what death would take away from him? Wisdom therefore knows to whom and when it should give, and it does not even lose a leaf of its tree. So let us consider what the fruit of wisdom is, and what the leaf.

The fruit is within; the leaf is what protects the fruit from the scorching sun or the cold. The fruit seems to be faith, peace, excellence of teaching, the pursuit of true knowledge, the understanding of the mysteries. A good life guards these fruits; a bad one loses them, even if it has received them. To the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous deeds? The fruit lies in the mystical, the leaf in the moral, compared with the contemplation of the heavenly mysteries.

For virtues without faith are leaves: they seem green but can do no good; they are tossed by the wind because they have no foundation. How many Gentiles have mercy and sobriety, yet have no fruit because they have no faith! Leaves soon fall when the wind blows. And some Jews have chastity, great diligence and care in reading, but they are without fruit; they are tossed about like leaves. These are perhaps the leaves that the Savior found on that fig tree, while he found no fruit.

The mystical things save and set free from death, while the moral things are adornments of beauty, not aids to redemption. That the mystical surpasses the moral the Lord himself teaches in his Gospel, speaking of Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his word while Martha was busy with serving and complained that her own sister was not helping her with serving at table: Martha,

Martha, Mary has chosen the best part for herself, which will not be taken from her. If the woman who served Christ at table could not be compared with the one who longed to hear the word, how could we compare one busy with work to one devoted to eternal knowledge? Yet in such a way that faith should not be lacking to the work of the one, nor work to the knowledge of the other, as with Mary, so that there may not be leaves without fruit, nor fruit left uncovered without its natural protection and exposed to harm.

We can also understand that Adam and Eve covered themselves with leaves, seeking bodily garments, because the resurrection of the Lord's body was being prophesied: the flesh, which before used to perish like leaves, would not perish in Christ, nor in all the just who, according to the Gospel, would shape their life and actions in imitation of the tree of wisdom born of the virgin.

For the Greek reads: ho ton karpon autou dosei, "which will give its fruit," which can be referred to the blessed man—in Greek, makarios [?] karpon dosei—while in Latin it is rendered "who," so that it reads: "who, being blessed, will give fruit" in his resurrection, when he can give it forever. It can also be taken thus: ho ton karpon autou [?], as standing for xylon, "tree," so that it refers to the tree, all of whose deeds will prosper. In this there is clear testimony that it was said of the Savior;

for whose deeds, if not his, can all be praised and have prosperous outcomes? Aquila, however, says "will be directed," which seems applicable to any man whom the Lord directs by heavenly favor; for a man's steps are directed by the Lord, and the prophet David asked that his prayer be directed in the sight of God. But the Lord himself also directed his works, so that they were bent by no crooked turn of error.

There follows: Not so the wicked, not so, but like the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth. That is: not like the blessed man, who is blessed because he did not walk in the counsel of the wicked, because he did not stand in sin, because he did not sit in the assembly of the pestilent who seek to pervert those who believe piously or live piously; who had his will in the law and will meditate on it, or, as Aquila put it, will resound in the law, so that his life may resound with the precepts of the law and his conduct echo them, like those whose sound has gone out into all the earth.

Perhaps here it is the sound of human teaching that goes out, but there, where it will be granted to see face to face, some fuller expression of the Word will seem to come about. The wicked man, then, will not be like this blessed one who has done these things, who will be like a planted tree, all of whose deeds will prosper.

For this reason the one who wrote it, or the one who added it later, as some think, repeated it, so that the statement might be made firmer by repetition, saying: Not so the wicked, not so, who will be like dust. For they are earthly, and just as dust is driven before the wind, so they too will be driven away and scattered by the Holy Spirit, who is wont to breathe like the south wind upon the fertile and fruitful earth of a soul bound for salvation.

It is to this wind that the Song of Songs says: Come, south wind, so that through the mildness of a softer air the fields of our heart may be loosened, which, gripped by winter frost, refused to open their lap to receive the seed. It is good for us that this wind should blow, for it brings the ships of Tarshish safely into harbour, carrying to the true Solomon whatever seems necessary for his temple.

But this wind blows only when that heavy north wind has stopped blowing. That is why the Church, or the devout soul, says: Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; that is: you, north wind, withdraw; and come, south wind, blow upon my garden, so that you do not scatter the flowers but preserve them. So the soul full of devotion has a garden, or rather is itself a garden that bears fruit; the soul that lies open to ungodliness has dust, which is barren of fruit. The Lord indeed made it fruitful, but it has gathered for itself the dust of ungodliness.

Why do you boast, you who are full of ungodliness? Because you are powerful in honours and abound in riches? Do you not notice that you are dust, and that you will be scattered and dispersed? I saw the ungodly, it says, highly exalted and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not. Why do you glory because many servants throng about you, many friends guard your sides, a great many horses

follow you, whose lineage you recount to us, as though it were the pedigree of your own ancestors? You show off your riches because you feed your companions at banquets. If only you fed the needy! If only you fed not those who minister to your amusements but those who help you with their prayers! You boast that as soon as you go out, people make way for you, and men turn aside from you as from a wild beast or an animal. 'Are these things not something?' Do you not hear that all these things pass away like a shadow? What use are the bordered robes of a consul, or triumphal tunics gleaming with gold?

Naked you will depart; no one there will recognize a consul. What good are countless estates? They are public, not yours; today you hold them, tomorrow someone else. When you go out, another comes in; you have scarcely moved your foot before another has stepped in. How many were there before you, how many will be masters there after you! And you think this is private property? Whom have riches ever redeemed from death? Indeed, whom have riches not driven to death?

Whom have his wealth called back from the underworld, whom has power exempted from punishment? Ungodliness is dust, just as the power of the ungodly is dust; it brings darkness, it cannot bring salvation. As soon as a strong wind begins to blow, it scatters it and breaks it up, troubles the air, and lays the ground bare; it is cast away like dust, vanishes like smoke, melts like wax.

From this many have raised no small question: whether divine Scripture seems to assert that a nature will perish, especially since it says elsewhere: I will grind them like dust before the face of the wind, and like the mud of the streets I will blot them out; and elsewhere: Behold, all your adversaries will be confounded and put to shame; for they will be as though they were not.

First, then, I ask whether they think ungodliness is in accordance with nature or contrary to nature. If they assert that it is in accordance with nature, their opinion is clearly mistaken. Let them say, then, whether sin agrees with nature or not. But it is certain that to sin is to stray from what is in accordance with nature. What, then, is so absurd as for them to say that being ungodly seems a lesser thing than being a sinner, when the bitterest of all things is whatever is seen to be done as an injury against God?

But if acting ungodly is not contrary to nature, then living ungodly is in accordance with nature, and should neither be counted as sin nor judged worthy of blame; for no one is blamed who acts in accordance with nature. Hence it follows that ungodliness is contrary to nature. How, then, along with the destruction of a habit, does Scripture introduce [?] natures,

that is, natures that will perish, when ungodliness is certainly not natural but contrary to nature? For what you do not have, you do not lose; nor can a substance perish that never existed. Even dust, when stirred up, is changed either into the substance of water, or into air, or into fire; that is, it often seems to pass into another nature. So it does not vanish into nothing, but passes into something else.

What, then, prevents the one who is ground like dust by the power and reason of the Word from being, not scattered into nothing, but changed for the better, so that from an earthly man he becomes a spiritual one; and from being blotted out like the mud of the streets in such a way that whatever seems rough and filthy is removed, and whatever is smooth and clean remains? And as for what it says of the adversaries of Jerusalem:

they are as those who are not, it could certainly have said: 'They will not be.' But since it said: they will be confounded and put to shame, you surely understand that they will exist in substance and in the progress of conversion, but they will not exist as adversaries, which is what they were. So through the failing of their wickedness they will not be; [they will be,] changed by faith and devotion. Again, elsewhere it is said in the person of a sinner: I will bear the wrath of God, because I have sinned, until he justifies my cause; for God, wishing to convert the sinner, punishes him and burns him in order to cleanse him.

That is why he says: and he will bring me out into the light. For fire burns wax too, and it melts so as to be purified; and we are tested by fire; and smoke, once all its material has been consumed, is purged away and does not pass out of its nature. So also the soul, cleansed of every stain, passes away into what is, not into what is not, as Balaam says: Let my soul die among the souls of the righteous; meaning that his fall and a certain habit of wickedness should die, but that he should pass over into the way and life of the righteous. For God wills all things to be saved. That is why Solomon also said: God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living.

He made the soul so that it might exist; he created man, whom he made in his own image, for incorruption. But men, straying from the gift of nature, made themselves liable to death, so that they are corrupted as earthly beings. Yet God drives them to repentance through tribulations, so that through repentance that accidental evil of wickedness may be burned up and consumed and may perish, and that place in the soul which was occupied by accidental ungodliness may lie open to receive virtue and grace. It is certain, moreover, that the nature of the soul is precious; made in the likeness of God, it is capable of receiving every virtue, since it has not been cheated of a share in heavenly knowledge.

Now there remains, I think, the question that is on many people's lips: how God, without whose will not even the most worthless sparrow falls, and with whom the hairs of the head are numbered, could have said through Isaiah: If all nations are reckoned as a drop from a bucket and as the tipping of a scale, they will also be reckoned as spittle. Will all nations, then, perish like a drop from a bucket, and as spittle perishes and is of no use for anything?

But you who know that our God did not count the nations as nothing to such a degree, since he said to Abraham: In you all nations will be blessed, and spoke through David to his Son, saying: I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and further on: All nations will serve him; you who have read that he offered his Son for every nation, in order to save sinners, ought to consider in this passage the force of the divine statement.

For in comparison with the heavenly creatures, which are many — such as the heaven, which is many times greater than the earth, so that many have reckoned the earth to be a mere point in comparison with the heaven; the angels, archangels, principalities and powers, thrones, dominions, thousands and tens of thousands and countless thousands — in comparison

with these, then, the nations are reckoned as a drop from a bucket, which holds all fullness. So the nations are reckoned as a drop falling from that heavenly fullness. For how could they seem very great, when the earth itself, on which the nations live, is the smallest portion of the world, and the nations are, among all that God has made, like the slight tipping of a scale? At the same time, learn from this scale that God made all things with justice, and that there is something natural in the nations themselves in which there seemed to be at least a small weight of justice; and that the spittle itself is, as it were, an inner portion coming from the whole of the body.

Rather, then, it is mercy that is proclaimed here, since he who came to seek what was lost did not despise even that drop as worthless; he lifted up the tipping of the scale, and deigned to give that spittle the substance of a good body, that is, to gather all the nations into the one body of the Church. Israel too can be counted among the nations, though by no means without a share in his divine justice, since Moses himself said of Israel:

Behold, a wise people, holding fast to instruction, a great nation. And so that you may know that God's goodness has overflowed beyond our merit, the apostle, interpreting this prophetic passage, says: God has shut up all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all; and he added: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who has first given to him, that he should be repaid? And the prophet, leading up to this passage, says: If all nations are reckoned as a drop from a bucket, and so on, so that you may recognize that this understanding agrees with the apostle's interpretation.

But what is clearer evidence that he does not seem to introduce natures that will perish than the holy prophet's own words that follow: For the ungodly will not rise in the judgment? He did not say: 'They will not rise,' but: 'They will indeed rise, but not in the judgment.' Whoever rises certainly exists and endures; but because he did not believe in Christ, he has already been judged, and so does not come to judgment, since the punishment of a judgment already passed awaits him. On the resurrection there is a great deal of testimony in the Scriptures, which we did not pass over in our books On Consolation and On the Resurrection.

As for what he says: The ungodly will not rise in the judgment, according to the Gospel the statement is unqualified, since not all will be judged. Yet the apostle says: For we must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. Many think these statements contradict each other, and do not notice that the Saviour was speaking of the faithless and ungodly, who did not believe in the Lord Jesus.

For this is what he says: Whoever believes in me is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. And this is the judgment: that the light has come into this world, and men loved darkness rather than light, for their works were evil. It is clear, then, of whom this was said: of those who did not believe in the Lord Jesus. The apostle

too, though he said 'all,' certainly spoke of those who believed but will have to give an account of their actions on the day of judgment. Indeed, he himself says elsewhere that the testimony of our conscience will be revealed on the day of judgment, when our thoughts will either accuse one another, as it is written, or defend them, and the secrets of the heart will lie open. And what could be clearer than what he says elsewhere: We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed? For the righteous will be changed into incorruption, while the reality of the body remains.

Daniel too says: The judgment sat, and the books were opened. So he shows that there will be a judgment, especially since the same prophet says elsewhere: Many who sleep in the mound of the earth will arise, some to eternal life and some to reproach and everlasting shame; and those who understand will shine like the brightness of the sky, and many of the righteous will shine like the stars.

What is this judgment of judges sitting, and what are the books that are opened, if not our consciences, which, like books, contain the record of our sins? And yet it is a poor thing to think of this as resembling a human trial. The judgment of Christ is something else: there conscience itself betrays itself, unable to hide from the judge of secret things; there thoughts are plain before him who used to say to people even as they were thinking:

Why do you think evil in your hearts? When he spoke to the Jews, he was speaking to everyone, so that no one would think that what he did could be hidden, so that no one would think that, shut in behind walls, he could escape a witness to his secret wrongdoing. And so the evangelist also testifies, saying: But Jesus knew their thoughts. In what sense, then, does it say: The books were opened? Not books written in ink, of course, but in the traces of sins and the stain of shameful deeds. The book of your conscience will be opened, the book of your heart will be opened, our guilt will be read aloud.
