There is a book where there is a tablet; indeed, there are inscribed books where there are inscribed tablets, which the apostolic teaching inscribes with the Holy Spirit, as we read when Paul says: You are our letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on fleshly tablets of the heart. So there are tablets of the heart inscribed by the Holy Spirit; these will be read aloud. If you have acted well, the writing will remain.

See that you do not take away the grace of the Holy Spirit; see that you do not erase it and write your shameful deeds in ink, lest the day of judgment come and the Judge say: 'Let the books be read, let the tablets of his deeds be read,' and say to you: 'I wrote your tablets; why did you erase my letters? I wrote my gifts there; how did you erase my gifts and write your disgraces? Have you not read that I write? Did I not tell you through the mouth of my prophet: My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe? And judgment belongs to the Word.'

So many of those who sleep in the mound of the earth will rise: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment. What Daniel calls to eternal life, the Saviour called to the resurrection of life; and what Daniel calls to reproach and shame, the Saviour called to the resurrection of judgment.

So it is not good for us to come to judgment, and it is not good not to come, lest we either seem to be condemned in advance or, in this stain of vices, undergo the weight of so great a judgment. The prophet prays that the Lord will not enter into judgment with his servant; how much more ought we to fear the Lord's judgment! Suppose the merciful Lord forgives: how much will be brought to light that I believed was hidden! What shame, what confusion there will be when I, who professed to teach others, am myself caught in the very thing for which I rebuked others!

And so, since the Saviour set out two kinds of resurrection, and John too in the Apocalypse, saying: Blessed is he who has a share in the first resurrection — for these come to grace without judgment, while those who do not come to the first resurrection but are kept for the second will be burned until they fulfil the times between the first and the second resurrection, or, if they have not

fulfilled them, will remain longer in punishment — so, then, let us pray that we may be found worthy to have a share in the first resurrection. There are those who rose at the passion of Christ, and they are truly blessed, for they received the grace of Christ and heard his voice, of which it is written: The hour is coming when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live; and: They entered the holy city. I think this refers to that heavenly city rather than to this Jerusalem which he left behind and which he reproached; for into this one they entered on foot, but into that heavenly one by their merits.

But let us also take care to rise from the mound of the earth while we are still here. There are those who, while living, are surrounded by a tomb and filled with the dead; their throat is a sepulchre, speaking not words of life but of death. If we rise from the dead here, we shall rise there too; if here we are not dry bones but have received the dew of the Word, the moisture of the Holy Spirit, we shall live there too; if here Jesus rouses us with his loud voice, as he roused Lazarus, and through his disciples looses us from the bonds of death, and brings us into Bethany, where Lazarus was — that is, into the house of obedience — and admits us to his banquet, then there too we shall feast with him for ever, there we shall recline with him, and there the ointment will be fragrant for us, whose pouring out only the traitor resented.

So the ungodly do not rise in the judgment, that is, into the portion of those who are to undergo judgment; nor do sinners rise in the council of the righteous. You see that the ungodly rise, yet do not rise in the judgment; and that sinners, though they do not rise in the council of the righteous, nevertheless rise in the judgment. Hence it appears that those who believed rightly and carried out their faith in works as well are not judged themselves, but rise in the council of the righteous; while sinners, who cannot rise among the righteous, will rise in the judgment.

You have two ranks; there remains a third, that of the ungodly, who, since they did not believe, have already been judged, and so do not rise in the judgment but to punishment. For they loved darkness rather than light; therefore their judgment is punishment, and perhaps the punishment of darkness. It might indeed be understood that those who have evil works yet believe in Christ, who wish to live rightly but are overcome by the allurements of sin, loved darkness more than light, that is, they loved both, but darkness more.

But since he spoke first about those who did not believe, I think it should be taken to mean that they loved darkness and not light; for Christ is the light. It is absurd, then, to believe that those who did not believe in the light even loved the light, which they did not know; for they did not know and did not understand; they walk in darkness, as it is written.

Next comes: For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the path of the ungodly will perish. Notice the sense: The ungodly do not rise in the judgment, because the Lord knows the way of the righteous. He certainly knows the ways of those whose steps he directs; for there are steps of men that are directed by the Lord. A man's ways too are directed by the Lord. The Lord knows these ways that are straight, that lead to that life of him who said:

I am the way and the truth and the life. This is the good way; but the way of the world is crooked, and he does not deign to know that way. For he knows those who are his own, who do his works; but to those who work iniquity the Lord says: Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity; I do not know you. They are not known, not through ignorance, but because they are unworthy of God's knowledge.

He says beautifully: and the path of the ungodly will perish. The Latin made a distinction, saying 'path,' and so distinguished path from way, whereas the Greek said 'way' in both places. Yet the Latin did not do so idly, since the Lord too said I am the way, not 'I am the path.' And he said that the path of the ungodly will perish, not the ungodly themselves; he preserves their substance, so that if they are converted they will lose only the path of ungodliness, which neither existed from the beginning nor will exist hereafter. So what is accidental perishes; what is substantial remains. The ungodly perish, then, in the sense in which it is said: The soul that sins shall die, meaning that they die by the sting of sin, not by the complete dissolution of their substance.
EXPLANATION OF PSALM 35

Since the prophet was going to describe in the following psalm what the pattern of the righteous man is, he first portrayed the pattern of the unrighteous. For we cannot know the form of righteousness unless we know the likeness of iniquity, since they are opposed and contrary to each other. In the one there is the simple condition of nature, in the other the deceitful cunning of wickedness; the one displays the images of the virtues, the other puts forward the inventions of the vices.

Reason itself teaches that this order is fitting; and if testimony must be taken even from the opposing side, the teachers of philosophy themselves have admitted it by following it. Who doubts that David lived long before the time of Plato, whom not only Plato's teacher but not even his grandfathers' grandfathers could have seen? For David lived at the beginning of the kingdom of the Jews, which continued through countless years, while Plato lived after the time of the captivity, by which the kingdom of that nation had already been dissolved.

So he who holds the first place over all in worldly wisdom, when he said that the form of justice could not be grasped unless they had first judged that the course of injustice must be examined, gave the example that those who wish to look for gold first smear themselves with mud. Justice, then, is the gold; iniquity is the mud. There is no doubt that our own writers said this too, since it is written: Like the mud of the streets I will blot them out; and truly mud, for it defiles those who come near it.

Let us therefore flee injustice, lest we be defiled with its muddy filth, and lest not our outer foot but, what is more serious, our mind sink into its pit. Philosophy indeed says that it is looking for gold, but it is turning over mud, since it seeks the divine in statues; but the rod shatters the potter's vessels. We look for the gold with which to cleanse our bodies, carrying about in our body the dying of Jesus Christ, so that the life of Jesus Christ may also be revealed in our body. The good gold is the blood of Christ, rich enough to pay the price, flowing freely to wash away every sin. We have spoken about the order; let us consider the title.

"To the end," it says, "for the servant of the Lord, a psalm [?] of David." In the whole body of the Psalter this is the only title in which he declares that he wrote a psalm "for the servant of the Lord." Who is this servant of the Lord? Let us see what the course of the psalm indicates about the one to whom it is addressed. Let us hear whom he is speaking to: "Lord," he says, "your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds; your righteousness is like the mountains of God, your judgments like the great deep."

To whom is this said if not to the Son of God? For these things belong not to human but to divine power. But what does it mean that the title declared this psalm to be spoken "for the servant of the Lord," when in a later title he preferred to call it "the prayer of Moses, the man of God," rather than "of the servant of the Lord"? I do not understand what the prophet's purpose was here, or rather the purpose of the Lord and Savior himself, who spoke in the prophet.

Truly his judgments are like the great deep: he kept the honor for his servant and ascribed the condition of servitude to himself. I think I understand; I think I have drawn something from spiritual grace. As we have said, this psalm was written against injustice, and so the injustice of the faithless weighs all the more heavily

— of those who refused to receive Christ Jesus the Lord, though he had taken on servitude for their sake. For what is so unjust as to be ungrateful for such great benefits, so that those to whom he was giving salvation should shed his blood? Indeed elsewhere, when he was speaking of his passion, he sharpens the odium of Jewish impiety by saying: "Do not turn your face away from your servant; because I am in distress, hear me quickly." "I am poor and in pain."

Come, Paul, explain to us how the Lord of heaven and earth could call himself poor, and what this poverty is. You certainly called him rich; how is the same one both rich and poor? Let us hear Paul's testimony: "You know," he says, "the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that for your sake he became poor, though he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich."

Come you too, Isaiah, and explain to us how Christ, who was accustomed to heal the pain of wounds, could call himself in pain. The physician came to cure the sick: what did he himself have to grieve over? Let us hear Isaiah's testimony as well: "He grieves for us," he says, "and we thought him to be in pain."

He described the feeling of a physician who, even though he himself had no wound to pain him, nevertheless suffered with the wounded. This, then, is what the Lord reproaches the Jews with in the psalm: "For your sake I was poor, for you I was in pain, and you laid impious hands on me, saying: Let us take away the righteous one, for he is useless to us. Let us put wood into his bread." He rightly says "bread" for his flesh. He brought them nourishment; in return for the benefit they paid him back with punishment.

No wonder, then, that they go hungry, who denied themselves the food of eternal life. And they put those two things together beautifully: "Let us put wood into his bread." The Jews did not know what they were saying, and yet they were speaking a mystery. The cross of Christ has given paradise back to us. This is the tree that the Lord pointed out to Adam when he said that the tree of life, which stood in the middle of paradise, was to be eaten from, but the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not to be eaten from. Adam went astray; he did not keep the commandments; he tasted what was forbidden.

Through a tree we began to hunger, until the flesh received its proper food. That is why the Lord joined flesh and wood in Christ, so that the ancient hunger might cease and the grace of life be restored. Blessed is the Lord's tree, which crucified the sins of all; blessed is the Lord's flesh, which supplied food to all!

So concerning the Lord's poverty and pain we have brought forward, I think, adequate testimonies from the saints, one of whom saw and spoke, while the other was chosen to speak. Let us now bring forward again the testimonies of these same proven men concerning the Lord's servitude, or rather his own testimonies, which he spoke about himself in both of them. Let us hear, then, what he says: "Thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to gather Jacob and Israel to him."

We notice, then, that he took on the form of a servant in order to gather the people. Listen, Jew: you turn grace into an insult, and you make the very thing that should have led you all the more to believe into an occasion for faithlessness. He came to call you, and you revile him. He said, "a servant from the womb." Listen, Arian, from what womb. Go back a little earlier: "From my mother's womb," he says, "the Lord has called my name." Let us hear what his name is, the name by which the Father called him: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and

his name shall be called Emmanuel," which means "God with us." For what other name does Christ have but "Son of God"? Take another. Gabriel also had said to Joseph about Mary: "She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus." Take the voice of God: "And you, Bethlehem of Judea, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah;

for from you shall come forth a ruler who will govern my people." Notice the mystery: from the virgin's womb came forth one and the same who is both servant and Lord, servant to labor and Lord to command, so as to root God's kingdom in human minds. The two are one, not one from the Father and another from the virgin, but the same one who before the ages was from the Father afterwards took flesh from the virgin. That is why he is called both servant and Lord: a servant for our sake, but by the unity of the divine substance God from God, ruler from ruler, equal from equal. For the Father did not beget an inferior son, he in whom he declared that he was well pleased.

"It is a great thing for you," he says, "to be called my servant, to establish the tribes of Jacob." Everywhere he keeps the titles of his dignity: a great God and a great servant. Even in the flesh he does not lose the name of greatness, he of whose greatness there is no end. And rightly was he secure, since, as the apostle says, "though he was in the form of God, he did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross."

He, then, is equal as the Son of God; he took the form of a servant in the flesh; he tasted death, he whose greatness has no end, because "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes," so that we may all believe in him and worship him with our inmost love. Good is the servitude that has made all free; good is the servitude that has won the name above every name; good is the humility that has brought it about that at his name every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. This is the end, then, toward which this psalm is directed: that we too may be servants for righteousness and not proud men given to arrogance. For servitude is the wage of freedom, but arrogance is the wage of death. But now let us take up the course of the psalm.

"The unjust man has spoken, so as to sin against himself." He did not state what he said, and so I think it should be understood this way: whatever the unjust man says is sin. For all injustice is sin, since where the instrument is faulty, how can the song not be faulty? The offspring of degenerate material is discolored. Whatever the unjust man says, then, is iniquity, and it falls back on its author,

like the offspring of the viper, which, as is commonly said, first tears open its own mother. So he sins against himself. I think nothing more sublime has been said than this sentence. In those who claimed the wisdom of this world for themselves I have read nothing like it, known nothing like it. And no wonder, since they spoke by human ingenuity, whereas this was poured in by the Spirit of God, the Spirit of truth: that the unjust man sins against himself, inflicts wounds on himself, runs himself through. For just as thorns grow in the hand of a drunkard, as Scripture

says, so too in the speech of the unjust man things grow that prick the one who speaks. The unjust man speaks and his inner conscience is wounded, because in every word he speaks he is not free from deceit. For what punishment is heavier than one's own, since he pays a penalty for every word? The serpent pours its venom into others, the unjust man into himself, for whatever he has poured out flows back upon him. The unjust man, then, is both useless to others and harmful to himself, while the life of the righteous is fruitful to others and sweet to himself. For Solomon says: "My son, if you are wise for yourself, you will be wise for your neighbors too; but if you turn out wicked, you alone will drink up the evil."

We notice, then, that righteousness is born for others rather than for itself. It looks to the common good, not its own, and counts another's good as its own gain. Blessed and glorious is righteousness, whose good benefits all; it usually starts from one person and reaches everyone. David was righteous: he spared his enemy and preferred to protect his innocence rather than his life, so that he would not be avenged at the public's cost, nor, by taking vengeance himself on the one plotting against him, set others an example of attacking a ruler even in wrongful causes.

Abel was righteous: he thought that the firstlings of his sheep, which the Lord had given him, should be offered to the Lord, and so he pleased God more, because he made no delay and proved his devotion. But the impious man, the transgressor of righteousness, the root of iniquity, could not bear this, and so he killed his brother because his brother's sacrifice had been approved by God more than his own offering. But the one who was slain spoke to God in the voice of his blood, while the one who lived was driven from the face of the Lord, and although punishment from the Lord was still held back, the consciousness of his sins tormented him.

The wretch hid, trembling and afraid, and though no slayer was yet at hand, the unjust man's very life tortured him. He had received a sign so that no one would kill him, not so that he might enjoy the sweetness of life, but so that death would not take away his misery and he would suffer his slayer every day by fearing him. He had indeed obtained protection against any slayer, but without any respite he was his own executioner, his own slayer.

What punishment is greater than to fear what you cannot avoid, and not to be able to escape what you have feared? So David splendidly expresses the most grievous summons of a sinful conscience when he says: "For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my offense is always before me." For the avenging image of our sin is spread before us and does not allow its defendant to rest. It imposes a wretched slavery and drags him into its chains so that he cannot free himself, since he sold himself willingly, he who was free not to take on the debt of sins and to keep the freedom of innocence.

So while we pray, sin spreads itself before us; when sleep has relaxed the senses of the body, sin comes back. Our error always confronts us like a harsh tax collector, or like a shameless moneylender dunning a debtor.

That is why the Lord says: "Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin." But the righteous man knows how to loosen the chains of his sins. He does not wait for an accuser but gets in first, so that by confessing he may lighten every offense of his and leave the adversary nothing to charge him with. And so Scripture tells you: "The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech." For he snatches the voice away from the adversary, and by confessing his sins he binds shut, as it were, the teeth

that were ready to seize the prey of hostile accusation. Judas Iscariot spoke so as to sin against himself. What did he say? "The one I kiss is the man; seize him." He said this, and with his own mouth drove himself to death. How many tormentors must we suppose there were within him, that he should bear down on himself as the exactor of so heavy a penalty and strangle himself with a noose!

The unjust man spoke and sinned against himself. The righteous man spoke: "Behold, I the shepherd have done wrong; and what has this flock done?" And all his sin was forgiven. So the righteous man spoke and benefited himself. Cain said, "Am I my brother's keeper?" and lied to himself. Ananias said that he had brought the whole price of the land he had sold, and he lied to himself, though he could have offered less without fraud. And so it is splendidly said: "And iniquity has lied to itself." For it lies first to itself when it lies to its own ruin; it sins against itself when it robs itself of the sweetness of innocence.

For what fruit is sweeter than purity and simplicity of heart, what food more delightful than that on which the spirit of a man with a good conscience and the mind of an innocent man feast? But iniquity, as Scripture testifies, weighs down the conscience like a talent of lead, and rightly David says: "Like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me," and Solomon: "As sour grapes to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to all who practice it."

Heavy is the punishment that hinders eating, clouds the sight, and, what is more, spreads a dark fog over the eyes of the inner mind, so that the unjust man cannot see what is true. And so he sins against himself who robs himself of what is precious.

So the unjust man speaks so as to sin against himself, but the righteous man speaks so as to benefit both others and himself. The one speaks for destruction, the other for salvation. Of the righteous and faithful it is said: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." The tongue of the one wounds, but the tongue of the wise heals.

So when David remonstrated with King Saul because, forgetting the benefit of his own deliverance, he was ungratefully pursuing to the death the man by whom he had seen himself saved so many times, and seeking the life of one who had exposed his own life to dangers for the king's safety, David said that the fruit of righteousness would not be lost to him, since he had not killed the man plotting against him when the Lord had delivered him into his hands. Iniquity came forth from the unjust; venom was poured out by serpents; the venom and the weapons of iniquity have perished.

That is why it is written: "The unjust man has spoken, so as to sin against himself." What did he say? "I will set my throne above the clouds and I will be like the Most High." The words have no effect, but they do have sin. It is indeed an empty show of boasting, but the criminal, in his spirit of pride, is not afraid to violate the divine majesty with insult. For if there had been any fear of God in his heart, he would not have presumed with reckless daring that he could carry out deeds full of deceit in God's sight, as though God, who searches the inmost parts, could not know what is hidden.

God sees all things. There is nothing that escapes him, no one who can deceive him; to him all that is future is present and all that is hidden is plain. For if this sun of the world often slips its light into the closed rooms of houses, how much more does God, supreme and eternal, search out and anticipate by his knowledge even the secret recesses of the human mind and every counsel of the angels! What else, then, does the unjust man do but seek iniquity and hatred for himself?

For it is written thus: "There is no fear of God before his eyes, for he has acted deceitfully in his sight, so as to find out his iniquity and hatred." What does "find out" mean? Everyone who seeks finds; so if evil is sought, it is sought in order to be found. But just as the man who has found the good he sought is praiseworthy, so the man who has toiled to find the evil he sought is blameworthy [?]. We ought to spend our labor on good things, not on shameful deeds and crimes. What, then, is it but the height of folly and madness to seek hatred and to find out by evil arts the iniquity that no good man has ever sought?

Let us consider, then, how the wicked seek their iniquity and hatred. Herodias, to be sure, was joined in lawful marriage to the tetrarch Philip, and abounded in the wealth of royal power. When Herod was on his way to Rome, she received him as her husband's brother by right of hospitality

and kinship. She joined her sins to his, and not long afterwards left her husband and changed the bond of her partnership. Did she not seek iniquity and hatred, she who deserted her marriage to find adultery? And because the holy Baptist steadfastly rebuked the unlawful marriage, saying to Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have as your wife a woman who left her husband against the law and has joined her husband's brother as though by law," the adulteress was so stirred that she wanted to kill him. But realizing that she could not easily bend Herod to the murder of a righteous man, she devised a way to bring it about.

It was Herod's birthday, which he was accustomed to celebrate with excessive luxury, as is the custom of most kings. She adorned her daughter so that a royal child should dance at the king's banquet. And when Herod was pleased by what ought to have displeased an uncle, he offered to let her ask whatever reward she wished for the disgrace of her dancing. She consulted her mother, and at her prompting asked for the head of the Baptist.

Herod gave in, because he had bound himself by oath to give his own niece whatever she asked, and he ordered John to be killed and his head brought. When it was brought, he gave it to the girl, and she carried it to her mother. It is true, then, that iniquity and hatred are sought out, since that woman obtained by the wicked arts of a fraud she had devised what she could not obtain by a simple request.

What shall I say of Judas the betrayer, who sought avarice and found sacrilege, saying, "What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?" Not satisfied with the spoils of the poor, he sowed crime upon crime until he reached the full measure of the gravest crimes, mixing the holy sacraments of love with outrages when he said, "The one I kiss is the man; seize him"? So truly that no one can doubt it was said of him: "The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit." He brought kisses on his lips and poured poison into hearts; he was plotting cruel tortures while he brought a pledge of affection.

The prophet did well to add concerning him: "He would not understand, so as to do well." For he did not sin by nature but by will. He was, after all, an apostle; he heard the divine commandments every day; he was learning the heavenly mystery. He could have understood so as to do well, if he had been willing [?]. He saw paralytics healed, sight restored to the blind, the dead raised;

ought he not to have understood that it was God who could do such things? But he would not understand, because as a greedy man intent on money he turned the vigor of his mind away from the knowledge of the divinity. For everyone who has gorged himself on shameful deeds does not want to understand what belongs to the heavenly commandments, lest he be called back from his vices. See the man who flees from understanding, who says: "Darkness covers me and walls surround me; who knows whether the Lord sees?"

For he does not want to seek and find out that God sees and knows all things, lest fear draw him back from crime. See King Ahab asking Naboth for his vineyard; observe Naboth answering, "Far be it from me to give up the inheritance of my fathers." Ought Ahab not to have understood that Naboth's answer was just? But he would not understand, so as to do well and not seek what belonged to another. Ought he not to have understood that Elijah truly served God, when he saw that at Elijah's word the sky was shut for three years and three months, and that at his prayers the rain was sent down so that all the parched land was watered? But he would not understand, lest he condemn faithlessness and follow faith.

"Moreover, he plotted iniquity on his bed," where he ought to have sought the truth... For on our beds our sins ought to prick our conscience, not be committed by our sinning there, as the prophet says: "What you say in your hearts, be sorry for it on your beds."

"He has stood in every way that is not good," it says, "but he did not hate malice." It is not without reason that he plots injustice who stands in the way of error and loves the malice he ought to hate. "He has stood" says more, as though he had long remained in the way of wickedness, stationed there a long time. For blessed is the man who has not stood in the way of sinners, not the one who never stops standing in it.

That is why the first precepts of the holy prophet David are to flee impiety, not to stand in sin, and to meditate on the law, so that you may understand what is good and distinguish just from unjust. In all things, then, we must watch the root from which growth springs, so that no harmful sap infects it from the beginning; and the vices of souls are far more serious than those of saplings.

Above all, then, we must take care that the habit of malice does not take root in human nature and the whole age that follows degenerate; for a bad tree bears bad fruit. For if we often do what we do not want and cannot avoid it, and do what we hate, bound either by some delight in wrongdoing or by the stealthy approach of sin, how can we avoid what we love? We are bound even against our will; how can we not be held fast when we are willing?

Paul barely freed himself from errors by wrestling in a daily struggle, so that, stripped of the chains of captivity, he might be saved by the grace of Christ; and do you think that by standing among offenses you can attain the reward of the heavenly promises? The crown is sought by wrestling, not by resisting; it is won by zeal, not by opposition. Even those who strive must ask for the support of divine mercy, so that the crown of righteousness may be bestowed in reward for their labors.

Next, let us consider what follows. "Lord," he says, "your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds; your righteousness is like the mountains of God, your judgments like a great deep." Did not Paul follow this passage when he said: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord"?

For when the human mind is troubled and hard, bitter struggles wear us down, we must ask for the Lord's help. And so he turns to the Lord himself, calls on him and begs him to stand by those who labour and help them. Mercy, then, must be sought from heaven, and the truth of God must be gathered from the oracles of the prophets, who veil the mysteries of divine knowledge like clouds.

For God made darkness his hiding place, so that you might first receive the rain of mystical fruitfulness, and then, steeped in heavenly dew, recognize the brightness of the light revealed, and be able to say: "From his fullness we have received." For who can easily grasp the secrets of God, whose righteousness is like the mountains of God, or, as Aquila

put it, "like mighty mountains," because his precepts are full of mighty power? This is why the apostle, seeing how lofty they are, ventures to say: "O the height of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?"

So he linked the height of the riches of wisdom to the height of mountains. Hear which mountains. The Son of God himself is a great mountain, and therefore: "Go up onto this mountain, you who bring good news to Zion," so that you may stand rooted and planted in Christ. There is a mountain that is, so to speak, the wisdom of God; there is also a mountain that is, so to speak, the righteousness

of God; there is also a mountain that is the knowledge of God; there is a mountain that is sanctification, a mountain that is redemption, a mountain that is resurrection. Scripture has shown us these mountains when it said: "But you are in him, in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." Or else they are mountains because the Son of God became an angel to the angels and a prophet to the prophets, he whose judgments are like a great deep. Hear something good: "Deep calls to deep at the voice of your cataracts"; that is, the scripture of the Old Testament summons the course of the New Testament to the completion of sanctification and the fullness of grace, with a kind of roar and torrent of spiritual overflow.

"Men and beasts you will save, O Lord, as you have multiplied your mercy, O God; but the children of men will hope under the shelter of your wings. They will be drunk with the abundance of your house, and you will give them the torrent of your delight to drink." What does "men and beasts" mean? Surely rational and irrational beings. To the rational belong judgments, to the irrational mercy; the one are governed, the other are fed.

So he added: "But the children of men will hope under the shelter of your wings." That is, not a brood of vipers but children of men, who live after the image and likeness of God, are placed not in pastures but at banquets. For some are in a place of pasture, others in the privilege of the sacraments: for the imperfect there is the juice of milk, for the perfect a table of refreshment. Of this table he said: "You have prepared a table before me." On it is the living bread, that is, the word of God; on it is the oil of sanctification, with which the head of the righteous is anointed and the inner sense is strengthened, so that the oil of the sinner may be done away; on it, too, is that cup which inebriates, "how excellent" or "how strong" it is. For the Greek said κράτιστον, which means "powerful" or "strong" or "mighty"; mighty indeed, since by it crimes are washed away or blotted out.

Good, then, is the drunkenness of the cup of salvation. But there is another drunkenness that comes from the overflowing of the scriptures, and yet another through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, those who spoke in various tongues in the Acts of the Apostles seemed to their hearers to be full of new wine. The house, then, is the Church; the abundance of the house is the overflow of graces; the torrent of delight is the Holy Spirit.

Do not let the name or the nature of a torrent trouble you, in that it is sometimes drier or thinner, so that its streams often stop. This torrent of ours stopped too: the torrent of spiritual flow once stopped among the Jewish people. But why do I say "the torrent stopped," when the sea itself stopped, as today's reading taught us, where the Lord says: "Behold, by my rebuke I will make the sea desolate (and I will make the rivers

a desert), and their fish will dry up"? These are the fish of the Jews, dried up by the drought of their unbelief, so that they cannot swim out. The torrent stopped, then, because of the sacrileges of the synagogue, for that people was dry in faith, barren in works, captive to sins. What should flow for people who did not drink from the sacred channels but defiled them, since they denied the fountain itself? Good is the torrent that stopped for them so that it might abound for us and, like a torrent in the south, take away the thirst of human captivity. Hence scripture also says: "Arise, north wind, and come, south wind", the south wind that is accustomed to blow through the shrubs of paradise.

We have stated the meaning; let us also consider the wording. Why did he say "you will give them the torrent of your delight to drink," and not "with the torrent," as if "from the torrent," unless he wished to express the eagerness of the drinkers, as though they would drink the torrent itself dry if they could? This is perhaps the torrent of delight that we read of in Genesis, the fountain which waters paradise and divides into four rivers that encircle the whole earth. From this fountain, too, flow the spiritual virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice. Good is the fountain of grace and splendour, of the same nature as that river of which it is said later: "The rush of the river gladdens the city of God."

Most fittingly, then, he went on: "For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light. Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright of heart." For after the heavenly benefits have been recalled, thanks are rightly given to their author, our Lord Jesus Christ, who came down to earth as the ever-flowing fountain of eternal life, to water the dryness of our hearts.

He is also the radiance of the glory of God the Father and the image of his substance. And therefore in his true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world, "we shall see," he says, the Father, for God is light. It is also rightly said, "In your light we shall see light," in keeping with the saying: "Whoever sees me sees my Father also." With you, then, O fountain of life, we shall see the Father present.

For just as you, God the Word, were with the Father in the beginning, so the Father who is in you is always with you; for he is with the one in whom he also is. And here the coming of the Lord and Saviour is prophesied, who on coming to earth would say: "I and the Father are one," that is: we are one light, just as we are one name; through the unity of light and of name we two are one. Indeed, the Trinity is one in unity of substance, yet with the distinction of each person.

"Trinity" signifies the distinction of the persons, "unity" the power. The words "For with you is the fountain of life" can also be addressed to the Father, meaning: with you is the one from whom life came forth, who was the Word, and who always was precisely because he was with you. All things were made through him and in him; he is the life of all things, and he revealed you to us, to enlighten the hearts of men to the knowledge of your majesty.

"Extend, then, your mercy to those who know you." A privilege is extended, so that those who are supported by the merit of knowing you may deserve mercy. Indeed, later on we find that eagerness for knowledge supported even persons of lower standing, for the Lord says: "I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me." That is: I will remember that harlot Rahab and that confusion among those who know me, or in their company, because that harlot recognized me, whom the people, though chosen, did not know.

Among those, then, who knew me Rahab will be remembered, so that she may obtain the reward her faith deserves. Hence we note that it was said in the gospel too: "Harlots and tax collectors will go before you into the kingdom of heaven." But since we are weak in carrying things out, though devoted in believing, extend your mercy to those who believe in you, so that our deeds too may match our devotion and faith, and the weakness of this body may not let down the zeal of our mind. Rather, let us glory in those very temptations and weaknesses in which the apostle gloried when he said: "Most gladly, therefore, will I rather glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may be extended over me."

Most beautifully, then, he added: "Let not the foot of pride come to me, and let not the hand of sinners move me. There those who work iniquity fell; they were driven out and could not stand." Some take "the torrent of your delight" above to mean fortitude in temptations, such as the martyrs had, in whom it pleased God to show himself the delight of a sweet and pleasing contest. For winters are taken to mean temptations (which is why the Lord warns us to pray that our flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath, that is, either in temptation or in leisure), and in winter a torrent rises, fills and swells. So the torrent can certainly be taken to mean a heavier temptation, the kind that comes in persecutions. And therefore it is well called the torrent of delight, because where the sin of persecution abounded, the grace of confession abounded all the more.

See how powerfully the prophet sets things in order. First he described the unrighteous man, who says, either in his heart or aloud, that he will sin to his own harm, or sin within himself. For the Greek manuscript has ἐν ἑαυτῷ, that is, "in himself," though not all of them do. And perhaps this is because "the fool has said in his heart, there is no God": lest the unrighteous man too should speak within himself and sin within himself, although it is the mark of a madman to deny God openly.

Many, however, flaunt unrighteousness as something to be praised; many think it glorious to rob, to harm even those who have done them no injury, and to cheat. So first he described the life of the unrighteous man; afterwards he added the mysteries of divine knowledge, so that we may fear God and turn away from iniquity and unrighteousness. He added a prayer that God would deign to deliver his righteous ones from the company of the unrighteous, so that over those too who are pure of heart divine righteousness may spread itself like a devoted watchman, lest the onslaught of sinners, like that of enemies, steal upon us and take us while we sleep.

So we must always keep watch and fortify the Lord's camp, because the enemy and adversary comes at night, when the senses are held fast by sleep and the body is heavy with food. We must pray that the righteousness of God may be extended over us, to make us stronger when we are set in weakness, so that each of us can say: "When I am weak, then I am strong."

Then he also prays particularly for himself, to teach us how we ought to pray to the Lord. "Let not," he says, "the foot of pride come to me," that is: let me not fall into pride. Indeed, elsewhere too he recalls this of himself, saying: "If I have not walked in great things." Here he prayed, there he fulfilled it; he would not have fulfilled it had he not prayed. We must beware of pride, which trips us up even in prosperity; indeed, Adam's fall in paradise was graver than if he had fallen on earth.

To fall from the heights is a headlong plunge; on level ground it is called a slip. The proud man's foot goes astray because he does not hold to his head, for "the eyes of the wise man are in his head." No wonder, then, if the step goes astray where there is no eye. Let the eye go ahead, so that the foot may follow. How, then, will you walk as a traveller in the dark? The foot soon stumbles at night if the moon, a kind of eye of the world, does not show the way. You too are in the night of this world; let the Church show you the way, let the sun of righteousness shine on you from on high, so that you have no need to fear a fall.

And since he had spoken of the foot of pride, he added: "and let not the hand of sinners move me." For just as the saints are members of Christ, so the wicked are members of the devil. "Let not the hand of sinners move me," that is: let not the deeds of those who sin move me from my post of righteousness. For often, when we see sinners abounding in prosperity and success, our feelings waver, and we are torn from the root of virtue as if by a hand of sinners. We must take care, then, that those whom the divine hand has planted in the house of God are not uprooted by a hostile hand. Yet it is fitting that this is said by one who is being beaten by persecutors. But those who are moved from their root, which had already clung to Christ, fall.

Hence he added: "There those who work iniquity fell." What is "there"? Is it where pride is, where the hand of sinners is? Or did they fall there where they stood, where they had once been planted? Or in the mire? Or on the spot, as if at that very moment and in that very place? It seems ambiguous. But elsewhere we are taught what "there" means, where it is said: "There, pains as of a woman in labour." Good is that pain for one who gives birth to faith, by which Christ is formed and born in the Church.

And elsewhere he says: "I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me"; for "the foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians, these were there", that is: where those who know me are, where the foundations are on the holy mountains, there the foreigners are too, because they also thought that they should believe in me. There, then, they fell, where they ought rather to have stood, just as Adam fell in paradise; and Christ came for falling and for rising, to be the ruin of the faithless but the resurrection of the righteous and faithful.

Indeed, they were driven out because unrighteous men could not stand in the holy place. Hence the apostle also said: "And you who stand, take heed lest you fall"; and he said it, of course, to one who stood not in body but in faith. We can also understand "there" of the future, as in: "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth," and: "Naked I shall go there." And how brief, yet how great, is the conclusion at the end!

"Let me not be proud," he says, "and so sin; let me not sin, lest I be moved; let me not be moved, lest I fall; let me not fall, lest I be driven out, as Adam was driven out of paradise, because in him the foot of pride first could not stand." Pride does not know how to stand, and if it falls, it does not know how to rise again. And so he also spoke beautifully of the proud earlier: "Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will be magnified in the name of our God" (for this is firm, that is unreliable), and he went on:

"They were bound and fell, but we have risen and stand upright." And in the book of the prophet Micah it is written: "Do not rejoice proudly over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise again." For we fell in this world, but in Christ we have risen again, to whom be honour, glory, power and everlastingness, from the ages, now and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.
EXPLANATION OF PSALM 36

All divine scripture is either natural, mystical or moral. It is natural in Genesis, which sets out how the heaven, the seas and the lands were made and how this world was established; mystical in Leviticus, which contains the priestly mystery; moral in Deuteronomy, in which human life is shaped according to the precepts of the law. That is also why the three books of Solomon seem to have been chosen out of a great many: Ecclesiastes on natural things, the Song of Songs on mystical things, Proverbs on moral things.

But since all the psalms make up one body, nothing in them is divided or set apart; rather, as occasion arose, no branch of teaching of this kind has been left out. For the psalms very plainly include the natural, speaking of angels and powers, sun and moon, stars and light, the heaven of heavens and the water above the heavens: "For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them for ever and ever; he laid down a decree, and it will not pass away."

They have also spoken of mystical things, when they wrote of hidden things, of the ointment of the sacred anointing, and of the completion of the tabernacle. Manifold is the grace of these, since the Lord spoke in the prophets at many times and in many ways. For the psalms foretold that the Son of God would come as chief of priests; the titles "for the winepresses" declared that he would suffer for us and cleanse our sins with his blood; the psalm "of the resurrection" proclaimed that he would rise again; and another title later on, in which "his land was restored," indicated that through the sacraments of faith there would also be a transformation of all things.

They have also woven together a great deal on moral matters, set out the various kinds of virtues and given precepts for living, with which they have healed the sores of our errors, renewed human conduct and changed our innermost feelings. Psalm 33 teaches this, which Saint Peter applied to our hearts in his epistle like a healing plaster, and so does this psalm, which has been set before us in today's reading. These two above the rest are found to be ethical, but this one, entitled the thirty-sixth, is the fuller.

For though that one is very sweet and clear, this one is sweeter still, because that one taught me to keep my tongue from evil, this one to cease from anger and abandon indignation; that one instructed me to speak without guile, this one trains me to be meek, for it has shown the rewards of meekness. What greater comfort is there for the human heart than meekness and simplicity, which ease all the pain of an injury received and shut out every stain of guilt?

Let us, then, set our hand to these remedies to treat our own wounds, lest, if we would claim to be able to heal others, it be said to us: "Physician, heal yourself." It is common not only among physicians but among ordinary people too that few profess medicine, yet very many say they know some of its remedies; or, as physicians' servant-boys do, let us too bring to those in need a remedy from another's medicine.

Let the rich man call in the master, the poor man the assistant. Whoever can grasp the heights of the perfect, let him take from there; whoever wants plainer things, let him graze in the valley, just as a little child who is afraid of the river drinks from the brook, and one who is afraid of deep water swims near the shore. Holy David has beautifully described the life of the unrighteous man in the previous psalm, and here that of the righteous; there the unrighteous man is set forth, here the righteous man is instructed; that one sins to his own harm, this one even takes away the sins of others. And so let us consider what is the first remedy of righteousness.

"Do not act wickedly among the wicked," he says, "nor be jealous of those who do iniquity." First let us learn what it means to be jealous (aemulari), although the force of this word is weaker in Latin than in Greek; for we read of such zeal both in a good sense and in a bad. Thus the apostle says: "It is good to be zealous for what is good always," and earlier he himself said: "They are zealous for you, but not well; they want to shut you out, so that you may be zealous for them"; and again he says: "Be zealous for the better gifts." In Romans you have: "I say, then, have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means! But through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make them jealous"; and further on: "For I say to you Gentiles: as long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will glorify my ministry, if somehow I may make my own flesh jealous and save some of them", that is, stir my own flesh; indeed, the Greek has παραζηλώσω. And here too it has μὴ παραζήλου ἐν πονηρευομένοις and μηδὲ ζήλου τοὺς ποιοῦντας τὴν ἀνομίαν, that is: do not provoke the wicked to jealousy, since they compete not over good but over evil.

What does it mean to provoke to jealousy? Let us explain with an example, if we can. There are certain unchaste women who tempt the hearts of other women's husbands. When they have made these men slaves to their ways and their disgrace, they are not content to keep their wrongdoing secret but make a point of flaunting their shameful conduct before the men's wives, to provoke them to jealousy and inflame them, seeking a kind of triumph from the pain and distress of virtuous minds.

The wives, unable in their womanly jealousy to bear the insult to their own marriage bed, either break the bonds of the marriage they agreed to, or fight it out in daily quarrels; and so jealousy breeds discord, and dissension breeds separation, which throws the whole household into turmoil. Learn, then, reader, from the example of a shameless woman, that it is the work of the most wicked and detestable cunning to stir another's soul with base jealousy, and that zelus is one thing and parazelus another.

For this is the perverse jealousy that creeps into the hearts of the good. By it the Jew too went astray: he strayed from the true and good teaching of the gospel and was turned aside by zeal for the law, just as the apostle says of himself that out of zeal for the law he persecuted the Church of Christ.

So although our God was often offended by the ungrateful feelings and complaints of the Jews, he never abandoned the people he had once taken up and chosen for himself. But the synagogue, like a wanton harlot, began to provoke him to the bitterness of jealousy by mixing itself up in the sacrileges of transgression. In the end it said to Aaron the priest:

“Make us gods, that we may worship them,” and they began to worship the head of a calf. That is why the Lord rang out through the great song of Moses, from his own mouth, saying: “They stirred me to jealousy with what is no god; they provoked me with their idols. But I will stir them to jealousy with those who are no nation; with a

foolish nation I will provoke them.” See how the Lord condemned the synagogue for its harlot's ways, so that he might turn their own cunning back upon them and they might be repaid in their own coin. They had rejected the Lord their God, by whom they had been taken up, through grave sacrileges, choosing for themselves gods to worship. He, on the other hand, took for himself a church from among the profane, so that the Jewish people would groan to see preferred to themselves those who had no law and no favour, and their feelings would be stirred to jealousy of them all the more because the ones chosen were of lower worth.

For before, the people had nothing to stir their feelings, since they regarded themselves as the only ones chosen by the Lord. But when they noticed that a gathering of newcomers had been called from the nations, laying claim to the law of the Lord, the oracles of the prophets and the Lord's new testament, then at last they began to be tormented by overwhelming feeling, once they realized that they had been rejected. In fact, if they see the ceremonies of the Gentiles, they are not moved; if they hear of the church's progress, they are racked with wretched envy. So this is fulfilled in Judea: “And I will stir them to jealousy with those who are no nation.”

Their torment is made heavier still by the fact that the ones they see preferred to themselves are sinners from among the Gentiles, who cannot even boast the name of any people or nation. For every community of any region usually claims a name for itself: Egyptians, Ethiopians, Syrians, Jews and Arabs all bear the name of their province and their lands.

We, gathered from different peoples, cannot take for ourselves the name of a single nation; and so, because we had no name on earth, we received one from heaven, that we should be called the people of Christ. But the Gentile thinks this foolishness, the Jew a disgrace. So what is written is true: God avenged the insult done to him by seeking a church for himself from what was no nation, and by preferring it, drawn from a foolish nation, to that ancient and royal people.

If you ask which is the foolish nation that has been preferred, listen to the one who says: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise”; and again: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool, that he may be wise.” So the Lord paid back the stirring of jealousy rather than starting it, so that it came not as a model to imitate but as a punishment for wickedness.

Indeed the Latin translator, wishing to distinguish between jealousy that strives after virtue and jealousy that gives offence, says: “Are we provoking the Lord to jealousy?” That is: are we giving the Lord the offence of jealousy by eating things sacrificed to idols, just as the Jews exasperated him by sacrificing to idols? Even among men, the attempt to stir up jealousy gives offence, and often the one exasperated turns out to be the stronger, which usually brings harm on the one who stirred the jealousy. How great a folly, then, to provoke the divine majesty and assail it with the offence of jealousy, when for him there is no difficulty in taking vengeance!

We must not, then, supply the goads of jealousy against ourselves to malicious people, who are spurred by the stings of envy to do harm even when they have not been provoked. So Cain killed his brother, because his brother's sacrifice was more acceptable than what he himself had thought fit to offer. In this it was not Abel who was jealous; it was envious Cain who pursued the favour of being preferred with the wicked murder of his brother. For Abel did not want to overshadow his brother's sacrifice, but to keep the proper discipline of sacrifice, so that no

sloth should delay the firstfruits, and no usurpation should violate them by diverting them to private use. Saul, too, laid plots for David, conqueror of the Philistines, a prophet and the preserver of Saul's own safety, because the young women's song had set David above him. He prepared to kill him with a thrown spear, and he would almost have shed the blood of his innocent son-in-law, had David not dodged the wound by twisting and bending his body. What malice was there in it, if the young women said, “Saul among thousands, David among ten thousands”? But how savage was the envy of King Saul, who turned a mistake of speech into the destruction of an innocent man!

“And do not be jealous,” it says, “of those who do iniquity.” He did not repeat what he had said, but changed it. For to rival covertly is one thing, to be jealous is another: covert rivalry involves cunning, jealousy involves simplicity. Yet even simplicity itself ought to be cautious and far-sighted, so that it knows what to guard against; for it was not said idly: “Be cunning as serpents and simple as doves.” So cunning ought to be spiritual, keeping us safe and knowing nothing of deceit; and simplicity ought to be spiritual.

Scripture seems to have drawn the distinction of covert rivalry in another place too, when it says: “And the jealousy of Ephraim will be taken away, and the enemies of Judah will perish; Ephraim will not be a rival to Judah, and Judah will not harass Ephraim.” But elsewhere it has: “So you also, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek to abound in them for the building up of the church.” It used “zealous” for good people who imitate what is good, but “rival” for the spiteful and envious.

The first point, then, is not to provoke malicious people to the malice of jealousy; the second is not to be jealous of those who do iniquity. For very often devout people, seeing that some have acquired riches by fraud and cunning and have risen to honours, are eager, out of ugly emulation, to follow their ways, so as to reach riches and honours by the same arts, or to trick young girls in arranging a marriage.

Yet what is the use, when riches themselves and all worldly glory quickly wither like grass, and perish like garden herbs at the very moment of their bloom? “All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man like the flower of grass.” So do not strive so hard after what cannot last for ever; do not be a rival and a spiteful man; do not be quarrelsome and contentious in jealousy. That is why Aquila said, “Do not contend among evildoers,” and Symmachus, “Do not strive.”

Do not be an imitator of iniquity and fraud either, but be an imitator of the apostles' teaching, the prophets' grace and the virtue of the saints, so that you may bear fruit and store up a harvest of goodness. Be like Joseph, who with an abundance of grain shut out the famine of long barrenness; like Habakkuk, who, while carrying lunch to the reapers, was lifted up by an angel and made his way along a path through the air, and, set back down on earth amid the fierce roaring of lions, served a sweet meal to a devout prophet.

So the prophet rightly says: “Hope in the Lord and do good, and dwell in the land, and you shall be fed with its riches.” What is the land he urges you to dwell in, if not your own soul? You ought to cultivate it well and plough it often with spiritual ploughshares, so that it does not grow rough from long neglect. For a good farmer works his field every day with watchful care and

guards his own land, so that the boar from the forest does not lay it waste and a thief does not snatch the ripe crops. So plough your land, so that when the one who sows the word comes, he may find your soul prepared, and the seed may not fall on the untilled ground of your heart, and the birds of the sky come and carry off what has been sown. If you ask what the land is, listen to the one who says: “Behold, the sower went out to sow his field. And as he sowed, some fell beside the road, some on rock, some on good soil.” And what fell on good soil are those who, with a good heart,

hear the word, keep it and bear fruit with patience. So let your heart be clean, let your soul be clean, so that you may bear the fruit of goodness, that is, of spiritual grace. For goodness is a fruit of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, modesty, self-control.” These are the fruits whose riches feed us and whose abundance fills us. In this land righteous Noah planted that fruitful vine, drank of its fruit

and was loosened in his inmost heart, when the twofold offspring of his virtues clothed him in the praiseworthy cloak of devotion. In another place, too, the holy prophet showed us these riches, in which he was rich in Christ and abounded in everything that leads to eternal life. And truly, who is richer than one who is rich in the Lord, so that he can say: “In the way of your testimonies I have delighted as in all riches”? For what could a man lack who was enriched by heavenly oracles? So in this psalm he urges us to seek that eternal treasure for ourselves and to take delight in acquiring it.

That is why he says: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart.” Why did he not say “your requests,” but “the requests of your heart”? Because the requests of the outer man and of the inner man are not the same, and not all of them are approved by Christ, since the law of the flesh often fights against the law of the mind. But the requests that belong to the inner man, who has been renewed in the Spirit, the Lord, when asked, grants and fulfils.

So he also says elsewhere: “May the Lord grant you according to your heart and confirm all your requests.” He says “according to your heart,” not “according to the craving of the flesh,” and he means: may he confirm the requests that come from the inmost heart, not those directed by the allurements and pleasures of this flesh.

“Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him, and he will act; and he will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like the noonday.” In this single little verse he has shown what you ought to be. For who reveals his way except the one who confesses the inner things of his heart to God, the judge of his secrets?

He rightly says “reveal,” that is: open your conscience, so that the shadow of this world or of the flesh does not weigh it down. For if seeds that are breaking through the ground are overshadowed, they grow thin; exposed to the sun, they grow fat. But why speak of seeds? The shade of the forest kills even young trees, keeping them from shooting upward, and prevents them from spreading their branching arms.

And he says beautifully, “Reveal your way to the Lord,” because human nature, prone to sin, draws a kind of veil over our minds, so that we do not confess our sins to the Lord, who is able to heal our wounds,

so that a person is ashamed to ask for medicine with his own mouth, for fear his disgrace should be exposed before men. So conscience keeps itself pressed down inside a person, though it cannot stay hidden, and it puts off confession until the wound festers, so that it is finally uncovered not by the healing power of faith but by the incurable violence of the ulcer. “Reveal your way to the Lord,” he says; that is, open up your way, do not hide it, as Cain hid his, wanting to stay concealed.

For everyone who does evil hates the light. David revealed his way when he said: “I speak my works to the king.” Open up your mind, so that there is nothing in it you fear to have censured. Paul revealed his too, when he made bold to say: “I am conscious of nothing against myself.” Let your conduct and your life be such that your way shines before your Father who is in heaven.

But since the whole human condition is subject to frailty, and it is not in our power to direct our path as we wish, he therefore tells you: “Hope in the Lord, and he will act”; that is, so that he may open up your way and not let you become the sort of person who flees the light for fear of being exposed, and loves darkness so as to hide your misdeeds, saying: “Darkness covers me;

who knows whether the Most High sees?” For how can the one plotting adultery not seek a night suited to his schemes, the one planning a falsehood not bring in a witness to his fraud, the one angling to corrupt a judge in order to crush an innocent man not look for a secret place for his wickedness? The robber lies in wait in lonely places and hides in the darkness of night, so that his crime may succeed.

So iniquity is darkness; God is light. And even if you wish to hide your righteousness, God brings it out into the light and does not allow your judgment to stay hidden, by which you chose what is good and rejected what is wicked. And he not only makes your judgment shine, but shine like the noonday. When this sun pours itself out in full splendour, it is noon; it was noon when Joseph feasted with his brothers, not having avenged the wrong done to him but having forgotten it.

“Be subject to the Lord and entreat him.” You are urged not only to be subject to the Lord but also to entreat the Lord, so that you may carry out your desire to be subject, just as he said above: “Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him.” It is fitting for you not only to reveal your way but also to hope in the Lord. Good subjection is not abject or base, but glorious and lofty; for the one who is subject to God is the one who does the Lord's will.

Indeed, who does not know that the wisdom of the mind is better than the wisdom of the flesh? Now the wisdom of the mind is subject to God's law, while the wisdom of the flesh is not subject to it, and the apostle added: “nor indeed can it be.” So be subject, that is, close to Christ, so that you may fulfil the law. Christ fulfilled the law by doing the Father's will, and so he is the end of the law and the fullness of love, because, loving the Father, he devoted all his work to his will.

That is why the apostle spoke of it as a glory: “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all.” And he himself [?] says: “Is not my soul subject to God? For from him comes my salvation.” Indeed, it was out of devotion, not weakness, that Jesus was subject to his parents Joseph and Mary. And the greatest glory of Christ is to pour himself into the hearts of all people and call them all back from the impiety of unbelief and the attachments

of paganism, so as to make them subject to himself. And when he has subjected all things to himself, when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in and all Israel has been saved, and there is one body in Christ throughout the whole world, then he himself will also be subject, offering his gift to God the Father, as the chief of all priests with access to the heavenly altars, so that the faith of all may be the sacrifice. So this subjection is one of devotion, in that

the Lord Jesus will be subject in his body, whose body and members we are. So, O man, be subject to Christ, that is, subject to the wisdom of God, subject to the Word, subject to righteousness, subject to power, for Christ is all these things. Let every person subject himself to God; for he teaches not

one but all to subject their heart, subject their soul, subject their flesh, so that God may be all and in all. So the one who is subject is the one who is full of grace, takes up the yoke of Christ, and carries out the Lord's commandments vigorously and without hesitation. But the one without subjection is the one who exalts himself in vain, puffed up by the mind of his own flesh, unused to devotion and shunning the observance of the dutiful service that by the very law of nature we owe to the eternal Creator. Finally, the one who is without sin is subject to Christ, since he has been redeemed by the Lord; but the one who is in sin cannot be called free, but a slave, held by the heavy chains of sin.

Next comes: “Do not be jealous of the one who prospers in his way while doing iniquity.” Here he clearly shows what he meant above: that malicious people are not to be stirred to malice by jealousy, and that those who do iniquity are not to be imitated. For it is not iniquity itself but the prosperity that comes to those who do wicked things that often tempts us to think them worth imitating, so that we may attain their success, and we say: “See, these are sinners, and they prosper in the world and have gained riches. And I said: So it was in vain that I made my heart righteous and washed my hands among the innocent, and I have been scourged all day long.”

If, then, David was scourged, we must take care that we too are not scourged, and that it is not said to us that riches, honours and powers seem to have been assigned to this generation as the wandering and uncertain works of money and the profits of iniquity, not as any rewards of virtue, and that therefore they come like a dream and vanish with the dream when you wake. It is certain that athletes themselves are crowned when they have won, not before they win.

Our wrestling match is with the world; conquer the world first, before you seek a crown. No one is crowned beforehand, unless he has completed the contest. Do those who run in the stadium receive the prize before they have finished the course? How many who were in the lead fall at the finish and are cheated of the reward of their speed! Are you more acceptable to God than Paul? He, the chosen vessel, the teacher of the Gentiles, never dared to ask for a crown for himself in this world. Listen to him saying: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will give me on that day.”

That Paul who was caught up to the third heaven, who heard things that it is not lawful for a man to speak, and who did not know whether he was caught up in the body or out of the body, as he himself testified: that Paul says the crown will be given to him on that day; and you insist on its being given to you here? So complete the time of your contest. An athlete does not wrestle only once, nor does a soldier fight only one battle, if he is to complete his term of service; and you too are wrestling with more than one passion.

If you have escaped the passions mentioned above, anger comes next, and so Scripture tells you: “Cease from anger and forsake indignation.” There are many vices that steal upon the foolish. Anger is a grievous passion; often it sets a man on fire against his will, and when he means to punish more mildly it sweeps him into fury, so that he kills the one he meant only to restrain.

Aroused, a man often runs an innocent person through with the sword; very many have killed friends and brothers out of indignation. That is why the wise man says: “Anger destroys even the wise.” It is a saying of Solomon that anger destroys not just ordinary people but even the wise themselves. And David warns the wise man, saying: “Cease from anger,” lest, once you are inflamed by it, it does not cease until its flame consumes you. “Forsake indignation,” he says; that is: nature carries you away, emotion stirs you, someone's fault or offence provokes you to indignation, but not without end, so that you know no limit:

forsake it, put an end to it, so that it does not drag you into sin. This is what he said earlier: “Be angry and do not sin.” He is not urging you to be angry; he yields to emotion for a time, but he provides a remedy, so that the force of the ulcer does not spread any further. When he says “be angry,” that is a concession to your passion. For a physician does not apply medicines to a sickness immediately. If the pain is burning, he applies poultices to soothe it; if a fever

is raging, he waits for the time for a remedy, and he usually even refuses drink to the thirsty. He does not say “Do not have a fever” while the patient's heat is burning; he says, “Wait for the fever to break and the disturbance to settle.” So too the prophet could not say to a man, whose flesh is stirred by passions of agitation as it is by various diseases, “You shall not be angry”; instead he says: “Cease from anger and forsake indignation, so that you do not sin;

for anger is a powerful teacher of sin.” Another physician also says: “Do not let the sun go down on your anger,” so that, while you put it off for a long time, the one does not come who is accustomed to rouse the body when it has grown warm in sleep, and goad you, plant thoughts in you and sink himself into the secret places of your heart, saying: “Avenge your injury; recognize that you are a man; it is womanly weakness not to take revenge.

So your slave was allowed to despise you, your brother to deceive you, your friend to mock you, and you still do not avenge the insult? You must ruin him; you ought to rise up with the sword and console your pain with your adversary's death. He was a real man who killed his enemy; he is rightly praised, because he avenged himself in such a way that no one else would dare to do him wrong.” By these goads a man is inflamed and stirred all the more, so that what is written is fulfilled: “Anger destroys even the wise.”

So do not listen to him, and do not envy him so as to act wickedly, since those who act wickedly will be cut off. Those who have no roots are cut off, like garden herbs or grass. Let the weak man eat herbs; but you, plant a vine in your field and lay out a vineyard. And if Ahab comes and says to you, “Give me your vineyard, so that I may plant herbs for myself,” do not give in to him, lest with your consent he sow what perishes and cut down what is eternal.

That is why Naboth is counted among the saints: he did not think that the inheritance of his forefathers should be given up even to a king, and he preferred to be stoned rather than hand his vineyard over to plunder. The inheritance of our forefathers is the true faith. Men like Haman have arisen, propped up by royal power, who thought that the Lord's temple ought to be handed over to them, and who threatened bitter punishments. But God forbid that, in a mind that serves the Lord, fear of punishment should outweigh the pattern of piety.

Faithlessness did not prevail, because faith stood firm. There is also a kind of vineyard in the hearts of the faithful, of which Isaiah says: “My beloved had a vineyard on a fertile hill.” The Lord planted this vineyard in our hearts, and so we read that God says: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true.” Let no one, then, take this vineyard away from the field of our soul, for that vineyard is blessed. And so it was said of the saints:

“By the fruit of their grain, wine and oil they have been multiplied.” So it is good to have winepresses within you overflowing with wine, so that wine may flow into your vessel from the vineyard of Sorek, that inebriating cup, how excellent it is! For Sorek is the vineyard of a new beginning, of a new justice. Hence it is also said to us: “Sing to your God a new song; his beginning, glorify his name from the end of the earth.” Let this vineyard, then, produce grapes, not iniquity. The vineyard of the Jews was abandoned because, as it is written, it produced iniquity and not judgment. Let us therefore bear fruit in Christ, so that we may deserve to live forever.

For those who wait for the Lord will possess the land, that is, the land of the living. There is a heavenly land which bears fruit for heavenly beings, of which he says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” This earth supplies food for the belly with much human sweat; that land of the Lord's good things

bears fruit without any toil, and in it lies the lasting possession of the just and the inheritance of the devout mind. And he rightly says: “But those who wait for the Lord will inherit the land.” For this is the land that does not pass away. Heaven and earth will pass away, but the words of the Lord will not pass away. And so that spiritual land of paradise will not pass away either, where those who keep the words of the Lord are found. Adam was placed in this land to gather the fruit of eternal life; but because he could not keep the words of the Lord, he did not deserve to remain in the possession he had received.

But whoever keeps the words of the Lord says with confidence: “I waited and waited for the Lord, and he looked upon me.” Adam, however, did not wait for the Lord (for how could he have waited, when he fled and was afraid to show himself?), and so the Lord did not deign to look upon him either, for the eyes of the Lord are upon the just. Indeed, so unwilling was he to see him that he searched for him, saying: “Adam, where are you?” Whoever is searched for is treated as absent. It is faith that brings us into God's presence; faithlessness makes the ungodly into exiles.

So no one is absent from God except the one who keeps himself absent, and that is why he says: “Let it be done to you according to your faith”; for whoever does not know will not be known.
