So Adam, as a sinner, could not keep his place. Cast out of paradise, he was banished to a village to do penance. He was granted a reprieve so that he would not perish utterly at once, and so that Eve might be saved through the bearing of children: the faith of holy Abel, the grace of the prophets, the posterity of the church.

But whoever refuses to be redeemed by these things and thinks he should persist in sin, of him the prophecy says: “Yet a little while, and the sinner will be no more; you will look for his place and will not find it.” For how could that place exist in the future, when the place of sin cannot last? This is the earth that opened its mouth to receive the blood of the innocent, and so it is on this earth that the place of sinners lies.

This earth passes away; how then could the sinner's place be found? I think that God commanded the firmament to be between water and water for this reason: to separate sins from virtues, so that the upper water, which praises the Lord, might remain at rest from error, while the lower would be liable to sin. Indeed, the one sees God, the other does not;

the water above the heavens sees him, the water in the abyss does not. Hence it is also said: “The waters saw you, O God, the waters saw you and were afraid; the depths were troubled; a multitude of the sound of waters.” Rightly are the depths troubled, for shapeless darkness lies over them, and so they cannot have peace. That is why the legion of demons begged to be sent into the abyss, and hurled itself with a great tumult into the waves to drown the herd of swine it had found. So sinners make for the abyss, where the gloom of darkness is.

“But the meek will possess the land and will delight in abundance of peace.” Rightly do they possess the land in whom God himself rests, as the divine oracle declared through Isaiah: “On whom shall I rest, if not on the one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?” Who are the meek, if not those whom no

goad of discord stirs up, whom anger does not disturb, savagery does not provoke, the frenzy of cruelty does not inflame? And so, because while living in the body they loved not wine, nor banquets, nor riches, but the peace of the Lord, in return for that delight in bodily pleasures which they thought they should forgo in order to gain eternal grace, they will delight in the abundance of peace which our Lord Jesus bestowed on the human race in his days, as the prophecy, which has not lied, declared: “In his days justice shall rise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away.” What, then, is the peace by which the people of all the churches has been multiplied, if not that of which the Lord said: “My peace I leave you, my peace I give you”? He gave peace who calmed the wars within our souls.

There follows: “The sinner will watch the just man and gnash his teeth at him. But the Lord will laugh at him, for he sees that his day is coming.” It is indeed the habit of someone indignant and seething with anger to gnash his teeth; but the heart of the wicked also has teeth of its own, which do not make a sound but tear. Ambushes, the schemes of wickedness, are the sinner's teeth.

So the sinner lies in wait for the just man because he envies him; for the life of the just man rebukes the sinner, and condemns him in silence with greater authority than if it spoke aloud. But the just man ought not to fear the sinner's gnashing, because wickedness cannot last forever. Ambushes are temporary, but the defenses of virtue are eternal. The sinner's death undoes all his power and deceit.

He adds more: “See,” he says, “sinners have drawn the sword, they have bent their bow, to bring down the poor and needy.” What is the sinner's sword but the opposite of the sword of the Holy Spirit? Scripture taught me about this sword; the apostle taught me, saying that we have the breastplate of justice, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. So the word of God is the sword of the Holy Spirit; conversely, the sword of the wicked one is an evil word.

With this, as with a kind of blade of his speech, the apostle Peter struck Ananias and Sapphira; with this sword Paul took away the light of the eyes from Elymas, who opposed his arguments, and poured into him the night of blindness. Now consider, I ask you, sinners quarreling, hurling bitter insolence and uttering reproaches and accusations. If you heard them, would you not say, “Sinners have drawn the sword,” when shameful speech is drawn,

as from a sheath, out of a wanton mouth, when it ought to have been restrained and put away? Just as the word of God is called a sword, and so is the sinner's speech, so too the bow that sinners bend is their mind, and the arrow they shoot is poisoned speech. For just as Christ, who is the Word of God, is an arrow, to whom it is said, “I have made you like a chosen arrow drawn from the quiver of God,” so too there are arrows of the faithless, which, shot from a kind of bow of iniquity, wound the unwary

innocent, unless their fiery darts are driven back by the shield of faith. So you must be watchful, soldier, in battle, because your fight is not only against flesh and blood but also against the spiritual forces of wickedness themselves, which cannot be seen. Have an abundance of weapons that are mighty before God, so that you can easily draw out whatever missiles you wish, lest the enemy overpower you while you are poor and unarmed. Be strong for God, rich for God, so that it may be said of you:

“A man's riches are the ransom of his soul.” Abound in the treasure of wisdom; be rich in word and in good works, so that you may be well defended. Flee the riches of the sinner, lest he find a place where he can wound you. Be merciful, so that you may remain invulnerable, or be able to heal yourself if you have been wounded. There is also a poor man whom the adversaries wish to wound, one of that number of whom the Savior said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

“And therefore,” he says, “let the sword of sinners enter their own heart, and let their bows be broken,” so that, just as the peace of those who bless returns to God's lowly servants from those who have not received it, so too the malice of sinners, by which they try to harm the just, may turn back to their own ruin, and they may be slaughtered by their own weapons and wounds. For darts often rebound on those who threw them.

This also happened in the recent war, when unbelieving and sacrilegious men were attacking a man who trusted in the Lord and were striving to snatch his kingdom from him, threatening the churches of the Lord with savage persecutions. Suddenly a wind arose which knocked the shields out of the unbelievers' hands and turned all their weapons and missiles back upon the sinner's army.

The enemy had not yet reached them, and already they could not withstand the battle of the winds and were being laid low by their own javelins. What is worse, the wounds of their bodies were no more grievous than those of their minds, for they lost heart when they realized that God was fighting against them. They had gone out to provoke, and from the quiver of their hearts they were drawing poisoned darts of faithlessness against the Christian people, but their impiety came back upon their own heads.

In the end they fell apart among themselves through their own treachery, and the Lord scattered the snares they had prepared for the faithful, so that not only could they not harm the godly, but they were stripped of their own forces, and their arms went over to the enemy. How much better if they had never drawn the sword from its sheath, that is, never uttered impious words! For if everyone must give an account for an idle word, how much more will he pay for words of sacrilege with grievous punishments!

“You have tested us by fire,” says David. So we shall all be tested by fire. And Ezekiel says: “See, the Lord almighty is coming. And who will endure the day of his coming? Or who will endure it when he appears to us? For he will come in like a refiner's fire and like a washers' trough. And he will sit refining and purifying as gold and silver are refined, and he will purify the sons of Levi and pour them out like gold and like silver, and

they will offer sacrifice to the Lord in righteousness.” So the sons of Levi will be purified by fire, Ezekiel by fire, Daniel by fire. But even if these are tested by fire, they will still say: “We passed through fire and water.” Others will remain in the fire. For the former the fire will be like dew, as it was for the Hebrew youths who were thrown into the blaze of the burning furnace; but the avenging fire will burn up the servants of impiety.

Woe is me if my work burns up; I shall suffer the loss of this labor. Even if the Lord saves his servants, we shall be saved through faith, yet saved as through fire; even if we are not consumed, we shall still be burned. How some remain in the fire while others pass through, let divine Scripture teach us in another place. The people of the Egyptians, of course, was drowned in the Red Sea, but the people of the Hebrews passed through;

Moses passed through, Pharaoh was hurled down, because his grievous sins sank him. In the same way the sacrilegious, who hurled proud insults against God, will be hurled into the lake of burning fire. While we are placed here, then, let us follow the pillar of fire, so that it may give us light while we are in this body and show us the way, and so that in the future the cloud of night may refresh us, and we may be able to find relief from the fierce flames.

But see what Scripture says: “May the Lord break the bows of sinners.” Yet he set his own bow in the cloud when the floods had ceased, so that calm might be restored. Hence we must believe that the wicked adversary bends his bow to stir up storms in peaceful minds and rouse up gales. Let us pray, then, that the Lord our God may break the bow of malice and help his poor and needy one, who in the fear of God knows that riches are not to be coveted, that the estates of the humble are not to be seized, and that widows are not to be stripped of the inheritances their forebears left them.

“Better is a little for the just than the many riches of sinners.” So it is not riches that are being accused, but the riches of sinners. Unless perhaps it is because the sinner said, “All these have been handed over to me, and I give them to whomever I wish”; and then because riches kindle the torch of greed all the more, and everyone, while he longs for more, does not avoid the byways of sin.

Hence the Savior also said: “Make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon of iniquity.” For wealth that lies in the devil's power, to be given to whomever he wishes, belongs to iniquity. The words “Better is a little for the just than the many riches of sinners” can also be understood this way: there is a kind of person who is rich in words, like the philosophers of this world who dispute about sacrilegious things, about the motion of the stars, about the star of Jupiter and of Saturn, about the generation of human beings, about the worship of idols, about geometry and dialectic. So the philosophers are rich in speech, poor in faith, and without any share in the truth.

And many priests of the Lord are simple men, poor in speech but lofty in self-denial and virtue. The former preach faithlessness to many; the latter uphold the faith with few words. The former lose their own priests every day; this poor man wins peoples for the church and for the number of believers. Whoever, then, hears these men and sees the quality of their works will say: “Better is a little for the just than the many riches

of sinners.” From this Solomon drew what he set down as his own saying: “In much speaking you will not escape sin.” So dialectic overflows with riches of words, while piety keeps the fear of God. That is why this man, sparing in words but rich in spirit, prefers to fear rather than to toss about hollow words about the truth. For fear is the discipline of wisdom; talkativeness is the shipwreck of innocence and virtue, and an incitement to lapse and guilt.

“For the arms of sinners,” he says, “will be broken,” so that their deeds cannot hinder the just, lest the rod of sinners be left over the lot of the just. And Paul says: “May God crush Satan under your feet.” For if his arm is broken, he himself will be crushed entirely, so that his schemes are trampled underfoot like a serpent's venom.

“But the Lord strengthens the just,” once the adversary's arm has been broken. That is why the just man says, “And you have strengthened me upon your hand,” and Job says, “The hand of the Lord has touched me.” So the Lord laid his hand on his servant and broke the hand and arm of the sinner, which he had laid on him by the power he had been granted. Thus the devil was deceived by his own words, when he said: “Lay your hand on him, and let us see whether he will not bless you to your face”;

for he did not dare to say “curse,” but left that to be understood. The Lord laid his hand on him and Job was strengthened; the man who was expected to curse began to bless. For when the divine hand touches the just, it heals them, it does not wound them. He put out his hand, and every blemish of the leper vanished; he touched the eyes of the blind, and when their blindness was driven out, the light of their eyes shone again. So always ask to be strengthened, for you too who stand, take care that you do not fall. We must stand, so that we may be strengthened by the Lord. The world is slippery, and we soon slip; so let us ask the Lord to deign to make us steady and firm.

Do not think that the Lord does not know your way; if you are just, he knows it. Believe the prophet when he says: “The Lord knows the ways of the spotless, and their inheritance will be spotless; they will not be put to shame in the evil time.” Whoever knows Christ is known by the Lord; he knows the just, he does not know the unjust. Therefore he will say to the unjust: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity; I do not know you.” That is: I do not know you because you are unworthy of being known by God; I do not know you because you yourselves chose not to know me. Your works do not know me, your deeds do not know me; even if you say that you know me, your sins refute you.

“Every sin is from the evil one, but whoever does not sin abides in me”: John wrote this. What shall I say of the Lord, that he disdains to know the ungodly? Paul disdains it, when he says: “If anyone among you is a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge what I write to you; but whoever does not know will not be known.” And elsewhere it is said: “The Lord knows those who are his.” Let us therefore belong to the Lord, so that the Lord may know us, and let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.

The Greek has: “The Lord knows the days of the spotless.” For there are days of Elijah, and there are days of Nebuchadnezzar. That is why the Gospel says: “In the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut.” It was night for the faithless, but for Elijah there was light; heaven was shut for the faithless, but open to Elijah; there was famine for the faithless, but plenty for Elijah. For he could not go hungry who was served food from heaven, nor did he hunger who himself fed others. So the just man is a day to himself in the midst of darkness, for the light too shines in the darkness. Joseph also was in Egypt, and noon shone for him, as he said above.

But to the sinner God said: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds?” Righteousness is light, for above he says: “And he will bring forth your righteousness like the light.” So you have something to shine within you, if you follow righteousness. The day shines for you, the night is bright for you, because for the faithful even the night will be lit up like the day. So the Lord knows the days of the just, because he himself enlightens every man coming into this world, that is, the one who lives according to the image and likeness of God, the one who recognizes himself as God's own man, so that he flees the neighing lust of horses, the rage of wild beasts, the timidity of hares, the cunning of foxes, the rapacity of wolves; that

man who lives as though he had come into this world as a newcomer, who was born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh, but of God. You have come, then; do not stay, do not cling to earthly things. And so that you may know that there are good days, hear him say: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced.” He has a good day who knows the Son of God as the good God and confesses him as Lord. And again he himself warns us to be careful, because the days are evil. Which days are evil? Surely those in which evil is known, the evil that comes from the evil one.

Or perhaps the days of this world are evil, because the world lies in the power of the evil one. But we also read of an evil day after this world: “In the evil day the Lord will deliver him,” that is, on the day of judgment, because of the punishments of many. For it must be that the unjust are tormented and the just suffer with them, since even the angels rejoice when a single sinner is saved from death. So they suffer with him when he is punished, even though we read elsewhere: “The just man will rejoice when he sees the vengeance on the ungodly.” I reserve this for its proper place, though you have often heard why he rejoices; but let us not pile one task on top of another.

“The Lord knows the days of the spotless,” because his grace and fullness show mercy to spotless innocence; they do not show mercy to those who go astray. These have no day, because they flee the light; of them it is beautifully said: “Their days pass away like a shadow.” So God's knowing is a matter of his favor, not of his sight. His eyes are light; those he looks upon, he enlightens; and so his eyes are the day of the just.

Hence “their inheritance will last forever,” because they sought eternal goods, not the profits of a temporal inheritance; and they will have nothing to blush for “in the evil time,” that is, the time of the heavenly judgment, and “in the days of famine they will be satisfied,” because man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God. But which man? “I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago (whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know; God knows) was caught up to the third heaven.”

That man, then, who is in Christ, who does not know himself to be in the flesh, who walks not according to the flesh but according to the spirit, who is caught up not only to heaven but even to the third heaven, and is caught up into paradise and hears words that a man is not permitted to speak, who glories not in his strengths but in his weaknesses: he lives not by bread alone but by every word of God. For the Word of God is life, because the Word was made flesh. Hence the evangelist said so admirably: “What was made in him was life.”

The Alexandrians and Egyptians read: "All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made," and then, after inserting a pause, they go on: "In him is life." Let the faithful keep that punctuation if they wish; I am not afraid to read: "What was made in him is life

",and the Arian has nothing to cling to, because I am not considering his poisons but recognizing the customary usage of sacred Scripture. For it did not say "the Word was made before every beginning"; it did not say "the Word was made." If you want to hear what it did say: "The Word," it says, "was with God." He was with God, working with him, ruling with him. It did not say "the Word was made"; it said: "The Word was God."

But God is not something made; he is the maker and creator. Open your ears and hear: "All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made." You learn that he is the Son, in whom dwells the fullness of the Godhead. Open your ears a little longer and hear him say: "What was made in him is life."

"In him," it says, "was made," not "the Word of God was made." Or if the words "was made in him" move you to slander, will you slander God the Father too, because the Son of God said: "But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been made in God"? Or because David said: "I will praise you, Lord, because you have heard me and have been made my salvation" — that is, you have turned to me for salvation, you have worked for my salvation? I could use other examples, but I do not want you to take my word for it, lest you think these are arguments of ingenuity rather than testimonies of truth.

Let the son of thunder himself — the one who reclined on Christ's breast, the one from whom the Lord did not keep his secrets, the one to whom Peter signalled to ask the Lord, and he asked and the Lord revealed it — let him explain what he meant when he said: "What was made in him is life." Hear him, then, interpreting, for he was already guarding against your slanders, Arian: "What was from the beginning, what we have heard and seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon and our hands have examined concerning the Word of life — and the life appeared."

It is the flesh, then, that appeared in Christ, or Christ in the flesh; he is our life in all things. His divinity is life, his eternity is life, his flesh is life, his passion is life. That is why Jeremiah too says: "In his shadow we shall live." The shadow of the wings is the shadow of the cross; it is the shadow of the passion. His death is life, his wound is life, his blood is life, his burial is life, his resurrection is the life of all.

Do you want to know how his death is life? We were baptized into his death, so that we might walk with him in newness of life. And he himself says: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." He is the grain that was dissolved in body and died for us, so that he might bear much fruit in us. And so his death is the fruit of life. Therefore what was made in him is life.

Flesh was made in him: it is life. Infancy was made in him: it is life. Judgment was made in him: it is life. Death was made in him: it is life. The forgiveness of sins was made in him: it is life. A wound was made in him: it is life. Mockery was made in him: it is life. Division was made in him: it is life. Burial was made in him: it is life. Resurrection was made in him: it is life. See how many things were made in him, by which our life was turned around, so that what had perished might be restored.

Lastly, a sale was made in him: it is life. Redemption was made in him: it is life. He was sold to death by Judas and bought by the Jews for death, so that we might be redeemed to life by his precious blood. This is the life that was made, this is the life that appeared, this is the life that we have seen, this is the life that was with the Father, because he who was in the beginning is the very one who was born of a virgin, so that there might be life for those who were going to die.

Let us question the very passage set before us. What does "a man in Christ" mean? It means one made in Christ, in whom all things were made, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before

all, and all things hold together in him, that is, in his power. A man in Christ, then, is one who was made in his image and likeness; a man in Christ is one who is wholly in Christ. For just as God the Father, through the unity and fullness of the Godhead, is wholly in the Son and the Son in the Father, so — to use this by way of example and not of comparison — through devotion and the affection of piety a man is wholly in Christ; for whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit.

A man in Christ, then, is not that earthly man, not the man of sin, but the man of Christ. Why then should it disturb anyone that "what was made in him is life," if man too — above all the inner man — was made in him, crucified in him, renewed in him, buried in him and buried together with him, raised in him? Why should it disturb anyone, as I said, that it is written, "What was made in him is life," when a man has said:

"In God we shall act with valour"? If it disturbs you that what was made in him is life, and you ask what this life is, take this answer: the life is surely the Church. She was made in him, in his rib; in him Eve was raised up again. And Eve means life — that is, what was made — because Eve, who had perished, was saved through the Church, that is, through the begetting of her children, as it is written, since a sober inheritance amended the fault of the forebear. Hence Paul himself was caught up to life, who before had been a persecutor unto death.

We have wandered rather far afield, in order to speak of that man who would live not by bread alone but by every word of God. Let us return to the psalm: "And therefore the spotless will not be put to shame in the day of judgment, and in the days of famine they will be filled."

"Failing like smoke they will fail." The Greek has ἐξέλιπον, that is, "they have failed." You see someone suddenly come to power and to the insignia of office; you judge him exalted. You see that success has come his way; and do you not then say of him: "Where is the man who was honoured and exalted? He has failed"? That is why the Greek said more: because at the very point where someone is thought to be honoured and exalted, his own failure overtakes him, so that you realize the river's currents have passed by sooner than they came, and while you wait for the streams to arrive, they have flowed past as you are still waiting. The humble and meek, on the other hand, while they are made subject to the rich and oppressed by them, have been exalted by their own humility and have suddenly shone out. That is why Paul took pleasure in weaknesses, not in powers.

But let us take care that no one should think he boasted of his revelations, and let us go back over those words, so that he himself may show himself a teacher of humility: "I know a man in Christ," he says, "fourteen years ago — whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know; God knows — such a man was caught up to the third heaven." He says the revelation came to him fourteen years earlier, and yet he kept it to himself and held it back all that time; nor would he have told it had he not judged it useful for us that he should, so that we might not be puffed up by revelations.

For if Paul did not boast in so great a grace, neither should we boast. He did not boast as a young man: would he boast as an old one? Moreover, he could not deny that he had been caught up to the third heaven, and yet he testified that he did not know whether he had been caught up in the body or out of the body. He boasts, then, not of knowledge but of ignorance, and proclaims God's grace toward him. What belongs to knowledge he denies; what belongs to love he confesses; for knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. And again, he said that such a man was caught up,

and stated that how he was caught up, whether in the body or out of the body, was uncertain to him. See the balance of wisdom! He set up one man in Christ and himself as another, the one who says "I do not know." What is another's he exalts; what is his own he humbles. "And he heard," he says, "unspeakable words." He did not say "I heard," but he did not deny that the other had heard. So out of modesty he preferred to present himself as a witness rather than a prophet, and shrank from appearing to be the judge of heavenly secrets. For to bear witness belongs to truth; not to shrink from the merit of a revelation belongs to one who boasts. That is why he says: "On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast."

But what does he mean when he says that a man — that man in Christ — heard things that it is not lawful for a man to speak? How can it be that a man was not permitted to speak what a man was permitted to hear? If the very man who heard is not permitted to speak, how was he entrusted with hearing what he was not allowed to speak? What is this distinction? And if it refers to another man, one outside, how could a man come to know what a man was not permitted to hear?

It seems, then, that it was not the grace of speaking that was lacking to that man who was in Christ — he did not lack it — but that the place, the time and the merit were lacking to those who would hear. For he heard in heaven, and therefore it was judged unfitting for him to speak on earth what he had heard in heaven, since even on earth itself there is this distinction, that what is sung in one region is not sung in another, according to what is written: "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land?"

Indeed, the Hebrews did not sing in the land of captivity what they had been accustomed to sing in their homeland. This is the land of captivity; the other is the land of freedom. This is the land of sin, that of eternal rest; this belongs to the valley, that to heaven. So in heaven Paul now proclaims those things which he could not proclaim before on earth; for the secrets of wisdom are to be spoken among the perfect.

And yet what does the mention of this revelation accomplish, if not to teach that one should by no means boast in revelations but in weaknesses? For weakness is both a remedy for revelation and an exercise of virtue, whereas revelation is a slippery path to pride. Indeed, so that Paul himself, who was caught up to the third heaven, might not be puffed up by the sublimity of the revelation, he received a thorn in the flesh.

Weakness therefore came to his aid, so that grace might not turn into danger. Weakness, then, is more useful than grace. That same weakness is also the workshop of virtue, as the Lord testified, saying that power is made perfect in weakness. Indeed, this very man after his revelation asked for the remedy of health and did not obtain it; but in his weakness he sought no remedy, and instead finished his course and found the crown.

"The sinner borrows," it says, "and will not repay, but the just man shows mercy and gives." This too fits the person of Paul, because the just man shows mercy and gives. See him dispensing the words of the Lord; see him lending out the Lord's silver at interest.

He received one mina and returned two; he received two and returned four; he received five and returned ten. He did not tie up what he had received in a napkin, but paid it out to the money-changers, and what he had paid out he got back with interest. In this way he also freed the one who had received it from a very great sin, so that the Lord's money should not be lost in his keeping, and he himself earned the right to be set over ten cities. What the ten cities are you may recognize in the letters he wrote, even though the apostles are not bound to a fixed number, since to them it was said:

"Go into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature." So this man dispensed the Lord's money from Jerusalem through the East and Illyricum and Italy. And so that no one should think he was lending out his own, he testified that the money was the Lord's, saying: "To those who are joined in marriage I give charge, not I but the Lord, that a wife should not depart from her husband," and elsewhere:

"Are you seeking proof of the Christ who speaks in me?" Indeed, the king himself, in whom is a figure of the Lord, said: "You ought to have entrusted my money to the money-changers." "My money," he says, not "yours." So the just man shows mercy and gives. Hear him say how he gives: "I teach in all the churches." But the sinner borrows and does not repay. See the rich man borrowing and not paying back, and the poor man receiving and repaying at once, so as not to remain in debt any longer. So much for the moral sense.

Now see the poor man in the mystical sense, that is, the simple man who fears the name of God: he hears the word about chastity and repays; he hears about mercy and repays; he hears about gentleness and does not grow angry. But the rich man, arrogant and proud, hears indeed, yet casts the words of God behind him; he hears the condemnation of luxury and indulges in luxury all the more.

Indeed, the Church repays what she received; the synagogue does not repay. Recognize that the Church repays: "They were yours," he says, "and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word"; and elsewhere: "For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me." So the Church paid back the money of love which she received from the Lord, but the synagogue did not pay it back. That is why it is said of the Jews: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin," because they certainly heard and did not believe.

It is proved, then, that sinners borrowed and did not repay. The sinner is therefore always in need, but the just man, whose conscience is rich, has abundance and gives. That is why the Jews were in want amid their riches — "the rich have been in want and have gone hungry" — while Christians have not lacked anything amid the riches of their simplicity.

So the just man is good, and therefore Scripture added: "For those who bless him shall possess the land, but those who curse him shall perish." How does the just man possess the land, and what land, when Scripture says, "Will you alone dwell upon the earth?" and elsewhere, "Woe to those who dwell upon the earth," which is a word of rebuke and curse? Of what land, then, is the possession blessed? Not of this one, which is hidden in darkness and filled with bitterness, but of that which flows with honey and milk, that is, which has the grace of sweetness and the radiance of eternal light.

Take the sweetness of good honey — indeed, beyond honey: "Pain and sorrow and sighing have fled away," because the grace of sweetness will shut out the bitterness of human frailty. And elsewhere: "And he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, nor mourning." Take also the brightness of milk: "And they will have no need of a lamp or of the light of the sun; for the Lord himself will shine upon them, and they will reign for ever and ever."

There is also a just man in the mystical sense, who shows mercy and gives: he who gave us all the words he received from the Father, who forgave us the debts of our sins and paid his own blood for our debts, so that we might not be bound by interest to another, but the good creditor might hold us as debtors to himself. And there is also that sinner who gathered what he did not bring forth

and borrowed what he did not hold, and will not give back what he received. Hear how the devil borrowed: "To you," he says, "I will give all this power and their glory, for it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whom I will, if you will fall down and worship me." Most wicked one, you received it for testing, not for death; that is, you received it so that

God's poor servants might be proved, not destroyed; you received it so that God might be worshipped, not denied. You received the things of this world; why do you snatch away what is eternal? You received what belongs to the world; why do you want to take away what belongs to Christ? Give those things to whom you will; we do not begrudge them. Why do you begrudge us the things we want? Do you want to be worshipped — you who, more wicked than all, are unworthy even of servitude?

"By the Lord a man's steps will be directed." The Greek said διαβήματα, that is, "passings," and so it is said to you: "If you pass through water, the rivers will not hem you in." Pass on, then; do not stop, just as a good traveller, when he comes to some marker on the road, does not halt but passes on. You too are on the road, as long as you are set on this course. Had Paul stood still, he would not have finished his course. See: that is why it says to you too, "You who stand, take care that you do not fall"; for one who has passed through has no need to fear falling.

"I saw," it says, "the wicked man highly exalted and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon, and I passed by, and behold, he was not." So the one who saw the wicked man highly exalted, and did not stand still, did not stumble; had he stood still, he would have admired him and followed him, and would have stumbled and fallen like the wicked man. That is why Moses, seeing the bush shining and not burning, said: "I will pass over and see this great sight." Whoever passes over from this world sees a great sight; whoever loosens the chains of this bond by which we are tied to this body sees a great sight.

Moses [it is read in Exodus] sees many miracles in the Exodus; no one else who is not in exodus sees such things. Moses himself passed over; the people of the fathers also passed over, for they were going out of the land of captivity. And so their steps were directed by the Lord: a pillar of fire gave them light by night and of cloud by day, so that neither the heat of the day would harm them as they journeyed nor the darkness of night hinder them on their way.

You too, by your deeds earn it and by your prayers ask for it, that your steps may be directed by the Lord, so that your feet may not be moved, for it is written: "But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well-nigh slipped." You must also take care not to abandon the straight path and let the byways of crooked roads lead you astray. That is why it is said: "Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight."

Let us then prepare the way for the Lord our God in our minds; let us make his paths straight, let us make the paths of our souls straight, so that we do not slip. Let our steps not slip like those of Lot's wife, who looked back and could not keep her steps; they slipped when she was suddenly turned into salt. Let them not slip like those of the Egyptians, whose steps the waves of the sea swept away. Even of the Hebrews who were with Moses, because they sinned in the desert, the footsteps fell, so that they did not enter the land of resurrection.

Is it not also fitting to say of those whose hopes have collapsed, whose labour has been poured out in vain, whose vows have come to nothing, that their progress has slipped away? For consider someone who for several years held to a zeal for uprightness, the guarding of chastity, a desire for a more careful life, the resolve of devout service, the duty of diligent observance, and then suddenly

was changed: he left the monastery, bade farewell to fasting, renounced continence, gave himself up to pleasures and pursued luxury. Some left the monasteries a while ago and are now teachers of luxury, sowers of incontinence, instigators of wantonness, detractors of modesty. Would you not rightly say of them, "Their steps have slipped," since they regretted having directed them well? They have performed a penance of a new kind — for their virtues — and do none for their sins. "But they went out from us," says John, "but they were not of us; for if

they had been of us, they would have remained with us." These people, then, have condemned their own way, and to them it is fitting to say: "O you who have forsaken the straight paths to go into the ways of darkness, who rejoice in evil and delight in wicked overthrow, whose paths are crooked and whose courses are winding," like their slippery and winding author. Why have you begun to hate the straight way, and why have you abandoned just counsel? The Lord did not direct you. But the one whom the Lord directs "will desire his way," as it is written, and will delight in his paths.

Yet it can be understood either way — the phrase stands ambiguously in the middle: both that the one who is directed by the Lord will desire the Lord's way, because with him as guide every labour is lightened, every obstacle removed, and encouragements supplied; and that the Lord himself does not spurn, but gladly accepts, the way of the man whom he himself has directed toward virtue. And it is well said that a man's steps are directed by the Lord, because it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy, to keep one's footsteps from stumbling. For neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth; to him alone the glory of virtues is rightly given.

In short, even the righteous man sometimes falls. But if he is righteous, when he falls he will not be thrown into confusion. That he falls belongs to his condition; that he rises again belongs to his righteousness, because God does not abandon the righteous man but strengthens his hand. Why did Scripture say "hand" and not "foot"? Is it perhaps because the one who falls does not slip by the foot so much, but, being weak, is often tripped up on slippery ground or stumbles against a rock? Here, however, understand the fall of the righteous man, that is, of the stronger man.

For among ordinary people who wrestle, if a man goes down on one knee or slips with his foot, he is counted as beaten. But an athlete who has skill in wrestling and wrestles for the crown will even go down on one knee deliberately in order to win. If he slips, he is not ruled out; and if he is pressed down by one who has the upper hand, so long as he holds himself up on his hands he is still lawfully in the contest, and the prize is not taken from him unless he is thrown flat on his belly or pinned by a lock of the arms. This is why the bouts are so frequent, because there are many kinds of falls, and most of them are unknown to most people. Indeed, they properly call their falls "ruins";

for in Greek they are called ptōmata [?]. So when a wrestler is gripped and hard pressed, he often rolls himself over, and the one who was thought to be underneath comes out on top, and as he rises he throws down the one who had been above. Scripture seems to indicate this when it says: "You have overturned his whole bed in his sickness." So it is said of such a man: "When the good athlete falls, he is not thrown into confusion." Many who are confident in their skill even want to be held, so as to win the sooner.

But even if he has been "marked," to use the technical term itself, both a first and a second time, he is not ruled out; he is allowed at times to renew the bout, and it often happens that he wins and that the man who got the better of him in the second round gives way. So too the righteous man, even if he has run into a stumbling block

and fallen, should not give up his zeal for devotion and faith; let him keep sober, do penance, and recover himself again and again. That is why Peter asks: "If my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him? As many as seven times?" And the Lord answered: "Not only seven times, but seventy times seven." And so that you may know that we are athletes, and that we are pushed, and that some fall and many are thrown down, listen to the one who says:

"The Lord upholds all who fall and sets upright all who are thrown down." Hence David too, or rather he who spoke in the prophet, says of himself: "I was pushed and overturned so that I might fall, and the Lord took me up." For Jesus did not fall; he was pushed. Indeed, since he himself sets upright those who are thrown down, how could he himself be thrown down? That the righteous man, when he falls, can rise again is attested by Scripture, which says: "Shall he who falls not rise again? Or shall he who has turned away not turn back? Woe to those who turn away with a shameless turning away, says the Lord."

Would that the athlete of Christ were unconquerable and unbeatable in wrestling, and glorious at every age and in every kind of virtue, as the apostle says: "But in all things we overcome through him who loved us!" What does "in all things" mean? There are athletes who are called boys, youths, and men, that is, paides, ageneioi, andres. Scripture too recognizes these ages among wrestlers, for David says: "Do not turn your face away from your boy," and: "I was young, and I have grown old."

Hence John also says: "I write to you, little children, because you have known the Father. I write to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning." So, being more mature himself, writing to his brothers, he marks out as mature those who are advanced in faith and devotion. These, then, are ages of virtue, not of weakness; for the boy who has known the Father, the God of powers, is not without strength.

These boys come from that Boy who, before he knew how to say "father" or "mother," received the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria. He is the Boy who is born to us, the Son who is given to us, whose government is upon his shoulders. He himself taught us that childhood is a virtue, saying: "Let them be, and do not forbid the children to come to me," and elsewhere: "Truly, truly I say to you, unless you are converted and become like this child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven."

Boys often defeat men even in bodily strength. Certainly, if we consider the age of boyhood, a boy cannot know the whole practice of wrestling or bear its force; yet we know that boys have often defeated men they could not even have carried, so far does vigour of spirit overcome the weakness of age.

And as the boys are, so are the youths, that is, spiritual. Scripture knows Paul as a young man, already close to his conversion; it knows also the young man Eutychus, who, while he clung intently to Paul's words, was overcome by sleep, fell from the third storey, and rose again; it knows too the young man John reclining on Christ's breast, who was so strong that he did not fear persecution and overcame the evil one.

He is the boy who left his natural father and followed the Father whom he knew to be eternal; the young man who, wrapped in a linen cloth, followed the Lord at the time of the Passion, having left all that was his; the more mature man who knew that God the Word always was and is in the beginning itself, and who proved that he abides in him.

Scripture has also taught us of spiritual men, when the prophet Agabus says: "So shall the Jews in Jerusalem bind the man whose belt this is," and Festus says: "There is a certain man left in custody by Felix." Before his suffering Paul is called a young man; in his suffering he is described as a man, since, having finished his course, he was already close to the crown.

We have come to know the ages that contend for faith and devotion. Let us also come to know the kinds of each contest. Let the course of Scripture teach us these too. In this worldly contest, then, there are some who wrestle in a simple and regular style and contend only with holds of the body; they do not know how to strike, and they are called palaestae. There are others who mix blows and the flinging of dust with the straining of their limbs, every right of striking being allowed them; these they call pammacharii, because they have against one another the freedom of every kind of struggle and fight. There are others who contend against one another with the caestus and are tormented with lacerated heads; these are called pyctae.

The apostle Paul undertook all these contests, as he himself shows. Thus in one place he says: "For our palē is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers"—and, to be brief—"against spiritual wickedness." In most Latin copies "conluctatio" is found; in all the Greek copies palē is written, for the Greek palē is the Latin "wrestling."

And truly it is palē, because flesh and blood and spiritual wickedness are overcome by patience, by bodily self-control, and by moderation of mind. Anger, fury, and slaughter are the weapons of the devil. Elsewhere too he indicates that he was beaten with blows beyond measure, saying: "in stripes beyond measure, in deaths often," and that at Jerusalem he was struck with fists. There, when the soldiers intervened and the Jews had at last stopped striking Paul, the high priest Ananias himself ordered those standing by to strike him on the mouth.

The apostle answered him: "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit judging me according to the law, and contrary to the law order me to be struck?" Surely he knew how to strike back, he who struck the high priest back with a heavier blow; for he himself was struck in body, but he gave back to the priest the warning that he would be struck in his soul by Christ. Writing also in the First Epistle to the Corinthians he says: "I therefore run not as one uncertain; I strive not as one beating the air." Where the Latin says "I strive," the Greek says pykteuō, "I box."

And truly, like a good boxer, he was beating not the air but the powers of the air and the heads of the Jews, because they did not have the Lord Jesus, the Head of all. So in every contest the apostle was proved, and when he had finished his course he received the crown. Hence he himself says: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me."

Christ also has those who in their boyhood defeated men of mature age, as Daniel, a boy strong in spirit, refuted those elders of the Jews and by the right of victory cast them down to death. He has others too who wrestled in their mother's womb before they were born. Thus Jacob supplanted his brother Esau and overcame the wicked one, and so came out of his mother's womb as to display the mark of victory and, as victor, to overturn the foot of his degenerate elder brother. Jeremiah was sanctified and approved in his mother's womb.

John the Baptist, though not yet born, recognized that the President of the human contest, the one who awards prizes to the wrestlers, had come, and by leaping in his mother's womb he earned the prize of a devout confession. Rightly was he already then marked out for the crown, he who before all others had entered his name for Christ's contest as witness of faith and herald of virtue. A good herald, who roused others to the contest; and truly a good herald, who cried with so great a voice that the secret places of heaven echoed at its sound.

What more need be said? He shook the earth and filled heaven. And so he received the name "voice," because a sacred voice went before the Word of God, as he himself taught us, saying: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness." The prophet Isaiah said this; John confirmed that it was said of him. We have heard what the herald said: "Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." This is a unique voice, the only one so resonant that it could be heard by all, so sweet that it soothed the hearts of all. So the Lord strengthened his righteous athletes so that they might win; for he never deserts and abandons his own.

And therefore the prophet added: "I was young, and I have grown old." So the Latin copies have it; but some, following the Greek, read: "I was young; for indeed I have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread." For anyone who wants to understand it simply, the sense is plain: that in the time of his life David did not see a righteous man forsaken. But this both covers only a short time and is hard to believe; for we see many righteous people in this world forsaken by men, when some of the powerful persecute them, and no one dares to approach them, seeing that he would himself be placed in fear or in danger of harm.

Hence Job says: "My brothers have gone away; they have acknowledged strangers rather than me. My friends have become merciless, and those who knew me have forgotten my name." David too cries out that he has been not only abandoned but even attacked by his friends and neighbours: "My friends," he says, "and my neighbours have drawn near against me." So if righteous people are found forsaken in this world, how could David have said things contrary to himself, unless you understand that the righteous man, even if he is forsaken in this world, is nevertheless not forsaken by the Lord?

For Job was not forsaken by the Lord when he sat on the dunghill; the Lord praised him with his own voice in the council of the angels and allowed him to be tempted so that he might crown him. He gave leave to tempt his body, but refused it for his soul. Nor was David forsaken, to whom he gave a kingdom so that he might rule the chosen people, and whom, when he was attacked in parricidal wars and driven out of the borders of his kingdom, he restored by right of victory.

Jacob too, Elijah and Elisha, John the Baptist, and the others who went about in goatskins, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and holes in the ground, though they seem to have endured many mockeries and bitter torments, were nevertheless not forsaken. For when Jacob was fleeing from his brother and wandering alone through the wilderness, he fell asleep, and rising he saw there a multitude of the heavenly host and said: "This place is called the camps of the angels." It was not enough to call it a camp, but "camps," such as would suit so great a multitude.

You see, then, that he thought himself alone, and yet the camps of the heavenly army were following him, just as in Moses' time, so that our fathers should not thirst in the desert, a rock, as it is written, followed them. For while we read in Exodus that when the people were thirsty Moses struck the rock with his rod, and water flowed, and the people of God drank, and we read again in Leviticus, or rather in Numbers, that Moses once more touched the rock with his rod and water gushed out for our fathers to drink, the apostle interpreted this splendidly, saying: "They drank from the rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ."

So the Lord did not desert them, complaining, grumbling, and transgressing though they were, but followed them. What shall I say of Elijah and Elisha, whom horses and a chariot of fire came from heaven to meet as they walked through the wilderness? How was Elijah forsaken, who was invited by Christ? How was he forsaken on earth who was caught up to heaven? How was he needy and naked and empty who left to his disciple the inheritance of a double spirit, so that the heir, endowed with a single sheepskin cloak, could stop rivers, turn the Jordan back to its source, feed the armies of kings in the desert, and supply drink to the thirsty?

At his bidding drink flowed down from heaven, and the dead on earth rose again. How was Elisha raised up, who, when he was surrounded by the army of the Syrians so that he might be carried off as a captive to the king, and his servant Gehazi said, "Master, what shall we do?", replied: "Do not be afraid, for there are more with us than with them"? And he said: "Lord, open his eyes, that he may see." And his eyes were opened,

and he saw the mountain and all around filled with countless horses and heavenly legions. Paul too, who said that he had been tossed about by perils at sea and perils in the wilderness, nevertheless testified himself, saying: "If God is for us, who is against us?" So he who was thus forsaken and abandoned by men abounds and overflows with God. For Elijah too was so abandoned that he said, "Lord, take my soul," and yet he was so strong with God that in power he was a terror to kings themselves.

How could the young David understand this? For a young man considers temporal things rather than eternal ones, because that age inclines to vices. But there are some who are old in youth and others who are young in old age. There are, I say, men whose minds are reckoned to have the gravity of old men, in whom an unblemished life is the age of old age, in whom white-haired prudence flourishes. Such was Jeremiah: when, with an eye to his age, he called himself young and excused himself on the grounds of his youth, because he seemed unequal to the office of preaching, the Lord said to him: "Do not say, 'I am young,' for you shall go to all to whom I send you."

Thus he did not consider young the one whom he judged fit for the grace of prophecy. Such a young man, then, was David, whose youth had been renewed and had flourished again, as he himself said, like the eagle's. So it must be understood thus: "I was young, but sanctified, but set as a prophet among the nations, able already to know the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom and to consider the true rewards of righteousness; yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken. Afterwards too, strengthened both by experience and by God's gift, I gained increase of wisdom; and the same grace seemed to me to remain upon the righteous."

We have explained as well as we could how he said, "I was young"; but let us consider how he added, "for indeed I have grown old." Youth is good, but old age is better; for "he who perseveres to the end will be saved." Hence it was not said casually of the patriarch Abraham that he was nourished in a good old age. And John began to write the Gospel and the epistles when he was old.

And since he shrank from writing himself "apostle," he wrote "the elder," and was not thought the less for it, he who was furnished with a kind of swan-like grace of old age. The Lord's chosen vessel himself, writing to Philemon, says: "Since you are such a one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus, I appeal to you for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my chains." So, wishing to pay him the greatest deference, he compared him to Paul the old man, not the young man,

and he gloried in being old at the very point when he was already held in chains. And see the difference: he is described as a young man at another's suffering, as an old man at his own; there as a young man, because he was keeping the clothes of the Jews, here as an old man, when he was putting off the garment of his own body. So too Peter is called old at the point where the contest of his passion comes: "When you were younger," he says, "you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you have grown old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish."

He said this signifying by what death he would glorify God. Before the contest he is called younger; in the contest, old, as one who had fulfilled the whole contest. This, then, is what David says, he who was a warrior in his youth and a man of peace in his old age: "I was young," he says, "but I do not want you to think me still young; for indeed I have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread."

What is the seed of the righteous? "The promises were made to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say 'and to seeds,' as of many, but as of one, 'and to your seed,' which is Christ." Hear the seed of the righteous: "My little children, with whom I am in labour until Christ is formed in you." And now, if anyone coming from the Gentiles hears our word, and the Lord deigns to help so that Christ

is formed in his soul, so that it bears the offspring of faith, Christ will be seed to him [there in both]. Abraham, then, was both father of a lineage according to the flesh and the one who first poured the word of the Lord into the hearts of the righteous. And so this seed of Abraham does not seek such bread as supplies bodily nourishment, because it has the bread of righteousness that came down from heaven. For just as those who have not done the works of Abraham are denied to be Abraham's sons, so those who have done his work are the seed of Abraham and are received among his sons. Elijah was the true seed of Abraham, to whom an angel supplied food, and in the strength of that food he walked for the space of forty days.

The true seed of Abraham did not seek this nourishment of the body, he to whom bread was brought from heaven; indeed ravens served him a daily meal. He was so needy in everything that he had nothing of his own, and yet he was sent to bestow food on others. Daniel was the true seed, to whom, when he was placed among the lions, dishes filled with the reapers' food were carried through the air by the prophet Habakkuk.

There is, then, a bread of angels which man has eaten; for so it is written: "Man ate the bread of angels." This is the bread of which David said: "The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing. He has set me there in a green place; he has brought me up beside the water of refreshment." Good David has taught me of the bread of angels, and he himself has taught me of the water of refreshment. This refreshment is spiritual; this refreshment is the rest of the inner mind. Good is the water that washes away sin and cleanses what is within.

Let us hear what this water is: "If anyone thirsts," he says, "let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." He said this of the Spirit, which those who were to believe in him were beginning to receive. So the righteous man, whose rest and refreshment is the Holy Spirit, lacks neither this bread nor the water of refreshment.

And how can he be in need who all day long is merciful and lends? What is it that the righteous man lends? Not bronze, not iron, not lead, but silver tried in the fire. This he brings to the Lord's table and distributes to those who ask, to one a single mina, to another two, to another five; he distributes it daily, and it never runs out.

But we have heard lending at interest condemned in the law, where Moses says: "You shall not lend at interest." Lending is of two kinds, one of money, the other of grace. Distinguish the two, for it is written: "If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still." So you too divide rightly, so that you do not sin. Let Moses himself, who warned that one must divide rightly, teach you to divide, so that you may follow what Abel was, who divided rightly, and shun what Cain was; he who did not know how to divide rightly was a murderer of his own kin. So the Holy Spirit divides

the divisions, he who works all things, dividing to each as he wills. He divides as he wills; you, as you can, as far as your understanding allows. Distinguish when the law speaks of money and when of grace. For it said to you: "You shall lend to the nations, of which [?] the Lord demands interest, but you shall not borrow." There is a money of lending, and there is also a grace of which the Lord demands interest; the money of lending brings bronze, grace confers faith. Lend faith, then, to the nations, so that grace may abound for you;

but do not borrow as one in need; rather lend as one who is rich and wealthy. Peter lent, Paul lent, John the Evangelist lent, or rather both Johns, and they were not in need; that is, they lent the money of Christ; they did not lend money at interest. Lend, then, and do not stop lending. Do you hear what Scripture says: "All day long he is merciful and lends"? The righteous man lends by day, the greedy man by night; for grace belongs to the light, but greed is the usury of darkness. And therefore the seed of the one who lends faith will be blessed, since it surely has the reward of blessing.

Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell for ever and ever. For the Lord loves judgment and will not forsake his saints; they will be preserved for ever. But the unjust will be punished, and the seed of the ungodly will perish. The just will possess the land as an inheritance and will dwell upon it for ever and ever. In these verses the prophet shows that we belong to the Lord. He is the judge of our thoughts and deeds and watches the merits of each person. He does nothing without judgment, but by judgment he distinguishes evil acts from good ones.

We must therefore turn away from evil and do good. So that you do not confuse good and evil, the first thing is to be free of crime, and the next is to bear the fruit of innocence, by which you may endure for ever. Do not think that your sins escape God's notice; that is how many people fall. He sees all things, condemns them, and wipes out the seed of the ungodly. This is not the seed of bodily generation, of course, but the succession of the inner mind and of ungodliness.

For Job, certainly, is marked out by the testimony of Scripture as born of the seed of Esau. How then did the seed of Esau perish in Job, when he was so great a man that he foresaw the Lord who was to come to earth and subdue the devil, the sea monster of this world? So what is sought is that wickedness should not be passed on to descendants.

Christ accomplishes this through the sacrament of baptism. Each person puts off what he was by birth and puts on what he is by rebirth, and becomes heir not of a family but of grace, so that he may gain for himself a lasting home in the eternal dwelling. And whoever has merited to dwell there for ever and ever will himself honor God for ever and ever.

Having trained the just man in moral disciplines, so as to teach you what one ought to be toward God [?] and what the form of perfect justice is, he wants the just man's mind to rise to wisdom and contemplation. He rouses his attention, so that he may gaze on heavenly things with an attentive heart, turn over the divine oracles within himself, and shape his

affections to what pleases God. He is to meditate on the law and let none of the Lord's commandments escape him, and he is to know the movements of the divine mystery. See, then, how from here on the holy prophet rises in his precepts: The mouth of the just will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment; the law of his God is in his heart. Nor will the Lord condemn him, it says, when he is judged. Wait for the Lord and keep his way, and he will exalt you, so that you may possess the land as an inheritance; you will see it when sinners perish. I saw the ungodly man exalted on high and lifted up beyond the cedars of Lebanon, and I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found.

The earlier verses concern morals; these concern understanding. What is the mouth of the just that will meditate wisdom, if not the mouth of the inner man? For there are two men in each person, one inner and the other outer. The inner man thinks and speaks what belongs to the mind; the outer, what belongs to the body. Yet the Lord at his coming joined both together and made the two into one man, so that they might not

fight each other with conflicting impulses, but be united with each other in a single will. Therefore the mouth of the just will meditate wisdom. For now even the outer man of the just has been brought over into the discipline of the inner man. Conformed to its nature, he performs its functions, so that the flesh meditates what belongs to the inner mind. But lest this seem incredible to you, listen to the one who says that the Lord Jesus has transfigured the body of our lowliness, so that it might be conformed to the body of his glory.

Who would dare to say that the flesh without sin had no share in the virtues of the inner man and could not pass over into its uses? That flesh was taken from the virgin and begotten when the Spirit of God came upon Mary, and in nothing did it depart from the disciplines of wisdom. It was beyond human power that the sick were healed by its touch, light was restored to the blind, and the dead rose again.

Fittingly, then, it is written: The mouth of the just will meditate wisdom, because the whole man is spiritual and certainly not earthly. For as was the earthly man, so are those who are earthly; and as is the heavenly man, so are those who are heavenly. So the earthly has passed away and the heavenly has remained. That is why the prophet, referring to the times of redemption, said 'will meditate', although one translator among several wrote 'meditates'. That reading is not foreign to the sense either, since to the spirit of the prophets future things are as present. Others think that 'mouth' stands for 'mind'.

Solomon explained this beautifully for us when he said: The discourse of the just is always wisdom, but the fool changes like the moon. That is, the fool often varies and does not hold to his opinion, and seems, as if in darkness, to shed light without holding on to it.

So let the meditation of wisdom always be in our heart and in our mouth. Let your tongue speak judgment, and let the law of your God be in your heart. That is why Scripture says to you: You shall speak of them when you sit in the house, when you walk on the road, when you lie down and when you rise up. Let us speak, then, of the Lord Jesus, for he is wisdom, he is the word, the Word of God. For this too is written: Open your mouth to the word of God. Whoever echoes his sayings and meditates on his words breathes him.

Let us always speak of him. When we speak of wisdom, it is he; when we speak of virtue, it is he; when we speak of justice, it is he; when we speak of peace, it is he; when we speak of truth and life and redemption, it is he. Open your mouth to the word of God, it is written. You open it, and he speaks. That is why David said: I will hear what the Lord speaks in me; and the Son of God himself says: Open your mouth, and I will fill it. But not everyone can grasp the perfection of wisdom as Solomon did, or as Daniel did;

yet the spirit of wisdom is poured into all according to their capacity, at least into all who are faithful. If you believe, you have the spirit of wisdom. That is why the wise man says: I believed, and therefore I spoke. Once you have believed, you will receive the grace of speaking. Whoever believes is redeemed. Whoever prays is redeemed too, if he devotes himself devoutly to prayer and perseveres in it: if he rises before the day, keeps watch often in the night and goes out to meet the morning sun, so that he is lit by Christ before the earth is lit by the rising sun. Whoever sings psalms is redeemed, and whoever is pierced with compunction is redeemed.

Therefore meditate always, and speak the things of God when you sit in the house. By the house we can understand the Church, or we can understand the inner house within us, so that we speak within ourselves. Judges sit in Jerusalem; thrones were set for judgment; the council of judges also sat, and the books were opened. The prophet says: Do all things with counsel. Judge your deeds with counsel; with

counsel drink wine; with counsel speak, so that you may escape sin and not fall into it through much speaking. When you sit, speak with yourself as one who judges. Speak on the road, so that you are never idle. You speak on the road if you speak in Christ, because Christ is the way. On the road speak to yourself, speak to Christ. Hear how you should speak to him: I want men, it says, to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger or dispute. Speak, O man, as you fall asleep, lest the sleep of death creep upon you.

Hear how you should speak as you fall asleep: I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob. Overcome nature by diligence; shut out the sleep of the body. We cannot shape our nature, but we can shape our diligence. David was a man, and he too allowed himself some sleep at night, but he shut sleep out by washing his bed every night and watering his couch with his tears.

So on his couch he always remembered his Lord and meditated on him, so that he might rise before the dawn and Christ might shine on him in the darkness, saying: Rise, you who sleep. This grace is not found in everyone, but diligence can be found in many. So do not wait for Christ to rouse you; rather, rouse Christ. Whoever thinks of him as he falls asleep rouses him. If you rouse him, he in turn will rouse you from sleep and raise you from death, saying to you: Arise from the dead.

So when you rise, or rise again, speak of him, so that you fulfil what you are commanded. Hear how Christ rouses you. Your soul says: The voice of my brother knocks at the door; and Christ says: Open to me, my sister, my bride. Hear how you rouse Christ. The soul says: I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you rouse and awaken love. Love is Christ. Hear also how you speak while you sleep: I sleep, and my heart is awake. That is the ordinary sense; now lift your mind a little higher.

Speak sitting in the house: in this earthly house of our dwelling, which is being dissolved, and in which we are exiles from the Lord. For while we are placed in this body and wish to be clothed over rather than stripped, we are exiled from Christ and groan heavily. As you sit in this house, then, confess your sins, because you sat and did not stand, and did not say:

Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem. Speak out instead, and do not hide your offenses. Speak sitting, so that you may hear the one who says: Rise, after you have sat, you who eat the bread of sorrow. Speak walking on the road, that is, as you run the course of this life. Speak here, so that you do not become mute there, as that man became mute who at first did not believe the angel of Christ, though later, when he had believed, he received his voice back.

Speak while sleeping and at rest, buried with Christ, so that you may rise with him in newness of life. Speak even when buried in the tomb, as the souls of the saints spoke when they sought vengeance on the one who caused their death: How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood? Speak finally when you rise, as he taught who said:

I slept and rested and rose again, because the Lord will uphold me. So there too the mouth of the just will meditate wisdom, until he himself reaches the loftier secret places of the tabernacle, full of heavenly and holy delight and gladness. Scripture has taught us this, as David says: These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me, for I shall go into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and praise, the sound of one feasting. So we shall speak while we sit in this bodily house, and when we have gone out from here and walk on the road, when we are caught up, if we merit it, to meet Christ, and while we sleep.

Now take the third anagoge, the ascent by which the soul of the just raises itself. For a certain spiritual sleep is to be understood here, of which Solomon says: If you sit, you will sit without fear; if you sleep, you will rest sweetly; and you will not fear the terror that comes upon you, nor the assaults of the ungodly coming upon you. You will rest sweetly and will not fear terror or the assaults of the ungodly coming upon you, if your tongue speaks the judgment of God and you always keep it before your eyes. Then you will leave no room for sin, and you will know that the price of wrongdoing will be paid in the requital of punishment.

He himself interpreted this in the ninetieth psalm, saying: You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, nor the thing that prowls in the darkness, nor the attack of the noonday demon. A thousand will fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you; yet with your eyes you will look on and see the requital of sinners.

For when the just man speaks the judgment of God, or speaks for himself what is just and full of true judgment, he does not speak in anger, nor out of the affliction of a grieving mind, nor out of pain, nor out of any passion. He speaks from truth and from equity, so that he is not swayed by feeling but weighs what he says on a true balance; for he judges what should be said and what should not be brought out. Like this is the saying: The lips of the wise are bound by understanding. This is because everything they say is seen to agree with true understanding, and by the prudence of their understanding they know what they ought to say and what they ought to keep silent. What should be kept silent they hold back with a kind of bolt

and fastening of the lips, while for what ought to be said the bonds of the lips are loosened. Rightly, then, he put first: The mouth of the just will meditate wisdom. For long meditation can have full judgment, which the just man will speak in due time, when he has seen face to face the things that are perfect. For now we cannot speak truly about things we do not comprehend. Indeed, not even Paul presumed to speak of them, though he was caught up into paradise and heard heavenly secrets. Not wishing to err in what he said, he declared: How unsearchable are the judgments of God, and how untraceable his ways! But now that he is released from the body, perhaps he comprehends the kinds of God's untraceable ways and his judgments, which are many, like the abyss.

The form of justice is described further and enlarged when Scripture says: The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not be tripped up. The law of God is in the heart of the just. What law? Not the written law, but the natural law; for the law is not laid down for the just but for the unjust. The law is in his heart, not superficially, as on the lips of the Jews; for it is with the heart that one believes unto justice. Whoever believes also speaks, but whoever speaks does not necessarily believe. Indeed, the people of whom it was said did not believe:

This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. If, then, the Gentiles, when they do what the law requires, are a law to themselves and know what they ought to follow or avoid, how much more does the faithful and just man, who lives according to the image and likeness of God, know how to discern what is seemly and honorable! He can steer by a kind of lawful rudder of natural wisdom, so that his steps are not tripped up like those of Esau, whom his brother supplanted because of his greed so that he fell, and whose steps he sent sprawling into death.

The more just a person is, the more the enemy lies in wait for him. That is why Scripture says: The sinner watches the just man and seeks to destroy him; but the Lord will not leave him in his hands, nor condemn him when he is judged. The sinner sees that the just man speaks wisdom with his mouth and meditates on it in his heart, that he speaks judgment with his tongue and keeps the law of the Lord in his heart. So he tries to bring the death of sin upon him, but the Lord protects him.

And so let us not fear the snares of the sinner, for God is for us. If God is for us, then, who is against us? Therefore God will not forsake his just one nor condemn him when he passes judgment on him; for he is a true judge, and so justice cannot be put at risk. Hence Aquila too rendered it: Nor will he condemn him in judging him; and Symmachus: Nor will he condemn him when the just man is judged.

But since the Seventy rendered it 'when he is judged', we think they were looking to the text: For the Lord himself will come into judgment. But into what judgment? Hear the one who says: Against you alone have I sinned and done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and may prevail when you are judged.

So the Lord offers himself to be heard and to have judgment passed on him, so that he may prevail all the more. Hear how he offers himself: My people, what have I done to you, or how have I grieved you, or how have I troubled you? Answer me. For I brought you out of Egypt and freed you from the house of slavery. And elsewhere: I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them. But you, remember, and let us go to judgment.
