This is a heavy judgment, when the Lord asks to be judged against man. For what could you answer the one who has bestowed everything on you and set you over all things? He made subject to you the Egyptians, to whom you had come as a stranger, and later drowned them in the sea as they pursued you. He destroyed and overthrew your enemies, he created and formed you, he redeemed you with his own blood, and do you hand yourself over to serve his enemy?

He forgave you all your sins, and do you commit graver ones? He calls you. When you come into judgment, what will you answer him? Unless he forgives you again, you are lost. And so holy David, seeing that by this kind of moral reckoning God's judgment would weigh more heavily on him, flees from judgment and begs for mercy, saying: Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no one living will be justified in your sight.

He confesses that he has been placed in darkness like one dead to the world. He said carefully 'like one dead to the world', not 'dead'. For those who die in Christ are not the dead of the world; the dead of the world are those who set the whole life they have lived in the world on destruction and death. And so, as if in despair, he flees to the remedy, saying: Hear me quickly, Lord, for my spirit has failed. For his spirit failed when such a judgment was set before him, a judgment in which truth would be examined rather than mercy bestowed.

Yet the Lord is so kind that, even though no one living is justified in his sight — for who, however just, is not liable to sin, or whose life is such that it could be judged worthy of the likeness of God? — surely one made in the image and likeness of God ought to be without sin, since he is in the image of God, who is without sin.

What punishment, then, does he deserve who has lost so great a grace of the Lord's workmanship and the likeness of divine beauty? But because God is merciful, even when he submits himself to judgment he does not judge the just man, but the unjust. He spares the just man as one who sins through the frailty of his condition; he punishes the unjust man as one who detests the ungrateful. Further, even if you have many works of justice, do not be impatient and arrogant. Do not think that you should demand the rewards of justice in this world, or complain that some adversities have befallen you undeservedly. For as long as you live, what you are owed is a contest, not a prize.

Wait, then, for the Lord, whether as helper or as rewarder, and keep his ways. This is what 'to wait' means: to keep the commandments of the one you think you should wait for. Even if you are crushed, even if you are afflicted, even if you are wasting away with sickness, still wait for the Lord; your hope will not put you to shame.

The Lord will come and will exalt you, so that you may possess the land as an inheritance. Clearly the land is a higher one: not this earthly land in the valley, but the land of the eternal promise, in which whoever is set is exalted by the Lord.

And you will see when sinners perish. For the just will be rewarded at the time when judgment is passed on what the ungodly deserve. But sinners do not perish in only one way. They perish for you beforehand if you do not admire their power or their riches, and if it does not move you to learn that they abound in honors, children and friends.

For these things belong to the world, and the world lies subject to worldly malice, and the prince of the world favors those who serve him, as in the saying: All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me. Why do you seek to have these things given to you, when the ungodly one who gives them cannot himself remain long among them? He himself passes away too: how can the things he bestowed not pass away? Only keep a steadfast mind and hold to justice; let no one move you, and you will see that the ungodly man is nothing.

Then listen to the one who says: I saw the ungodly man exalted on high and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon, and I passed by, and behold, he was not. I saw him in this world, I saw him with the eyes of the body; I saw him boasting too and exalting himself with his words, thinking himself to be something when he is nothing. How does he exalt himself? I will set my throne above the clouds, he says, and I will be like the Most High.

He exalts himself so that you may see him like the cedars of Lebanon, exalted on high. They are tall, and they stand on a very high mountain, so they are rightly said to be exalted on high. The ungodly man also seems exalted on high, since he has set himself on that mountain of which it is written: If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mountain: Be lifted up and cast into the sea. 'That is, to this demon,' he says, 'by whom this boy had been seized and oppressed, whom you marvel to see healed. Therefore you have more love in Christ than power in the devil.' You see the cedar on

the highest mountain, exalted on high, but it is broken by the wind, burned by fire, worn away by age. So it is with the rich man in this world. He shines indeed like Lebanon with a certain splendor of worldly favor, he relies on the power of the world, he exults in wealth and riches. He seems to you to be something until you say: Passing by, I shall see. For as Moses passed beyond material things in spirit and mind and saw God, so you too, if you pass beyond this place and lift the step of your mind to the grace of God,

will see that he is nothing, though on this earth he seemed to himself most powerful. That is why God the Word says to your soul and to your mind: Come here from Lebanon, my bride, come here from Lebanon; you will pass over and pass through. If you pass beyond worldly things, you will pass through to paradise. Hear one passing over: Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom; and hear again one passing through: Amen, amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.

What does "and behold, he was not" mean? Certainly, in the beginning was the Word, and whoever sees the Word and shares in the Word surely also exists himself, because the Word of God always is, and the word that comes from him is not "Yes" and "No", but "Yes", and it abides in the one who follows God. But whoever does not know the Word does not exist, because he does not cling to the one who said: "I am who am." Whoever clings to him is one spirit with him; and where the Spirit is, there is life too. That is why Scripture tells you about God that he is the one "who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they were"; that is, he calls the Gentiles, who were not, as though they were his own people, who were. For our fathers, who were God's chosen, did exist.

And elsewhere it says: "The Lord knows those who are his"; he does not know those who are not. And Esther says: "Do not give the sceptre of your kingdom to those who are not." Rightly, then, the righteous man says: "And I passed by, and behold, he was not." That is: I saw him exalted on high in the world before I had considered that the world is nothing; but when I passed in mind beyond the world, I saw that the one who had before been exalted on high in this world no longer existed.

You too, if you are righteous, pass from the things that are present to those that are to come, and the present will pass away for you. "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." For the righteous man, then, all things pass away. The wicked man passes away: "He is like vanity, and his days pass like a shadow." And not only do present things pass away for the righteous man; even as soon as he has turned his attention to the things that are to come, these things are already passing away.

See how present things have passed away for the righteous man. Certainly in the time of the prophet David there was the synagogue, and the Church from the Gentiles did not yet exist; yet he speaks of future things as though they were present: "Bless our God, you Gentiles"; and before that he says: "God has gone up with a shout of joy." He passed beyond the times of unbelief that were to come, not in his lifetime but in his mind, and with the devout piety of faith he celebrated the Lord's resurrection, which was to come many ages later, saying: "Sing praise to our God, sing praise;

sing praise to our King, sing praise." He dances and rejoices as though he were himself present at the sacred mysteries of the marriage union of Christ and the Church. He also stated the reason for the celebration, saying: "The Lord has reigned over all the earth." So if we pass by, then the things that are to come also seem to us to have passed by; just as, if you sail past the land, you see it too pass by and, as it were, move away from you. Sailors often flee the land, especially in a storm; and yet, while they are sailing away from it, it is rather the land that seems to flee from the sailors.

So you too: if you flee this world, it too will flee from you; if you pass by this earth, it too passes you by. You are also sailing on this sea and tossed about in this world: flee the land, it has rocks, it has stones, as it is written: "Throw the stones out of the way." If you hurry across this airy deep toward the harbour of divine delight, you will see that all these things have passed you by. For what difference does it make whether they have passed away or whether you judge that they have passed you by?

There is also another wicked man who seems exalted and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon, yet if you pass by, he will not be, nor will you find his place. Look, I ask you, at a Jewish scribe who recites the sequence of the ancient Scriptures but does not follow it. You hear him repeat it with his lips, and you admire him as learned. You ask him what he understands by it; he answers according to the letter and runs through the history.

He seems to you exalted on high and lifted up, if you consider the letter. Pass over to the spiritual understanding, for the law is spiritual; you see that he is nothing, and then you say: "I saw the wicked man exalted on high, and I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found." I sought him where he ought to have been, where life is; I did not find him; he

was not there where life was, because he was dead, and so his place was not found either. For what place does a dead man have, one who did not exist and never had? The man who was in the letter never existed, for "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." So I sought him in order to find him; he did not offer himself to be found. That is: I wanted to convert him; he would not offer himself to me to be converted. I did what belonged to one who seeks; he shrank from what ought to have belonged to one who returns.

Indeed, the soul that wishes to be converted seeks the Word, and when it has found him it says: "I held him and will not let him go"; that is, the Son of God, the Word of God. But the unrighteous man, who would not be healed, I sought and did not find; so do not imitate him.

"Keep innocence and look upon equity." Whoever keeps innocence sees equity, since whoever is pure sees God, whose rod is straight and whose justice upright, so that he turns away from those who have turned aside to the pursuits of depravity. Good is the innocence that sees God. Others, in fact, have rendered it: "Keep perfection"; for the perfect man is the one who does not know malice and is ignorant of deceit.

Therefore, he says, "keep perfection, because there are remains for the peaceable man." A man's remains are what is said of the dead body, of what he has cast off. They are called remains because they appear to survive after a man's death; for what is kept for the resurrection survives. "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality."

So the remains a man has are rather the hope of resurrection, the faith of conversion and the grace of love, since the wicked do not rise to judgement, while the life of the righteous is known to God and is approved at the Lord's judgement. This passage fits beautifully with the saying: "A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace."

"But the unrighteous will perish together; the remains of the wicked will be destroyed." The remains of the righteous are virtues; the remains of the wicked are wickedness, unbelief and sin. These will be wiped out, so that they no longer exist.

"But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord": not from the world, not from an element; "heaven and earth will pass away." I do not entrust my salvation to heaven, because it too passes away, since it was said of the many heavens: "They will perish, but you remain." I entrust it to God alone, who remains, who can forgive sins, so that he may be my protector in the time of trouble, and help me, and deliver me, and rescue me from sinners at the time of his judgement, and save me, because I have hoped in him. In him alone have I hoped; for he does not want us to serve both him and another. Whoever serves him alone is set free, for to him belong praise, glory and everlastingness from the ages, now and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.
EXPOSITION OF PSALM 37

I wrote two books on penance some time ago, and I think I must write about it again. First, because it is useful to pray for the pardon of our sins even every day; and then because those two books contained an exhortation to penance and an account of the progress it brings if it is practised, whereas now I must set out how penance ought to be done, for doing it is of no use unless it is done as it should be. In this holy David has set before us a teaching to follow; he seems to me to have tasted sin precisely so that he might teach how sin can be blotted out. For where did medicine take its beginning, if not from a wound? While the first age of the human race teaches others what helped it, and shows others how

it healed its own wound, practice created the art and sickness the instruction. For this is the first and strongest school of medicine, shaped by experience, not by guesswork. And so the first physicians were called empirics, from experience, and the other schools derived from it and drew from it some of the sap of their own strength. And what is more powerful as an exhortation to penance than that the holy prophet David taught us to repent of our sins? For who would disdain to humble himself before God when a king has humbled himself, or who would hesitate to afflict his soul when so great a prophet afflicted his, paying the price of tears for the redemption of sin?

And although he has spread precepts for doing penance throughout the whole body of his writings (for which of his psalms is not a remedy for a sinful conscience, since in one place he has shown how he was driven to sin and in another how he was troubled, so as to demonstrate not only how wounds are to be healed but also how they are to be avoided, and to teach us by his own example? And who would believe that he himself stands firm where even a stronger man has fallen?), nevertheless in the thirty-seventh psalm he expressed a greater force of inner grief and mournful lament.

Indeed, at the very outset the title itself tells us that precepts of this kind are being set out, for this is what we read: "In remembrance," it says, "concerning the sabbath day: a psalm of David." For the remembrance of sins is the complete definition of penance: that each person should chastise his sins with the scourge, as it were, of his daily speech and condemn the shameful deeds he has committed. For so we are taught, as God says: "Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified"; and the apostle says: "With the mouth confession is made unto salvation."

But perhaps it may trouble someone that he did not say "the remembrance of sins" but "concerning the sabbath day", or, as another version has it, "of the sabbaths". What, then, is the sabbath, if not the rest of things to come and relief from things present, on which the law commands that human labours cease and burdens be laid down? And what burdens are heavier than our sins?

Let these be laid down on the sabbath days, that is, in this present time of our life. For every week is completed in seven days; this world was formed in six days; on the seventh day the Lord rested from his work, he who rests in our gentleness, as he himself said: "On whom shall I rest, if not on the humble and gentle?" So set yourself free every sabbath, lift off the weight of error, so that you may deserve to come safely to the rest of that sabbath to come; for if you carry heavy sins from here, you will have no rest there. Unburden your mind, then; cast off everything

by which your conscience is weighed down and oppressed, so that your flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath. This life is spent in labour, that one in rest. Let the end of this world find you lighter, so that you are not unable to flee because you are weighed down with sins. Flee beforehand, so as to get ahead of it. He flees the world who is not held fast by the world's enticements, who has freed himself from all its cares. Flee also the wrath to come, that is, the day of judgement. He flees it who does penance; for this is how John the Baptist defined it, saying: "Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? Bear, then, fruits worthy of repentance."

You heard it read today that John was baptizing at Aenon near Salim. Aenon means "eye of punishments", Salim "he himself ascending"; that is what the interpretation of the names gives. So whoever chooses to be baptized

foresees punishments, and therefore takes refuge in the sacrament of baptism, in order to lay down every sin and not begin to be liable to punishments. And perhaps the one who is baptized with the baptism of repentance foresees punishments, whereas the one who is baptized in Christ looks to grace. John's baptism, then, is the eye of punishments, Christ's baptism the eye of graces. Yet, though John baptized at Aenon, he baptized near the one ascending; for this is what that interpretation also contains, that Salim means "he himself ascending". Close,

then, to Christ was the one who announced his coming. For the Son of Man, who came down from heaven, is the same one who also went up into heaven, so as to fill all things. But since "as is the heavenly one, so also are those who are heavenly," he too goes up into heaven who lays aside earthly things and is buried together with Christ, so that with Christ he may rise from the death of sin to newness of life and to a share in the inheritance, and become, as it is written, an heir of God and a joint heir with Christ.

Doing penance, then, is the true medicine, and it was rightly preached when the physician came from heaven, one who would not inflame wounds but heal them. A good physician, who taught us how to seek remedies in this earth of our body, when there sprang up for us the flower of a healing herb, he who by sin condemned sin in the flesh.

So the flesh, which before had been the poison of sin because it was the enticement to sins, became an antidote. Hear how the flesh is an antidote: the Word of God became flesh, put his hand into the den of asps, drew out the poison, took away sin; that is, by sin he condemned sin in the flesh.

And so that this can be considered more fully, let us go over that very passage of the apostle. For it is written thus: "God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, also by sin condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." The Son of God, then, came in the likeness of sinful flesh. He who took on true flesh certainly did not come in the likeness of flesh, but in the likeness of the flesh of sin, that is, of sinful flesh;

for through the serpent's deceit, and infused with his poison, our flesh had become the flesh of sin. Once it had become liable to sin, it had become the flesh of death, because it was owed to death. Christ took on in his own flesh the likeness of this flesh, already guilty and already condemned, because, although he had taken on the natural substance of this flesh, he had nevertheless taken on none of its contagion, nor was he conceived in iniquities and born in sins,

he who was born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin. What, then, does "by sin he condemned sin in the flesh" mean? Is it said on account of the likeness of sinful flesh? Or because Christ took on our sins not by committing them but in their character, not as guilt but as a mystery of his mercy, and he who himself did no sin was made sin for us? Or is it rather that, even by means of this flesh of sin, that is, this flesh of ours that is liable and condemned, he condemned sin in the flesh by teaching

how we, while placed in the flesh, may walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit? For to walk according to the flesh is sin, since whoever conducts himself according to the wisdom of the flesh lives for luxury and pleasures and wantonness and the desires of the flesh; for the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, and so those who are in the flesh cannot please God. And so he condemns sin by sin who, lifting himself away from the vices of the flesh, lives according to the Spirit, wholly devoted to God and intent on the heavenly oracles; this is why Christ came, to do not his own will, that is, the will of the flesh, but the will of God. So if anyone follows him, so as to do what pleases God and to restrain the craving of his flesh, he is an imitator of Christ.

We have set out what we think; you who read, choose which to follow. There is no error where the attitude of devotion is simple and every understanding is faithful. Christ condemned sin by taking on the likeness of sinful flesh, so as to abolish the offences of our flesh. He condemned sin so as to crucify our sins in his own flesh, being himself made sin for us, so that we, who were the captives of death and the prey of the serpent, might become in him the righteousness of God.

This taking on of sins, then, is an act of devotion, not of guilt. Through this sin the eternal God, who did not spare his own Son and made him to be sin for us, set us free. Further, Christ condemned sin in the flesh by means of that very flesh of sin which, with a kind of judicial vigour and a censor's authority, hates the vices it used to love and shudders at the impurity it once thought pleasure.

It separates itself from wantonness, renounces desires, forswears crimes and shameful deeds, drives away greed, which makes effeminate what manliness the flesh has. Here you have that imitator of Christ, himself condemning sin in the flesh by sin: "So I run," he says, "not as at an uncertain goal; so I fight, not as one beating the air; but I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be disqualified."

We have not digressed needlessly, I think, since this too pertained to the healing of man. Providing for this healing, God, just as he commanded this earth to bring forth the wholesome juices of herbs and trees to cure the wounds of the flesh, so he also filled the course of the divine Scriptures with wholesome precepts by which the weakness of the soul might be healed.

So how grievous it is that dumb animals know how to treat themselves and seek out healing herbs for their wounds, and do not refuse to choose them, while human diligence does not seek them, even though a physician has been sent to human beings, to point out the seeds of healing medicine in the ancient Scriptures and to bring new ones himself! Let us take examples, then, from the earth itself, of how many things are wholesome that are carelessly judged harmful.

The serpent nourishes poison, has a harmful bite, wounds the flesh; but in its very poison you will find an antidote, if you look for it. In fact its flesh is burned, and from its ash theriac is made, which usually blunts the force of the poison so that it cannot do harm. So the fault does not lie with the earth that produces the serpent, but with the one who does not know how to beware of the serpent.

The serpent itself can benefit you, if you understand, or rather if you do not despise the physician's instructions. Learn to imitate the one you think you must flee: "Be wise as serpents," he says, "and simple as doves." Guard your head as the serpent does; even if you are torn in all the rest of your body, you will revive. Your head is Christ, for he is the head of man; if you have kept the faith, then even if you have died, like the serpent you too will rise again. Imitate the serpent, which sheds its outer self so that its inner self may be renewed; imitate the serpent, which vomits up its poison.

Blessed are you if you too vomit up your evil thoughts and lay aside the poisons of your malice. There is a well-known story, supported by the authority of writers, that a serpent approaching the water woos with its hissing the embraces of a female snake; that she, looking to her own safety, promises the union he seeks on condition that the serpent vomit up its poison; that he, captivated, obeys her commands, lays down his weapons and, in the manner proper to their mating, puts his head into her mouth; and that when their intercourse begins to grow hot, whether through some violence of nature or the heat of lust, the female clamps her jaws and presses down with bites amid the kisses of lust, and so the serpent's head is cut off.

Do you not recognize a mystery of the faith in the nature of the serpent? That serpent in paradise first provoked the woman to the adultery of sin. But when its poison had been poured out into this world, the offspring of that woman, avenging the deception of his mother and the serpent's fraud, stripped it of its weapons and cut off its head. But if the poisons have prevailed and sin, in which lies the sting of death, has crept in, follow the example of physicians, so that the serpent may die for you, even if late: crush its poison, grind up its body, and know that it must be tempered by mixing it with healing juices, so that it not only loses its strength and venom but also becomes a remedy made out of poison.

That spiritual serpent dies for you if you die to sin and your sins die to you. Its poison is crushed in this way, if your deeds sting you with remorse; all its power is abolished in this way, if you cover the crime you committed with good works and temper it with faithful confession. Hear how the power of the dragon himself is crushed: "May God crush Satan," he says, "under your feet." First crush your heart, where the dragon's lair was, so that he finds nowhere to dwell. Crush the dragon's flesh; his flesh is our sins.

That is why God says to you: "The nations feast on him"; and further on he says: "runs ahead to die [?]. The flesh of his body cleaves to him." For just as the saints are the body and members of Christ, so sinners, who do not abandon sin but cling to it, are the body and members of the dragon. Therefore we feast on the body of Christ, but they feast on the body of the dragon. We who strive to cling to Christ feast on the daily remission and pardon of sins; but they, who join sins to sins every day, feast on an unbroken succession of shameful deeds and crimes.

Crush this flesh, then, and sprinkle over it the contrition of your heart; then pour the water of the Jordan over all of it. For the Jordan means going down and going up, since whoever goes down into the sacred font also goes up, so as to seek the things that are above; for whoever is baptized into Christ goes down into Christ's death and goes up into his resurrection.

But if you have already been baptized and have gone astray, pour out the water of tears, not false but true, so that you may cry from the depths to the Lord your God, and it may be said of [?] you: "A voice was heard in Ramah [?], weeping and great lamentation: Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted, because they are not."

Rachel is the Church, in which the people of God is blessed. Let her weep for you, let her lament your sins and weep greatly, so that she does not easily accept consolation, as those do who grieve greatly. She would not be comforted because you who once were have ceased to be; but by this perseverance in grief and weeping let her earn the right to say: "My son was dead and has come back to life; he was lost and has been found."

Or perhaps Rachel would not be comforted over the children of the Jews because they are not, though she had certainly borne them so that they might be. And so she did not accept consolation when the little children were killed by Herod, because they did not believe in the coming of Jesus either, filling up the measure of their wickedness by killing even little children, so that among them the Son of the Virgin too might be put to death. So the Church of the Lord would not be comforted over the Jews, because they are not; but over the Christians, who have been gathered from the nations, she feasts and rejoices, because those who were not have begun to be.

So you have put in the water of the Jordan, the water of grace; drink this first. You have put in the water of tears, the water of repentance; this is the second cup, so that you may restore the first. Drink water from your [?], drink water from your weeping, so that you may say: "And I mingled my drink with weeping." Your weeping, then, is your drink, and your tears are your food.

"My tears," he says, "have been my bread." If tears are bread, then out of the sin of iniquity you have the food of conversion, as you read in the Gospel: "the one who is forgiven more loves more." This is why we often see that some who were careless Christians before, after committing some

sin, become more careful, and through repentance commonly emerge from it perfect. So just as conversion comes out of sin, the remedy comes out of the poison. Hear this remedy: "The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech." Sin is poison, iniquity is poison; confessing one's own crime is the remedy for the fall. And so the remedy truly comes out of the poison if you declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified.
But now let us take up the psalm, so that it may itself teach us how repentance is to be done. It begins like this:

"Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your wrath." Whoever does penance must be ready to bear reproaches and to undergo insults, and must not be upset if someone throws the crime of his sin in his face. For since he ought to accuse himself, how can he not bear another rebuking him? And if he should not fear being rebuked by a man, how much less by the Lord his God, against whom we all sin even in what is hidden, especially since condemnation in the present is absolution for the future? But those who are not condemned in this world "will not be scourged with other men."

Woe to me if it is said of me: "He has his reward"! If a good deed is condemned by this sentence, how much more heavily is a crime burdened! For if an act of mercy that is boasted of in easy words is cheated of eternal fruit, how much more is the punishment of iniquity put off only to grow by the addition of bitter interest! So whoever does penance ought to offer himself to punishment, so that he may be punished here by the Lord and not be reserved for eternal torments; and he ought not to wait for the time, but go out to meet God's indignation.

See how David's deeds agree with his prayers. He had offended the Lord by ordering the people to be counted. He forestalled God's messenger by confession, declaring that he had sinned greatly and acted very foolishly, not as if reminding One who had forgotten, but as if pressing One who delayed, so that he would not put off any longer the anger his offense deserved. "I have sinned," he says, "greatly, in doing this thing; and now, Lord, take away the iniquity of your servant." Hear how sins are blotted out, as Scripture says: "His sin has been paid off [?],

for he has received from the hand of the Lord double for his sins." So he does not ask that his sin be wholly remitted, but that it be blotted out by a moderate payment, that is, that its memory may be blotted out for the future. And so the Lord, appealed to as if by the voice of one pleading with him not to postpone the punishment of the error committed, sent the prophet Nathan to him; and he came to the king and said to him: "Choose what you want done: three years of famine upon the land, or that you flee for three months before your enemies while they pursue you, or that there be death in the land for three days.

And now know and see what answer I am to give to him who sent me." See how God teaches by what moderation his indignation may be softened: if we do not refuse the lashes altogether, but ask for a lighter kind of punishment rather than an escape from it. He set out three things, so that David might choose the one he thought more moderate. See too how he calls us to penance, so that we may offer ourselves to suffering: he commands him to choose, so that even in the punishment some privilege of choice may be kept, and by this word he treats his defendant gently. And David said to Nathan: "I am in distress over these three; but let me rather fall into the hands of the Lord, for

his mercy is great, than into the hands of men." Did he ask to be let off the punishment for his error? Had he done so, he would have been branded as shameless, ungrateful for God's moderation. A modest confession helps the accused most, and a punishment we cannot escape by a defense we lighten by our shame. He chose not what was free from the lash, but what he judged more moderate, so as to entrust himself to the gentleness of God, who knows how to forgive, rather than to the power of men, who frequently go beyond the measure of revenge. The One who cannot err shows mercy; the one who shares in error does not.

Nor did holy David's faith deceive him; even in the very offense he earned the grace of divine compassion. For he who had proposed to inflict death on the land for three days did not let even one day pass, but at the hour of the midday meal he gladly pardoned, and, to use the words of Scripture, "he repented of the evil." See how Scripture urges you not to shrink from repentance either, if you follow God, as you ought to follow him.

He did well to add "of the evil," since all punishment seems harsh. That is why the day of judgment too is called an evil day, and blessed is the one who is delivered from it by God, as it is written: "The Lord will deliver him in the evil day." "And the Lord," it says, "told the angel to spare." But see that when the Lord wishes to forgive, he gives the grace and the confidence to plead. And David saw the angel striking and said: "Here I am. I have sinned, and I, the shepherd, have done wrong; and these in the flock, what have they done? Let your hand be upon me and upon my father's house."

If the Lord had commanded the angel to spare, how was the angel still striking, unless it was because the Lord, though he wishes to forgive, wishes to be asked, and works so that he may be asked? Nor would the man have seen the angel striking unless the Lord had revealed the angel to his eyes. So Elisha also says: "Lord, open now the eyes of this boy, that he may see"; and the boy's eyes were opened, and he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots around the prophet. Do not be troubled that a little servant is a lowlier person than a prophet or a king, for the sight of horses and chariots is also lowlier than the holiness of angels.

Perhaps to some who read carelessly it may seem harsh that David, humble of heart and meek as he was, who spared his enemies, chose the death of the people rather than his own flight or famine on the land. He avoided famine for the people because it is held to be worse than death and all punishments, and it is followed by pestilence as well, which pollutes the air and heaps up the dead. He did not ask for his own flight

because the prophet could intercede for the people, as in fact happened, but the people could not intercede for the prophet. For it is written: "If the people sin, the priest will pray for them. If the priest sins, who will pray for him?" And yet, when he saw the people being slain, he offered himself to the striking angel, so that he himself might be struck instead of the people. It is a greater thing that, not terrified even by the sight of the dead, he offered himself to the sword, than if he had asked to be released from the condition laid down. So in his choice he followed reason, and in his grief, devotion.

But see the Lord's grace: he too departed from the condition he had laid down. Is it any charge against mercy that he threatens more and exacts less? He who keeps his promises in bestowing rewards draws back from what he prescribed in exacting punishments. When he is angry, he puts off the guilty; when he has mercy, he hastens to absolve. He frightens in order to correct, warns in order to amend, and comes first in order to forgive.

So elsewhere too the prophet says of the Lord: "In the hand of the Lord is a cup full of unmixed wine, well mixed; yet its dregs have not been emptied." The cup is full to frighten, but not emptied to strike. The cup was full when

death was ordered for three days, but the mercy of God intervened and held back the angel's hand before he emptied that cup. And that you may know that the cup is punishment or the sword, hear him saying: "Take this cup of unmixed wine from my hand, and you shall make all the nations to whom I send you drink it, and they shall vomit and go mad before the sword." And to Jerusalem it is said: "You have drunk the cup of wrath from the hand of the Lord; for you have drunk the cup of ruin and emptied it, and there was no one to comfort you." Jerusalem drank the full measure, because she sinned beyond measure.

The Church of the Christians has not known how to empty the cup of wrath, but she has emptied ointment, for whose sake Christ emptied himself, so that it might be fragrant everywhere. She received this gift from the hand of the Lord, but she does not know the cup of death. I read of two cups, one of death, the other of life. Christ emptied the cup of death in his own blood and served a new cup, so that we may say: "I will take the cup of salvation," the cup of the new covenant, which is poured out for the forgiveness of sins. This cup is poured out and no dregs are found in it, because it cleanses every offense.

We have said how the Lord bends his anger in punishing; let us say how in rewarding he anticipates our prayer, and let us show it by an example. Hear one of the two thieves saying to the Lord: "Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom." The Lord answered: "Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." He was still asking to be remembered when the Lord came into his kingdom, and the Lord was already granting him the heavenly kingdom. How swift is mercy! The petitioner's prayer is slower than the Rewarder's gift.

That is why David held to moderation and did not pray for remission, saying: "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your wrath." "Wrath" in Greek is called thymos, the onrush of anger. So this is what the Latin translator wanted to express: "Do not rebuke or chasten me either in anger or in the very onrush of anger." Chastening, moreover, is instruction; in Greek it is called paideia [?], of which it is said: "Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord."

For God is not open to passion so as to be angry, since he is impassible; but because he punishes, he seems to be angry. It seems so to us because we ourselves are accustomed to punish with agitation. Yet even among men there are often found those who, when they punish, are not agitated, but carry out punishment and inflict torments with the greatest patience. Why then should you wonder at this in God, when you sometimes recognize it in a man?

We said above, about the day of wrath, that wrath means punishment. Indeed it is common usage to say of someone who has been punished that he has fallen into the wrath of the laws, not because the laws have wrath, but because he has fallen into their severity. So too elsewhere it says of the ten plagues of the Egyptians: "He sent his wrath upon them by evil angels," that is, punishment; for the law does not know how to be angry, though the minister of the laws does. Therefore the author of the laws does not know how to be angry either, for his will is to frighten, not to punish. So, emperors, imitate the divine example: be more severe in framing laws and merciful in exacting punishments.

Let the severity of the laws restrain insolent boldness, and let the mercy of rulers rescue the guilty from punishment. The prophet, then, recognizes his fault, sees his wounds, and asks to be healed. Whoever wants to be healed does not dread being rebuked, but he wants to be rebuked not in wrath but by the word of God. The word of God is health; for so we read: "He sent his word and healed them." He wants to be instructed not in anger but in teaching, as if you were to ask a physician not to cut your wound but to apply a medicine. The medicine presses hard but does not cut; there is pain, but not beyond the measure of pain; it stings but does not draw blood.

And he added: "For your arrows are fixed in me." He seems to say the same thing as holy Job, but they are different. For Job too says: "For the arrows of the Lord are in my body, and their fury drinks my blood; when I begin to speak, they pierce me." Job complains of the wound of his body; David laments the wounds of his soul. And perhaps David is doing penance for sin, while Job pleads the cause of human weakness and, as a champion of our frailty, asks for the Creator's help as a remedy for his handiwork.

So the one prays, the other pleads a case, and therefore David's pain is sharper, because the wounds of the soul are heavier than those of the flesh. Job says the arrows of the Lord are in his body; David laments that they are fixed in him. Job's blood is drunk, David's is shed; Job is pierced, David is wounded; the hand of God touched Job, but upon David it was made firm with heavy weight; David weeps that his soul is filled with mockeries, Job that his body is filled with sores. By the hand of God we understand his power to punish.

This hand scourged the king of the Egyptians for the wrong done to Abraham in the assault on Sarah's chastity; this hand plunged the chariots and horses and peoples of the Egyptians into the depths of the Red Sea; this hand weighed down the mind of King Saul, so that he hated the kindness of the one who had saved him, and, for his transgression of the heavenly command, deserted by his companions, bereft of his sons who were slain, defeated by the enemy—and no spectacle is more shameful for a king—he turned his own sword against himself, so as not to live on as an old captive, outliving both his sons and his kingdom.

David experienced this hand in himself, and he lamented in his children the incest of one and the fratricide of the other; and, what is heavier for a devoted father than threats to his own life, he wept at once for the disgrace of his offspring and for the ruin of family love. One of them was

inflamed to incest out of affection for his sister, the other was armed for fratricide out of zeal for chastity. How the borderlands of the virtues deceived them into the gravest crimes! If only the one had not loved his sister, or the other had not avenged her! In the end David himself, driven from his country's borders by his son, fled from the enemy he wished to have as his heir; he was afraid to win, lest he be defeated by the loss of his fatherly love.

But perhaps someone may ask how the hand of God could have been in fratricide or incest, since that is the work of the enemy. Let us learn, then, that even where the devil wounds, it may be said that the arrows of the Lord wound. For we read that when the Lord, in the council of the angels, turned to the devil and praised his servant holy Job, so that the envious one, the adversary of the human race, would burn—for the praise of a man of lower nature is the condemnation of one who was cast down from a higher state—

the devil answered that Job did not worship the Lord for nothing, since by God's will he abounded in everything. "But stretch out your hand," he said, "and touch all that he has; let us see whether he will not bless you to your face." And God gave the devil power to lay his hand on all that Job had. When this had been done and holy Job remained steadfast in his strength, since Job was not shaken either by the death of his children or by the loss of his property, the Lord again spoke to the devil, mocking him because he had destroyed all that Job had and killed his

children, and yet had been unable in any way to move Job himself from his steadfast virtue. And the devil answered: "Whatever a man has he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand," he said, "and touch his flesh and his bones." And again he received power to lay his hand on Job's body, but on condition that he preserve his life; and when he had gone out from the Lord, he covered holy Job with sores. We notice, then, that it is called the hand of the Lord when a man is tempted by the devil's attack, since Job too said that it was the hand of the Lord that had touched him, and he spoke of the arrows of robbers as the arrows of the Lord: "And he has handed me over," he says, "into the hands of the unjust."

So he himself has resolved the question: when the devil wounds, the arrows are the Lord's, because he granted the devil the power to wound. After all, if you order your servant to be beaten, is he not said to have been beaten by you, even if someone else standing by does the striking? There is also this reason: the Lord gives the tempter power so that the dispositions of men may be tested in temptations. Persecution happens so that faith may shine, virtue may stand out, and the inner mind may be made plain to all.

So temptation, like an arrow, penetrates a man's inner parts, like the sword of God that searches what is within. And the sword is the word of God, powerful and sharper than the sharpest sword. Hear what is said to Mary about this sword: "And a sword will pierce your own soul too, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed."

For all things are revealed by the word of God, in whose sight all things are naked and open. The soul itself is divided, the inmost marrow and the thoughts are laid bare, and finally, as Scripture says, there is no creature that can hide itself from his knowledge. So let us sell everything in order to buy the Word, and let us store him up within our hearts.

Lastly, the devil himself testifies that a man gives all he has for his life, and admits that the price of a whole fortune is not worthy of the redemption of a single soul. Why do we spare our fortune, when even the devil judges it cheap in exchange for salvation? I have said too little with "for salvation": he testifies that it is little even as the price of error.

For he says: "All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me"; and he showed not only the riches of the world but also its honors and kingdoms. If it costs so much for the devil to be worshiped, how much ought a Christian to offer in order to be raised with Christ? But let us send the devil away like the scapegoat into the wilderness; for he is no faithful witness to the truth, even if at times he disguises himself as an angel of light.

The testimonies of the divine Scriptures abound for us, teaching us that there is nothing more precious in man than faith, and that no fortune is so great that it can be compared with the price of our salvation and our soul. By faith Abraham left his homeland and his land and even the kinsfolk he could see, and followed the One he could not see as though he beheld him;

Moses too valued the price of his soul above all the riches of Egypt. But why speak of exalted men? Rahab the harlot, a foreigner from the world outside, nevertheless thought her soul must be redeemed not only by despising everything she had but even at the risk of her life: she refused to give up the spies of Joshua son of Nun to her fellow citizens when they searched for them, and she chose to hide rather than betray those who were enemies of her country, yet envoys of faith.

She was not frightened by the threats of her fellow citizens, the dangers of war, the burning of her city, or the perils of her own family. Learn, man, learn, Christian, how you ought to follow the true Jesus, when a woman despised all that was hers and followed Jesus in a figure, because of the likeness of the name. So Solomon put it admirably: "A man's riches are the ransom of his soul." Ransom your soul, then. Money is cheap, but it becomes precious through faith; it is cheap when hoarded, precious when scattered. For so it is written: "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever."

If, then, you are such that you can despise not only all that is yours but even your very flesh for the sake of righteousness, than which no possession can be richer—for a pure man is a precious possession—then even if rivers close over your head, you pass through; even if the Lord gives power to tempt you, he still commands the devil himself to guard your soul, according to what is written: "That you may destroy the enemy and the defender"; for he tempts as an adversary and defends as a servant.

For it is written: "And the unicorn will be willing to serve you." He serves who does not carry out what he wishes by his own will, but obeys imperial commands against his will out of necessity. See the depth of Christ, who turned back upon the devil the price of his own malice. The devil compels us to do what we hate; for, as the Apostle said, "I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate." The Lord turned this back upon him, so that he too often does not do what he wants, but does what he hates: he guards the very soul he wants to overcome.

We condemn the corruption of the flesh and yet follow it, like that widow who broke the pledge she had made to her husband and afterwards wishes to marry, which she shunned before. The devil is an enemy to the saints, and he is made to serve as their defender so that he may be punished the more, in that he who longs to do harm dares not do it. And how much more bearable it is to love the virtues even if you cannot fulfil them, than to hate the virtues and be unable to harm them!

"There is no health in my flesh," he says, "because of the face of your anger." Isaiah has explained this passage for us: "You were angry, and we sinned." Yet what is the face of the Lord's anger? Is it perhaps this: "The eyes of the Lord are upon those who do evil"? For if the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, how is the prophet weakened by the face of God's anger? Consider also what David himself said in a later psalm: "For you have rescued me from all my troubles, and your eye has looked upon my enemies."

For just as he looks upon the good deeds of the righteous, so he also detects the hidden deeds of sinners. Unless perhaps you refer this to Christ, who was rescued from all who were crushing him when he stripped himself free of the Jewish people, who crushed him with their frequent sacrileges and daily impieties, and called his enemies to grace, whom the eye of God saw and loved. So, because God is merciful, there is no reason at all to despair: though he is angry, he forgives; though he strikes, he heals; though he hands the flesh over to destruction, he saves the spirit. So do not fear the weakness of the flesh, for when a holy man is weak, he is stronger.

But what does he mean when he says: There is no peace in my bones because of my sins? What are these bones? Are they the soul's or the body's? But the saint would not be so concerned with bodily pain when the soul too is struggling, since it is the mark of a saint to be willing to have the flesh scourged for the soul's sake, as Paul too scourged himself, so that his preaching would not be rejected. The inner man has certain bones, just as he has his other members, the eyes and the nostrils of the mind, as Job said: The divine spirit which is in my nostrils.

So there are also bones, which form a kind of framework of love. That is why Adam said of the partner of his love and fellow heir of the grace of life: This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. The apostle interpreted this when he said: This is a great mystery, but I speak of Christ and the church. Who would doubt that the mystery of Christ and the church is spiritual and not carnal? Even within marriage every good man is bound by the beauty of virtue, not of the flesh, and loves his wife for her character, not for her use. Then listen, for he speaks not of the flesh but of inner virtue: My bone, which you made in secret, is not hidden. It is virtue, then, not flesh, that knows the hidden things of God the Father.

So the soul's virtues have no peace when our sins rush together before our eyes and flood our minds. The chosen teacher of the Gentiles explained this well in the second letter to the Corinthians, saying: For even when we had come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were afflicted in every way: fighting without, fears within.

The sins of the Macedonians troubled him; how much more does each of us find our own sins disturbing, so that we can have no rest! Our own guilt is a heavier adversary to us. It harasses the idle, afflicts the healthy, saddens the joyful, unsettles the calm, stirs up the gentle, wakes the sleeping. We are defendants with no one accusing us, we are tortured with no one torturing us, we are bound without chains, we are slaves though no one has sold us.

That is why Scripture also says: You were sold by your sins. These, then, are the sins that are always against us, as the prophet said: They have sold us and they rule over us. A slave who is sold leaves his former servitude to pass to another master; we do not lay down the yoke of the former sins, and we are bent beneath new ones as well.

That is why the saint groaned, saying: For my iniquities have risen above my head; like a heavy burden they weigh heavily upon me. That is, my iniquities have passed over my head and tower above me, so as to weigh down my senses; for the eyes of the wise man are in his head. And so Nabal was wicked and hard, because malice and iniquity had locked up his senses. That is why he could not bear even Abigail's word. His heart hardened, and he collapsed as if he were sick.

Or consider whether this may be the head of which the apostle speaks, which a man puffed up by the mind of the flesh does not hold fast. This head is Christ, for the head of every man is Christ. This is the head which, through the joints and ligaments of the whole people, grows with the growth that is from God, because Christ rises up in all of us through each of his members. So when our sins weigh heavily on us, and a kind of leaden talent of iniquity presses us down toward earthly things, let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke from us, so that we may lift up the eyes of our mind and hear him saying:

Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Indeed, avarice burdened Egypt, and money harassed the merchandise of the Ethiopians, as it is written: Egypt has labored, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabaeans, men of stature, shall pass over to you. Egypt labored before it knew the truth, but it labors no longer now that it has passed over to Christ. The Sabaean men who once fled now follow willingly, because the bonds of love hold them, and these are stronger than adamant. That word of Isaiah also fits this passage beautifully: Every head is in pain and every heart in sorrow. From

the feet to the head there is no wound or scar or inflamed sore. For iniquity grows inflamed when it lords it over our head, exalting itself and seizing that place so that Christ, the teacher of repentance, cannot hold it. These iniquities have no small power, if you consider that man of iniquity who is to come by the working of Satan, with all power and signs and lying wonders and every seduction of iniquity. The apostle showed that we must beware of him, because he will receive the working of error, so that the faithful may be proved and the unfaithful judged.

Rightly, then, does he say that, placed as he was beneath iniquities, and his own iniquities at that, which is worse, his scars had grown foul and rotten because of his folly. The remedy came only slowly to one who was still lifting up burdens of iniquity. Yet health was restored to holy Job, who scraped the pus from his sores when he was covered with sores from his feet to his head. And Lazarus the poor man, who lay at the rich man's gate while dogs licked his sores, was carried away by angels from the stench of his scars and placed in Abraham's bosom. So holy David has hope and a remedy for his health, because to him the wounds of his sins do not smell of ointment but give off a stench, and because he is afflicted and bowed down by them and takes no delight in them.

Now look at some wanton youth, notoriously lustful, who spends his life in debauchery, like that rich man who reclined in fine linen and purple and feasted splendidly every day. His floors swim with wine, his ground is strewn with flowers and fish bones, and his dining rooms are filled with the scents of various burning incenses. See how he thinks himself happy and judges that he smells sweet! Yet he bears grave and long-standing wounds in his soul and oozes corrupted blood, and still he notices no stench from his scar. His nostrils are blocked with filth, and he cannot say: The divine spirit which is in my nostrils. That is why the rich man could not find the remedy of salvation, while the poor man found it; and in the end one is in torment in the underworld, the other at rest.

So the holy prophet David also found the remedy of everlasting salvation. He confessed that the wounds of his soul stank to him, and he said that his own scars had rotted because of his folly. But there is also a folly that brings salvation to believers through the foolishness of preaching. So the prophet, already moved by the spirit of the gospel, shuns

the wisdom of this world, by which God is not known, which covers its wounds and does not reveal them to the Lord. Better, then, the folly that has eyes to see its own sores than the wisdom that has none. And so, admonished by the spiritual gaze of his folly, this great king declares himself afflicted with miseries, so that he may find the remedy of repentance, which Judas, who acquired a field with the reward of iniquity, could not find.

I am [?] with miseries, he says, and bowed down to the end; all day long I went about in sorrow. To what end does he say he is bowed down? Is it to the proper end of penance, or further? If we take it in a mystical sense, it is as far as Christ, who is the end of the law, who allowed himself to be stoned and allowed his dead body to be wounded.

But those wounds gave off no stench of penance; they gave off the fragrance of grace. Indeed, from his wound came no decay of death, as with other men; a fountain of eternal life welled up, as Scripture teaches us, saying: And water shall leap up with delight from the fountains of salvation. So water leapt from the wound so that we might drink salvation; all the sinners of the earth shall drink, so that they may lay down their sins. Look at each point. Christ was afflicted with miseries so that he might make blessed those men who had been placed in miseries. Let no one call the just man wretched, for he himself said: No one shall make you wretched. He was bowed down so that we might be raised up; he was saddened so that he might gladden us, as it is written: For if I sadden you, who is there to gladden me but the one who is saddened by me?

So whoever is saddened by the Lord Jesus Christ gladdens Christ, and is gladdened by Christ in turn. Therefore we too recognize that we must make satisfaction, and not perfunctorily. Let us be bowed down to the end, that is, let us bring Christ not only our faith but also our perseverance in suffering, and let us rejoice in our sufferings, as Christ too rejoiced in his. He took them upon himself for his poor servants; let us undergo them for our Lord.

This, then, is the end: That I may fill up, he says, what is lacking of the tribulations of Christ in my flesh for his body, which is the church, of which I have been made a minister. We see what we must take upon ourselves, we who take up the priestly ministry: we ought to endure the sufferings of the body bravely, not only for ourselves but also for the Lord's church. But David added the sufferings of the soul as well.

Indeed, he says himself: For my soul is filled with mockeries, and there is no health in my flesh. I am bowed down and humbled exceedingly; I roared from the groaning of my heart. And all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you. My heart is troubled, and my strength has left me, and the light of my eyes is not with me. We observe, then, that the soul's toil is greater than the flesh's.

Understand, then, what mockeries fill the soul: in temptations the devil seems to mock it and taunt it as it struggles hard. Symmachus, however, says 'loins', where the seeds of human generation lie. That is why the wisdom of God bids you keep your loins girded, so that your chastity may not be loosened. And so that you may know that the loins hold the stirrings of lust, which are often aroused by the devil when he strives to scatter the members of Christ and make them

the members of a harlot, Scripture says: Behold, his strength is in his loins and his power in his womb. A man's seeds are in his loins, and a woman's in her womb. So the devil makes sport with these, to bring about adultery, incest and fornication. And so whoever commits fornication sins against his own body, not outside the body. First, the flesh is weakened as it melts away in lusts and does not keep the restraints of chastity. Second, the seeds, which

should serve to beget offspring, produce defilement of the body rather than the fruit of posterity. These, then, are called mockeries, perhaps because in them the heat of the body often mocks a man without the act of intercourse. That is why the Seventy rightly said 'mockeries of the soul', because the devil mocks a person's affections and strives to pour out his strength in vain, to empty his virtue and loosen his fortitude.

And so elsewhere he says: And my reins are loosened. In this the blessed apostle also strengthens us: we should fear neither the mockeries of the soul nor the weakness of the flesh, because Christ is the strength of both our soul and our body. As a physician he heals the sick; as the strength of all he strengthens the weak. Indeed, though our outer man is wasting away, yet the inner man is renewed day by day.

So holy David, wearied by these mockeries of the soul, had bowed himself down and humbled himself exceedingly. This was not because he gave way to iniquities that set themselves above his head, as we said, or yielded to the enemy. In later passages he teaches that one must not yield to him, saying: How much evil the enemy has done in your holy places! And those who hated you have boasted in the midst of your feast. They set up their signs as signs, and I did not know them, as on the way above the summit. As in a forest of trees they cut down its doors with axes.

He means: When my enemies set the signs of their iniquity above the summit, I did not know them. And what is the summit but your head, where the senses are, where Christ is wisdom? 'I did not know' means I did not acquiesce, I did not consent to them or add the assent of my own thought. That is why he says elsewhere too: I did not know the wicked word, and I did not know the malicious who turned aside from me. Indeed, though Christ knows all things, he did not know sin; for he knows what is his own, that is, what belongs to the virtues, not what belongs to vices.

And so Scripture tells you: The Lord knows those who are his. But to the wicked he says: Depart from me, for I do not know you. And he spoke through Jeremiah, saying: I was led like a lamb to be sacrificed, and I did not know. How did he not know what he had foretold would happen? But he means: I did not know their thoughts, their malice; I do not want to know things of blood. Indeed, I will not gather their assemblies of blood.

I blot out their iniquities and do not remember them; I do not want to know what I came to forgive. I did not know the wood that is to burn, nor what is laid on the woodpile, whether straw or hay, so that the flame may consume them all the faster as its fuel. I want to know the things that will last, so that they may receive the fruit of their reward.

I want to know the things that are built on the foundation, so that they may be improved, not those by the road, where passers-by plunder the grapes. I want to know what belongs to the vine, the sure trees that bear fruit, not those gathered into a bundle and made ready for burning. That is: I am not a witness or partner to the things that perish. So what is at fault is not fellowship in just anything, but fellowship in crime.

And why did he not know those who glory in what is fruitless and frail? Because with their evil deeds and the axes of their iniquity they overturn the entrances of the faithful soul, and with cruel acts they split the forecourts of the devout mind, so that Christ cannot enter through them. Each of us must guard his own gates and doors, so that when Christ comes and knocks, the ministering powers who go before him and run ahead may say:

Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, you eternal gates. Those who have governed themselves well are truly princes, so that Christ may enter their souls. Solomon's saying is similar: If the spirit of one who has power rises up against you, do not leave your place, for care will calm great offenses. For diligence and faith hold the higher place, and faithlessness the lower. So let good diligence rise up to you, which shuts out the snares of the

enemy and takes away sin, so that the malice of the one who has power cannot do harm. In the Canticles [?] Ecclesiastes saw this malice under the sun, that is, in this world; that is why Scripture called this place 'under the sun'. So he saw it under the sun, not above the sun, where the angels have peace and the heavenly powers have holiness. Or perhaps he meant 'under the sun of iniquity'; for the devil presides over malice, and Christ over the virtues. And so, to overcome the spirit of the one who has power, a power he received for a time, David bowed himself in prayer, bending his neck like a ring, and humbled himself in supplication. For the prayer of one who humbles himself pierces the clouds and passes beyond the heights of the elements, so that it may draw near to Christ.

And he roared from the groaning of his heart. Whoever utters only a groan, without words, roars. This, then, is that glorious prayer, when the Spirit intercedes for us with unutterable groanings, as the vessel of election declared. This is the groaning which God does not despise, for he does not despise the young servant bereft of his father, nor the widow when she pours out her speech.

So the apostle sets groaning above all else as a sign of the Holy Spirit, as we read. Let us guard the doors of our soul, then, so that the entrance of our confession is not split open by the axes of much talking. Let nothing insolent or proud come out of our mouth, and let us not raise an axe or a hammer, which do not enter the Lord's church. Shut your doors when you pray, so that the wicked spirit does not thrust himself in and wring sin out of you where we wish to gain the profit of piety.

Whoever prays in this way, his groaning is not hidden from the Lord. Indeed, holy Peter's groaning was both known and heard when he wept most bitterly. It was not that the tears were bitter; bitter was the feeling that shed them. Even the faithless Ahab's groaning would have found grace, had his lasting envy not heaped up the offense. For it is not a perfunctory groaning that is praised, but one that brings conversion; for it is written: If you turn and groan, you will be saved.

Let us also set all our desire before the Lord. What is desire? I have read of desire for something good: With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you; and: The hart desires the fountains of water.

But I think that one who is doing penance, who afflicts himself, ought to recount the sins he has committed, not his good deeds. Indeed, I believe we are taught this by the little verses in which he says: O God, I will declare my life to you; you have set my tears in your sight. For he is not declaring his life as innocent when tears are shed, since tears usually serve as envoys on behalf of offenses. Unless perhaps we should understand it this way: even if someone is innocent, he cannot be secure, since he must fight against the most grievous enemies

every day. And so even where the conscience shines with joy, the fight is still tearful. In connection with these verses, then, we may take the word as 'covetousness' rather than 'desire'. For the Greek has epithymia, and both covetousness and desire are called epithymia; but covetousness is said of both good and evil. It is said of good in: My soul coveted and fainted for the courts of the Lord. But in the law it is otherwise: For I would not have known covetousness had the law not said:

You shall not covet. Here it is certainly said of evil. Indeed, the words that follow teach us that sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, works all covetousness in a person's affections. Yet we can also take it this way: 'I set all my desire before you', that is, I make plain to you what I desire to obtain. Then it seems to refer to a series of petitions, not to a boasting of virtues; for boasting is insolent even in the blameless, while supplication is praiseworthy even in a sinner.

The prophet also added that when his heart was troubled, his strength left him. The danger is great if the heart, with which we believe unto righteousness, is shaken. In grave illnesses, if pain is felt and its sensation expressed, this shows that a cure is possible. It is more bearable to feel pain than not to feel it: if you feel pain, it is a sign that life still remains, but if there is no sense of pain, it is a sign of final death. In the same way the heart shows signs of health when it recognizes the causes of its disturbance.

Indeed, David's heart was troubled against Nabal, a pestilent man, and he found grace. Abigail came to meet him to soothe his anger, and she received the sanctification of a blessing. But Nabal, with his hard and rigid heart, could not bear his wife's word; stunned, he grew stiff and fell into death.

But what strength deserted the prophet, the flesh's or the mind's? If it was the flesh's, then health is certainly not to be despaired of, for strength is made perfect in weakness. A certain judge and combatant in the wrestling match between mind and body discussed this at length. He knew how to regulate the contest between the two, restraining the flesh whenever he saw it growing stronger, so that it would not lead the mind captive into the law of sin. So he held the flesh in check and joined to it the strength of the mind, and in this way he was found worthy to reach the crown.

So in what the prophet says, if the strength of the flesh deserted him, the strength of the mind prevailed. But if we take it that the strength of his mind deserted him, it is no wonder if in the gravest temptations a man with a troubled heart thinks that the strength of his mind has deserted him. Let the prophet himself teach you, when he says: The Lord is my strength and my praise. So he was seeking the Lord, and therefore, so as not to deserve to be deserted,

he thought he must seek him more often, and whenever he wavered, he thought he had been deserted. In the same way the apostles wake the sleeper so that he will not be asleep to them, not because they believed he had really fallen asleep. In the same way Elisha, to take examples from earlier times, says: Where is the God of Elijah? He did not think him absent, but sought his presence in his benefits. In the same way Jeremiah followed him as a physician, saying: Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved. I have not grown weary in following after you.

In the same way the church sought him in the Song of Songs and asked the daughters of Jerusalem to awaken love. She sought so that she might find him whom she held fast by her love and never felt to be absent. So David too was not complaining that Christ had deserted him; he judged that while Christ was present he could not be troubled.

Finally, so that you may know that this is rather to be understood of Christ, he added: And the light of my eyes is not with me. What is the true light of all, if not Christ? Of him John says: He was the true light that enlightens every man coming into this world, for he is the one who enlightens both the eyes of the body and the gaze of the mind. Let us ask, then, that he may always pour his light into us and always be with us, as he was with David. That is why David dared to say: For with

you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light. He surely, as a prophet, had seen a great light; for us, let his lamp shine, so that we cannot go astray. The lamp is the word, just as the true light is the Word that enlightens the whole world. Indeed: Your word, Lord, is a lamp to my feet. That lamp the prophet too was seeking: not a lantern, but a lamp. John found the lamp and pointed it out; the persecutor came with a lantern and pointed him out. For a lantern has an enclosed light, not a free one.

The light of the Jews is like a lamp under a bushel, or torches under a veil: it can be seen, but it is not seen. We, however, with unveiled face behold the eternal glory of the Lord, so that we may be re-formed into his image from glory to glory through the Holy Spirit. So the crowd of persecutors came with lanterns, and that is why their eyes could not see the enclosed light; they came with torches, which have more murky smoke than bright light.

Indeed, it is with torches that the corpses of the dead are customarily burned. So the Jews who were persecuting the author of salvation were already carrying the fires for themselves. They came with weapons, signifying that they, who refused the Lord's peace, would perish by the weapons of the Romans, even to the destruction of the whole city and the temple.

My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood against me, and my neighbors stood far off; and those who sought my life used violence, and those who sought my harm spoke vanity and plotted deceit all day long. But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and was like a mute who does not open his mouth; and I became like a man who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth.

Who those may be who discuss these matters subtly, I shall see later. To me it seems that in this verse above all the Lord's saying is first to be kept in view: that in times of temptation a man's enemies include even those of his own household. This, then, is what holy David confesses, purely, sincerely and with sorrow. For it is true grief and a confession of the inner heart when one lists everything by which the hidden depths of the mind are pierced with the bitterest feeling and embittered by the gall of one's own household.

The prophet therefore laments that he was attacked by his friends and neighbors, by whom he certainly ought not to have been attacked, but helped. This plainly agrees with the complaint of holy Job, for he too rebuked those three kings as miserable comforters, who brought greater struggles upon him when they had come together out of friendship to comfort him. This is something we must certainly guard against. For consolation ought to be gentle, not

harsh; it should soothe grief and calm the fever rather than stir up agitation. Surely the medicine of the body itself can teach us: it customarily applies softer remedies to inflamed wounds, to relieve the pain. And so wounds are first poulticed and only afterward cut, lest the very harshness give offense and the incision aggravate the wound. How much more, then, ought we to take care, when we come to console, not to speak hastily or perfunctorily! For seven days Job was silent,

and his friends were silent; nor would they have spoken had Job not burst out into speech from grief. For you must consider where to begin, so that your consolation does not give offense by the very words. Even silence itself is medicine, and the one who is quick to speak does more wounding. Why are you surprised that he wounds another, when he himself is often wounded, since in much speaking sin is not avoided? For if a physician waits for the right time to treat, so that the aids of medicine are applied once the illness has come to a head, lest an illness still raw and unripe, as they say, resist the remedies of the cure and be unable to feel their benefit, how much more ought we to take care

that a healing word should come from us at the right moment, one that would be seen not to inflame mourning but to soothe it! The force of grief presses hard; the heart of an afflicted woman who has lost her husband or children to an untimely death is crushed: why do you hurry, when she will not listen to you until her grief cools? We have often seen quarrels stirred up over consolations. You came to grieve, not to quarrel. You must seek the very order of your words, so that you do not incur sin before God while you are wishing to console a man; so that when you say, 'Hear this,' and many other things that do no good, he does not reply: Hear, you miserable comforters; so that you do not bring a contest of garrulous debate into another's mourning; so that you do not fail to come when you should, or come and speak too harshly. Finally, as to what is said about [?], let holy Job teach you: At once the most grievous temptations came upon me; they surrounded me, watching me. My brothers have departed from me; they acknowledged strangers rather than me; my friends have become merciless. This, then, is the natural sense also in the holy prophet David: he complains that he was attacked by his friends and abandoned by his neighbors.

But a mystical sense of devotion is not to be rejected either: that he may have said this of the angels who stand guard over those who fear the Lord, to rescue them from temptations they cannot bear. How then do those who have been assigned to help stand far off? Yet they do not separate themselves; rather, the one who is pressed by temptations thinks that they are far away, since he longs to have them closer, and supposes that they are ignoring him, when they are awaiting the time to help at the nod of their commander, who has ordered his athlete to contend longer so that he may win more gloriously.
