And this seems to fit better with what follows, because when the angels relaxed their protective watch, the enemies lay in wait, seeking to find in his soul something with which to harm him. For they are permitted the power of more severe temptation when graver guilt is found in the soul. Hence you have in the Book of Kings what King Ahab said to Elijah, when the prophet rebuked him vehemently and announced his death to him:

Have you found me? he said. And Elijah answered: I have found you, because you have done evil in the sight of the Lord. You see, then, that God's prophets and priests should not rashly affront kings, if there are no graver sins for which they ought to be rebuked. But where the sins are graver, there it seems the priest should not spare them, so that they may be corrected by just rebukes.

Yet in this place David says that they seem to have found nothing, and so his enemies spoke vanity, since they found nothing they could say in accordance with the truth. 'Or else it is because, even if I sinned, I was cleansing my sins by the sorrow of repentance; and in this they spoke deceitfully with me, to confound me with reproach and call me back from my conversion.' And consider whether he did not rather mean this: that they sought out his wrongdoings, but when they wanted to accuse him, they were forestalled, because he himself had laid open his wounds, becoming his own accuser; and so the force of their accusation was weakened, and what they said was empty of truth, since it could no longer harm one who had already confessed his guilt.

'Shut out, then, from the malice of accusation, they resorted to deceit,' he says, 'so as to rise up against me and insult me, to provoke me to some agitation; but I, seeing their deceit, like a deaf man did not hear.' Consider the force of the words. He did not say, 'because I pretended not to hear what they were saying,' but he said, 'I did not hear,' meaning that by the resolve of his mind he shut out the voice of the speaker, and did not open his mouth, like a mute.

Blessed is the one who can have such strength that when provoked he is not angered, and when stirred up he does not wish to take revenge. Enemies work at this, to provoke us to anger: they curse so that we will curse, they accuse so that we will throw the accusation back, they revile so as to rouse us to return insult for insult. Hence Peter wrote splendidly in his epistle of the Lord Jesus that when he was cursed he did not curse, and when he suffered he did not threaten.

The just man, desiring to shape the pattern of his life after his likeness and image, is silent when accused, forgives when injured, takes no notice when provoked, and does not open his mouth, so as to imitate him who was led like a lamb to the slaughter and did not open his mouth; and though he could have a reply to make, he prefers to be silent rather than speak.

For the Lord Jesus himself truly was silent when he was accused, and when he was struck he did not strike back. Indeed, when he was struck he answered: If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me? See how he spoke with a kind of childlike feeling, as though truly weak, as one who could not avenge himself. So you too, if you have the means to refute your accuser, will do better to be silent, lest by refuting him in return you betray your agitation; for it is better to overlook an injury than to avenge it by refuting.

Good is the mute who does not know how to speak evil, from whose mouth no accusation knows how to come out. This is the truly blessed mute, who, while silent, speaks within himself: 'The Lord gives me an instructed tongue, for when I must speak a word.' Such things Zechariah spoke within himself when he had been struck dumb. And truly, because speaking had not profited him, he was struck dumb so that he would not speak, and he was heard by Christ so that he might speak. Indeed, he wrote what Christ would hear, and he received back the voice that

Christ granted, and Christ added a grace he had not had before, so that he prophesied the one whose commands he had not believed before. Why do I speak of the Lord of all powers, when the woman Susanna, not unsettled even by the weakness of her sex, uttered no word against those by whom she knew she had been condemned to the danger of death? She was accused and was silent; she was led to death and covered herself with silence, so as not to lay bare her modesty. Yet within herself she spoke to God, who heard her the more because she was silent, whereas if she had wished to speak, perhaps she would not have been heard.

You too, then, who have resolved to make satisfaction for your debts to the Lord your God, purify yourself before him alone in your inmost heart; look to him who can wash away sins. Whoever thinks you deserve reproach is helping you. Indeed, when David was being cursed and his commander Abishai wished to avenge the insult to him, David said to him: Let him alone, let him curse, for the Lord has told him to, so that you may see my humiliation, and the Lord may repay me with good for this curse. You see, then, that you are helped by those who revile you, so that the Lord may hear you and forgive your sin.

For since you ought to be your own accuser, to heap up your misdeeds and offer yourself to punishment, how can you wish to deny the charges against you? Penitence calls for patience; patience lessens great offenses. How can you be angry with others when you yourself stand guilty in your own conscience? How can you be agitated, when you ought to be an object of pity? One who is reproved — and, what is more, by himself — ought to tend his own wounds, not wound another. No one heals himself by wounding another. Physician, heal yourself. If a physician must, how much more must a guilty man heal himself first!

You confess your own sin, yet you profess yourself physician of another's. Even if what you retort is true, it is not the time for it; for God said to the sinner: Why do you recite my righteous decrees? You have taken it upon yourself to reprove from the law, you who yourself stood against the law. Why do you waste the time for tears? Why in quarreling do you listen to or speak empty words, when it is written for you: You shall not receive an empty report, and when you have read in the Gospel that judgment must be undergone for every idle word? Even if another speaks, be silent; even if another reviles you, stop your ear.

David conquered his adversaries by keeping silent, and because he became like a mute, he received back his voice, for he turned to the Lord and spoke, saying: For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, O Lord my God. For I said: Let my enemies never rejoice over me. Look at each point. David was silent; his enemies were speaking, provoking him to say something himself.

They kept saying, 'Let us hear your voice'; he, silent, spoke within himself: 'What need is there for these things to be heard by those whom they cannot benefit? In you, Lord, I have hoped; to you alone I speak; hear me, you who are able to hear. I have always asked of you that my enemies should never rejoice over me; for even if I have sinned, you forgive sin; even if I have fallen, you raise me up; so that those who delight in the sins of others may have no grounds for exulting.'

For we who have sinned more have gained more, because your grace makes us more blessed than our innocence would. We have this thought also in the book of the prophet Micah: Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise again. The fall that comes from weakness is not grave, provided there is not also a deliberate will not to rise from it. Have the will to rise: he is at hand who will make you rise again.

So David spoke in his heart, asking to be heard by the Lord and that his enemies should not exult over him, and asking too that he might persevere in his resolve to be converted, lest, while the steps of his resolve — the feet, as it were, of his soul — were shaken, his adversaries should speak against him proud words full of boasting, as those do who long to insult.

Yet, though he is shaken as a man is, he says that he is ready for the scourges, so that he may atone for his error at least by punishment. Even if the Lord's scourges cease, he recalls that he is scourged by his own grief, so that there may be nothing in his fault for judgment to condemn, since a good confession has forestalled it. This, then, is what he says: And while my feet are shaken, they spoke great things against me — because they are so ready for mocking insult that when my feet were shaken they had their boasting ready. Or else it means this: while my feet are shaken, thinking that I would fall, they have already spoken proud and boastful words.

But since in a later psalm he himself said that his feet were almost moved, lest any doubt arise from this, consider that here we are taught the disposition of penitence, while there the notion of that error is ruled out, that the riches and great success of the wicked should move us.

Such a manner of expression is found in the divine Scriptures. So it is elsewhere too: When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted — although the saint wishes to be proved not by a display of words but by the power of the Spirit. So we must always look to the sense, which even the repeated translation from Hebrew into Greek and from Greek into Latin tends to weaken.

For all the foregoing, then, there is a fine remedy: he is ready for the scourges and offers himself to the Lord, to endure whatever scourges please God. I read, it is true, that holy David chose a kind of scourge that he would endure with equanimity; but he chose because he was ordered by necessity to choose one of three conditions.

Where no such order is given, however, the humble servant of God is ready for anything, whether he must undergo bodily illness, or flight before the face of an enemy, or the death of his children, whom he does not fear to send on ahead, since he can receive them back undismayed. For he knows that if he is punished here with temporal punishment, he can lighten for the future the penalty of everlasting affliction. He asks, then, that his petition be received, and that he himself be chastised so that he may be received; for the Lord chastises every son whom he receives.

If you see your servant confessing his own sins and offering himself to punishment of his own accord, you are moved and you forgive: and do you doubt the Lord's mercy? A judge, who in very many cases is not allowed to hold back the sword because he serves the laws, can nevertheless grant remission of penalties; and do you still hesitate over what you may ask of the Lord of the laws and author of mercy, whose will is law and who has the right to pardon — provided only that you ask for your sins to be forgiven you, and do not think of your honors or feel ashamed before your friends, afraid of seeming to have lowered your dignity?

The friend of God, the prophet of God, a king chosen by God himself and anointed to the kingdom, offered himself to the scourges of his own accord and was not ashamed: and are you ashamed? This bashfulness will not help you much when you come to God's judgment; rather, you will regret this shame when, set in the sight not only of men but also of angels and all the heavenly powers, you begin not to deny your own sins. How will you excuse yourself, when you have committed so many? You will plead the weakness of our condition, since no one is without sin.

The answer will be given you: 'Then you ought to have done penance. I had given you a remedy; why did you refuse it?' You will go on to plead your shame, that you were embarrassed because of your honors. He will say: 'If you were ashamed of me before your friends, I too will be ashamed of you before my Father who is in heaven. Learn that what is written is true, that there is a shame that brings sin. David set his grief before his eyes, so as never to forget it; David himself declared his iniquity; David thought about his sin, not about his wealth; David was not ashamed to go over his sins, so that he would not be put to shame for them when he stood at my judgment:

and were you ashamed? My servant Job would not be at rest today if he had been ashamed before those three kings, his friends; nor would David himself, if he had been ashamed to confess his own offenses. So, because he was not ashamed to lay open his sins to me, neither will I be ashamed to unlock my secrets to him. And because neither of them was ashamed to place the price of his deeds in my power, to commit himself to my judgment and will, neither will I be ashamed of such

servants, but will call them friends, since they strove to do my will. And so, because they were in sorrow before, they are now in consolation; you, because you were in delights, are now in torments. A great chasm lies between you, so that neither their grace can pass over to you nor your punishment to them.' Do you hear, then, what David says? Listen, while you are still permitted to correct and amend yourself; if you amend here, you will rest there. Do not let the sweet things of the world and the pleasures of this age delight you; they tend to vomit up bitter gall. He did not seek pleasures, though set upon a throne, who chose the death of the saints rather than the life of the wicked.

My enemies, he says, are alive and have been made strong against me, and those who hate me wrongfully have been multiplied; those who repay evil for good slandered me, because I followed close after righteousness. But how much more illustrious is he who died daily to give life to his people,

and offered his body to the wounds of death, as he himself says: in deaths often! For an honorable death is the redemption of a life, even of a stained life, or the confirmation of an innocent one; and the issues of death are in the hand of life. That is why the apostle preferred to die daily, to prove the merit of his life; for it is written: Do not praise a man during his lifetime. For those who live die; those who die will rise again. So the one who dies in order to rise is nearer to salvation than the one who lives only to die.

And who is it that dies daily, if not one who carries about the death of the Lord Jesus in his flesh, so that all sins may die in him? The enemies of David were strengthened and multiplied in this world; but there is no sound strength except that of one who is strengthened in Christ. Indeed, those who hate the righteous man wrongfully are strengthened in the world; so their hatred is not just but unjust, since they hated wrongfully.

But see the difference. In a later psalm he says: those who hate me without cause; here he has: those who hate me wrongfully. But there he speaks in the person of Christ, here in his own; where he speaks in the person of Christ, he is hated without cause; where in his own, wrongfully. For a man may be proof against some one wound — say injustice, intemperance or unchastity — and yet be open to other wounds; but in Christ there could be no opening through which he could receive the wound of any sin, for he was free from guilt, untouched by any offense, and spotless from all vice. There are some, however, who think that both psalms run their course in the person of Christ, who was making satisfaction to the Father for our sins. Here, then, he would be saying that he was assailed against justice, there against grace.

And he rightly adds, to prove that he was assailed unjustly: because I followed close after righteousness. How great is the force of the word through the addition of this one syllable, that he says he 'followed close after' righteousness, not merely 'followed'! For the one who follows close behind is nearer than the one who simply follows, just as the nearly equal is nearer than the unequal, and an heir's coming is called a succession rather than an accession.

And yet, although he follows after justice, he does not think it is due to his own virtue but to heavenly grace if Christ does not desert him, and so he prays the more earnestly, saying: Do not forsake me, O Lord; my God, do not depart from me. That is: men have forsaken me; my friends have attacked the one dear to them; my neighbours did not come near. They fled from me as from a dead man and loathed me, because I desired to confess my sins to you, because I offered myself to your scourges

to be wounded, because I chose the scars of wounds over the banquets of kings and the boasting of the powerful. Do not you alone forsake me; hold fast to your poor servant, you who raise the needy from the earth and lift the poor from the dunghill. Upheld by your company, I shall count myself more thronged than those whom crowds surround. My scars have indeed festered, but I still long for the scars of your blows, which form over wounds once they are healed, so that afterwards no sore appears.

Good are the scars of triumphal wounds, in which the victors of this earthly battle take pride: how much more illustrious are the wounds that are seen to have been received for faith and for the glory of your name! This is the scar that opens heaven, wins the kingdom, finds immortality. This, then, brothers, is the blessed scar, since blessed are those who have washed their robes in their own blood. Thus the flesh of death began to be a robe of glory, the very flesh in which even Paul, God's chosen one, was once in peril, had he not asked to be delivered from the body of this death, as we read.

And so let us who are in this body of death pray that that good physician, the beloved of God, may not forsake us, the one whom the patriarch David begged not to depart from him. Let us entrust ourselves to him, ready to be cured with whatever medicine he wishes. No one tells the physician of his body how he is to be treated. The physician knows what medicines suit each wound, and which ulcer's rot must be cut away with the knife, lest it creep on to the ruin of the whole body.

If the physician names the kind of treatment by which the sick man ought to be cured and he scorns it, the physician goes away and leaves the sick man. See the man who wants to be cured, consenting to every kind of treatment; mark the order. First he opens his wounds to the physician and says: 'Cure me, but I beg you, not in your anger, for my infirmities cannot bear harsh medicine.' Christ's medicine is correction; for the Lord corrects the one he wishes to convert. That is why Paul too says to the physician: Reprove, entreat, rebuke. So the one who asks to be reproved does not refuse to be cured; he only wishes the penalty to be lightened, that he may not be reproved in fury nor corrected in the violence of anger.

And see the progression. First he asks to be reproved, then, which is more, to be corrected. Next he not only confesses his sins but even counts them up and accuses them; for he does not want his offences to lie hidden. For just as fevers cannot be relieved while they are deep within, but when they break out they bring hope of their ending, so the disease of sins burns hotter while it is covered, but if it is brought out by confession it evaporates.

And so the just man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech, before the infection of the sore spreads inward; for the memory of offences weighs on the conscience unless medicine is sought. And if the physician delays, the sick man ought to offer himself so that he may be cut the sooner, just as David offered himself to the Lord's scourges, saying: 'Repay me double for my sins, so long as you punish me here; do not desert me, do not turn your face away from me, do not disdain and shudder at the stench of my wounds.

Job too, your poor servant, was struck with sores from his feet to his head, and he found the remedy for his health, although his wound came from virtue and this one from error. His wounds stank, and physicians could not cure them. You spoke, Lord, the mysteries of your sacraments, you exposed the serpent's poisons, and by the medicine of your word alone the wounds of your servant were cured, because you did not desert him;

do not forsake me either, Lord, do not depart from me. Men have forsaken me, because my wounds, which I thought should be laid open to your mercy, are filthy to them. They say: Go away from us, for you are a sinner; depart, lest you defile us. But you, Lord, heal and are not defiled, you help and are not contaminated, because you are the God of salvation, Lord, and your hand is accustomed not to destroy but to heal.'

We have finished the psalm, together with the interpretation of a verse which some Greek manuscripts contain, but not all the Latin ones. For before the nearest responsory there is the verse: And they cast me off like a loathsome dead man, that is, those who repaid me evil for good. But you, do not forsake me, O Lord, do not depart from me (for this follows), that is:

Do not forsake me, you who are accustomed to heal even a stinking corpse. Indeed we have this in the Gospel: when he had come to the tomb of Lazarus and said, Take away the stone, Martha said: By now he stinks, for he has been dead four days. He answered her: Did I not tell you that if you believe you will see the glory of God? And he called Lazarus, and he came out whole. Let us too, then, believe, so that from our wounds we may gain the medicine of salvation and future glory.

In prayers and supplications, then, penance must be carried out with grief and tears, so that we may deserve to see that glory of God. And do not let it trouble you that mourning, grief and mortification of the body are very heavy sufferings; even if they seem very heavy, yet sufferings of this kind are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, as the apostle Paul bears witness.

Let us not be reluctant, then, to bear lighter things here, so that there we may obtain what is full of praise and glory, carrying off everlasting rewards for temporal labours, through the Lord Jesus, to whom be praise, honour, glory and everlastingness, from before the ages, now and always and for all ages of ages. Amen.
EXPLANATION OF PSALM 38
Title: To the end, for Jeduthun; a song for David himself.

In the preceding psalm the pattern of penance is set out; in this following one the pattern of patience is marked out. David wrote this psalm and gave it to be sung to Jeduthun, a man learned in the Levitical and priestly disciplines, who was most skilled at composing a sequence of psalms and led the singing before the ark of the Lord. So, because it was not Jeduthun who wrote this psalm but the prophet David, who gave it to Jeduthun, a man skilled in singing, to be sung, the title is inscribed in this way.

Indeed, in secular literature too there were some who wrote and others who were accustomed to sing on the stage, whether songs or comedies or tragedies. And they sought the Olympic crown, which is why their writings bear witness at the end to a hymn of victory. But David, who did not seek these garlands of withering crowns but longed with devout affection for that incorruptible and undefiled reward, the inheritance of heavenly things, wrote a hymn not as a victory epi-

nician, but to him who granted victory to those who believe in him, who is the end of all that we ask with a devout mind. For whether you seek wisdom, or pursue virtue, or truth, or the way and justice, or resurrection, in all things you must follow Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God, the truth, the way, justice, the resurrection. Toward whom, then, should you strive, if not toward the perfection of all things and the summit of the virtues? And that is why he says to you: Come, follow me, that is, so that you may deserve to reach the consummation of the virtues. So whoever follows Christ ought to imitate him as far as he is able, meditating within himself on his precepts and on the examples of his divine deeds.

And so David meditated within himself on what he remembered Christ had spoken in him, so that, when some people were troublesome to him and tried to provoke him to strife, he might put on patience and shun the zeal for disputing, from which empty uproar and quarrels often arise. Many, envying his virtues and believing he could be drawn away from his purpose of gentleness and his disposition of humility, kept assailing holy David; and especially the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, against which the just have a hard wrestling, drove the agents of their wickedness to provoke him. So, lest amid the frequent contests of those clamouring at him and

the tumult of dispute some offensive word should slip from him, the holy prophet resolved to keep silent. O silence, strong shield of a watchful defence! O most faithful foundation of steadfastness, on which whoever can stand need not fear a slip of the tongue! For many, though made firm with a steady heart, have yet often fallen through the error of careless, wavering speech. So the prophet, seeing himself tried by such snares and by the vain uproar of disputants, silently took counsel within himself, imposing on himself a law of silence; and when he kept silent before those who insulted him and provoked him to say something (such are the contests and the talk of insolent men: 'Answer us, if you presume to be our equal; you see for yourself that you are beaten and have nothing to reply'), and when he seemed almost driven by their taunts to speak, he called himself back, so as to speak in his heart:

I said: I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue; I set a guard on my mouth while the sinner stands against me. That is: I resolved, I confirmed, I commanded myself, I said to my heart: 'I will guard my ways.' If I had said it to others, my word would have to stand; how much more firm must be what I have laid down for myself! If someone deceives a stranger, it is unseemly; if a neighbour, it is serious; how much more serious, then, if someone thinks he may cheat himself of what he has promised himself, so that by his own verdict he is judged unfaithful to himself and contemptible! To whom, then, can a man seem worthy who is worthless to himself?

Let us therefore keep our soul steadfast, so that our lips, hasty to speak, do not burst out into offence. Job too overcame his affliction by silence, and by his quietness he surpassed even his endurance. The flesh is not to be trusted; we would have lived if Eve had kept silent. So that first sin came forth from the voice, and that most wicked and cunning serpent first tempted us through the voice. Would that either Adam had been deaf or Eve dumb: he, so as not to hear his wife's voice; she, so as not to speak to her husband and, through the service of a slippery voice, pour the serpent's poisons into her husband!

Cain too, although by murdering his brother he violated human nature and impiously blotted out the rights of kinship, yet by his voice added sacrilege to his crime, denying to God the death of the brother he had killed. Why should I speak of individuals? The very people chosen by the Lord, for whom Moses opened the sea in silence, ungrateful for heavenly benefits, kept murmuring, and so brought on itself God's displeasure. Then it rejected Moses himself, the leader of that pathless and unheard-of journey, and demanded of his brother Aaron that gods be made for it to worship.

Hence he too, considering the great dangers of the voice, said: I will guard my ways. What, then, are these ways of man that must be so carefully watched, lest they incur some graver offence? So great a prophet urges us to consider this more carefully, and his son Solomon, the interpreter of his father's mind, urges us to examine it more keenly, for he wrote: Three things are impossible for me to understand, and a fourth I do not know: the track of an eagle in flight, and the way of a serpent on a rock, and the paths of a ship sailing on the sea, and the ways of a man in his youth (and of an adulterous woman,

who, after she has done it, washes herself and says she has done nothing wrong). So he said that three things were impossible for him to understand, and a fourth which even he, who bore the seal of wisdom among men, did not know: namely, the course of the ways of a man in his youth. If the knowledge of these ways is either inexplicable or difficult, can guarding them be easy? That is why David himself, not without reason, offered no defence for the sins of his youth but asked that they be forgotten: The sins of my youth and of my ignorance, he says, do not remember. Not without reason, then, did Solomon say that he did not know what his father, in whom the grace of God was greater, testified that he had been ignorant of.

And perhaps he referred the sins of youth to the heat of the flesh, and the sins of ignorance to slips of speech, which mostly pour out not from our considered judgement but from a certain impulse and rush of talking. Knowing this to be dangerous, the prophet says: I believed, therefore I spoke. Upon the foundation of virtue, then, the voice is safe; without a foundation it is slippery. That is why the chosen interpreter of divine Scripture rang out as with the sound of a trumpet: With the heart one believes unto justice, with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Faith is what comes first in believers; confession is its carrying out.

Let us hear, then, how the holy prophet David resolved to guard his ways, or why: So that I do not sin, he says, with my tongue. If the prophet guards against this, do you not? If he in whom the grace of God was speaking feared this, do you not fear it, you who do not shun words of error and delight in theatrical talk? Do you not dread it, you to whom it is written in the Gospel that you will render an account for every idle word? If there is danger for an idle word, how much more for a wicked one!

Not everything that is idle is also wicked, but everything that is not fruitful is dangerous and fit to be uprooted; for every tree that does not bear fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. When the mind is stirred and agitated by adversaries who goad, clamour, mock and accuse, a word spoken in agitation slips out; therefore silence is both safe and seemly, for it keeps caution with dignity.

For what are our lips but a kind of chains of ours? Indeed, each person is bound by the chains of his own lips. That is why the wise man keeps silent at the right time and considers within himself when he ought to speak. Of this Solomon himself says admirably: The lips of the wise are bound by understanding. So when you see a wise man keeping silent while the insolent mock him, you will say: He has bound his lips with understanding, that is, he wisely keeps silent, so as not to be bound by the chains of his own lips.

He has set a guard on his mouth, he has hedged his ears with thorns, he has put a bar on the doors of his mouth; he guards the treasure of his heart and the silver of his speech, so that he may bring it out, tested and refined, when it is fitting, lest some thief or troublemaker should first break into his heart and drag him captive to those to whom he may sell his wickedness.

Judas was contemplating selling Christ, but the great grace of the Lord and a certain fatherly tenderness kept calling him back, softening his fury; nor would he have broken out into crime had not the adversary plunged himself into his heart, since he thought he could deceive Christ. So when some people are troublesome to you while you wish to keep

justice, do not doubt that they are the agents of that most wicked sinner who is the author of all crimes. David saw with prophetic eyes and recognized his figure; that is why he kept silent, so as not to do the will of the one who longs to throw our disposition into turmoil. He held back his voice, he closed his gates with silence, he set patience as a defence in it and kept watch with the guard of silence, so that the enemy might not creep in, nor any stray and careless word go out from the barriers of his mouth. That is why the patient man who restrains himself is stronger than one who captures cities. The just man is his own barrier, his own ever-wakeful guard.

So while he was setting up this defence for himself, he spoke in his heart: I set a guard on my mouth while the sinner stands against me. The enemy is always present, because he is always lying in wait. Even if you do not see him, he is present; even if you do not feel him, he attacks. If you do not see, believe the one who sees: He stands, he says, against me. Whoever sees his own sin also sees the sinner mocking him in what he has done; but whoever has foreseen the sinner can avoid sin.

David saw the sinner standing against him when Shimei cursed and stoned his king and cried: Get out, you man of blood. For he would not have been so reckless as to be moved neither by reverence for so great a king nor by fear of his armed men, when any one of his soldiers could have killed the reviler; but the devil had made him mad, driving him to his death. Therefore David fought against the author rather than pursuing the agent. For what great thing would it have been to take vengeance on a feeble man whom another was driving to fury, when by his death the sinner would have had his will fulfilled?

The devil is conquered not by the sword but by the word of God; so let man's tongue be silent, and let the word of God speak. Indeed, Christ too kept silent when he stood before Pilate's judgement, to give us a pattern of silence, because the bodily tongue is quick to err and prone to fall. But there are also those who speak while silent, like Moses, who stood astonished and silent, and to whom, though he was silent, God said: Why do you cry out to me? Or like Susanna, who kept silent in her dangers, and the Lord heard her. So if the word of God is in you, you will both keep silent in the word of God and, though silent, cry out so as to be heard by Christ.

Meditate, then, on the things of Christ, on which the prophet David meditated within himself; for Christ had earlier spoken in him the things which in this psalm he says he meditated within himself. For thus it is written: But I, when they were troublesome to me in anything, clothed myself in sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer will return into my bosom. What does 'in anything' mean?

It means that an untimely word slips out, or emotion is stirred, most of all when we are in some pain or sadness, or the mind is sick with indignation, or hampered by some anxieties, or taken up with disputes. Who, then, are those who are troublesome? Understand it first of the very author of sin

and his angels, then of those who prefer to be his followers rather than Christ's. A wife is driven on, as with holy Job; a friend, as that same book shows; a son, like Absalom; a slave, a freedman and a member of the household, because a man's enemies are even those of his own household, so that they harass him one by one. What remedy, then, is there against such sicknesses of the soul, if not patience, if not silence? And what is harder still, the one who provokes you most is the one who has enjoyed your benefits, and among them the one who owes you more exasperates you more, so that you are all the more stirred by the bitterness of an ungrateful man or the indignity of some lowly person.

So the just man, even if a friend is insolent to him, grieves for his friend, because his friend is falling in this way, because he is being driven on by the tempter. If he grieves for a friend, much more for a wife or a son, if he finds them too insolent to him; and if a brother harasses him, as Esau did holy Jacob, he grieves and seeks to reconcile his brother to himself or to flee from his presence, as Rebecca advised, so that his brother's anger might find no opportunity to do harm; and if it is a neighbour or a member of the household, he grieves; and if it is a servant or a freedman

or a slave, he bears it patiently and in all these cases keeps silent, so as not to answer the one by whom he sees the offender driven on. So someone of the household reviles him: he grieves and is silent; a freedman reviles him: he is silent; a slave reviles him: he is silent. In this way the one who spreads a snare for his soul with the bait of the voice is defeated. So you too be silent when an unworthy person reviles you; be silent when a slave, and especially your own, insults you, and say in your heart: I am silent, but you, Lord, do not be silent; and add: Do not depart from me, as the prophet David said, that is: Do not leave me alone among those who attack me; for he is not alone to whom God is present. Take the testimony: Behold, he says, the hour is coming when you will be scattered, each to his own, and will leave me alone; but I am not alone, for the Father is with me.

So the just man is silent toward those who are insolent to him; the just man prays. Hear the just man praying: Instead of loving me they slandered me, but I prayed. The just man blesses those who curse him, as the apostles did, as Paul declares, saying: We are cursed and we bless. The just man loves his enemies. See how one is taught to climb gradually, step by step, to the increase of the virtues, as the Lord says: Love your enemies.

The just man prays for those who slander him, because the Lord commanded this too, adding: Do good to those who hate you, pray for those who slander and persecute you. He is just in every respect who keeps and observes these things: first, because he is silent and does not answer his enemies; then, because he prays, that is, his disposition is not idle. And he who prays prays for good things, not for whatever might harm his enemy. It is more, then, to pray than to be silent. The just man blesses those who curse him.

This is more than praying for oneself; for, secure about himself, he blesses one whom he does not fear, or even one whom he formerly feared. The just man loves his enemy. To love is more than to bless, because the love of the mind is greater than the grace of speech. The just man does good to one whose hatred has assailed him; the just man prays for those who slander him. Love is good, and devotion is good; both belong to God, and both are God, because God is love, as John said in his epistle.

That is why both are joined together: Love your enemies and pray for those who slander and persecute you. Love is the fulfilment of the law, but this too is the fulfilment of the Gospel: to pray for those who slander and persecute us, asking pardon for their sins, just as holy Job was chosen by divine judgement so that his prayer might wipe out the offence of those kings who had slandered the just man.

So pray whether you are weak or strong: if you are weak, you pray for yourself; if you are strong, you pray for your enemy. Prayer is a good shield for weakness: you pray, and the Lord protects you. It is a good shield for the victor too, so that you defend your enemy, whom you could strike, and he is not slain by someone else, and, what is more, not by Christ, who said:

Vengeance is mine; I will repay. This is the prayer that returns into the bosom of the one who prays. It brings back the fruit of what he wished to obtain, so that the gifts he asked of the Lord come back into his soul and mind. This same prophet taught you so later on, saying: So will I bless you in my life, and in your name I will lift up my hands. As

with fat and richness let my soul be filled. The bosom of the soul is the secret place of its prayer, the inner chamber of the will, and a kind of innermost store for the vows that return to it. Hence we read that the just rest in Abraham's bosom: those who have put on a faith like his and shown the same will in good works rest in his grace, in his repose, in his calm.

But someone may wonder, since the Lord said through David's mouth that he humbled his soul with fasting, how David himself says later on: If I was not humbly minded, but exalted my soul. Let him consider that what concerns the wisdom of the mind is one thing, and what concerns the humility of the heart is another.

The wisdom of the mind is lofty, but the wisdom of the flesh ought not to be puffed up. So he humbled his soul with fasting to teach that the swelling of our flesh must be chastened, and the prophet exalted his soul through the sublime grace of God, since he who exalts himself will be humbled and he who humbles himself will be exalted. This means, in the first place, that the proud are struck down and the humble raised up as a fitting reward for what they deserve. But that is not all. The word of God is sharp on every side, like a sword sharp on three sides, and so I think it can also be understood that he who exalts himself knows how to humble himself, and he who knows how to humble himself also knows how to exalt himself. Paul shows this when he says:

For I have learned to be content in whatever state I am. I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound. So David too, by not thinking humbly of Christ, exalted his soul, which the Arians humble and cast down. And by exalting his soul through the vigor of his understanding and the grace of faith, he showed forth with devout affection the virtue of humility.

That is why he said: I was dumb and was humbled and kept silence from good things. He knew when he ought to humble himself and when he ought to be silent. He was dumb so as not to raise a din himself in quarrelsome dispute with those who reproached him. He was humbled to cast down the swelling of the proud, or to teach them by his example how they ought to humble themselves. He kept silence from good things, because a good conscience needs no defense of words: it rests on its own testimony and is its own judge. And so the just man says: Who will contradict me, or who will resist me? And Paul says: For to me it is a very small thing to be judged by you or by any human day.

Against slanderers and sinners the just man is content with his own judgment, but he reserves to Christ the judgment of his merits. And so he added: He who judges me is the Lord. Most beautifully he chose as judge one whom no fraud deceives, from whom nothing hidden escapes, and who is not offended by the lapses of our weak condition, since he knows how to pardon frailty. Silence, then, is useful in every case. If you acknowledge a sin, be silent, lest you make it worse by denying it; if you acknowledge none, be silent, secure in your innocence. The words of others cannot fasten on you a crime that your own conscience does not admit.

There follows: And my sorrow was renewed. He utters these words while still placed on a lower step of virtue: his sorrow was renewed when old sins were cast up at him, sins that had been blotted out and that oblivion seemed already to have covered over, or that good works had hidden by making amends for them. Later on, as one grown stronger, he says: They saw me and shook their heads, because they threatened him but could do him no harm. And he added:

They will curse, and you will bless. This too he says as one grown stronger, heedless of insult or shame, since the Lord's blessing made up to him abundantly for everything. So in this thirty-eighth psalm, as in a kind of meditation, and not yet set in the full perfection of virtue, he says that his sorrow was renewed.

For the strongest man does not feel the hurt of a scar, and one who is stronger cannot fear a blow. In a boxing match the stronger man often waits to be provoked by some blow from the weaker, so that, stung, he may rise up more fiercely. He is so hardened by long training and endurance that, as if insensible to pain, he cannot feel a blow: when struck, he laughs; when provoked, he threatens. But if the weaker man happens to take his opponent's blow on the healed scar of an old wound, he feels the pain renewed. So it is with someone reproached with earlier sins which he duly

grieved over and wept for, so as to close the wound of his sins with a scar by fitting satisfaction. If he is perfect, he is silent before those who revile him, and no sorrow is renewed in him. Even if he has sinned, he is secure, since the gifts of God are without repentance, and so God does not usually undo and renew what he has once forgiven; for he himself said: I, I am he who blots out iniquities, and I will not remember them. But if he is imperfect and forgetful of the heavenly commandments, his pain comes back as if the scar had been cut open.

My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will blaze up. Graver wounds, as we know, are cured by caustic medicine or by applying fire. So the wise man is his own physician; yet even as physician he cauterizes his own wound. And so, if he has not been fully brought to a state of unimpaired health, his heart steams, he runs a fever, he is inflamed by the insults hurled at him, and even if he is silent, he chafes within himself.

If a stone is rubbed against a stone, it strikes fire. So too a good conscience is kindled with shame if the memory of its offenses is renewed, and in that very meditation a fire blazes up. It is not an evil fire, for it scorches but does not consume. Such was the fire Moses saw in the bush, when the bush was burning but was not consumed.

There is, then, a fire that lessens sin and feeds on guilt with its heat. There is also a fire stirred up by meditation on the heavenly Scriptures, like the one of which Jeremiah speaks: And there was a flaming fire in my bones. Or like the one Cleopas and his companion on the road spoke of together when Christ joined them after the resurrection, saying: Was not our heart burning within us when he opened the Scriptures to us? That is why the Lord came: to send this fire on the earth, to enlighten the souls of all, to kindle zeal and to burn away guilt.

I spoke with my tongue: Lord, make known to me my end, and the number of my days, which is, that I may know what is lacking to me. Good is the fire that made the prophet speak. And see whether it is not the same fire that was seen on the day of Pentecost, when the disciples were gathered in one place and the Holy Spirit came down upon them with great force and they spoke in various tongues. For so it is written, that their tongues appeared divided, as of fire.

This, then, is he who said to Jeremiah: Behold, I put my words in your mouth as fire. So David too received this tongue of fire, so that, kindled with the ardor of divine knowledge, he might say: Lord, make known to me my end. He is not asking about his death, for that is no end for one who will rise again. He is asking about the end of which the apostle said: For that is the end, when the Lord Jesus hands over the kingdom to God the Father and abolishes all principalities and powers

and when death, the last of all, is destroyed, so that evils may cease and eternal goods take their place. And therefore it was said: Sorrow, sadness and sighing have fled away. Paul too worked this end in men, saying: For who is it that makes me glad but the one who is made sad by me? For by rebuking he stirred up sorrow, sadness and sighs,

so that they might repent and thereby earn irrevocable pardon and a salvation that God would never regret. That, then, is the true end, which will be the end not of one man but of all. How, then, did he say 'my end'? But consider who is speaking. It is a man, certainly: either one among men, sharing their common nature, or one who is portrayed as the pattern for all and is being trained toward the perfection of the complete man.

Hence he added that the number of his days, which is, should be made known to him, so that he might know what he lacks: what he lacks for perfection, that is, not for the life of this body. The prophet David longed to be set free from that life, saying: Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged! I have dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar. Indeed, he wished to know the number of the days, not of the nights as well. Here

there are days and nights, but there are days alone; there the light is perpetual and unending. And so he added: which is. 'Which is,' he says, not 'which passes away'; for heaven and earth will pass away, but faith remains, and so does the day of Christ, because he is the same yesterday and today and forever. And as for the number he seeks, hear this: In my Father's house, he says, are many mansions.

So the Lord Jesus gives each a place, that is, a mansion suited to each one's merits; for each is in his own order. He went ahead, then, to prepare a place for those who believe in him. That is why he also says: If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again to you and take you to myself, so that where I am you may be also. And where I am going you know, and the way you know. There is, then, a way by which Christ ascended when he rose again.

He ascended above all the heavens to the throne of God. But men who deserve it ascend from the first heaven to the second, then from the second to the third, and from there by stages up to the seventh heaven or thereabouts, and into the very vault and summit of heaven. If, then, there is a number of ways and a number of mansions, there is surely a number of days by which one reaches the height of heaven.

Behold, he says, you have made my days old. Another version has: You have made my days palaestae. If with the Seventy we take the days as 'old', we understand them as days spent according to the old man. But our old man has been nailed to the cross; so the old day too has passed, and the new has come. For the day of man is one thing, and the day of Christ another, the day which Abraham saw and rejoiced, of which David too says:

This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and be glad in it. So the holy man exults in the day of the Lord, in the new day on which the Lord God has shone upon us and given those who are remade a new light, an innocent and unimpaired life. Therefore the just man, secure in the new light and the grace of God, says: I will have a new heaven and a new earth and a new light. For there no lamp will shine, nor the light of the sun or of the moon, but the Lord will give light over his people. Those things, then, I have desired, those I have longed for, and so I have not sought the day of man.

But if we take the days as palaestae, we understand from the name that they are full of contest and toil, since palaestae is the name for wrestlers who wrestle in the games for the crown. So, since our wrestling too is not only against flesh and blood but also against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, our days,

that is, the days of this life, are spent in toil and sorrow. Hence later on he also says: Our years were spun out like a spider's web. The days of our years are seventy years in all, and if in the strong, eighty years, and most of them toil and sorrow. Hence the apostle Paul too labored more abundantly than the other apostles, so that by contending lawfully he might reach the crown he longed for.

Yet the measures of architects are also said to be called palaestae: with them buildings are measured to reckon the size of the structure or the extent of the space, and also the site where the buildings are to be placed. And God spoke through Isaiah: Who has measured the water in his hand, and heaven with his palm, and the whole earth with closed hand? Who has set the mountains in a balance? So let us see whether this word should perhaps be taken in this sense: that God knows the days of all. To him nothing is beyond measure; he grasps all things by a kind of measure of his knowledge; to him nothing is beyond reckoning, nothing unexamined and uncounted. He it is who says: But even the hairs of your head are all numbered.

This, then, is what the prophet says: Behold, you know my days; my daily acts do not escape you; you have set my sins before your eyes, and therefore my substance is as nothing before you. For what is man, that you are mindful of him? Man has become like vanity, man is in sin. If he has some uprightness and virtue, he is rightly ranked above the other earthly creatures and excels in the sight of the animals over which he is set, but in the sight of God his substance is as nothing. Hence elsewhere too he says: For no living man shall be justified in your sight. Symmachus expressed this more plainly, saying: And my life is as nothing before you.

There are some, however, who think the days are called short, because Symmachus put spithamas. A spithame is a span. And since God is said to have measured heaven with his span, a palm or span being the part of the hand of one who measures something and grasps it, they suppose the days are so named as being short. Yet, as we said above, the knowledge of God can be understood through measure, and this heavenly knowledge means that all things were made to measure. So the prophet's days can be understood not as short but as great, since God measured them with the span with which he measured heaven.

For he would not have called the days of his life short who afterwards said: Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged. Unless perhaps it is because, on account of men's sins, God made the days of this life shorter: formerly it stretched to nine hundred and to seven hundred years, and now it is confined within the course of a hundred years. So it should be understood thus: Behold, you know my days, which are subject to sin. For the days of this life, which is subject to sin, are short, but the days of eternal life are without end.

Or else it may be understood thus (for it is our part to seek the truth by argument, yours to choose which view to follow): Lest sin should grow, he says, you have shortened the days of the human life we live on this earth. And yet, though in this short course of life the swiftness of death brings an earlier end to sins, my substance is as nothing before you. For although we were made in the image and likeness of God, yet while we are placed in this body a certain earthly contagion weighs us down. It would not weigh us down if, when we put on grace, we chose to strip off the old man rather than to put the new on over him;

for the old man stripped off would cause us less toil than the old man with the new put on over him. What we strip off we cast away; what we put something on over, we enclose. And so we groan and labor until this mortal garment of the old man, made subject to error, is swallowed up by the newness of its spiritual life. In the same way, if a great deal of honey is poured over poison, the venom is destroyed only with difficulty and very late; and even much water struggles a long while with the gall of poison if one does not spit the poison out but swallows it. Therefore penance is laborious and grace is sweet, because where there is grace sin is stripped off, and where there is penance it is swallowed up: in the one case it is forgiven, in the other it is hidden. And so it is written: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered.

And he paused a little, groaning over the misery of the human condition, because he had said: Nevertheless all things are vanity, every living man. And after the diapsalma, taking breath again, he says: Although man walks in the image of God, yet he is troubled in vain; he lays up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it. See how he first softened the harshness of his statement, and then completed the reasoning of his words. He softened it by saying that man walks in the image of God.

Blessed are you, man, who walk by faith in the likeness of God: blessed because you have faith, more blessed still if you had no avarice. The eternal good of the mind is one thing, the vain fire of carnal desire another; for faith fights for God, avarice for the tempter. Avarice heaps up what benefits itself, faith what profits others. What, then, is so vain as not to know for which heir one is toiling? For who knows whether a son or one's own grandson will survive? Often the heir named in the will dies an untimely death and goes to the grave before the testator; or

he survives and devours the inheritance, or squanders it in luxury, or in his utter folly fails to keep it, or loses it by proscription. So if you see someone zealously amassing riches, you will say: He is troubled in vain; he lays up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it. For he cannot take what he owns with him, and when he dies he will leave his riches to others. Often an enemy and an ingrate succeeds him, and the successor mocks his predecessor: those whom the one loved the other persecutes, those whom the one brought up the other sells.

The Greek, however, does not have 'in the image of God', but only 'in the image'. In what image, then, does man walk? Surely in that image to whose likeness he was made, that is, to the image of God; and the image of God is Christ, who is the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance. Christ, then, is the image of the Holy One. This image came to earth for the image [?], so that we might no longer walk in shadow but in the image;

for he who follows the gospel walks in Christ. That is why he says to his disciple: Get behind me, so that you may follow me. That is why the Jewish people went astray: because they walked in shadow. And that is why the Christian people do not go astray: because they walk in the image, with the sun of justice shining upon them. It is a good image, not formed in the wax of a bright painting, but expressed by the fullness of the Godhead.

In this image the Father and the Son are seen together, because the unity of the working of both shines forth in it. Although Christ has already risen, his image is still shown to us in the gospel. I read that he raised Lazarus, and I believe it was the work of the Father and of the Son: the Son called, the Father heard, Lazarus walked. I read that the demons confessed him; they also confessed the Father, since they entreated the Son of God, and they were cast out in him or through him, as it is written: But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?

First, then, the shadow went before; the image followed; the truth will come. The shadow is in the law, the image in the gospel, the truth in heaven. The shadow of the gospel and of the gathering of the church was in the law; the image of the truth to come is in the gospel; the truth is in the judgment of God. So the things now celebrated in the church were foreshadowed in the words of the prophets: a shadow in the flood, a shadow in the Red Sea when our fathers were baptized in the cloud and in the sea, a shadow in the rock that poured out water and followed the people.

Was not the sacrament of this most holy mystery present there in shadow? Was not the water from the rock, like blood from Christ, a shadow? For Christ followed the peoples who fled from him, so that they might drink and not thirst, be redeemed and not perish. But now the shadow of the night and darkness of the Jews has departed, and the day of the church has drawn near. We now see good things through the image, and we hold the good things of the image. We have seen the high priest coming to us; we have seen and heard him offering his blood for us.

We priests follow as best we can, so as to offer sacrifice for the people. Though weak in merit, we are made honorable by the sacrifice. For although Christ is not now seen to offer, yet he himself is offered on earth, because the body of Christ is offered. Indeed, he himself is shown to offer in us, for it is his word that sanctifies the sacrifice that is offered. He himself stands by the Father as our advocate, but now we do not see him. We shall see him then, when the image has passed away and the truth has come. Then the things that are perfect will be seen no longer through a mirror but face to face.

Ascend, then, O man, into heaven, and you will see those things of which there was a shadow or an image here. You will see them not in part, not in a riddle, but in their fullness; not under a veil, but in the light. You will see the true light, the eternal and everlasting priest, whose images you saw here: Peter, Paul, John, James, Matthew, Thomas. You will see the perfect man, no longer in an image but in truth. For as is the heavenly one, so also are those who are heavenly: they too will surely be in glory and beauty, in the grace of the resurrection, no longer in the body of death and the ugliness of corruption.

See that you do not carry the image of the earthly into the place where the light of heavenly things shines. Here in this world, if anyone keeps the images of a tyrant who has already been defeated and has perished, he is rightly condemned. Then how can you bring the image of the enemy and adversary into the city of the true emperor, unless you want the emperor himself to condemn you? And if you try to carry in the image of the earthly, the prince of this world will challenge you. He will say: 'This image is mine, and what you are offering is mine.' What will you do, caught in the act, when he says to you: 'Greed is mine, ambition is mine, riches are mine, and I recognize their image in you'?

For he is both adversary and defender. But if you are like Jacob, you will say to Laban, who disguises himself as an angel of light: 'See whether you find anything of yours with me.' Then he will search, and finding nothing he will go away refuted, because you have hidden and wiped out every idol of the vices. Blessed is the one who can say: 'The prince of this world will come, and he will find nothing of his in me.' For he seeks what is his own, not what is Christ's. So if you follow Christ, do not reach for riches you do not have, and do not increase the riches you do have. Instead, let the poor man find that you are rich for his sake.

Bring the needy into your house, break bread for the hungry and clothe the naked, so that a treasure may be stored up for you in heaven which will pass over with you. Christ became poor though he was rich, so that by his poverty he might make us rich. So do not be troubled in vain over riches. Do not be roused from sleep to think how you may keep your money and increase your wealth. Do not go out by night and keep watch at the judge's house so that you can seize what belongs to others, bring a lawsuit against the poor, or live in fear of the tax collector. That disquiet is vain.

And therefore the righteous man said: 'And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is before you.' Christ is our hope and our patience. He has become our redemption, he is our expectation, so that each of us may say: 'Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he looked upon me.' Look upon us, then, in your judgment, and let your mercy look upon us, so that we who have no confidence in our own merit may be set free by your mercy, for in your power lies the substance of our soul and of our life. And therefore let us not fear the death of the body, but him who can either save or destroy our soul. The soul's substance is virtue, which God poured into human hearts after his own likeness.

Whoever, then, possesses this substance of his soul says: 'Deliver me from all my iniquities.' The one who prays to be released from all his iniquities is not confessing a lapse into a single crime. For he knows that unless the Lord forgives, no one born under sin can be saved, since the very inheritance of a guilty condition has bound him to guilt.

'You have made me,' he says, 'a reproach to the fool.' Who is the fool, if not the one who commits sin and chooses evil over good? Therefore the author of sins is himself more of a fool than his servant.

So when we sin, we are handed over to the adversary as a reproach, so that like an enemy he may accuse and betray us on the day of judgment. Let us therefore take up the reproach of Christ's cross, which Moses took up and preferred to the royal treasures of Egypt. That is why he was not handed over to the fool as a reproach. Other manuscripts read: 'Do not make me a reproach to the fool.' But it is rather David's custom to confess his own reproaches and sins, and not to blush at his sins and reproaches, since he knows that in confession there is pardon, and in condemning one's own sin there is righteousness.

This meaning is made plain by what follows, for he added: 'I was mute and did not open my mouth, because you made me.' That is: 'You made me a reproach to the fool; that is why I was mute and did not open my mouth, so that I would not incur greater sins. I recognized your will: that I should blush for a time and afterward be saved by asking for pardon.' So reproach is sometimes beneficial, just as even the destruction of the flesh is beneficial, as the apostle testifies when he says: 'I have handed him over for the destruction of the

flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.' David himself also testified that reproach is beneficial, when he said to Abishai: 'Let the Benjaminite curse me, for the Lord has told him to, so that he may see my humiliation, and the Lord will repay me with good for this cursing.' And indeed the Lord saw his reproach, as he went along weeping, barefoot and with his head covered, and he took his reproach away. It is clear, then, that reproach comes from the Lord, and that it is more beneficial to endure reproach than to drive it off. For David, when he was made a reproach, fled and was humbled; he made amends to the Lord with bare feet; he did not strike back at the man who threw stones; he did not allow vengeance on the man who cursed him; and after this he was restored to his kingdom intact. And then victory followed.

So reproach is beneficial. But what does he mean when he adds: 'because you made me'? Is he not saying that he was mute and did not open his mouth because he recognized the Lord's will, and that he therefore endured patiently, so that satisfaction might be made to the Lord for his sin through reproach?

Hence he also added: 'Remove my blows from me.' How is this consistent? In the previous psalm he offered himself to the scourges; here he asks that the scourges be removed from him. Surely this is because he has already paid, from the Lord's hand, double for his sins, by blushing for them and by enduring reproaches. The scourges are the compunctions of his heart and of his thoughts; they are also the scourges of rebukes. Let us consider, however, whether he said that the substance of his soul is before God for this reason: that the adversary could not attack it unless he had received power from the Lord. For what the Lord has made, he also protects.

Indeed, an angel stands round about a man to shield him, so that no one may harm him. The angel does not withdraw unless the Lord orders it, so that his athlete may fight his contest. So, as being the Lord's own substance, the soul trusts that pardon for its iniquities can be granted by its creator, and it asks for this because it knows that its maker is merciful.

Next, since he has been made a reproach, he does not resist, but allows the sinner to stand against him. And the conscience of his substance, which is good, keeps silent, and it can curb the fierceness of the body, so that virtue may take its place and guilt be laid aside. Finally, because he was made by the Lord, he confidently reckons that his sin can be forgiven him all the sooner, since he has been able to endure the strength of the Lord's hand.

And this certainly belongs to a good substance, even though he says that he failed under the strength of the Lord's hand. A strong hand heals as quickly as it strikes hard; a hand that is strong to wound is strong to heal. That is why he himself says: 'I will strike and I will heal,' so that the one who has come through healed does not even remember the wound. Indeed, this hand of the Lord took everything away from holy Job

and restored everything, and even increased it all abundantly, so that he got back double what he had lost. And do not be troubled that he said he failed. There is such a thing as failing and rising stronger, for the Lord upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are crushed, and whoever is lifted up rises with strength. Paul failed under the strength of this hand: the persecutor fell, and a preacher of the gospel rose up. This is what he means by: 'Under the strength of your hand I failed.'

And he added: 'With rebukes for iniquity you have instructed man, and you have made his soul waste away like a spider.' The Greek has ὑπὲρ ἀνομίας, that is, 'for iniquity', and constructed the whole verse so that the phrase applies to both parts (κατὰ κοινοῦ), namely: 'With rebukes for iniquity you have instructed man.' That is why the Wise Man said: 'Who will give me scourges for my thoughts and a seal for my lips?', so that he might scourge his heart with his own thoughts and seal his lips, and so both

lessen his old sins and not renew them by speaking further, and so that, instructed by his own rebukes, he might take up the exercises of virtue. The soul wastes away when sin is diminished; or rather, when the soul wastes away, guilt is laid aside. It grows fat when sins are heaped up. That is why the Lord says of sinners: 'My spirit will not remain in them for ever, because they are flesh,' and elsewhere Scripture says: 'The heart of this people has grown fat.' That is also why Jeremiah first saw a rod of the nut tree and then a boiling pot, so that the soul of the prophet as he began might waste away, that guilt might depart and grace come in.

But why first the rod and then the pot? Because whoever is not corrected by the rod is thrown into the pot, to burn and waste away. And therefore it is said to the prophet Ezekiel as well: 'Take a pan for yourself, and you will take on the iniquities of the house of Israel and bring them to an end; and they will waste away,' he says, 'in their iniquities.' And elsewhere in the same book the Lord says: 'But I will make a great firebrand, and I will heap up the wood and kindle the fire, so that the flesh may melt and the broth be boiled down.'

These testimonies signify that the souls of the faithless waste away when fire is applied, so that they shed a kind of fatty fluid of carnal grossness. The souls of sinners, then, are thrown into the pan, so that a certain flesh of sin may drain away, which had clouded over the vigor of the soul and mind and had soaked the soul, as if in a kind of broth, with certain enticements of desire. So pans of a sort await us. Let us therefore crush our heart here, so that it may become fine and lay aside all hardness and a kind of greasiness of carnal lard.

This is what will be suffered by those who lived in luxury in this life and believed, after the Jewish manner, that they ought to practice shameful sport rather than any works of virtue. For Jacob grew fat and became thick and rose up to play, and that play led him away from the truth of faith into the error of faithlessness. Rightly, then, did Paul discipline his body, so as not to feed the flesh of sin; for by luxury we make our members instruments of sin, but by sobriety instruments of righteousness. So it is not nature that sins, but fault.

Nor again should we pursue empty and vain things, so that we are not judged to be weaving a spider's web, since sins can have no lasting substance. So when you see people eager to enlarge their estates, heap up power and grasp after splendor, you will say what Isaiah said: 'These men weave a spider's web in all things,' a web of a single day, which cannot last but is quickly torn, and all its work comes undone; for it is not set on any solid support but hangs in empty air. Nothing slack, nothing soft befits a true soldier of Christ; for see, those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings.

All greedy people think themselves clever and industrious. What is more clever, what more diligent, than the spider, which is always intent on its work day and night and produces its garment without any cost or expense? But everything it makes is vain. So it is with every man who does not build his work on the foundation of Christ. He too is troubled in vain night and day, since, like the spider, he is often entangled in the ruin of his own work in the very midst of his wicked labors.

And therefore the wise man, who recognizes the vanity of this world, does not pray for a long tenancy of this life. He hastens toward eternal things and longs to be released from the toil and pain of this body, as the prophet is known to have desired when he said: 'Hear my prayer, O Lord, and my supplication; give ear to my tears. Do not be silent toward me, for I am a newcomer with you on the earth, and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were.'

An inhabitant is one thing, a newcomer another, a sojourner another. An inhabitant belongs to the place and lives in the place of his birth; a newcomer has come from somewhere else; a sojourner lives somewhere for a time and moves on as the years change. So this is what David means: 'I am a stranger with you while I am on earth; I am not now an inhabitant of your paradise.' He explained this himself by adding: 'and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were.' The apostle Paul also made this plain when he declared that while we are in the body we are on pilgrimage away from the Lord, because, although faith is in us, we walk by faith and not by sight, that is, not face to face as if present; for we still walk in a riddle, not in the truth.

Then he added: 'We are bold, therefore, and confident, and would rather be on pilgrimage away from the body and be present with the Lord.' 'We are bold' is a word of faith's trust in God, not of rashness. And 'we are confident' means: we assent willingly and longingly. It is not that we rest the authority of fuller knowledge chiefly on our own judgment and so wish what we desire to be true; rather we desire to draw near to the Lord, from whom the distance between things to come and things present seems to separate us. So we are bold to be present, 'and therefore,' he says, 'we strive.' You recognize the word of one who still wishes to arrive, not of one who has already arrived. So what this saying shows is desire, not achievement.

Question, then, the very desire behind his words; or rather, listen to him speaking, or better, listen to him in his uncertainty, when he says: 'Therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him': absent as yet by faith, present by sight. From this it can also be understood that, both while we are placed here and when we are there, we desire to please our judge, who is also the redeemer of our souls. For we must stand before him by sight, so that each of us may receive the reward of his works by a fitting allotment: the righteous in rest

or the wicked in affliction. So he sheds tears because, having come to earth as a newcomer, he lingers here, cut off from his homeland and held back in a long exile. Picture for me now Adam, cast out of paradise and banished to an outpost, gazing at the place from which he was thrown down, weeping bitterly because he remembers what he lost and from what height he fell. And therefore let us give thanks to God, who has freed us from perpetual exile by opening the door through which we may return to our homeland. That is why the apostle dared to say: 'So you are no longer newcomers and pilgrims, but you are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God's household.'

Wishing to regain this before Christ came into the world, David said: 'Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart and am no more.' That is: forgive me here, where I sinned. Unless you forgive me here, I will not be able to find the rest of forgiveness there. For what remains bound on earth will remain bound in heaven, and what has been loosed on earth will be loosed in heaven. For the prophet, as a herald of the Church that was to be gathered, foresaw by the spirit of the gospel the Lord's acts of pardon, and the Lord revealed to him what was to be commanded

to the apostles. Indeed, this was the old ruling: that whoever had bound himself on earth would depart from the body in chains. Therefore the Lord gave the apostles the just power of forgiving sins, which had formerly belonged to his own judgment, so that sins which ought to be loosed would not remain bound for long. Listen to him saying: 'I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven as well, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven as well.' 'I will give you,' he says, 'the keys of the kingdom of heaven,' so that you may both loose and bind. Novatian did not listen to this; the Church of God listened. That is why he remains in his fall and we in forgiveness, he in impenitence and we in grace. What is said to Peter is said to the apostles.

We do not usurp a power; we serve a command. Otherwise, when the Lord comes later and finds bound those who ought to have been loosed, he may be angry with the steward who kept bound the servants whom the Lord had ordered to be loosed. For he says that the one who knew his master's will and did not act according to his will shall receive many blows, while the one who did not know and did things deserving blows shall receive fewer.

Rightly, then, does David ask to be forgiven, for he knew that this was not granted to the priests after the order of Aaron but was reserved for the gospel. So whoever is not forgiven is in exile, and remains in the hardship of pilgrimage. It is here, then, that pardon must be sought; for it is here that it was said: 'Blessed are you who weep, for you shall laugh.' Here is the place to ask for pardon. Let us therefore weep on earth, so that we may deserve forgiveness.

Unless sin has been forgiven here, we will have no rest; if there is no rest, there will be no eternal life; if there is no eternal life, we will not exist. That is why he asks to be forgiven before he departs, so that he may exist. 'For if it is not forgiven,' he says, 'I will not be with those who are, with those who are found worthy to ascend into paradise.' But whoever is not will be consumed with those who go down into the pit, as one left behind in chains and prison.

So he does not say 'I will be no more' as a final verdict, since elsewhere he says: 'I will sing to you on the harp, O God, Holy One of Israel. My lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed.' So he is confident of redemption. And listen to him saying elsewhere: 'I will please the Lord in the land of the living.' So he who is confident that he will please will exist. It can also be understood this way, since he said: 'I am a newcomer with you on the earth, and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were,' and therefore: forgive me, so that I may cease to be a pilgrim;

release me from the exile to which I have been banished. If you release me before I depart from here, I will no longer be an exile and a pilgrim. For when you have forgiven me, I will not be a pilgrim, but I will be a fellow citizen of your saints; I will be with my fathers, who were once pilgrims themselves but are now citizens. I will be a member of God's household, so that I may not fear punishment, but may be found worthy of grace through our Lord Jesus, with whom to you be praise, honor, glory and everlasting power, with the Holy Spirit, from all ages, now and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.
EXPOSITION OF PSALM 39
