In the preceding psalms he preached repentance, and then spoke of his own patience and of man's disquiet. But in the thirty-ninth psalm he proclaims the new testament. For whoever repents of his evil deeds is waiting. Yet the mark of the perfect is not to be waiting but to have waited, for no one will be saved except the one who perseveres to the end.

That is why he added: 'Waiting, I waited for the Lord.' Where can this rightly be said if not in the gospel? In it the one who was awaited has now come to us. In it the shadow of the law no longer darkens our sight; instead the truth shines, because Christ has shed his light. He heard the prayer of his own and brought us up out of the pit of misery and out of the miry clay, where we were held fast, sunk in the whirlpool of our sins. Our whole person was stuck there, and our mind could not pull itself free, buried as it was under the stain of many crimes.

Thanks be, then, to the Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, our redeemer, who came down from heaven to forgive us all our sins. He came to rescue us from the pit and slime of this world, from a kind of muddy swamp of the earth, and from the body of this death, and to set the inner footsteps of our soul firmly in his own flesh, so that, made firm in the word of God and set free through the cross of the Lord's body, we may now walk no longer in the reproach of disgrace but in the forgiveness of sin.

So, made firm and rooted in Christ, he recalls that his feet have been set upon a rock. That is why the apostle says: 'They drank from the rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.' He is a rock because he follows the thirsty and steadies those who are slipping, so that the thirsty may not lack water nor the slipping a firm support.

So, Lord Jesus, at last you came to me as I waited. You directed my steps in the gospel, and put into my mouth a new song, which is the new testament. Now we sing with joy a hymn to our God, because we have come to know the precepts of new virtues: to leave all that is ours in order to follow Christ, and to love our enemies. We have also taken in a new way of life, so that we offer prayers to the Lord for those who persecute us. See, we bless those who curse us; we do not know how to boast of our works or to hide our sins; and like the angels we even refuse marriage.

Why say more? From that wretched sinner a blessed man has been made, who no longer looks to the varied vanities of this world. For this whole world is vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, as the wise Solomon said. What is it but vanity to pursue things that cannot last and all pass away like a shadow? And by 'false madnesses' are meant the battles of wars, in which so much blood has been shed for the sake of a temporal possession; or the factional quarrels of the theater; or the frenzied passions of the circus; or the deadly teaching of heretics; or the feigned gestures and contrived words of false prophets, imitating heavenly oracles. For so the prophet said: 'Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked to vanities and false madnesses.'

So there are also true madnesses, perhaps those of the prophets, who prophesied in ecstasy, filled with the Spirit of God, so that to some they seemed to be mad. For, heedless of their own safety, they often ran among the peoples naked and barefoot, like holy Isaiah, crying out not what they themselves wished, but what they were commanded by the Lord. From these things, then, it is understood that the remedy of salvation has flowed in upon us, because the one who was awaited is here.

Adam, cast out of paradise, waited for him, so that he might be freed from his long exile. He waited for him in righteous Noah, who was kept back as the seed of those to come, so that from him the seeds of righteousness might spring up among men. He thought that the one who had

been found worthy to survive the flood was himself the author of the common salvation, himself the prince of wisdom, who had tended the vine and become drunk with its fruit. For what is the vine but wisdom? So David, the interpreter of the heavenly oracle, revealed to us when he said: "Your wife is like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house." This was because in Noah there was the fullness of wisdom that was awaited in Christ. Christ, filled with a new mystery of wisdom, which eye has not seen nor ear heard, hastened to bring us an unheard-of mystery: he would lie naked and pour out unheard-of cups of overflowing wisdom, so that, forgetting what lay behind, we might rise again to new ways and to the new sobriety of eternal life. Thus through the foolishness of preaching God would be acknowledged, whom this world did not know through wisdom.

And so, in that figure of the father asleep and uncovered, the one who laughed at the foolishness was cursed, while those who showed reverence obtained the grace of blessing. Therefore those who believe that the death of the only-begotten Son of God, the Father and Creator of all, should be thrown up against our faith as a stumbling block or a reproach are held bound by the chains of their sins to the endless misery of the curse; but those who accept that death as the release of the whole human race are upheld by the protection of eternal power. For the cross of Christ is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks, as the Apostle said, but to us who believe in our Lord it is the power and wisdom of God.

He was awaited in Moses, when Moses divided and crossed the waves of the sea and opened through the billows a path on foot, impossible for human strength; when the rock followed and poured out water to satisfy the inmost parts of the thirsting fathers in the middle of the desert.

He was awaited also in Aaron, the chief of the priests, who stood between the living and the dead, and set up the serpent against the plague of death, so that destruction might not pass from the corpses of the dead to the living. For what is so proper to Christ as to stand as advocate for the peoples before God the Father, to offer his own death for all, to drive back slaughter, and to restore life to those about to perish?

He was awaited also in Joshua son of Nun, and he certainly came, for Joshua received both his power and his name, so that he might lead the people into the land of promise and truly be called by the name Jesus. He dried up the streams, turned the waters back to their source, and made the sun stand still until he had completed the victory in power. But that was still a figure, not the truth. Then at last the true commander of the heavenly host shone forth, and Joshua son of Nun worshipped him, although he had not yet appeared truly in the body but had still come only in figure.

When, then, did the true one come? Hear him saying: "I have proclaimed and spoken; they are multiplied beyond number. Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me. Then I said: Behold, I come; at the head of the book it is written of me; I have willed to do your will, my God." What could be clearer than that the true Jesus came to us with the gift of his gospel? He spoke, and countless peoples of believers were gathered, where before hardly a few believed one by one. He came in the flesh, and the sacrifice of the Jews ceased, the offering for sin ceased, because the one who forgives sins had come. The remedy of the law was not needed where the author of the law was present.

"Then I said: Behold, I come; at the head of the book it is written of me." It is indeed written of Christ at the beginning of the Old Testament that he would come to do the will of God the Father in the redemption of mankind, where it is written that God formed Eve, as a figure of the Church, to be a help to man. For what can be our protection in this weakness of the body and the turmoil

of this world except the grace of the Church alone, by which we are redeemed, and our faith, by which we live? At the head of the book it is written: "Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh." Who it is that spoke, and of whom this mystery is, hear him saying: "This is a great mystery, and I say it of Christ and the Church." Hence he also admonishes that a man should love his wife as Christ loves the Church, since we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. What greater salvation, then, than to be with Christ and to cleave to him in a kind of unity of body, in whom there is no stain nor any filth of sin?

It is written at the head of the book that the sacrifice of righteous Abel pleased God, while the offering of the fratricide displeased him. Did not the Lord Jesus plainly signify that he himself was to be offered for us, so that in his passion he might consecrate the grace of a new sacrifice and abolish the rite of a murderous people? And what could be more explicit than that the son was offered by the holy patriarch and a ram was sacrificed? Did this not plainly show that it was human flesh, which is common to all earthly living things, and not the divinity of the only-begotten Son of God, that would be subject to the sacred wound of the passion?

It is written at the head of the book that a man would come who would command the heavenly powers. This was fulfilled when the Lord Jesus came to earth and angels ministered to him, as he himself deigned to say: "Hereafter you will see the heavens opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man."

It is written at the head of the book: "You shall have a lamb without blemish, clean, full-grown, a male of one year, and the whole congregation shall kill it." Who this lamb is you have heard from the one who said: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world." This is he who was killed by the whole people of the Jews, whom they still pursue with hostile hatred. And indeed he had to die for all, so that in his cross there might be forgiveness of sins and his blood might wash away the defilements of the world. But woe to those who denied the author of their own salvation! "You have taken counsel," he says, "but not through me." How could he approve the murder when he did not approve the counsel? And yet how great his kindness! He shrank from their counsel, yet if they turned back he did not refuse them the remedy.

It is written, moreover, not only at the head but throughout the whole compass of the law, that a man would come to preserve the human race who would will all that God wills. From this you understand that he who is of the same will is of the same divinity. Hence also he came willingly to the sacrifice of the passion, and rightly foretold: "Willingly will I sacrifice to you."

But perhaps you will say: "How then did he say in the gospel, 'Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me; yet not as I will, but as you will'?" There seems to be a difference of will. But we understand that what is expressed according to the unity of the Godhead, where he says, "I and the Father are one," is one thing; and what he spoke according to human feeling is another. By this he taught man that he ought to be cautious and not

presume what he cannot easily fulfil, lest, while seeking a reward, he fall into sacrilege. Hence he says: "When they persecute you in this city, flee to another." Rightly, therefore, here too, when he was about to undergo the passion of the body, he began to be sorrowful and troubled, and taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he first said, "My soul is sorrowful," and afterwards added, "Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation; the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." You see that everywhere he speaks as a man, prays as a man, is sorrowful as a man, and as a man said, "My Father, if it is possible." What, after all, is impossible for God? But it belongs to man

to doubt, and to God to confirm. That is why he took with him the more eager ones, as chosen witnesses of his final judgment, who would recognize the mystery of his words. Indeed, the others were sleeping; these alone kept watch with faithful minds. Hence also, through Jeremiah, before he had yet taken a body, he himself says: "I was led like a lamb, and I did not know." What is there that the wisdom of God, which is always in the secret place of the Father, does not know? And that is why the Son of God has declared all things, because he is himself the wisdom of God the Father.

How did he foreknow that he would be led like a lamb, and yet say he did not know where he was being led? Or how, earlier, did he say through the mouth of David himself: "God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" How is the Son forsaken by the Father, who says, "And I am not alone, for the Father is with me," and elsewhere, "I was handed over and did not go out," and elsewhere, "I arose and am still with you"? Unless you are to notice that he is expressing the feeling of men, who think, when they are in danger, that they have been forsaken by their Lord.

Then hear what follows: "Far from my salvation," he says, "are the words of my transgressions." That is: the words of transgressions are one thing, the mysteries of eternal salvation another. Words do not prejudice power; the divine substance is upheld by its own strength. A man is seen, a man is heard; God is recognized in the works. And yet of this man it is said: "He is a man, and who shall know him?" What does "who" mean? Not that no one will, but that it is someone rare, someone wise, as in: "Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?" and "Who

is wise and will understand these things?" And elsewhere: "The senseless man will not know, and the fool will not understand these things." You too, then, when you read the gospel, recognize what you read as a wise man and not as a fool; let the brightness of eternal wisdom enlighten you. They are words indeed, but they themselves cleanse, they themselves enlighten, they themselves strengthen, they themselves give life. Hence Peter says: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we will not leave you."

Then, so that we should notice that he speaks as a man, a little later he said: "Behold, the hour draws near when the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners." And to Judas, as he kissed him, he said: "Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?" That is: do you pour poison into a kiss, through which the grace of love is poured out, a kiss that is the token of holy peace, a kiss by which faithful friendship is sealed, a kiss by which holy faith is signed? With this kiss, then, do you hand over to danger one whom, because of the exchange of a kiss, you ought

to revere? And do you, a man, hand over the Son of Man, who came down from heaven for the salvation of men? For so it is written: "The Son of Man who is in heaven is the one who came down from heaven." Do you hand over the Son of Man who made you, a sinner, into an apostle? Do you hand over the Son of Man who came to wash away the sins of all in his own blood? I do not refuse the kiss; see to it yourself, you who have violated the sanctity of the kiss. Or have you not read that the wounds of a friend are better than the willing kisses of an enemy? Not without reason was Judas struck by the weapon of such great condescension, a heavier

blow than if a thunderbolt had struck him. Indeed, he who betrayed the Lord's majesty could not bear his patience, so much so that the guilt of so great a crime could not be washed from him. So he went away and returned the money; that is, he condemned his own avarice as the cause of such great impiety, and gave back the price of treachery to the synagogue. The betrayer is not excused, for he could find no place for repentance; but the sacrilege of the Jews is made worse, since they are convicted even by the words of the betrayer. He acknowledged his crime, saying that he had betrayed innocent blood; they both took back the price of the crime and pursued the Prince of righteousness with fiercer zeal.

Therefore, to the everlasting condemnation of all these, the thief who was crucified is set free, because he recognized Christ in his own torments, whom they did not recognize in his benefits, and he confessed his sin to Christ, who knew how to forgive; for on his cross he saw in his mind the kingdom of the Lord, which Judas could not see at Christ's supper.

Therefore the thief's prayer was followed by a heavenly voice such as this: "Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." You were exulting, dragon, because you had taken an apostle away from Christ; but you have lost more than you took, now that you see a thief carried over into paradise. There is no one who can be shut out, when a thief, your own servant, has been received and has reached the place from which you yourself were cast down.

We have added these things on account of that little verse in which he said, "I have willed to do your will, my God"; that is: "I have one will of divinity with you, Father; and because there is one will, there is one substance and the inseparable majesty and power of the Trinity." But the voice of the flesh is different, and yet it too consented to the will of God, saying, "Not what I will, but what you will," and elsewhere, "If this cannot pass unless I

drink it, your will be done." To fear death is a common feeling, and Christ took it on in order to crucify it, as he also crucified the flesh; for he struggled for me, so that he might conquer for me. Although Christ's flesh was strong and not subject to sin, yet he took on sins; he took on weakness, though he had nothing in himself to grieve over. Then hear him saying:

"For he grieves for us, until he brings forth judgment in truth." For he did not take on some other flesh, but this one, as the Apostle teaches, saying: "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal immortality." Although he was born of a virgin and of the Holy Spirit, yet he is the son of man, because the virgin was human. And therefore what is born of the flesh is flesh, and he who is born of man is called man: the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.

For this reason he, being incorruptible, took on this flesh in order to make it incorruptible, and, being immortal, in order to make it immortal. If anyone, then, follows him, he will put on immortality; if anyone does his will, he will not die for ever, but Christ will say to him: "Today you will be with me in paradise." What does "today" mean? That is: "You have passed out of the night; you will be with me in the light.

Do not fear the darkness, you whom eternal light has received." He also added beautifully, "You will be with me in paradise"; that is: "Do not doubt about the flesh; you have seen me too in the flesh. Do not fear that you also may fall from paradise as Adam fell, but hear that you will be with me, in whose presence you cannot fall."

The flesh had fallen in paradise before it was taken up by Christ. You will be received there where he too is who received it, who did not lie when he said: "I will that where I am, they also may be with me." The shepherd will not leave his flocks, though you can no longer fear the wolf in paradise, of whom it was said: "I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven." Therefore, before the consummation, the adversary is cast down into the fire and bound with everlasting chains, so that you need no longer fear any snares.

Adam, too, was deceived by the serpent so that he fell, and he was swayed by his wife. Therefore there will no longer be marriages in paradise, but all will be without the celebration of weddings, like the angels in heaven. God had not said to Adam, "You will be with me," because he knew that he would fall, so as to be redeemed by Christ. Happy fall, which is repaired for the better! Therefore the loving shepherd, the good merchant, no longer abandons his flock and his own goods. There will indeed still be, even in paradise, a fight of the angels with the serpent until he is cast down; but he who is with Christ will have nothing to fear.

Adam was not with Christ when he was deceived; for if he had been with Christ and had remained in his command, he certainly could not have perished. He did not remain in Christ, because he did not abide in his word. Hear, then, who remains in Christ: "If you remain in me," he says, "and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you wish and it will be done for you," and further on: "If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love." Do you want to know that Adam was not with Christ? The Lord said to him: "Adam, where are you?"

He who seeks him as one absent would surely not have said "Where are you?" if he had known that he remained in him. But let us hear who made him absent: "They both hid themselves," it says, "from the face of the Lord." Christ sees all, but whoever hides himself is hidden, since whoever does not know will not be known; for the Lord knows those who are

his own. He wants all whom he has made and created to be his own. O man, would that you did not flee and hide yourself from Christ! He seeks even those who flee, and does not want those who hide to perish, but cries out, saying: "Adam, where are you?" That is: "Man, where are you? I placed you in the light; you have sought out darkness."

So in paradise, where it is always morning, evening came, since all sins are darkness. That is why you have the words: "They heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise toward evening." At the same time recognize the mystery: in the morning you went astray; toward evening you are set free. For how can there be evening where Christ is?

For although his throne is above the heaven of heavens, yet Christ is in his saints. How then can there be evening where God is, since God is light? So it was that a light shone around Saul on the road when Christ met him, and the persecutor was blinded by the shining light of God. Why, then, was he blinded, except that he had not recognized Christ? For if he had known the Lord of light, he would not have lost the light of his eyes. And indeed, when he recognized him, he received it back. It is evidence that he did not know Christ that, on hearing the voice, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" he answered, "Who are you, Lord?" He would not have asked who he was if he had known.

Hence the Lord also says to him as to one who does not know: "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. It is hard for you to kick against the goad." And he said: "Lord, what must I do?" See how fittingly each plays his part. The physician threatens in order to correct, and holds fast in order to heal. The sick man first asks who the physician is, whether he is capable, someone by whom he can expect to be healed; when he has heard who the author of the medicine is, he asks for the remedy and finds health. Then, when Ananias came to him, not only was his blindness driven out, but he also received a light he had not had, so that he might see Christ, whom he had not seen before.

But let us look at what follows, though first repeating the little verse that seems to have been discussed: "Behold, I come; I have willed to do your will, my God, and your law in the midst of my heart. I have proclaimed your righteousness well in the great assembly; behold, I will not restrain my lips. Lord, you have known your righteousness; I have not hidden it in my heart."

From the preceding verse, then, we understand: "Behold, I come: not only will I do your will, but I will also do your law in the midst of my heart." Others read: "in the midst of my belly." For the mind also has a womb, which conceives the seeds of thoughts, of which Isaiah said: "We have conceived in the womb and brought forth the spirit of salvation." With this womb Paul too was in labour, who says: "My little children, for whom I am in labour until Christ be formed in you." Christ, then, is formed not in a

bodily womb but in a kind of womb of the soul. With this womb the Apostle gave birth, as it is written: "I begot you through the gospel." That is why some read "in the midst of the heart" and others "in the midst of the belly," so that you may understand the womb of the inner man, which is taken to be in the midst of the heart, and in which we keep the precepts of the natural law, a law that is not only guarded but also carried out in our hearts. Hence it is also written that it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.

For there are those who by nature do what the law requires, like the Gentiles, who do not hear the law and are a law to themselves, who keep the precepts of a law unknown to them. So in this passage Christ, as the one who gathers the Gentile people, took on our person, so as to say that he does the law in the midst of his heart. For the people of the nations fulfilled the law they had not heard, so as to recognize Christ, whom the people of the Jews, who had received the law, did not receive and did not think worth recognizing, for it is written: "The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger;

but Israel has not known me." This, then, is the womb of believers, in which the Holy Spirit works and which he is accustomed to fill with spiritual seed, as the Lord Jesus testifies in the gospel, saying: "Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." These rivers come from that river of which we read: "The rush of the river gladdens the city of God." Of those, then, from whom such spiritual rivers flow, it is well said: "The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voice, from the voice of the spiritual waters," which praise God above the heavens.

Whoever has lifted up his voice can say: "I have proclaimed your righteousness well in the great assembly." Why did he add "great," except that before it was not great? And which is great, except the one gathered from every part of the whole world,

when the peoples of the nations were called from east and west, from north and south? Yet where do we read elsewhere of a great assembly? "I will confess to you, Lord, in the great assembly; among a weighty people I will praise you." The great assembly, then, is where the people is weighty: that is, not restless and fickle, the people that sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play. A weighty people is one that keeps faith with its God, that is not changed by any fickleness and does not waver and drift, but is grounded in Christ by love, so that it can say: "For I am confident that neither death nor sword nor tribulation can separate me from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus."

Whoever preaches in the great assembly does not hide God's righteousness in his heart. He raises his voice with all his strength and proclaims Christ. He is not afraid to preach him before the people and is not ashamed of his cross, but glories in that passion of the Lord. He does not follow the letter of the law but digs out its deep mysteries, so that by them he may reveal the glory of the Lord Jesus, who, the law signified, would come to the Church, the great assembly that was to be gathered. Righteousness, then, is faith. Indeed, "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." "See, I will not restrain my lips; Lord, you know it." So too elsewhere: "You know my sitting down and my rising up."

He says to the Father: "I have not hidden my righteousness in my heart; I have spoken of your truth and your salvation." This whole psalm is spoken in the person of Christ. That is why he says "my righteousness", though a man too may speak of his own righteousness without arrogance if he believes God and confesses that his faith is reckoned to him as righteousness. He loves truth and mercy who preaches the true faith and forgives sins. For Christ came for this very purpose: to establish faith and to grant the forgiveness of sins.

And since we have said that this whole psalm is in the person of the Saviour, the Apollinarians might perhaps say: "See, he said, 'A body you have prepared for me,' and not a soul as well." Let them hear him say further on in this psalm: "Let them be put to shame and confounded together who seek my soul, to take it away."

These are the points in this psalm that we judged (difficult). The rest we considered plain and easy, needing no interpretation. If these verses come up for treatment in another psalm in which they seem to be repeated, we will deal with them more fittingly there, with the help of the Lord Jesus, to whom be praise, honour, glory and everlasting endurance from the ages, now and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.
EXPLANATION OF PSALM 40

The order is fitting: he who said in the previous psalm, "See, I come," in this one has now come and suffers. And this psalm is numbered the fortieth because the Lord Jesus fasted for forty days, so that by that number he might bring to completion the perfection of man, who had perished. For just as man had lost grace by craving the forbidden fruit, so his strength had to be restored by fasting, so that he who had perished in Adam might be restored in Christ. That is why it says "to the end": because he himself is the end of our hope. Toward him we direct our efforts, to him

we bring our prayers, because he is the fullness, he is the consummation of all things, he is the sum of all virtues. Therefore it says "of David himself", as of the one who alone of all took our sins upon himself in his own flesh; who alone, the Lamb of God, took away the sin of the whole world; who alone blotted out the handwriting of the decree by the shedding of his blood, took it out of the way and nailed it to the cross. He is called so as Wisdom, knowing how to undo the ancient sin of the world; as Redemption, knowing how to renew man from his guilt; as Sanctification, knowing how to sanctify him for grace. This, then, is the title; this is the beginning.

"Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor." Open your ears, you who are beginning to learn the sacraments of the Lord's passion. That is why it is said to you: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." That is why in the Gospel the Lord touched the ears and lips of that deaf and dumb man, so that he might know what he was hearing in the mystery, and also what he should say and when he should say it. For it was not written idly: "The Lord has given me a learned tongue, so that I may know when I ought to speak a word." You must know, then, what you are hearing, know what you ought to say, and know also when you ought to say it.

Hear him, then, as he says: "Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor." Blessed indeed is he who has compassion on the poor man, who takes in his needs and knows what evil want brings on the destitute. But what is this opening doing in the Lord's passion? It is true that he suffered for the sake of the poor. Yet he himself rebuked Judas when Judas said of the ointment that Mary had poured on Christ's feet: "This could have been sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor."

The other apostles had felt the same, but from a different motive: he out of greed, they out of mercy. Judas was looking to his thieving; the disciples were thinking of food for the poor. He answered them all together: "Let her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but me you do not always have."

So "Blessed is he who understands concerning the poor" must be understood in another sense here. Here he speaks of faith, elsewhere of mercy. Faith comes first, mercy second. With faith, mercy is precious; without faith it is bare and unstable, for faith is the stable foundation of all the virtues. Blessed, then, is he who understands the need and poverty of Christ, who for our sake became poor though he was rich: rich in his kingdom, poor in the flesh, because he took on this flesh of the poor. For we had become very poor indeed. Through the serpent's deceit we lost the precious garments of the virtues; we were shut out of paradise, cast out of our homeland,

banished into exile, stripped even of the covering of the body, which before had been fenced and protected by the virtues but which our sins afterward laid bare. If, then, he was needy and poor in the flesh, he was certainly needy and poor in the suffering of that flesh. So he did not suffer in his riches but in our poverty. And therefore it was not the fullness of the Godhead, which dwells in him bodily, as Scripture testifies, but the flesh that suffered. Understand this, pursue this, hold on to it, so that it may not be said of you:

"He would not understand concerning the beggar and the poor." For even if you have doubts here, you certainly cannot doubt the verse in that psalm spoken in the person of the Saviour against the betrayal of Judas, where he says: "And he persecuted the poor man and the beggar." Understand, then, the poverty of Christ, so that you may be rich; understand his weakness, so that you may receive health; understand his cross, so that you may not be ashamed; understand his wound, so that you may heal your own wounds; understand his death, so that you may gain eternal life; understand his burial, so that you may find resurrection.

But perhaps you will ask: "How is Christ rich in poverty?" Even if my own wit fails, the help of the divine readings does not fail, since the Apostle has said: "The Lord Jesus became poor though he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich." What, then, is this poverty that makes men rich? Let us consider it; let us turn our attention to the venerable sacrament itself. What can be purer or simpler than it?

No one is drenched in bull's blood, as the sacred rites of the pagans are said to require; the sinner is not washed in the gore of goats and rams, for he is not purified that way: the flesh is washed, but the guilt is not washed away. Instead, it says, "Draw [?] water with delight from the springs of salvation"; and a heavenly table is prepared in your sight, and "how splendid is the cup that inebriates!" These are the riches of simplicity, in which lies the precious poverty of Christ. There is also a good poverty in one's way of life, of which the Lord said:

"Blessed are the poor in spirit"; and in the Psalms we find that "the Lord will save the humble in spirit." There is also an abundant poverty in a slender offering, if faith abounds. That is why the Apostle says: "And their deep poverty has abounded in the riches of their simplicity."

So that we may understand from his other sayings as well that he called himself poor, we have it written elsewhere: "I am poor and in sorrow", that is, he sorrows for us, as we read, for there was nothing in himself for him to grieve over. As he sorrows for us, then, as Isaiah, who saw him in the spirit, explained, so it was for us that he was sad, in keeping with his calling his soul sorrowful even unto death, though not on account of death. And he called the flesh weak, the flesh that submitted to the weakness of death so that it might break the sting of death and by it set us free on the day of judgment, which he called evil, and not lightly.

For so he went on: "On the evil day the Lord will deliver him," since that day seems bitter, for it sentences more people to punishment. The road of virtue is narrow, the road of sin broad; that is why fewer walk in virtue and more are engaged in wickedness. So it happens that the number of those who will receive the prizes of reward is smaller than the number of those who, as the wages of grave sins, will carry away an adverse sentence at the judgment. It was as if in sorrow, then, that he called the day of judgment evil. For if the angels rejoice over the acquittal of one sinner, how much more will men

be wasted with grief at the condemnation of so many men! And rightly does he grieve for the sheep that he carried back on his shoulders and called back to his fold when it had strayed. The Son of God speaks with our feelings, because the day of judgment, which we fear, is bitter to us. It seems evil to all because it is full of terror: on that day God judges not only a man's public acts but also his hidden ones, and each one is compelled to lay open what he has done or what he has thought. And so many are condemned and few are crowned. But even those who are crowned will grieve;

for the righteous will be crowned, and the righteous man counts his brother's hardship as his own. And who am I to pass judgment on that day on which man will be admitted to the councils of the angels? Let us hear the Lord's own verdict: "The hour will come," he says, "in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of Man and will come forth, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment." Those who have acted wickedly, then, will be judged, and that is why the Judge himself calls the day evil and harsh, so that you may know that he who suffered with us in the prophets suffers with us in the Gospel.

But we may also take "on the evil day" in this way: it is "in an evil time". For the world is set in evil, and so the days of this world are evil, and "sufficient to the day is its own evil." It is no small thing to be delivered here from the snares of the sinner. Whoever is free from wrongdoing here will be free from punishment there, and will not have to undergo the severity of judgment.

And therefore we need vows and daily prayers and the advocacy of the chief of priests, of whom John the evangelist says: "We have an advocate with the Father, the Lord Jesus, and he is the propitiation for our sins." This, then, our advocate and the propitiation for the sins of the whole world, prays for the one who understands and believes in Christ, and says: "May the Lord preserve him and give him life and make him blessed." May he preserve him from dangers, give him life as one set in the darkness of death, and deign to make him blessed by adding good works.

"And may he cleanse," it says, "his life on earth." He did well to add "on earth", because unless a man has been cleansed here, he cannot be clean there. Or else take it this way: "may he cleanse on earth", for how can anyone be clean in the mud, when the earth smears him? So the Lord's hand is needed, the hand that made the body from the earth, so that it may deign to cleanse it.

"And may he not deliver him into the hands of his enemy." Who is the enemy but that lion who goes about roaring, seeking whom he may devour? Other Greek copies have: "And may he not deliver him into the souls of his enemies." It put "souls" for "hands" because the souls of enemies lie in wait for the good and try to overthrow the righteous man by their schemes. "Souls" is also used for persons: "all the seventy souls who went down into Egypt." That is also why David preferred to commit himself to God's power rather than to the snares of his enemies, who did not know how to spare of their own will.

It goes on: "May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain; you have turned all his bed in his sickness." What is the bed of pain but the flesh of weakness? And it is well called the bed of pain, because it is the body of death from which the Apostle prays to be delivered, so that he may rise as if from a kind of tomb, in which the soul lies sick and is laid down, as it were, on a little bed. Symmachus said "bed of misery", Aquila "pallet of misery"; the Seventy thought it should be put more expressly as "bed of pain".

These verses, then, should be used with those who are held for a long time by bodily illness, so that they may have God's medicine, by which they may deserve to be healed. The bed of the soul, then, is the weak flesh, with whose sickness our soul suffers. If the soul has the Lord as its helper, he says to it: "Rise, take up your bed and go to your house."

Strengthened by this word of God, the one who was sick rises, takes up the bed on which he lay, and returns to his former state of health. This is what it means to go back to one's house: to dwell in the home of the most robust health. He who dwells there governs, and he who governs has the grace of virtue supporting him. But the Lord also turns the whole bed in the sickness of the ailing man whom he deigns to stand by. What is turned changes its state, either from health to sickness or from sickness to health. Here, then, the one who is sick is turned toward the remedy of health.

So it was with the Lord Jesus: although he was wounded for our sins, he did not remain in that weakness but turned himself to something better for the salvation of all. And so weakness was undone by the passion, and death by the resurrection. Just as he turned himself to the redemption of the peoples and did not feel the sting of death or the weakness of the wound,

so he turns to life the one who believes in him, even when he is gravely ill, in order to free him from death. "All his bed", then, means that he turned the weakness of all men in his own weakness. For he took on the weaknesses of all in his own flesh, raised himself onto the cross, and turned the weaknesses of all in the weakness of his own body. That is why Isaiah says: "By his bruise we have been healed." Wrestlers have this trick: they put themselves underneath the men they engage and grapple with, so that they seem able to be pinned. Then suddenly, just when they are thought to be beaten and crushed, they turn themselves with a certain skill and throw off the man on top. The one who was being carried falls, and the one who was carrying him is found on top, so that he lays out his assailant.

So in the spiritual wrestling-ground the Lord Jesus, taking up our burdens, put himself underneath in that bout of his passion. In the appearance of weakness, so that the adversary would judge him a man like the rest whom he could easily overpower, he laid aside the arms of divinity and put on the covering of humanity. Sure of victory, the tempter came closer and chose to wound him in the side with a soldier's spear, reckoning that he too, like Adam, could be laid low through a rib.

But the Lord Jesus, wounded in his side, brought forth life from the wound. He emptied out all sin and threw down the adversary, from whom he snatched the dying thief. And in that death, in that burial of his body, when he was thought to have been overpowered and crushed, he turned himself by his own power: the adversary fell, and the Lord rose again.

It goes on: "I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you." This can also be said in the person of King David. Seeing in the spirit so great a victory and the grace of Christ, he asks that in that forgiveness of all sins God may have mercy on him too. For although as king he was not bound by human laws, he knew that he was nevertheless answerable to God for his sins. So he confesses his sin in order to receive forgiveness and obtain the gift of the general pardon. It can also be expressed in the person of the Saviour, who asks God's mercy for us and said that he had sinned because for our sake he was made sin.

At the same time he teaches us that when we are engaged in any struggle against the enemies of God, we should implore God's help and confess our sins ourselves; and above all when we are hard pressed and ground down, we should prostrate ourselves in grief and bitterness, so as not to seem to have kept silent, so that medicine may be brought more quickly to our wounds and, once healed, we may resist the adversary. For how can a wounded man fight? From this we learn that we are wounded by the stings of our sins. A wound looks for a physician; the physician requires confession.

From here on the Saviour begins more and more to open up the sacrament of his passion, and there is no doubt that it agrees with the Gospel. For the Jews cursed him, sought his death, laid snares for him and pressed him hard, unable to bear the glory of his work, which grew daily. So the prophecy announces what was fulfilled in the Gospel: "My enemies spoke evil against me: When will he die, and his name perish?"

Madmen, to believe that the author of life could die! But the Church was overturning their wishes, believing that even when he died according to the condition of the body he would increase his name. And so she sang to him, saying: "I will remember your name from generation to generation," and she repeated: "Your name is ointment poured out."

"Let them die [?] who presume that you can die; I will not die, for I know you as the arbiter of life and the author of salvation." For we know that at the time of the passion and resurrection the disciples were gathered together and praying, when Magdalene announced to them that the Lord had risen, and when the Lord showed himself to them in his risen body though the door was shut, and when Thomas saw his wounds and believed.

So the Jews jeered at him as dead, but the Lord was revealing himself alive to the apostles. When the Jews said, "See, the whole world has gone after him," when they said that he was leading the people astray by his miraculous works, what else were they saying but, "When will he die, and his name perish?" And so at his passion they shouted: "Away, away with such a man from the earth! Let him be crucified, let him be crucified!" What they asked for came to pass: he was taken away from the earth. He rose again, ascended into heaven, and restored his kingdom, made from us, to the dwellings of paradise.

A clear prophecy about Judas the betrayer is added in the verses that follow: "And he came in to see; he spoke vain things; his heart gathered iniquity to itself. And he went outside and spoke." That is how we find it punctuated in the Greek manuscripts. So Judas came in, seeking to betray the Saviour, to see what he was doing or saying, so that he might catch him in his words and report it to the Jews. But he found nothing, for he understood nothing.

Scripture rightly says that he was not inside with Jesus, since he had withdrawn from his teaching and abandoned his instructions. He wanted to enter but could not get in, because his own treachery shut him out. For "every impure or greedy or unclean person, which is the service of idols, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God." So he not only tried to enter and did not enter, but also wanted to see and did not see. Indeed, Jesus spoke in parables, but Judas did not hear.

Indeed, he did not see the divine mysteries; for not all who think they hear the word of God actually hear it. If all heard, Jesus would not say, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." And so, because he did not hear and could not see, he spoke vain things instead of true ones, and thought he could deceive Jesus when he said, "This could have been sold and given to the poor," though he was providing for his thefts, not for the poor. He called "Rabbi" and "Teacher" the one whose teaching he was straying from, and the devil, who had entered his heart, was gathering it to himself and increasing its iniquities.

For he was wicked to himself, unjust to himself, he sinned against himself, plotting within himself a treachery that could not stay hidden. For Jesus was not deceived; he was betrayed willingly and testified: "One of you will betray me." Indeed, Judas confessed it, saying, "Is it I, Rabbi?" And the Lord said, "You have said it." Even so Judas did not understand that he was found out; had he understood, he would not have betrayed him.

But nonetheless "he went outside and spoke." The verse suits those who betray someone's secret. It says well, "he went outside", for outside are the wolves, outside are the robbers. Inside was Moses in the cloud with Joshua, outside were the Jews; inside was Zechariah the priest in the temple, outside was the multitude; inside, the Holy Spirit cries to the Father in our hearts, outside, our adversary keeps watch like a lion for his prey;

outside are the unbelievers, inside the faithful. And therefore God will judge those who are outside, but Christ will acquit those who are inside. So Judas went out and spoke. He went out from the faith; he went out from the council and number of the apostles; he went out from the banquet of Christ to the robbery of the devil; he went out from the grace of sanctification to the snare of death, as he spoke vain things to the faithless.

He went outside, for he was leaving the inner mysteries of life; he went out, for he did not know the inner meaning of Scripture. Had he known it, he would have understood the one who says: "Shall not he who sleeps rise again?" He would also have understood this: "But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my familiar friend, who always took sweet food with me; in the house of the Lord we walked in harmony." So he did not understand this psalm, nor the hundred and eighth, nor others, nor the other testimonies of the Scriptures. Of him and of the other unbelievers John the evangelist rightly says: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us."

So the traitor did not stay with the apostles. He went outside and whispered with the faithless. Divine Scripture used this word to show that faithlessness has no authority, since it is afraid of being caught in what it says. But to the faithful it is said: Lift up your voice with strength. See how far the apostle Judas had fallen. He had been sent to preach the faith to the nations with a herald's full authority, and now he whispered into the ear of those plotting against his master what he was afraid to have overheard. Did he not condemn himself by his own judgment?

He was ashamed to be heard saying what he was not afraid to do. He was ashamed because he was plotting evil against the author of his life, his sanctification and his honour. He did not repay kindness with gratitude. Instead he returned evil for good to a good master, something that even worldly people usually condemn. He was ashamed to be caught being ungrateful and ashamed to be seen as greedy, since he was betraying the safety of his maker for money. He was ashamed to be seen as faithless.

In the same way the Jews faithlessly bribed false witnesses against the teacher of the faith. They had them say that he had preached that the temple of God built by Solomon should be destroyed, when he had been speaking of the temple of his body: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. These people were truly outside, because they were shut out from knowing the heavenly word.

They set forth a wicked word against me, he says. That is, they put forward against me speech that was unlawful and against every law of God and man. They made bargains over human blood, which Judas sold with the utmost wickedness and which the Jews, in a crime no less great, thought they should buy. They were utterly foolish, as if he who sleeps would not add something so as to rise again. Let us consider what this 'addition' is.

All the creatures of the earth, the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea are by nature born and die. But God had made man more precious than the other living things of the earth, and he gave him a special grace: that after dying he should live again. This is what is called the 'addition' that renews the former life. So too with King Hezekiah. The Lord had decreed that he had completed the span of his life and had told him through Isaiah to set his house in order, because he was going to die. Hezekiah prayed to the Lord and wept bitterly, and the Lord took pity on him and sent him this message:

Behold, I add fifteen years to your time. And elsewhere holy David says: You will add days upon days to the king, and his years. So something has been found that can be added to man. But nothing can be added to God, for it is written: Nothing can be added or taken away in him in whom all things are perfect and full. When Christ rose again, he certainly rose in what he had taken on, and in that nothing could be taken away from or added to the fullness of his divinity. For God is incorporeal and

immortal, and his supreme nature and fullness of power are signified without any addition of flesh. The flesh in Christ belongs to the dispensation of salvation. He took it up by the claim of mercy and the right of love, to redeem it from captivity, to wash it when it was defiled and to raise it when it was dead. And he puts it beautifully: Shall not he who sleeps add, so as to rise again? He did not say 'is it not added', but 'shall he not add, so as to rise again', because the Son of God raised himself. As we said above, he told the Jews:

Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. The flesh received the addition, being taken from man and received from a virgin. But as God he himself brought about that addition, rising by his own power so as to be the author of his own resurrection. When you read both that the Father raised the Son and that the Son raised himself, recognize that this was the work of divine power. The Father and the Son have one power and a common operation, since the substance of the Trinity is one and the same.

'But why do I accuse the others?' says the Lord Jesus. 'Is it any wonder that the people did not know me and condemned me to the cross, when my own apostle demanded a price for betraying me, when my table companion sold my death? For the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, has magnified his supplanting against me.' Some think Judas should be excused because he returned the money he had received as the price of the sale.

But see, he is condemned beyond the unbelief of the Jews, for more is required of the one to whom more is given. 'Why should I complain about others?' he says. 'The man of my peace, to whom I had given my peace and to whom I had wished to leave my peace, brought the persecutors and handed me over, and he in whom I hoped deceived me.' Did he not know who would betray him? He had foretold it about him: One of you will betray me.

[He said this about Judas, as is written in the Gospel.] Certainly he knew. But to condemn him all the more, he said he had put his hope in that man's faithfulness. Aquila translated 'I had trusted', and Symmachus 'I was trusting'. For our charge is heavier against someone in whom we say we had the greatest hope or confidence, if he later betrays our hope and our good opinion.

At the same time he shows how great the power of divine sanctification is. It shuts out malice and corrects a corrupt character, if the pattern of a better purpose is added. How many people we know who have been converted! Zacchaeus, that tax collector who pursued gain with a greedy heart, was changed. Afterwards he made up for his wrongdoing by paying back fourfold. He condemned the greed in himself, renounced the profits of his earlier life, and where there was no one to claim them, he paid them to the poor.

The thief himself changed his wickedness for a better purpose. He recognized Christ on the cross, confessed the Son of God, and called him king with his own voice. At a time when many righteous people were wavering and even the apostles were hiding, the centurion, the executioner himself, did not deny him. But why speak only of the time of the Gospel?

Rahab was a harlot who lived on the wages of faithlessness and lust [?]. Yet when she saw the spies Joshua son of Nun had sent, she put on faith. With danger close at hand she held fast to righteousness. She did not betray those she had taken in, but protected them with faithful kindness. That is why he says he had hoped. It was as if he had rightly assumed that the apostle would lay aside his former ways and follow better ones,

and that he who had received the office of sanctifying others would himself keep the grace of holiness and hold fast to the duties of sincerity. He rightly says 'I hoped', because he gave man the freedom to choose what he would follow. I have set before you good and evil, he says. If you choose evil, it is not nature that sins but the will of the one who chooses. If every person who chooses evil is condemned, what shall we say of Judas, who betrayed the one he was joined to in the sweetness of a shared table?

Who ate my bread, he says, has magnified his supplanting against me. Why did he add 'my bread'? He could have said 'who ate bread with me', unless you understand the bread that belongs to Christ in a special way, that is, the nourishment of the heavenly word. For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.

So elsewhere he says: You who always took sweet food with me. We do well to use these verses against people who have thought it right to kill those they are known to have dined with. We are told that pagans, often enemies and even robbers, keep this rule and spare those they have shared a table with. [The very sharing of food makes them gentle. Hence, because of this kind of

affection that comes from the grace of the table, if we consider the words, he did not say 'sweet food' without reason. For how can food be sweet that quickly spoils? But see whether by sweet food he did not mean the words of life. No bitterness spoils this food and no corruption of death taints it. That is why he also said 'always'. No one can always be eating, but we can always hold fast to the word of God, night and day, if we meditate on the law of God day and night.

And what does 'magnified' mean? The Greek has emegalynen, that is, 'made great'. The Lord explained to us both of these things that might trouble us, saying in the Gospel: He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me. Let us consider where this expression comes from. We were once unbelieving, he says, going astray, slaves to desires and pleasures. Let us confess our error so that we may be washed clean. When I was a boy I saw an athlete who had thrown his opponent strike him on the forehead with his heel, as a sign that he was triumphing over the man he had beaten.

This is what he means by: He has magnified his supplanting against me. With this word he showed the boasting of someone who gloats. So Judas too lifted his heel against Christ when he betrayed him, but he did not lift it without punishment. Adam still lifts the heel that was wounded by the serpent. Christ had certainly washed Judas's feet, and Judas had heard him say: He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet, and he is clean all over. But what grace had washed, faithlessness had defiled. So Judas lifted his heel to be wounded. Truly, the one who lifted his heel against Christ did not hold fast to the head.

Adam lifted it over himself, but this man lifted it over Christ, and so the serpent wounded him more gravely than the rest. He lifted his heel when he offered the treacherous kiss with which he meant to supplant his maker. That is why it is written in the prophet: He has magnified his supplanting against me. Esau also says of his brother: He has supplanted me twice now. Whoever supplants uses a trick to throw down or wound his opponent. So Judas too is said to have supplanted him, because with his kiss he inflicted a wound. By that kiss he gave the persecutors the signal to seize the Saviour.

So he supplanted like a serpent, which pours poison from its mouth and wounds the heel with its tooth. This man too wounded not Christ's divinity but the lowest part of his body, the heel. Judas also lifted his heel like an arrogant and proud wrestler, meaning to strike the Saviour's head with it. But he could not strike Christ's head, because the head of Christ is God. His own head, however, he tied in the knot of a shapeless noose, and so took away from himself the remedy of salvation.

See whether you can reverently apply what the holy patriarch Jacob said in Genesis when he prophesied about his sons: Dan shall judge his people as one tribe in Israel; and: Let Dan be like a serpent sitting by the road and on the path, biting the horse's heel, and

the rider will fall backward, waiting for salvation from the Lord. We do read that Samson, of the tribe of Dan, was a judge in Israel. But someone else who is still to come is meant here: one who will come from that tribe and afflict the people with the torments of sacrilegious impiety. This is the Antichrist,

who will sit in the temple as though he were God. He is truly 'judgment', as the meaning of the name has it, for Dan means judgment. And it is well said that he will judge his own people, since he will himself be liable to everlasting punishment. For whoever does not believe is already judged, but whoever believes will not be judged, because he believes in the Son of God, the redeemer of his soul. That is why one who is free from judgment says: It is the Lord who judges me. So he will judge the people of impiety, not the people of faith. Those who are judged are the ones who fall in the ruin of faithlessness, not those who rise in the freedom of faith.

So he will sit by the road and lie in wait on the path like a serpent, to wound those who pass by and bite the heel of our horse, for he will not be able to wound the souls of the faithful. And on what road will he sit, and on what path? Surely those from which Christ the Lord, as we read, called the people of the nations to his supper, saying: Go out into the roads and along the hedges and make them come in, so that my house may be filled.

And since we read that Judas likewise magnified his supplanting against Christ, Judas himself seems to be meant in this passage, as the one who was to bite the heel of the horse that Christ the Lord rode. Hence it is said: Your riding is salvation. For his flesh was to take on the sin of the whole world, so that salvation might take the place of destruction and eternal life the place of death.

So the horse was wounded, the only horse that does not fail as a hope of salvation. The horse was wounded that took on the sins of the whole world and carried our burdens without growing weary. The horse was wounded that never learned to neigh in lustful frenzy. Perhaps that is why heaven was opened to John the Evangelist and a white horse was shown to him. On it sat one with diadems on his head, and on his thigh was written a name: King of kings and Lord of lords. He was white because he was spotless and had known no stain of sin. For if lust is dark, holiness rightly glows and shines.

This horse, then, was wounded but not slowed down. With that very wound he rose from the tomb and ran up to heaven above all the angels and archangels. He proved swifter than all the cavalry of the heavenly army, and even than those fiery horses by which Elijah was carried away. And he is rightly swifter, since he went up above all the heavens and above the heaven of heavens to the throne of almighty God, and sits there. As Scripture has taught us: From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of power.

This horse was also shown beforehand in a figure, in the time of the Maccabees. On it sat that commander of the heavenly army, gleaming in golden armour. He struck down and overthrew Heliodorus, who had tried to plunder the deposits of widows and the other things entrusted to the sacred treasury. Afterwards, won over by the prayers of Onias the priest,

he restored him to life. So the golden armour truly shone on him, because he alone rode this horse and conquered. On this horse no one else came through free of guilt: not Enoch, who was taken away so that wickedness would not change his heart, not Abraham, not Isaac, not Jacob, not Moses. For all are under sin, all under death. Indeed, death reigned from Adam to Moses. He alone committed no sin. Christ alone took away the sin of the world, and he said to death: Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?

How, then, did Judas magnify his supplanting against him, and how did the rider fall backward? On Judas's side, he acted with treachery. On Christ's side, he suffered willingly. We often see a stronger man let himself be struck, so that when he is provoked he may rise up more fiercely and be roused more forcefully. So the serpent bit the horse's heel and spat out the poison of its treachery,

and the rider willingly threw himself down. He fell willingly, in order to lift us up. Yet what does Scripture mean when it says: And the rider will fall backward? Why backward, unless to guide from behind those who follow him? Peter was behind him, the one to whom he said: Get behind me. The apostles and the other disciples were behind him. So he fell backward, because he saves those he falls upon. For everyone who falls on this stone, he says, will be shattered, but anyone it falls upon, it will cleanse.

Other versions have 'it will winnow him', and others 'it will crush him'. Whoever winnows grain cleans it of chaff. Whoever crushes something reduces it to powder, so that the fine powder may serve for a healing drink or some other medicine. From this we gather that we must take care that no one who has once been received by Christ through baptism should stray from his body, that is, be cast out of the Church.

That is the ruin of everlasting death. But take the man who comes to believe in Christ, so that Christ's death may find him, his cross take him up, his nail pierce him, his blood pour over him and his burial wrap him round, and so that the grace of the resurrection may lift him up, wake him from sleep and bring him to life from death. That man, I say, he sets free from the world. He cleanses him from sin, heals his wounds, bends him away from the hardness of impiety and softens him into the gentleness of devotion, so that with a circumcised heart he may breathe in that sweet and incomprehensible Spirit and drink the cup of eternal salvation. So the rider fell backward.

Here is another reason why he fell backward. Everyone is behind him and no one is before him. So he fell not for himself but for everyone, so that by falling on us he might soften the hardness of our hearts. He fell on Adam, whom he was seeking, in order to find him. He looked for him behind, so that as the good shepherd he might put him on his shoulders and carry him with him into paradise when he redeemed that thief.

But perhaps you will say: 'The persecutors fell backward too, for it is written that the chief priests whom Judas the traitor had brought, and the others who had come to arrest the Lord Jesus, drew back and fell to the ground.' That is exactly what I am saying: he chose to fall on sinners, not on the righteous. The righteous have no need of a physician, but sinners do. If the shadow of the apostles healed, how much more does the flesh of Christ protect from death those it touches!

Indeed, he touched a leper and cleansed him at once. And so that you who read may know that he wished to set even his persecutors free, ask Christ's witness. When Peter denounced the Jews for killing the author of life, he showed them the remedy: they should repent and so become worthy to have the sin they had committed forgiven. Why, then, do you doubt that he fell in order to raise others up, when he himself said: I will strike and I will heal? Yet notice the difference in the wording.

In Genesis we read: The rider will fall backward, waiting for salvation from the Lord. This means that he does not turn his eyes away from God or turn his own mind back, but claims the privilege of his resurrection and raises himself by divine power. But here we read: they drew back and fell to the ground. Whoever is earthly falls to the earth, and whoever is heavenly clings to heaven. Even if he falls in body, he does not fall in power, but always strives toward the things above. He always looks to the Father, so as to carry out the Father's will toward us.

If only these men too had not drawn back, but had received Christ, as Joseph received him and buried him in a new tomb! The faithful do not fall to the earth. The faithless fall and go down to the lower parts of the earth, as it is written: Let them go down alive into hell. So the persecutor falls onto the earth and into hell, but Christ falls upon those who will rise again, Christ falls upon the rock, Christ falls upon the Church. Hear how he falls upon the Church. Behind him was

Peter, following him as the Jews led him to the house of Caiaphas, the leader of the synagogue. This is the Peter to whom he said: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church. So where Peter is, there is the Church, and where the Church is, there is no death but eternal life. That is why he added: and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Blessed Peter! The gate of hell did not prevail against him, and the gate of heaven did not close against him. On the contrary, he destroyed the entrance of hell and threw open the gates of heaven. So, while he was placed on earth, he opened heaven and shut hell.

This passage may also fit the story of the Samaritan. He did not pass by the man coming down from Jericho who had been wounded by robbers. He took him up and treated his wounds, pouring in oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal and brought him to an inn. Why do you doubt about a good horse, when you read of a good beast of burden too, and when you read that many horsemen, and very many with chariots and carriages, enter that Jerusalem?

Do not be troubled by what you have read: Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will be made great in the name of the Lord our God. They were bound and fell. Elijah did not fall, though he went in by chariot. For where the name of God is, no one is bound and all are set free. In the name of our God the poor man is safe, and the rich man too, the noble and the lowborn, the weak and the powerful. Wealth is no obstacle to faith, so long as we know how to use wealth.

So, having the name of God within him, he says: But you, O Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I will repay them. He certainly does not say this as though he doubted the resurrection, since he had the power to say: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. Rather, he gives man a pattern, so that he may hope for mercy from God and resurrection from God. Next, he is not asking to be raised up himself. He is asking that Matthias be raised up for him in place of Judas, so that the number of the apostles might be complete. Since the son of perdition had to perish so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, it was right that a son of salvation should be put in his place. Now take a third meaning.

He asks that he be raised up, that is, his body, and the body of Christ is the Church. Judas was a figure of the unbelieving Jewish people, who bought or sold Christ for money, as those do who value money more than religion. So he means that in place of the destruction of the faithless people, the grace of resurrection will come to the Church for him. That is why the Church herself says in the Song of Songs: If you rouse and stir up love, when she was asking the young women about Christ, for Christ is love.

As for his saying, I will repay them, we take it to mean that they will be tormented by the growth of the flourishing Church. Then they will learn what the punishment of faithlessness is, when they see the splendour of faith and grace. Or else, since the Lord is good, he who could have said: They repaid me evil for good, and since the word 'repay' is neutral and can be used of good or of evil, he says that he will repay them with good. For although blindness has come upon part of Israel, when the full number of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved by the mercy of Christ.

And he added: “By this I knew that you wanted me, because my enemy will not rejoice over me.” Above, he spoke of his passion as a man; from here on he now reveals his majesty: that he alone is without sin, he alone is the one over whom the sinner could not ride roughshod, he alone is the one whom the Father loved as his only Son. Why, then, did the enemy not rejoice over him? Because, although

he accepted death for us, he nevertheless rose again, and he himself mocked the enemy, whose victory he destroyed and whose sting of death he broke. And we too, though we are sorrowful in this world, and the enemy rejoices in our grief and in the contrition of our heart and mind, nevertheless destroy his joy when we rise again. That is why Micah also said: “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; but I shall rise again.” It is resurrection, then, by which all the enemy’s chains are loosed and all his triumph is wiped out.

There follows: “But because of my innocence you have upheld me and established me in your sight for ever. Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, for ever, from age to age; so be it, so be it.” The innocent man harms no one and sins against no one. That is why Christ is marked out by the authority of divine Scripture as being without sin and without deceit; and this is what is declared here as well, where he says: “But because of my innocence you have upheld me.” What upholding is meant here? For elsewhere too we read: “You upheld me from my mother’s womb.”

Therefore, because he who was born of the Spirit and of a virgin was born pure of every taint of human generation, the Father upheld him, since no ordinary taint of bodily generation darkened his birth. He upheld him when he rose again, because no stain of falling had spattered him. Spotless he returned to the Father, from whom he had come forth spotless when he descended to earth. That is why the Father says to him: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you”—that is: I recognize in you the privilege of my own begetting, you whom no stain of sin could defile.

You lived among sinners, you took upon yourself the sins of all, you were made sin for all, you were made a curse for all; yet no habit of sin could pass over to you. You lived among sinners as though you were living among angels. You made the earth to be what heaven is, so that there too you might take away sin. Today I have begotten you, in whom I am well pleased. You have proved yourself the Son, for you have fulfilled the Father’s will in all things.

Today I have begotten you, in whom I recognize the light of a spotless offspring. You are the same to me yesterday and today and for ever. There is no night in you, because you are wholly day. Rightly is he said to be established in the Father’s sight for ever, because he is always with the Father and truly in the sight of him whose radiance of glory and image of substance he is. But just as the Father is well pleased in the Son, so too the Son blesses the Father; for the Father honors the Son, and the Son honors the Father.

“Blessed,” he says, “be the Lord, the God of Israel”—that is, the God of the people that sees God, which believes him to be both its Lord and its God—“from age to age; so be it, so be it.” In the Hebrew it has “Amen, amen,” as those who have read the book written in Hebrew letters have affirmed. The Greek here said genoito, genoito, which means “so be it, so be it.” This word has various mean-

ings: sometimes it belongs to one who commands, sometimes to one who prays, sometimes to one who confirms something. It is the word of one who commands when a superior lays down for an inferior what must be done or followed. It is the word of one who prays, as in: “Your will be done”; for no one commands God, but pours out a prayer. It is the word of one who confirms when a prophet or a priest or some holy man gives a blessing and the people answer: “So be it, so be it.” Here, then, it seems to me to be a confirmation of the blessing rather than a prayer or entreaty, especially because the word itself is repeated.

And though the Hebrew word seems to have been changed, the same sense has been expressed. For just as, when the priest gives a blessing, the people answer “Amen,” confirming for themselves the blessing that the priest asks of the Lord for the people, so in the psalm the response is “So be it, so be it,” as if to say “Amen, amen.” That “amen” is a word of confirmation is clearly shown in the Gospel, where the Lord, confirming his own words, says:

“Amen I say to you.” But the force is greater where the word is repeated, which we find more frequently in the book of the Gospel according to John, because he above all spoke of heavenly and profound mysteries, as it is written: “Amen, amen I say to you, unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God”; and elsewhere: “Amen, amen I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you.” Two examples are more than enough; anyone who looks for the rest will find them.

“So be it, so be it” is also the sign that a book has ended. For the Psalter appears to be divided into five books. The first book ends with this psalm, that is, the fortieth. And it is fitting that the fortieth psalm, reaching as far as the Savior’s passion, should be the one to bring the book to its end, since the Lord’s passion is the end of Lent, the forty days, so that the second book might begin with the mysteries of renewal; and this book, as befits what follows the forty days [?], contains more perfect sacraments.

For it foretells the sacraments of baptism, when it says: “As the hart longs for the springs of water”; and the rest of the saints who will have reached the heavenly tabernacle; and the descent of the Holy Spirit, when spiritual grace was poured out with, as it were, the voice of heaven’s cataracts, since the Spirit was borne along with great power, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles; and the entry of the renewed man to the altar; and the Savior’s ascension; and the sanctification of the virginal life.

This book ends with the seventy-first psalm, in which the peaceful kingdom of Christ, spread over the whole world, and the forgiveness of sins are announced in prophetic words; there, after first pronouncing the blessing of the Lord, he added: “And the whole earth shall be filled with his majesty. So be it, so be it.” The third book likewise ends with the eighty-eighth psalm, and there it has: “Blessed be the Lord for ever. So be it, so be it.” The fourth book ends with the hundred and fifth psalm, and there it has: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age; and all the people shall say: So be it, so be it.” The fifth book runs to the end, where instead of this word the prophet says: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

But perhaps someone will again be troubled at how I can assert that there are five books when there is one Psalter. But the Gospel too is one, and we cannot deny that there are four books. That the Gospel is one we have shown elsewhere, unless I am mistaken, and if it is demanded again we can easily demonstrate it, since the Savior said: “Amen I say to you, wherever the Gospel is preached”; and the Apostle: “I am astonished that you are so quickly turning to another gospel—not that there is another, except that there are some who are perverting you”; and elsewhere: “For I make known to you, brothers, the gospel.” Nowhere do you find this body of four books referred to in any other way than as “the Gospel.” So too, because the psalms also form one body, Scripture said: “On the ten-stringed psaltery, with song upon the harp.” But again, because there are five books, it said elsewhere: “On the instruments of psalms.”
