It is fitting that there are five books and one Psalter, since the outer man is given life by five senses, and in turn our inner man, that hidden man of the heart, who alone is found rich before God on the testimony of the apostle Peter, is brought to perfection by five spiritual senses. “He who has ears to hear,” he says, “let him hear.” There you have one sense.

And just as there are those who have eyes and do not see, so there are those who, though their eyes do not see, are believed to see more. That is why the prophets were called “seers,” even those who could not see with their eyes. Good too is that fragrance of which the Apostle said: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God”; and so Job also said: “And the divine Spirit that is in my nostrils.” The fragrance of Christ and of the Holy Spirit is therefore one and the same to God, because there is one fragrance of the Trinity. There is also an inner food, of which the Lord said: “My food is to

do the will of my Father who is in heaven.” There is also an inner touch, by which that woman in the Gospel touched Christ, who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years and had not received healing from the physicians, but received it from Christ. It is the touch of faith by which Christ is touched. Indeed, people did not see her, but Jesus saw her, and he testified that he had seen her, saying: “Someone touched me; for I too perceived that power had gone out from me.” To be known by Christ is to be granted healing. Since, therefore, it is evident that there are ten senses in man, David, who sang both outwardly and inwardly—outwardly with the body, inwardly with the heart—says in the psalm: “On the ten-stringed psaltery I will sing psalms to you.”

The psaltery, then, is the man made perfect in Christ, in whom, just as the strings resound when skillfully played in harmony, so the melodious works of the virtues resound in concord, so that he can say: “I will sing psalms to you, O God, upon the harp, Holy One of Israel. My lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed.” Paul says of himself: “Fighting without, fears within.”

This man rejoices both within and without, but Paul was still in the struggle, while this one was at rest, because he knew that he had been granted the redemption of his soul. One who sings psalms is in gladness; one who wrestles is in anxiety. Yet Paul too knew how to sing psalms, but he was still holding himself back for further progress, so that he might sing psalms once he had been more fully proven. And that is why he said: “I will pray with the spirit, I will pray with the mind also; I will sing psalms with the spirit, I will sing psalms with the mind also.”

And since he has shown that the office of singing psalms is twofold, Scripture has also taught that there is a twofold voice, as the prophet says: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and my voice to God, and he heeded me.” What is the point of “my”? For he could have said: “I cried to the Lord.” But what voice is truly ours, if not this one, which is the better, which does not know how to go astray? For in much speaking we fall into sin and cannot avoid it.

That voice of the prophet is the one that reaches God, the one with which Moses, though silent, cried to the Lord, the one with which Hannah too cried in her prayers when she did not move the lips of her mouth, and she obtained a son whom she had long failed to obtain when she had cried out with the voice of the body. Of this voice the Lord said: “But you, when you pray, go into your room, shut the door, and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will repay you.” What does “will repay” mean? It means what you have asked for, what you have prayed for.

For just as sinners receive from the hand of the Lord double for their sins, so, on the contrary, the righteous receive what they have asked for, fulfilled. Hear how they receive it. Your prayer goes up to God and comes down to [?]. That is why we also read in the psalm: “And my prayer shall return into my bosom,” that is, so that it may bring back its fruit to the one who asked. Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who has opened to us such great mysteries, from age to age, that is, from the infinite to the infinite. So be it, so be it.
EXPOSITION OF PSALM 43

The title of the psalm is: “To the end; for the sons of Korah, for understanding.” Having run through the mysteries of the Lord’s passion, of baptism, and of entry to the most holy altar, the holy prophet David teaches how Christ trains his athlete, whose name is to be entered in the contest of the saints. For just as, without any labor of ours, not from works but from faith, he forgave us our sins by his grace, and with the greatest indulgence and kindness admitted us to compete for the crown, and did not let our former shameful deeds stand against us, though by them we would have been judged unworthy of so great a contest—for even in those who undergo this purifying contest a disciplined way of life is required—so, in turn, lest we grow slack after so great a forgiveness of sins and fall back into our former shameful deeds or into idleness, this psalm warns us that many and heavy contests are set before us, so that no one is crowned unless he has competed according to the rules.

We must wrestle, then, against the allurements of this flesh and the heat of the blood; we must wrestle against the spiritual forces of wickedness. No adversary is more dangerous than the one within our own house; no foe is more harmful than the one whom the power of a heavenly substance supports. When I say “no one,” remember the divine word in which the Lord said that among those born of woman no one is greater than John the Baptist; for he who was born of a virgin is above all. And so let us fear no one, we who have Christ, since, if Christ is for us, who is against us?

Let us contend, then, to the end, so that, with everything done away that formerly fought in our body against Jesus and the will of the Lord, we may devote ourselves to the exercises of true virtue and serve our God and Lord alone. For this is the end, as it is written: “Christ the firstfruits, then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has done away with every rule and authority and power,” so that death may be destroyed last, and we may begin to be subject to God, keeping within us the heavenly kingdom where before there was a cesspool of sins.

Rightly, then, it is headed “To the end; for the sons of Korah, for understanding,” so that in grasping it not common hearing but spiritual understanding may be at work. Aquila, indeed, put “a psalm of discipline.” And so Scripture says to you: “Apply your heart to discipline, and prepare your ears for words of understanding”; and elsewhere: “Love wisdom and discipline.”

Wisdom is what wells up from the mind; discipline is the pattern of the virtues grown together into a kind of second nature, and a judgment of the mind made firm by the teachings of knowledge. Scripture has also taught us to understand obscure speech, the prudence of sayings, and the riddles of Proverbs; and on its authority we gather that these are the chief virtues of prudence: that wisdom is always giving birth like a fruitful mother, discipline keeping us in check like a sterner schoolmistress, and understanding finding things like a careful investigator and searching out true justice and judgment.

Let us show these things from the testimony of the sacred reading. Wisdom says: “Like a spring from paradise I said: I will water my garden, and I will yet pour out teaching like prophecy”; for like a devoted mother she pours her offspring and good thoughts into the mind of man. Take also the testimony concerning discipline: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of God, nor lose heart when you are rebuked by him;

for whom God loves he rebukes.” Discipline is stern in rebuking but sweet in correcting, so that we may not drift and wander astray but be received by Christ; for “discipline that is untested wanders,” as it is written. But here he has used “discipline” for one’s way of life. Yet, like wisdom, discipline too is called by the same name whether it is perfect or imperfect;

but where discipline or wisdom is named without any qualifier, the terms take on the meaning of perfection. Untested discipline, then, drifts, but tested discipline does not drift. Concerning understanding too, the same Scripture lays down that “understanding is good to all who practice it.” And since understanding holds within itself both the grace of wisdom and the order of discipline, we are surely taught that both wisdom and discipline are good to those who carry out their precepts in their service. We have spoken of the title; let us take up the psalm.

“O God, with our ears we have heard.” So Symmachus. Theodotion said “in our ears,” as did the Seventy as well. Why does he say “with our ears”? If “we have heard” was not enough, then surely, if that was what he wanted, “with ears we have heard” would have been complete. Since, then, “our” has been added, what does this mean, if not that you should understand that what belongs to the mind is truly ours, and that it is better than what belongs to this body?

And so this same prophet speaks as if of something else when he says: “I will not fear what flesh can do to me”; and elsewhere: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and my voice to God, and he looked upon me.” That is “my voice” which is heard by Christ, not the one that echoes in public. He who remembers that he was created in the image and likeness of God does not wish what is corruptible and earthly to be his. Indeed, Scripture teaches us that man was first formed in the image of God, and afterward made from clay. As if [?]

the superior, then—for the superior is the one that is older—the vigor of the soul, which steers and rules this body, says: “With our ears we have heard.” Who is this, if not the one to whom it is said: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear”? For there are those who have ears and cannot hear the mysteries, of whom Jesus says in the Revelation of John: “Outside are the dogs and the sorcerers and the unchaste,” whose ear for hearing is blocked by lust for shameful deeds and by the rust of money. Let us consider, then, what they say they have heard and from whom they recall having heard it.

“Our fathers,” he says, “have told us.” Who are these fathers? The title says that the psalm was written for the sons of Korah, to be sung by them, since they had received the office of singing psalms and had been appointed to this kind of duty. But Korah, Dathan and Abiram, along with others who had risen up against Moses and Aaron in stubborn defiance, were swallowed up by a chasm in the earth in the desert and perished. Once they were dead, what other fathers could have told their sons of the wondrous works of the Lord?

For wisdom does not enter a malicious soul. If, then, they did not tell their own sons, much less would they have told strangers, who would have shunned the offspring of the faithless. Who, then, are these fathers? Perhaps they are those of whom it was said: “Ask your father, and he will tell you.” You ask him when you read Paul; or if you do not read him and something troubles you, seek the answer in him. For he is a good father, one who can teach and form the Lord Jesus in us, as he himself testified, saying: “My little children, for whom I am in labor until Christ is formed in you.”

The evangelist John shows you these fathers when he says: “I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning.” These are the fathers whose old age is a spotless life. So, in the gathering of elders, lay your finger on your lips, that you may hear what will profit you and come to know the sacraments of eternal life, and not, an insolent recruit, make a din over your teachers and presume to speak when you still ought to be learning. Let us hear, then, what these fathers told the sons of Korah.

“The work,” he says, “that you wrought in the days of old.” Let us ask what these days are in which God wrought great and wonderful things. Scripture teaches us that there are certain glorious days in which the divine deeds shone forth, since we read that the sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes; and it shall be that whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.

For on that very day Christ rose again for mankind, and so it was said of it in particular: “This is the day the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.” Although God made all days, to this day above the others has been granted the special privilege of the divine work, for on it all sin was taken away; the other days are days of sinners. This, then, is the day that the Sun of Justice lit up; for justice too has its risings and settings, which is why it is written: “In his days justice shall rise.” There are, then, days of Christ in which

justice has risen; there are days of Christ in which abundance of peace has risen; there are days of Christ in which wisdom has risen. Hear how wisdom rises: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool, that he may be wise.” And so Wisdom, who chose the foolish things of this world, says: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works.” For just as in the days of King Uzziah and in the days of Nebuchadnezzar faithlessness arose and captivity held sway, so in the days of the Lord Jesus faith arose, which spread the splendor of its brightness and light over the whole world.

For what days are better than those in which the vision of God shone upon us, as Jacob said? For thus it is written: “I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved.” And at once the sun rose upon him. Who is this sun, if not the one who made the days of justice shine, the days in which Christ was born on earth of a virgin? Jacob saw in a figure, and said that he had seen God; the Jews saw in truth, and did not believe.

That is why for them the days were cut short, while for us they were made bright, since for them the day was failing, while for us it was drawing near. And so holy David, shunning the blindness of the Jews, says: “Do not take me away in the midst of my days.” For the day of the Lord is great and glorious not, of course, by the length of its time, but by the brightness of its justice or grace. There are, then, half-days, cut short by the darkness of impiety and the filth of faithlessness, in which the sun set upon the prophets, as it is written. For just as the Sun of Justice rises for the righteous, so it sets for the unbelieving.

But an objection arises, because the Lord says, “For the sake of the elect the days will be shortened,” and this seems contradictory unless you pay careful attention and go back to what comes before. For the Lord says: “Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or ‘Look, there he is,’ do not believe it; for false christs and false prophets will arise and will perform great signs

and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect.” And so, that the elect may not be deceived, the Lord warns us what we should follow: we must not be caught by the words of false prophets, nor be deceived by any wondrous deeds of theirs, but we should believe that Christ is coming only when days full of justice have begun to shine. For Christ will be revealed in the full light of his majesty, and just as lightning comes from the east and spreads its light over the whole world as far as the west, so

the Son of Man too, coming with his angels, will illuminate this world, so that every person may believe and all flesh may be saved. Let us not, then, believe the Antichrist, of whom the false prophets will say, “This is the Christ”; for the days of the Antichrist will be days of faithlessness. Let us not believe those who will say, “Christ is in the desert, Christ is in the inner rooms”; for when Christ begins to draw near, all things will already be full of Christ. But when we have seen the things that Christ foretold in his gospel, then let us believe in his coming, lest, while we seek the true light, we fall into the darkness of unbelief.

We must beware, then, of the signs of faithlessness by which the days are shortened and diminished. For the sun will be darkened and the stars will fall, that is, the righteous of God; for there are those who shine like stars in the heavens. When you see these things, believe that Christ is still delaying; for where Christ is, there faith is brighter, and where the Antichrist is, there the days are halved. The prophet David would certainly not have complained about these days if this were to be referred to the shortness of time, since he himself said elsewhere: “Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!”

How could he lament either the postponement of that heavenly dwelling or the delay of this earthly one, when he had earlier prayed not to be brought down in the midst of his days, if the shortness of days seemed to offer a shortcut that would speed up this journey? From this we also gather how we ought to understand the saying, “Honor your father and mother, that you may live long on the earth.” For many who honor their parents are often snatched away quickly and die at an early age, while many who show less respect to their parents enjoy the long wages of old age; and unless we take that long life to be eternal life, Scripture is found to lack the support of truth.

This is why the Greek put it more expressly: “that you may be of many days,” that is, polyēmeros; for whoever diligently keeps the duties of devotion lives in the light of days, a stranger to the darkness of night. And so of the one who reads Deuteronomy it says, “He shall read it all the days of your life” — not, of course, by night but by day, because day shines for the one who reads the mysteries of truth and the oracles of divine devotion. Let us consider what follows.

“Your hand destroyed the nations, and you planted them; you afflicted peoples and drove them out.” We know, indeed, that the Lord uprooted and overthrew many nations so that the people of the Jews might find a possession for themselves, nations whose lands the Lord declared he would give to the seed of Abraham. But since this psalm proclaims the gospel of the Lord and the times of his coming, it seems to me that it is not

recounting what the Jews did in the past, but signifying what was to come: how the people of the nations would believe. So it confirms the faith of the Church before it announces it, and lists the victories of her devotion. She did not drive out savage nations by her own arm or her own sword, nor put hostile troops to flight in battle, but took possession of the lands of her enemies without any bloodshed, by gentleness and faith; for faith alone did the fighting. And so she earned triumphs

that faithlessness could not reverse but only increase, because the Church of the Lord is not defeated by her persecutions but proved by them. Let us learn, then, who these nations are that the Church has conquered. I speak of old names but new mysteries: they are the Canaanites, the Hittites and the Amorites, the Perizzites and the others whose names we will set out below. These

are the names of peoples, but they stand for the weaknesses of the passions, the incitements of human sins and their disgrace. The first thing, then, is that a person in Christ has tamed himself and conquered himself so as to live for himself; for he lives for himself who lives for God, so that he may live the eternal life of Christ. The people of the Church, then, did not fight with military weapons and iron spears, as the people of the Jews fought. They fought in figure; we fight in the spirit. They fought against foreigners; we have the war within ourselves, and so we must first conquer the passions of our own body.

Hear the apostle Paul fighting against the nation of the Canaanites: “I see,” he says, “a law of my flesh warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin.” Now our flesh rises up, now it casts itself down: it rises up against the mind and casts itself down before power, and when it sees itself under pressure it abandons its steadfastness and, ready to submit, is led away into the law of sin, so that it deserts faith and succumbs to faithlessness, and, left helpless under the sway of Hittite weakness, it yields to falsehood instead of truth, serves crime, acquiesces in error, and like an Amorite speaks bitter things in place of sweet; for faith is sweet, faithlessness bitter. This is why Peter expressed so splendidly what faith is when he said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe. How then can you tell us to leave you?” For, captivated by the sweetness of heavenly words, he did not want to depart from Christ; but whoever denies Christ separates himself, or is separated, from Christ.

But neither the crafty disputation of the Amorites, which through philosophy leads some away from the truth; nor the shameful abasement of the Jebusites, which subjects and prostrates itself before those who run the worldly race, a race that cannot last forever but fails at the gates of death, from which the prophet David rejoices that he has been lifted up; nor the Kenite, who is possessed by his own money, as a miser is with insatiable craving; nor the Kenizzite, who thinks there is lasting possession in riches, sets a vain hope on perishable things and boasts of an empty reputation; nor the Rephaim, who claim to bring healing to others when they cannot cure their own wounds.

And so, if anyone takes refuge with a physician of this kind, he must spend his whole inheritance before he receives any progress toward health, like that woman in the gospel who for twelve years could not stop the flow of blood of bodily pleasures until she took refuge in Christ. For she understood that no one is a perfect physician except the one who came down from heaven, of whom she knew it was said, “He sent his word and healed them,” and she noticed that of him it was said, “See, I have put my words in your mouth, and I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to destroy and to ruin and to tear down and to plant.” For although God often spoke in the prophets, in whom did he speak more clearly than in his own Son, who, expressing the whole power of the Father, said, “My teaching is not mine but his who sent me”? It was not Jeremiah, then, who went into exile at the time of the captivity, but the Lord Jesus who by his words uprooted the vices of the Gentiles from the depths of their hearts, destroyed the faithlessness of the nations and the perverse inventions of crafty thoughts, and abolished every trace of iniquity. Then afterwards he poured in faith and the discipline of self-restraint, so that the sacraments of virtue would not turn sour, as in a tainted vessel, from the mingling of vices.

This is why the apostle says so beautifully to you: “But death reigned from Adam to Moses.” What is Moses but the law, since he himself is the interpreter of the law? But the end of the law is Christ Jesus. Sin, then, reigned in this world, and in sin death, cruel and an unbearable kind of punishment for sin. Moses indeed taught us to lift up our hands to the Lord, establishing the discipline of devout worship.

He taught how Amalek, the crafty-tongued, was to be conquered: that we should lift up our conduct and our works to Christ, for thus faithlessness could be destroyed; but if we let our soul sink, bent our affections downward and turned our minds away from the pursuit of self-restraint, [?] we would be overcome by vain things, and there would be no

remedy, unless Jesus raised up the arms of Moses, already sinking like the weakness of the law, and supported them by his mercy. But the help of the law would still have been weak had not Jesus himself come to earth, who took our weaknesses upon himself, whom alone our sins could not weigh down, nor could they make his hands sink — he who lowered himself even to death, death on a cross, on which, stretching out his hands, he raised up the whole world that was about to perish, lifted up those who lay fallen, and drew to himself the faith of all nations, saying to a man, “Today you will be with me in paradise.” This, then, is to destroy and to plant: that what is vicious is uprooted and what is better is planted in the heart of each person.

Of this Moses says splendidly in the canticle of Exodus: “Bringing them in, plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, in the dwelling you have prepared.” He was asking that the Lord bring his people into those nurseries of lofty virtue and wisdom, and that they be planted there in his works and instructed in the disciplines of the heavenly commandments, and that in this people he prepare for himself a dwelling of his holiness — which the Lord deigns to bestow not by right of inheritance nor in view of our merits but by his own grace. For how could we return to the place where we were unable to remain, unless we were supported by the privilege of eternal redemption?

And so the prophet said beautifully: “For not by their own sword did they possess the land, and their own arm did not save them, but your right hand and your arm and the light of your face, because you were pleased with them.” What, then, is the land that is not taken by the arm nor possessed by the sword, if not the land of promise, of which this same prophet said, “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living”? It is fitting, then, that its possession is so glorious, for there the adversities of the world do not rule, but the eternal good things of the Lord bear fruit.

Therefore it is not acquired by the sword but possessed by gentleness, as the Lord Jesus testified, saying: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land.” Let no one, then, be unpeaceable, no one arrogant or proud, but meek and humble of heart, claiming nothing for himself but attributing everything to grace; let him not glory in his own strength but believe that he has been protected by the right hand of God, saying, “The right hand of the Lord has done mighty things, the right hand of the Lord has exalted me”; let him remember also that he has been preserved by the sword of God, and that he is illumined by the face of almighty God.

In all of these Christ is protector, right hand, defender and sword. This is why Simeon said to Mary: “And a sword will pierce your own soul too.” For the word of God is a sword, which, sharper than any sword, pierces right through to the divisions of soul and thoughts, so that nothing hidden escapes its knowledge. Christ is also the radiance of the Father's face, and so he says, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also,” since he is the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance.

To him, then, all things should rightly be referred. To him Moses, to him Aaron, to him too the fathers dedicated everything they did, so that they might triumph over their enemies. For Joshua son of Nun did not say, “Let the sun stand still over Gibeon,” out of confidence in himself, but because he trusted in Christ, whom he recognized as the commander of the heavenly army and whom he humbly worshiped. And so he was found worthy to uproot savage nations and to lead the people of the fathers into the land of promise, because he attributed nothing to his own works, believing that human works are unworthy of so great a reward of heavenly glory, which the Lord

has determined to bestow on those who believe in him more out of his own mercy than in view of our deeds. This is why Abraham too readily believed God, so that he might find with him the grace of justification rather than store up the wages of his own work; for the gifts of the giver are richer than the wages of the worker. For this reason the Lord also answered the man who begrudged the equality of wages: “If I am good, why is your eye evil?” Our fathers, then, as the nearest kin and heirs of the patriarchs, did not claim that being planted in the land of promise was due to their own merits.

That is also why Moses did not lead them in, lest this be thought to belong to the law rather than to grace; for the law examines merits, grace looks to faith. This is why the apostle, following the faith of the fathers, says splendidly: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.” For it is not Joshua son of Nun, because he led them in or because he planted them, but God, who gave growth to the people, who holds the first place in glory.

Do not be troubled that he said above, “Your hand destroyed the nations, and you planted them.” For from this you gather that not everyone who plants or waters gives the growth, but the one who can give the growth can himself plant, just as the Lord is said to have planted the nations. For he planted who gave the planting its effect — yet in those who by faith in Christ have deserved to please the Lord, to whom alone it is said by God the Father: “You are my Son; in you I am well pleased.”

Those, then, who share in Christ obtain from him the grace of pleasing. And he says beautifully, “You were pleased with them,” so that the distinction may be seen to be properly kept. For rightly God is well pleased in the Son, because he is equal to the Father and found unlike him in nothing; he is pleasing by right of the divine nature and by unity of substance. And rightly the Father is well pleased in the Son, because the Father is honored in the Son as the Son is in the Father. But God was pleased with us because he himself granted us to be able to please him. Scripture has taught us devoutly that this too was a gift given specially to man, not something arrogantly usurped.

For it is fitting that God should be pleased with those whom he made in his likeness and whom, through his image, he willed to have the privilege of heavenly grace. In his image, then, God is well pleased; but with those who are according to his image, God is pleased. In them he is pleased with his own gift and his own present, which will be revealed when that which is perfect comes, because, when what we are appears, we shall be like him, as it is written.

Therefore the one who does not trust in his own arm, that is, in his own working, but in the grace of God, believing that it is not a person's deeds that justify him but ready faith, says to the Lord: “You yourself are my king and my God, who commands salvation for Jacob.” It is no perfunctory thing to say, “You yourself are my king.” Not just anyone says this, but the one in whom the kingdom of God is; and in the one in whom God reigns, sins surely do not reign, for God's kingdom has nothing in common with crime.

And who calls God his own except the one who shows him a disposition full of reverence and devotion? For to the righteous it is said, “I am your God.” Thus Thomas too, when he touched Christ's side with his own hand and found clear signs of an undoubted resurrection, answered: “My Lord and my God” —

Lord, because he redeemed his poor servants; God, because he not only rose again but also raised himself. And he commanded salvation for Jacob, because there is salvation in each of his oracles, salvation too in each of the dwelling places, salvation in the ministries of the angels who are assigned to protect human beings. Salvation is conferred on man, then, by the command of God, not by his own working. For God preferred that man should seek salvation by faith rather than by works, so that no one would glory in his own deeds and fall into sin. But whoever glories in the Lord gains the fruit of devotion and escapes the sin of boasting.

This, then, is the one who can say: “In you we shall toss our enemies.” What does “toss” mean? The Lord gave horns to many animals so that they could defend themselves against the attacks of wild beasts. And so the ox often resists the lion and tramples the bear; the stag too, timid as it is, nevertheless protects itself with its horns; and the ram butts the wolf. So animals that have horns are said to toss. But man has no horns: how, then, does he toss?

See, then, what Scripture says: “In you,” it says, “we shall toss our enemies.” You are our horn, Lord Jesus, and so, just as we do not trust in our own arm, so we do not have our defense for tossing in our own horns, but in Christ. For faith has its own horns, which it borrows from Christ. Indeed it is not for nothing that we read in the blessings of Moses: “May he who was seen in the bush come upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the one glorified among his brothers, the firstborn. The beauty of a bull is his, the horns of the unicorn are his horns; with them he will toss the nations together to the ends of the earth. These are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and these the thousands of Manasseh.”

Who was seen by Moses in the bush if not the firstborn Son of God, who said, “I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob”? He showed himself to human eyes because he was going to come so as to be seen by all. The bush burned and was not burned up because he intended to burn this earth, which was sprouting thorns and briars for us, through the discipline of self-restraint, rather than to consume it through the hardship of death. This is why the prophet says: “Burn my kidneys and my heart.”

He revealed, then, a sign of a bodily splendor to come, by which this flesh would shine through the resurrection. For what did the harmless fire signify but the lights of those who rise again? This is why the apostle ventured to say that, as star differs from star in brightness, so also is the resurrection of the dead. Let this one, then, he says, come upon the head of the tribe of Joseph, to exalt the head of his people; let him come also upon the crown, to pass over the crown of the hair, to cut away the excess of sins and to sanctify the adornments of virtue.

This is the one glorified among his brothers, as he himself says: “I will declare your name to my brothers.” What greater glory is there than to pour the knowledge of the Godhead into the hearts of the nations? It was he whom Joseph saw in a vision, when the sheaves of his brothers bowed down to his sheaf, and the sun and moon with the stars bowed down to him. That sheaf is understood as a figure of the flesh; for all flesh is grass. He

took up this grass of ours so that it might sprout his wheat and bear the fruit of the resurrection. Do you want evidence? Hear him speaking of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it will bear much fruit.” Finally, so that you may know that Moses is speaking of the Son of God, he says: “glorified among his brothers, the firstborn.” Certainly Joseph was not the firstborn among the sons of Jacob — Reuben was; for Joseph came after many others. But he is called firstborn who was to come in order to gather the peoples of the nations.

This is why Scripture says beautifully: “The beauty of a bull is his.” For as a bull leads the herd, so Christ led the people of the Gentiles to the Church and brought them into the pastures, so that each could say: “In a place of pasture, there he has settled me; beside the water of refreshment he has set me.” The herds have followed the beauty of this bull as he went before them, as far as our frailty allows, so that they might obtain eternal life. This bull bellowed, and death fled.

“The lion roars, and who will not fear?” Truly he is “the bull, the greatest victim,” to borrow testimony even from our adversaries; for what greater victim is there than the one who cleansed the sin of the whole world by his own blood? Hear how the holy prophet Jacob too calls him a bull, when he revealed the Lord's passion, whom the Jews later persecuted: “In their fury,” he says, “they hamstrung a bull.” And to make plain that he was speaking of the Jews, he added: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

This is the man who wrestled with Jacob and touched his thigh; at that touch the patriarch's sinew went numb, signifying that from his line according to the flesh would come the one who was to be hamstrung by the Jewish people in the passion of his body. Not understanding this mystery, they decreed that the children of Israel should not eat the sinew.

And so they have cheated themselves of redemption through the sacred blood and renounced the benefits of the saving passion, so that they may not attain eternal life, for it is written: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. But whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood will have eternal life.” Take another interpretation.

What is a sinew but that by which the whole body is bound together? The body of Christ is the Church, which is bound by the bond of love. What else did the Jews do in Christ but loosen every bond of love? Rightly Peter is chosen as priest, who bound himself with a threefold bond in the spirit of divine love.

Take this too: Moses pointed to him as well. He added: “His horns are the horns of the unicorn; with them he will toss the nations.” But do not be afraid because he tosses them, for he said: “I will strike, and I will heal.” Good horns, with which he encircled the whole world! Good horns, with which he tossed that lion, our adversary! Good horns, through which he made it impossible for us to fear the horns of the adversary! For Satan too has his horns, as Daniel testified when he said: “I watched, and that horn made war with the saints and prevailed against them, until the Ancient of Days came.”

This is the Ancient of Days. And who is the one-horned beast but the only-begotten Son of God and the one Word of God, which was in the beginning with the Father? With his horns this Word put to death and brought to life the peoples of the nations, so that they became the ten thousands of Ephraim to the ends of the earth, and the thousands of Manasseh. For the people of the nations was to believe in him and fill the whole world, and afterwards the people of the Jews too was to believe, turned from forgetfulness to grace; for a people that would turn to Christ so late had forgotten its own salvation. That is why Saul is credited with thousands and David with ten thousands: the harsh one rules over few, the gentle one over many.

Yet I do not object if someone thinks that “the firstborn of the bull, his glory” was said as though of Joseph, and thinks the passage should be divided so, since God gave horns to his saints as well. For he exalted the horns of his people, and Hannah, mother of the prophet Samuel, says: “My heart has exulted in the Lord; my horn is exalted in my God.” Joseph certainly had spiritual horns in the Lord. So let it be taken of Joseph, provided that in him there is a figure of Christ, to whom it is said: “Joseph, my son, increased, my youngest son; return to me.”

For it is not Joseph who returns to Jacob; it is Christ, raised from the dead, who returns to God the Father, as it is written: “His going forth is from the height of heaven, and his circuit to its height.” Still, “return to me” may be taken of Joseph, since the people returns to the land of the Canaanites, among whom the patriarchs had lived before. That is why Isaac says to Jacob: “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites,” and sends him to Mesopotamia to find himself a wife there. But did the masters of arrows lie in wait for him?

Is it he who, because of the blessing of his mother’s womb, is blessed throughout the world, and not the Lord Jesus, whom a virgin bore? And so he is blessed not only above men but also above angels and archangels and above every exalted heavenly power, as Scripture testifies: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us.” For the Lord God himself is King of kings and Lord of lords over the things that are in heaven.

Because of these horns of the Lord Jesus, David too, singing to the sound of the horn trumpet, was heard by Christ, and Moses taught that the rites of sacrifice were to be celebrated with the sound of the trumpet, as it is written: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month.” For whom was this written, if not for us? The ancients were accustomed to reckon months from the new moon. And the moon is the Church, which is lifted up by spiritual and gospel preaching “in abundance of peace,” as the prophet said. In Christ, then, we shall toss our enemies.

“And in his name we shall spurn those who rise up against us.” What is a name but that by which each one is properly signified, something he does not share with others? “Man” is a common word; unless you add what he is called, he cannot be made known. A name, then, is what is proper to each, by which he can be understood. That is why I think Moses too, wishing to learn what is proper to God, something special about him that he did not share with the heavenly powers, asked: “What is your name?”

And God, knowing his mind, answered not with a name but with the thing itself; that is, he expressed the reality, not a title, saying: “I am who am,” since nothing is so proper to God as always to be. So let those who deny that Christ is coeternal with the Father see that they deny God, to whom it belongs always to be and never at any time not to have been. By this knowledge of what is proper to the Godhead, then, Moses wished to spurn those rising up against him, or, as Aquila and Symmachus put it, to trample those who resisted him, like serpents and scorpions, which the Lord too says in the Gospel

are to be crushed under spiritual footsteps, so that they cannot block our way, the way that leads to the secret places of paradise. We have in us, then, the desire to know God; we have the Word of God, which is the name of the Father. This truly is what is proper to God: that he is the Father of Christ. And so the one who came to do the Father’s will came in the Father’s name. That is why he says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you have not received me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive,” signifying that the Jews, who would not believe in Christ, would believe in the Antichrist. So whoever believes in Christ does not hope in his own bow or his own sword, but places his hope of victory in his name.

And so he says: “For I will not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me.” Even if we must hope in a bow, it is in God’s bow, which he set in the cloud so that the human race might cease to fear the flood. With this bow he protects us, and with this bow he also shoots the arrows with which he strikes our enemies and adversaries.

Hence he says: “For you have delivered us from those who afflict us, and you have put to shame those who hate us. In God we shall be praised all the day, and in your name we shall give thanks for ever.” Hear how he delivers us: the arrows he shoots from heaven pierce the inner parts of our earth, so that every earthly impulse dies away and is stilled, as he says further on: “From heaven you shot forth judgment; the earth trembled and was still.”

This, then, is how we are delivered: when the hostile and adverse powers are put to shame, or when the wisdom of this flesh, blunted by heavenly commands, blushes at its crimes and is confounded with shame at its vices: the adulterer in the flames of his lust and the fire of his mad love; the greedy man in the heat of his boundless desire, who by seizing what belongs to others craves the more, the more he has grabbed; the drunkard in his drunkenness; the criminal in his crime.

They are put to shame most grievously even here, but they will be put to shame far more when they see the saints of the Lord rising again and that word of the Gospel fulfilled which the Lord spoke: “Many of those who sleep in the tombs of the earth will rise again, these to eternal life, and those to reproach and everlasting shame.”

So when those begin to be raised to everlasting shame, the saint of the Lord will say: “In God we shall be praised all the day, and in your name we shall give thanks for ever.” The rich man is praised for his wealth, the profligate for his banquets, the fornicator in the night, the powerful man in this life, which has its nights; but the saint will be praised not in this life but in God, for he longed to please the Lord in all things and can say: “The Lord is my strength and my praise.” He will be praised all the day, because he lived honorably and did not hide his deeds or his faults, but laid them open to the eternal King, walking in the day, not in darkness and hidden places.

Hence the apostle too says: “Let us walk honorably, as in the day,” that is, not in taverns and hovels, not in bedchambers and debauchery, where the wicked man thinks the walls hide him, so that he can escape God’s knowledge, though everyone’s vices lie unveiled before God, and the sins of men cannot be hidden from the divine knowledge. So the saint will be praised in the world to come, because he did not seek praise in the present but grace in what is to come.

See the difference, though. While he is here, he glories in the Lord; there he will be praised in the Lord, and for a short time he will receive the reward of eternity. Aquila, however, put it: “In the Lord we shall glory all the day,” and Symmachus says: “We shall sing a hymn to God every day.” The sense of all of them agrees: that we should never cease from God’s praises, whether by singing a hymn or by singing God’s glory together at every moment. For whoever sings a hymn sings it with a pure heart and in the spirit, and shuts out every kind of human passion, so that no grief, no bitterness of pain, hinders his service or embitters his feeling, but in singing a hymn to God he stands firm, unmoved and unshaken, like David himself, who says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall be always in my mouth,” and like Job, who, when he had lost his children, when all his servants had been killed and his goods plundered, said: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

“But now you have rejected us and put us to shame, and you will not go forth, O God, with our forces.” Since holy David himself said in another place, “For the Lord will not reject his people,” how can he say here, “You have rejected us,” especially as he is speaking of a people for whom he lists no small marks of its own virtue? For it is no small thing to say that storms and various temptations came upon them

and that they did not forget the Lord their God or deal falsely with his covenant, and so on. Hence the holy apostle too interprets this and says that the Lord was so far from rejecting his people that he presented him as saying: “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people that does not believe and that contradicts.” Relying on the authority of this saying, he says: “I ask, then: has God rejected his inheritance? By no means! For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” But it can be said here that he did not reject the people because a remnant chosen by grace was saved.

And so it seems that, in the few, he did not reject the people, yet that, while not rejecting the whole people, he rejected very many of it. That is why he added God’s answer, that he had preserved the people not only in a few, but had kept for himself seven thousand men who had not bowed the knee before Baal. Granted, this was said by the apostle in keeping with the gospel, since the Lord had passed over to the Gentiles; but the time of the divine answer should be referred to a zeal for faith that was still burning, when the grace of the prophets still overflowed among the Jewish people. So if in Elijah’s time the Lord denied that his people had been rejected, much more so in the time of David or of the sons of Korah, when the faith of the chosen people still shone brightly.

Still, let us question holy David himself, so as to gather how the Lord did not reject his people. For since God is “a God who draws near, not one who is far off,” as the Scripture of the Old Testament has it, surely the one who draws near does not reject. It belongs to God’s mercy to be the cause of death to no one and to consider that all are to be redeemed. But see to it that the one who is rejected is not the one who removes himself far from the Lord, as David says: “For behold, those who remove themselves far from you shall perish; you have destroyed all who go whoring away from you.” What does “go whoring away from you” mean? That in the sport of their

shamefulness they abandon you, withdraw from you and stray from your commandments. Indeed, you find it written elsewhere: “But God judges adulterers, destroying them from himself,” that is, by estranging them from you, you have destroyed them. So whoever separates himself from the Lord is himself separated from the Lord; whoever does not know the Lord is not known by the Lord; whoever ignores is ignored, as the Lord himself said: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity; I do not know you.” For he does not deign to know the servants of injustice and the authors of iniquity. The sinner, then, is not rejected; he rejects himself. It is in this sense, then, that he says: “But now you have rejected us and put us to shame.”

How God rejects, however, the next verse explains: “You will not go forth, O God,” it says, “with our forces.” When God does not help, he seems to reject; for anyone who does not feel the aid of God’s help being given him thinks himself rejected and abandoned. But what does he mean by “You will not go forth, O God,” and what is meant when

God is sometimes said to go forth, or go out, or rise up, or come down? For God, who is above all things, does not move bodily, or go out of one place, or pass to another, nor does he really rise up, as though lying on some bed or sitting bodily on some seat. These things are said so that you may understand when, and toward whom, he is said to go out, and for whom to rise up. For in this very psalm we read:

“Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord?” And we must take care that he does not at some time seem to fall asleep because of our blameworthy deeds, as we read in the Gospel that while the apostles were still imperfect, Jesus Christ slept as far as they were concerned. But when they were struck with fear and dread of shipwreck, they woke Christ from sleep. So to the faithless the Lord Jesus sleeps; to the faithful he keeps watch.

So too the one who is faithful goes in to God, while from the negligent God seems to go out and depart. Certainly the Lord draws the imperfect and those still weak to himself, as you have read the maidens saying: “Draw us; let us run after the fragrance of your ointments.” But Moses, who was already stronger and chosen by the Lord, is read both to go up and to go in to the Lord his God, as it is written: “Moses went up the mountain, and light surrounded the mountain. And the majesty of the Lord came down upon Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it for six days; and on the seventh day the Lord called Moses from the midst of the cloud. And the appearance of the majesty of the Lord was like a burning fire on the top of the mountain before the children of Israel. And Moses went into the midst of the cloud.”

So, just as Moses here went into the cloud when he was first called to the mountain by the Lord, so later, when he was more perfect, as he entered his tent, the pillar of cloud came down to him and stood at the door of the tent. And all the people stood and worshipped, each at the door of his tent. And the Lord was in the cloud, for “he made darkness his hiding place.” And so that you may know that it speaks of the Lord, it says: “And the Lord spoke to Moses.” That Moses’ tent is recorded as being pitched outside the camp, so that he might meet God, does not seem to be a contradiction; for whoever seeks God goes in, as it were, to God, and enters with his whole mind into the knowledge of him.

So the righteous man goes in to the Lord, as Moses went into the cloud; and God is in the cloud. Indeed, “behold, the Lord comes on a light cloud”; and you have it written in the Gospel: “But when you pray, go into your room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”

So God is within, as in your own room. Hear elsewhere too that God is within: “Behold,” it says, “the Lord will go forth from his place, and will come down and go up upon the high places of the earth, and the mountains will be shaken beneath him and the valleys will melt.” Scripture says this, and already then it signified that he would leave the Jewish people and pass over to the Gentiles. And indeed we find this expressed in the psalm too, where David says: “And he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course.”

In these ways, then, we have found God going out or going in, just as the Lord Jesus also says that he comes to the man who fears him: “Behold,” he says, “I stand at the door and knock; and if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with me.” We have said these things, then, because of the prophet’s words: “You have rejected us, and you will not go forth, O God, with our forces.”

Let us likewise understand that God went forth with the forces of the Jews when Joshua son of Nun worshipped the commander of the heavenly army, and so conquered without the sword and destroyed without any siege the city of Jericho, which had very strong walls. For when God went forth with the forces of his servants, victory followed; indeed, the angel went forth at Hezekiah’s prayers and laid low the countless troops of the Assyrians.

But sometimes the Lord also seems to abandon for a time those he wishes to be crowned in the contest, so that they may conquer by faith and their devotion may not grow slack amid good fortune and prosperity. Indeed, those who have fallen through a run of prosperity and the enjoyment of good fortune are often set right by adversity. That is why we often find that the Jews fell after victory and were corrected after servitude, because by their prayers and laments they made God return to them.

Hence that saying too, which was spoken in keeping with human nature and human feeling, does not conflict with this view, when the Lord said: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” Not that the Lord was forsaken, for he says elsewhere: “For I am not alone, because the Father is with me”; but in keeping with human flesh and feeling, a man set in a hard contest seems forsaken by the Lord. Indeed, Scripture does not say idly that after the first temptation the devil departed from him “until a time,” that is, until the contest; for when the great contest of the sacred Passion arrived, the adversary came back to tempt him again.

A man, when he is set in a state of uncertainty, thinks himself deserted by his God. But just as we take it according to the feeling of the flesh that he appeared to himself forsaken as a man, the man whose course Christ worked out in his own body, so too in his divinity he knew that he was never forsaken by the Father, for he himself said: “I am in the Father and the Father in me,” and indicated that he was not alone.

He also adds this verse: “You have turned us back before our enemies.” It is not well with the one who is turned back, for “no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” Indeed, Lot’s wife, because she looked back, could not reach the top of the mountain, that is, the higher things, but was turned into salt, a substance that quickly dissolves and cannot last long. So it is with those who follow temporal things and do not follow eternal ones: here they lose their savor through their own folly, and they cannot have the grace of things to come.

Yet there are some who, though placed behind, forget what lies behind and stretch forward to what lies ahead, so as to reach the prize. And to Peter it is said, “Get behind me, Satan,” so that he might be the better spurred on; and in order of rank the one who is behind Christ comes first. So then, “before our enemies” means: because they afflict us and they pursue us, you willed us to be at the rear, so that we might stretch forward to higher things and always keep our eyes ahead, pursuing our enemies and eager to pass beyond their place.

Theodotion, then, has it as the Seventy translators do, that is, as this verse has been set out. Aquila has: “You turned us back from the one who afflicts us”; Symmachus: “You set us last before every adversary.” What things are adverse to us, if not the pleasures of this world, full of delights and wantonness, which are incitements to lust? Lot’s wife was led astray because she had behind her the luxury of the Sodomites and the allurements of that region. How was she led astray? Because she looked back.

So you too, do not look back at your enemies; God has set you last in this world. Or: whoever by humility makes himself last does not turn back but always looks ahead. And so that you may know who your enemies are, hear the one who says: “Hear, O Israel: why is it that you are in the land of your enemies? You are defiled with the dead.” Yet who is so much your enemy and foe as the prince of this world and his allies, who persecuted the Lord Jesus even to the cross, not knowing his power? For had they known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty.

So even if you are last, do not follow your enemies; follow the Lord Jesus, take up his cross and walk in his footsteps. For whoever follows Christ does not look behind him, that is, at the luxuries and allurements of sins, and so he can say with the saints: “Our heart has not turned back.” From this we understand that even one who is ahead of his enemies becomes last and hindmost in heart if he looks back at them and turns the affection of his mind to carnal rather than spiritual things.

Likewise one who is last can be first in heart, if he considers the things that are in heaven and not those on earth. Hear how one who is last in this world may be among the first with Christ: “I think that God has displayed us apostles as last of all, like men condemned to death, so that we have become a spectacle to this world, to angels and to men.” He called himself last, and yet he showed that he was first when he said: “But our citizenship is in heaven.”

It continues: And those who hated us plundered us for themselves; you have given us up like sheep for food and scattered us among the nations. You may perhaps be surprised that the speakers, who, as we have said, show the utmost constancy of faith in the later verses, should say here that they were plundered by those who hated them. But do not let this alarm you. Many are plundered here, and yet their minds cannot be separated from Christ.

The apostles were seized, beaten with rods, thrust into prison and separated from one another, and yet they remained with Christ. Indeed, by the very fact that they were seized by the faithless their merits grew and their grace in heaven increased. For whoever is plundered by men is not thereby also defeated. Look at the apostle Paul rejoicing in his dangers; see him glorying that he was let down through a window in a basket. See how holy Jeremiah, holy Ezekiel and holy Daniel were led into captivity and plundered by the Assyrians, yet suffered no captivity of their own faith, nor did they sin against the covenant of the Lord. Even in captivity they kept the precepts of the divine law, and they did not think they should take any of the forbidden foods, contrary to the ordinance of their fathers.

Hence Theodotion rightly said: And those who hated us exulted over us. For the taunting of enemies does no harm to good minds, nor does plundering by enemies. And so the saint, who is sure that plundering cannot hurt him, says: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress? and so on. But in all these things we overcome and are more than conquerors through him who loved us, knowing that neither death nor life, nor angel, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come can separate us

from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore whoever is such a man is not separated from Christ. Thus, even if he is plundered in body, in spirit he is free; and not only is he not exposed to plunder, he even seeks for himself a praiseworthy plunder, like those of whom it is written: From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven is taken by force, and the forceful plunder it. So he is the victor who, though placed amid earthly things, knows nothing of being a captive of faithlessness. Not only is what is excellent in him not plundered; rather, he himself plunders what is eternal.

There are also those who become sheep for food. Good is our Lord Jesus Christ, for he became the sheep of our feast. Do you ask how he became so? Hear the one who says: Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. And consider how our fathers, in a figure, tore apart the lamb and ate it, signifying the passion of the Lord Jesus, whose sacrament we feed on every day.

Through that very sheep, then, they have become flocks for food, as Aquila said, or flocks for eating, as Theodotion put it, or the pasture of those who eat, as Symmachus said. But a good feast is not only not to be feared by the saints; it is even to be desired. For otherwise the kingdom of heaven cannot be reached, since the Lord himself has said: Unless you eat my flesh, you will not have eternal life. It is proved, then, that our Lord is the feast or the nourishment of those who eat, as he himself says: I am the living bread which came down from heaven.

And so that you may know that all these things were done for our sake, from the time he came down, the saint says: We are all one bread. Let us not fear, then, that we have become sheep for food. For just as the Lord's flesh and his blood redeemed us, so Peter too endured much for the Church; and the holy apostle Paul and the other apostles also suffered much, when they were beaten with rods, when they were stoned, when they were thrust into prison.

For by that endurance of wrongs and that experience of dangers the Lord's people was founded and the Church gained its growth, as others hastened to martyrdom, seeing that through those sufferings nothing had been taken away from the virtues of the apostles, but rather that in exchange for this short life immortality had been won for them.

The verse that follows also shows this, for they said: You have scattered us among the nations. Theodotion said the same; but Aquila and Symmachus have: You have winnowed us in the nations, or among the nations. For the holy apostles were sent to the nations and scattered among the nations, as were also the holy prophets, of

whom we spoke above, so that from that scattering very much fruit might spring up. For just as our Lord Jesus Christ fell into the earth like a grain and died in order to bear much fruit, so too the holy apostles were scattered to bring good seed among the nations, so that the fruit of the nations might sprout in their likeness. Indeed, Scripture reports that the Lord said this: For this reason I have sent you, that you may go and bear much fruit, and that your fruit may remain.

So the Lord became like a seed, according to what was said to Abraham: And to your seed, which is Christ. Christ, then, is the seed of all, and for that reason he allowed himself to fall and be scattered, so that he might transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to his own body. This saving seed, then, sprouted for all men, and the holy apostles, shaped from it after his image, were sent out like seeds to different places and

scattered, so that the nations gathered into the field of the Church might shine with various fruits throughout the whole world. These, then, are called the scattered ones, as the same David says in a later psalm: The Lord builds up Jerusalem and gathers the scattered ones of Israel. For they were scattered to produce new fruits and afterward to be carried, like new wheat, into the barns of the Church.

This scattering, however, does not take place below, that is, not on earth, but in heaven. The precepts of the law confirm this, where the Lord says: If your scattering be from the height of heaven to the height of heaven, from there I will gather you, says the Lord. What is this scattering from the height of heaven to the height of heaven? Who is so great that he could be sown in this way?

If a man is born on earth, he began from the bottom, not from the top. If these things trouble and disturb you, go back to the earlier words of this holy prophet and hear who that great one is who made such crops fruitful on earth that their fruit reached the storehouses of heaven. He is the bridegroom who like a giant ran the whole of this way, pathless for others but open to him; and from him it began to be open to mortals as well, yet in such a way that they would ascend, while he alone first descended, so that afterward his saints might be worthy to ascend.

Hear, then, how the sowing was from the height of heaven to the height of heaven: From the height of heaven, it says, is his going forth, and his meeting reaches to its height. To what man could this be attributed? Moses barely climbed to the summit of Mount Sinai, and that because he was called by the Lord and urged on by a heavenly voice.

Who would descend from the height of heaven but Christ, who even when he came down to earth remained in heaven? For no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven. You see, then, that both when he descended and when he ascended he was in heaven and remained there. For he himself said: I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord. He is the one who is in heaven. Let this be enough said about the scattering.

As for the words you have winnowed us, though they differ in wording, they agree in sense. For just as those who were scattered were proved, so those who were winnowed also earned the right to be approved. For as wheat is winnowed and separated from the chaff and is clean, but if it has not been winnowed it cannot be clean and remains clotted and mixed with chaff, so too a man, unless he has been winnowed by temptations, cannot separate from himself whatever is frail, that is, his chaff.

Hence it was also said to Peter: Simon, see, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have asked my Father that your faith may not fail. See what he says and understand: Peter is winnowed, so that he is driven to deny Christ. He falls into temptations; he said certain things that were, as it were, full of chaff, but he said them in word, so that he might be more firmly grounded in his heart.

Then he wept and washed away his chaff, and through those temptations he earned that Christ should intercede for him. How much greater is that protection than the trial of his distress! And so he gained more than he suffered, for he gained Christ as his advocate. The adversary is driven to tempt the Lord's saints to his own loss, for while he tempts he makes them better, so that the one who is tempted, who seemed weak to himself, is able to instruct others too.

Indeed, Peter is set over the Church after he had been tempted by the devil. And so the Lord indicates beforehand what it means that he afterward chose him as shepherd of the Lord's flock. For he said here: But you, when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers. The holy apostle Peter, then, was turned to good fruit and was winnowed like wheat, so that he himself, together with the Lord's saints, might be one bread, to be our nourishment. For when we read the acts of Peter and learn the precepts of Peter, it becomes for us nourishment of eternal life and salvation.

You have sold your people, it says, without a price. Buying and selling seem to be one and the same kind of contract; but if you consider the disposition of the buyer and of the seller, each sells what he values less and buys what pleases him. For, leaving aside that class of men who carry on the trade of selling slaves, no one readily sells anyone except one who displeases him and whom he thinks unfit for his use; and again, each wants to buy one whom he has judged suited to his needs or his service. Even those who invest their outlay in selling slaves and pursue profit certainly hold those they sell so cheap that they value them less than money; and often they prefer to keep rather than sell those whom they have judged better suited to their business.

So God too sold what was worth less and bought what was worth more. He sold the people of the Jews, not through any harshness on God's part but through their own fault. To them it is rightly said: See, you were sold for your sins, and for your iniquities I sent away your mother. In this way the people of the Jews was sold and the Christian people was bought: the one sold by sin, the other bought with blood. Hence Peter says:

You were bought not with corruptible things, silver or gold, but with precious blood. What precious blood is this but that of the spotless Lamb, that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ? So the people of the Jews is without price, but the Christian people is precious. The one has no price because it has sin; the other is held at a price, for its sin has been forgiven.

Hence it is rightly said to the children of the Church: You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. If you are told not to become a slave of men and lose your own freedom, much more are you told not to become a slave of sin, and again, not to become a slave of the serpent, your enemy and adversary, but to serve the Lord alone, who redeemed you by his own love, for he himself is the redemption of his servants.

So the Lord sells only a bad servant; he certainly does not sell a good one. For although Joseph was sold, the prophet did not say, 'Joseph was sold by the Lord,' but: Joseph was sold as a slave. His own brothers sold him; yet the Lord, as a figure of his own passion, redeemed him from slavery and restored him to favor.

So his brothers sold him and took the money, but the Lord not only gave him back his freedom but also heaped honor upon him. That he was a figure of the Lord Jesus is shown by Scripture, which says: My son, sought out with jealousy, return to me; and elsewhere: The firstborn of the bull is his glory, because God the Father has exalted the horn of his anointed.

Whoever is sold, then, is cheap and without price, as one who rather is not than is. Hence Aquila too said: You have handed over your people so that it should not be; and Symmachus: You have handed over your people without substance. For those who are rejected by Christ are not; but those who are chosen by the Lord are, since the Lord has called the things that are not as though they were, and the nations of the Gentiles were chosen so that the faithlessness of the Jews might be destroyed. That people, then, was handed over to nothing, because it was sold by its own sin; for guilt has no substance.

Hence, I think, it is said: And there was no abundance in their exchanges; that is: you scattered us among the nations for nothing. For you receive nothing in exchange for handing over a man's soul, since nothing is more pleasing to you than a soul's conversion. But if it refuses to be converted, it hands itself over to nothing, to be made the property of sin and wickedness. So you sold a degenerate people without price and without exchange. Hence he says in a later psalm: For there is no exchange for them. Why is there no exchange for them? Because, it says, they did not fear God.

There is a twofold understanding of why the people of error had no exchange. First, a man cannot redeem his soul with silver or gold or possessions. For what exchange will he give for his soul, since those things are temporal and perishable, while the soul endures, either for reward or for punishment? Second, the wicked did not have that change either which takes place at the resurrection, of which the apostle says:

We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed. It can also be understood this way: although a few who were redeemed were worthy to be changed, such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Moses, the change itself did not reach everyone. There is also this sense: that there is no abundance in the exchanges for grave sins, according to what is written, that the sins of some men are manifest, going before them to judgment, while those of others follow after. Those that are grave and manifest go before and are sunk without any doubt, while those that are lighter are often relieved by good works; for blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. But where iniquity weighs down the scale, it is not recalled by any exchange of good works.

So if anyone from the people of the Jews was redeemed, he was not redeemed because he was highly valued, nor because he had abundance in his exchange, but he was redeemed freely, as the apostle teaches you when he says: A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. And where there is grace, it is certainly not by the merit of works or by the justification of virtues, but by the generosity of the giver and the choice of the redeemer.

Scripture has taught you this as well, in the words of the apostle Paul: But if it is by grace, it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. What then? What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain. Recognize why it did not obtain it: because it wanted to justify itself, because it sought to boast of its own works, because it did not offer faith or acknowledge grace. And so the chosen obtained it, those who heard the one who called and received the one who came.

Rightly, then, it is said in the person of that people: You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and a derision to those who are round about us. Who these neighbors are, and how they might seem to have belonged to the neighborhood of the people of Israel, is not easy to discern. If a spiritual neighborhood is sought, some light of knowledge is lacking for searching out the mystery of Christ, especially since we have learned in the very book of Solomon entitled Ecclesiastes that the more wisdom is sought, the deeper it is found to be. For so it is written: He said, I will seek wisdom, and it went far from

me, much farther than it was, and its depth is in the deep; who will find it? Hence diffidence arises in me about searching the mysteries of the divinely inspired Scripture and examining its words, a thing which he was worthily able to do who spoke wisdom among the perfect. I see perfect men here, and I would not wrongly call you perfect, since I see that you have faculties trained to distinguish good and evil. Yet even he who knew how to take more solid food sought help, so that the word of the Lord might run in him. Nor could this man either lay claim to this without prayer, that his praise might be pleasing to God; for it is the declaration not of one who presumes but of one who prays.

Still, so that we may not seem to have shrunk back altogether, let us consider who were the neighbors of the tribes of the Jews. To review the old history: the Philistines were reckoned neighbors of the tribe of Judah; on another side the same people bordered on the tribe of Reuben. The Ammonites, too, were in the desert, and those in the territory of Tyre and Sidon adjoined Galilee, that is, the tribe of Zebulun and the tribe of Naphtali, which were in Galilee, as Isaiah said:

The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan. From this one can gather what was the particular character of each of the tribes, that they were joined to certain particular neighbors, so that the knowledge of the heavenly sacraments might gradually flow into the nations as well. This can certainly be understood from that Canaanite woman who came out of her own territory to meet the Lord Jesus as he passed by, and, putting her idols behind her, to worship the true author of salvation. To her

our Lord Jesus Christ bore witness that her faith was great. The grace of the gospel was indeed already shining forth, and the light of his majestic presence; but because she came out of her own accord, begged for mercy, confessed the Lord with a devout voice, and, though treated as if with disdain, persisted in crying out her petition, this woman received no small privilege, being the first to come out from the nations of the Gentiles and, by her persevering entreaty, earning so great a testimony from the Lord.

In this passage I have learned that some have been in doubt about what he means when he says: I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, as if the Lord, who came so that all might be redeemed, seemed to have looked for nobility of chosen birth in saving souls. But he deigned to show his purpose: that he by no means wished to reject those whom he had first chosen, and that he often sought, with a kind of fatherly affection, to call them back even when they strayed and wandered. But when they abandoned their own Maker, knowing that he was God of the mountains, not of the valleys, and that the kingdom of heaven is seized not by the disdainful but by the forceful, he gradually turned to the Gentiles, so that the devotion of the nations might be more fully proved and the obstinacy of those others deservedly condemned.

What, next, does he mean when he says: It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs? He certainly called the Israelites, that is, the people of the Jews, children, and the people of the nations dogs. What then? Is it for the rich or the more noble to receive the heavenly sacraments, and not for those who strive more with devout fervor of mind toward the knowledge of the heavenly mystery? And if some Israelite is slack and careless or stubborn and casts the words of God behind him, while a Canaanite is eager to set his mind on acquiring the sacraments, is the one who is indifferent to be preferred to the one who brings zeal? Certainly not.

And so we must pay careful attention to what he meant. When he had said: It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs, and the Canaanite woman answered: For even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters' table, he praised her zeal and humility, for she did not claim for herself the depth of wisdom from the start, even though she had already come out of the territory of Tyre and Sidon, but believed that certain crumbs of the saving word

that fell from her masters' table should be gathered up. For whoever searches the words of Scripture carefully and closely is accustomed to reach the heights of the mysteries. Hence it is said to her too: Great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish; that is: may the door of the word be opened to you, and may the saving mystery of eternal life shine upon you.

So let whoever is a neighbor come out and long to see Christ and cry out in prayer, just as this Canaanite woman came out of her own territory, saw Christ, and cried out with unceasing voice so as to obtain his mercy.
