And so, as the Canaanites believe, let the Jew be in reproach, since he himself did not believe; let him grieve to be mocked and groan to be derided by those who are round about.

This prophecy seems to concern the nations that were going to believe, especially since what follows shows this, for he says: You have made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples. On the apostle's authority we know that through the Jews' transgression salvation came to the Gentiles, and that what was done among the Jews in figure has served for our instruction. And truly they were made a reproach

to the Gentiles, because the Gentiles preferred the reproach of the Lord's cross to all the riches of the world. But whoever thought that cross a reproach, and shrank from it as a reproach, has truly remained in lasting reproach. Yet those who could say, "For we have not acted wickedly against the covenant of the Lord, and their heart has not turned back from the Lord," do not seem to be Israelites according to the flesh. So consider whether they may be recalling that they were mocked and derided by those set round about them, of whom the Lord says: Many young bulls have surrounded me;

for persecutors surrounded him when, according to the counsel of his will, he underwent his passion. Hence he also says elsewhere: Surrounding me they surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them. It is better, then, to keep to the straight way, on which the wicked cannot walk. They quickly fall, because they do not walk uprightly. That is why those men also fell as soon as he looked at them, when they wanted to seize the Lord Jesus. So because of these people, who are used to walking round about, the Lord has posted an angel to drive back the enemies who lie in ambush from behind. The angel of the Lord therefore encamps round about those who fear him, and protects and guards them; for the wicked walk round about, as it is written. See, then, the difference.

The wicked walk round about, but the angel encamps round about those who do not walk round about, and he encamps there to rescue the righteous from the snares of their persecutors. So it seems that the righteous, the spiritual Israelites, are the ones who say these things. They were subjected to the temptations of the world and became a reproach to their neighbours, that is, to those who did not dwell in Jerusalem, their homeland. They were also mocked by the spiritual hosts of wickedness and by the powers against which the righteous are accustomed to wrestle.

History, indeed, may teach you that the Jews carried off to Babylon were nevertheless held to be far better than the Gentiles, even though they seemed to have been subjected because of their sins. For those round about them who insulted them were worse, since they themselves were bowed down under the weight of grievous sins.

The first sense, then, is to be taken of our fathers in captivity, whom the Assyrians insulted and mocked in Babylon, and over whom that most wicked king Nebuchadnezzar ruled. The second sense must be referred to higher things: the most savage king is the devil. He is the Assyrian Nebuchadnezzar, who is in the habit of laying snares for the good in order to draw them into sin through the enticement of the flesh.

Notice this king, then, in the passage where the apostle says: I see the law of my flesh warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin, that is, to that law of fleshly enticement. The adversary is a lion who presses hard on those who are liable to him and wears out the righteous. Hence Aquila fittingly rendered it: You have made us a scorn and

a pageant to those who are round about us. For those who were made a spectacle to this world, to angels and to men, were reckoned as contemptible as this. Even though they do not sin against God's covenant and are not turned back from the Lord by the enticements of the flesh, they still seem to be paraded about as in a kind of procession and despised, since sinners are in the habit of insulting the humility of the righteous, so as

to count the cross of the Lord and Saviour and the humility of the righteous as a reproach. So the apostle, as though set in a kind of theatrical pageant, says: I am content in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in distresses. In these [?] he takes pleasure who counts all the things of the world as loss so that he may gain Christ, seeking him alone through life and death; for him to live is Christ and to die is gain, so that he may be found in Christ.

These Israelites go on to add: You have made us a parable among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples. Among what nations were they set, if not those that were going to believe? For the things that befell the Jews happened as a likeness [in figure], so that the destruction of the Jews might become a type and figure for us, and so that from that likeness we might seek its meaning for the present by way of parable, and be warned by their example. Furthermore, all things Jewish are like parables, that is, like figures that need to be solved. That is why the Lord spoke to the Jews in parables, so that the unlearned would not understand but the wise would. The apostles understood, and asked the Lord about whatever puzzled them; but the Jews neither understood nor wanted to learn what they did not understand.

Learn what a parable is. Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. The Jew understood this only according to the letter. He did not know which of the two sons received the father's inheritance, because he leaned toward carnal things. The parable needed to be solved. Then the teacher of the Gentiles and the faith of the nations came, and understood that those two women are the two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, which bore the Jewish people into slavery; this is Hagar. And it is called Sinai because by interpretation the name means 'its measure'; for the law has measure, but grace overflows.

Sinai is also said to mean 'reward', and this fits the Jewish people, who preferred to be justified by the reward of works rather than by the grace of faith. So the Jerusalem that was under the law was in slavery with her children, but the Jerusalem above is free. And therefore Sarah, whose name means 'princess', has freedom, because whoever is righteous and blameless is master of himself.

From the two covenants, then, come two peoples: one of the Jews, the other of the nations, which has believed in Christ. The people of the Jews that did not believe is in slavery. It is the one born according to the flesh, because it interpreted divine Scripture according to the flesh and according to the letter, not according to the spirit. But the one from the free woman was born through the promise, that is, the one to whom the promise comes by faith.

He is the son of the Church, holding the freedom of grace. It is on his account that the Church says: Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac; and the apostle says: So, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free. This, then, is the solution: what the Jew did not know, the faith of the Gentiles has solved, poured into the minds of the nations by Paul their teacher. That is why their deeds are set before us in a parable.

The Lord, too, said: I became a parable to them. Those who sat in the gate were busy against me. He became a parable because, he says, you say: Physician, heal yourself. He became a parable because he rebuked those who sat in the gate; for at our going out we ought not to be idle but active. That is why it is written: See that your flight is not

in winter or on the sabbath, that is, not in idleness but in activity. So the Jews sat sluggishly, because those who did not know the courts of the true Jerusalem could not stand; had they known them, they would have sought that Jerusalem. So they sat wearily in the gate. And he did not only say 'they sat', but also that they hated the Lord who reproved them in the gates. For in the gate was the one who was about to undergo the passion of his body, through which he would pass from the earth and return to heaven. He was in the gate when he said: Walk while you have the light.

What, then, does I became a parable to them mean, if not that Christ is the end of the law, and that his death solved the riddles of the prophets? What had been unknown to the Jews when it was being prophesied was afterwards made plain by the effect of the Lord's passion. He became a parable to them because he presented himself as one of no account, putting himself in their way and not shunning their uprisings, and leading them on to the time of his good pleasure, so that he might die for all people and the human race might be cleansed by his blood.

Likewise it is written in a parable: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain. The apostle solves this parable, saying: Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Or does he not speak entirely for our sake? For it was written for our sake.

Who is it that ploughs, if not one who ploughs in hope, so that he may reap at the Lord's judgement? So, like good farmers, when our ground has been ploughed in hope through bodily continence, let us sow not carnal but spiritual things, since from carnal things corruption is reaped, but from spiritual things eternal life is gained. Let the deeds of our forebears, then, be a type and figure for us, and the law a type written in our hearts, so that in it we may have a kind of figure of things to come, not the truth itself. Let the law be to us as a figure, and the gospel as the light and seal of the truth.

So the Lord showed himself to the Jews in a parable, but they did not understand the parable, because they did not receive the physician who would heal the souls of those in distress and free them from every sickness and disorder of infirmity. He also became a parable because he took on flesh, which the Jews crucified, not understanding the spiritual parable.

For they understood so little that, when they crucified the author of life and saw the Lord's saving flesh hanging on the cross, they shook their heads. Had they understood, they would surely not have mocked but groaned. And yet that very shaking of the head became a likeness for them, so that it signified not what they meant by it but what the mysteries declared. For they shook their heads, mocking the Lord after the common custom, just as people who are eager to mock the righteous shake their heads if they happen to see them worn down in this world.

This shaking of the head has a twofold meaning. On the authority of Scripture, those who shake their heads appear blameworthy, for Matthew says: Those who passed by blasphemed the Lord Jesus, shaking their heads; and Mark: Those who passed by blasphemed him, shaking their heads. That those who pass by are regarded as blameworthy is taught by this same prophet, who says of the vineyard of Sabaoth:

And all who pass along the way pluck its grapes. The next verse, indeed, indicates this: The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed on it. And later he says: And those who pass along the way have not said: The blessing of the Lord be upon you; for one who passes by and does not stand in the courts of the Lord does not give a blessing. So the Jews shook their heads over the Lord Jesus as people passing by, since they could not have a firm and solid footing of faith. But they were shaking

their own head, for Christ ought to have been their head, and the faithlessness of the Jews ought not to have dislodged and thrown him down. But because they did not allow themselves to be members of Christ, Christ was not their head. Nor was the law their head, since the people of the nations stripped them even of the law. The word of God was not their head, because they had lost the prophets and did not have the apostles. Let this be enough about the blameworthy shaking of the head. There is, however, also a praiseworthy shaking of the head: blameworthy in the Jews, praiseworthy in the people of the nations.

For what is the head but the seat of the senses? The eyes of the wise man are in his head. These eyes, that is, the senses of your mind, must be kept moving, so that they do not grow sluggish with some torpor. Move, then, your prudence, move your wisdom, move your thoughts by comparing heavenly sayings and discussing prophetic words, so that you do not sin against God's covenant, but your faith stands firm. For there are heretics who move their senses, but so as to stir up faithlessness, not faith.

But now we must speak more explicitly about this shaking of the head that has been set as a likeness among the people. Who is the head of the peoples but Christ? For the head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ; but the law too is the head of the woman understood in the spiritual sense. Thus the Jewish people is under the law as under a husband, because the law is called nomos in Greek, and so the synagogue is joined to nomos as to a male. But she is joined to the bodily law, not the spiritual one, that is, to the Jewish ritual of the law; she is bound by its fetters and knows nothing of the sacraments of lawful marriage.

But if the law has died, that is, the bodily interpretation of the law, then the people, as though its first husband were dead, may lawfully marry a second husband, the one who rose from the dead. The gospel too is the head of this woman. Hence some, interpreting mystically, have held that once the Jewish ritual has been put to death, this woman marries the gospel according to the law, as though marrying the brother of the deceased, because the law announced the gospel. So the law was the first husband, and afterwards came the marriage to the second husband, that is, the sacraments of the gospel; for the two covenants are like two marriages. The one marriage is the old covenant, which was dissolved by the death of the first husband.

And therefore that woman to whom the law is dead rightly enters a second marriage, that is, the new covenant. Thus one woman is joined to two brothers: her former sins die, and afterwards better sacraments are renewed. The apostle has clearly set this out for us, saying: For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives; that is, she is bound by her husband's law, so as to owe him chastity.

But if the husband dies, she is released from the law of the husband, that is, so that she may marry whom she will, provided she marries after her husband's death. For while her husband lives, he says, she will be called an adulteress if she is joined to another man; but if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of the husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man.

He has also shown elsewhere that this mystery pertains to Christ and the Church as well, for it is a great mystery. Here too he did not pass it over, saying: So, my brothers, you also have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, who rose from the dead. How have you been put to death to the law, unless the shadow of the law dies for you when you approach the heavenly sacraments? For you ought not to approach the gospel except

freed from the hindrances of bodily interpretation. Otherwise it is adultery to mix false with true. But it is spiritual chastity if your soul, stripped of all the hindrances of errant understanding, approaches God's word without wrinkle. So just as Christ is the head of the Church, so the law is the head of the synagogue, that is, of those who are under the law. For their sake the apostle made himself as one under the law, though he was not under the law, so that he might win those under the law. And again, the teacher of the Gentiles became as though he himself were without law, so that he might gain for Christ those who were without law. And he aptly said that he was not without the law of God but remained under the law of Christ.

Yet the law was not the head of the synagogue from the beginning, for Christ was the head of the ancient synagogue which Moses founded and established. Listen to one who says that it was founded by the word of the Lord: By faith, he says, Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the grandson of Pharaoh the king; for he chose to suffer with the afflicted rather than to enjoy temporal pleasures, and he considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt and preferred it to them; for he

looked to the reward of God's promises, which is the grace of the resurrection. But when, because of the faithlessness of the Jews, the word of God died to the unbelieving and fell from the hearts of the Jews, the spiritual understanding of the law perished, and the synagogue married bodily ritual and the observance of faithlessness. That was not the sobriety of a spiritual marriage but an adultery against chastity. Therefore the synagogue could not be

free, since she had married badly and had not believed that Christ's resurrection would come. Hence the Church rightly married him, the Church for whose sake Christ died according to the flesh by the holy dispensation, so that the Jewish soul, which had formerly been bound by sin, might be released through Christ's death from the bond of its transgressions. So a woman does not marry another man unless her husband has died, that is, unless she has been released from the bond of lawful love; but if her husband has died, she is freed.

Indeed, the law required her to be joined to her husband's brother if her husband had left her no offspring. That bond was tied more by the interpretation of the letter than by spiritual grace. Moreover, the brother of the deceased had the choice not to take his brother's wife to raise up offspring for the deceased if he did not wish to. Hence he was ordered to loosen his shoe, so that he would be released from the tie of union with the woman he had shown to be outside his favour.

For thus it is written: he loosened his shoe and gave it to his neighbour, saying: This shall be a testimony in Israel. And the kinsman said: Take it and acquire it for yourself. And he loosened his shoe. And those standing by said: May the Lord make the wife who is entering your house like Rachel and like Leah, who together built up the house of Israel and did valiantly in Ephrathah.

But this bound the Jew through an interpretation of the letter. Otherwise it was a figure showing that Christ would come to earth, who as a brother would raise up offspring for the dead people, since it was said: I will declare your name to my brothers, and: theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh. Or else it showed that the gospel would bring about the restoration of the dead law in later generations, so that the course of the gospel would raise up the offspring that the law had not left behind.

No wonder, then, that by their perverse interpretation they shook their head, so as to dislodge from themselves wisdom, the author of their salvation; or at any rate, by shaking their own head they caused a shaking of the head not among a few but among the peoples. This shaking of the head came about when their sound went out into all the earth, so that all the earth became the Lord's and the kingdom of the Lord was among the nations. Hence he also says later: The Lord reigns; let the peoples rage;

you who sit above the cherubim, let the earth be moved. Aquila aptly rendered this with the word metastasis, that is, a transfer from place to place: from Judea to the peoples of the nations. How the law was moved can be shown clearly from the reading in the Gospel, where Scripture says: The scribes and the Pharisees have sat on the seat of Moses. So observe and do all that they tell you, but do not do as they do; for they do not do what they say. They bind heavy burdens and lay them on people's shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with their finger. They do everything to be seen by people.

What does 'the scribes sat' mean, if not that the letter is written? That is why scribes are called grammateis in Greek: they follow the interpretation of the letter, not the understanding of the spirit; but the letter kills. Those, then, who follow the letter that kills, and echo it in their very name, are the scribes and Pharisees, that is, those who are divided from the unity of the truth; for phares means 'division'. And the Pharisees divide

the words of the law in such a way that they echo them and meditate on them, but do not see the spiritual mysteries and sacraments of the law. For if the law is spiritual, then surely the precepts of the law are spiritual and its works are spiritual. So, while speaking what Moses wrote, they bind heavy burdens with the bodily aspects of the law (for whatever is contrary to the yoke of Christ is heavy), and by their errant teaching they lay heavy burdens on the ears of their hearers. These burdens they themselves are unwilling to move even far enough to shift them from the bodily things of the law to the spiritual words of Scripture. For this is how we should understand that they are unwilling to move them with their finger: not even for the slightest point and moment do they cross over to spiritual understanding.

There is also this, for it is written: But if I cast out demons by the finger of God. What the finger is, Scripture itself explains when it says in another book of the Gospel: that I cast out demons by the Spirit of God. The finger of God, then, is the Spirit of God; for God is spirit and has nothing bodily in his substance, but is wholly spirit. So whoever casts out a demon by the finger of God casts it out by the Spirit of God. Hence holy David also says: For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, that is, the heavens are the works of your Spirit; as it is also written: By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.

To conclude the discussion, then: the scribes and Pharisees refer nothing to the inner man. Just as the inner man was made in the image and likeness of God, so in what he thinks and meditates on he ought to think of spiritual rather than carnal things. They, however, strive to refer everything to the outer, earthly man, and so all their works are done to be seen by people, not to please the Father who sees in secret; for they are afraid to reveal their own works.

This, then, is the shaking of the head that took place among the peoples, or, as Aquila and Symmachus put it, among the nations. For all the nations shook their heads at the idea of interpreting the law spiritually. Let no one think that he will be saved by the letter of the law, for the letter of the law carries a curse, while the Spirit brings a blessing.

No one can be justified by the works of the law, because all who are under the letter are under a curse. Let all, then, flee the curse of the law and take refuge in the grace of blessing, so that they may have blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus. He died for us so that faith might pass over to the nations; and although he was first the husband of the synagogue, he did not abandon her, and he also redeemed us.

He did not abandon her, so that a remnant might be saved; he redeemed us by choosing the peoples of the nations. This choosing of the Gentiles, then, is salvation for the Jews, for the remnant was saved not through its own works but through the election of grace. It is therefore the grace of Christ that both redeemed us and gave life to the remnant. The shaking of the head took place among the Gentiles, but from this shaking the Jews received the grace of no small change, since their remnant was saved.

Next comes: All day long my shame is before me, and the confusion of my face has covered me. Why is it that this psalm is spoken sometimes in the person of one, sometimes in the person of many? For at the beginning it started with many speaking: O God, we have heard with our ears, and what follows. Then it says: You are my king and my God; again: Through you we will winnow our enemies; and afterwards: I will not trust in my bow; and: In God we shall be praised all day long; and:

All day long my shame is before me. What is the meaning of this change, which is often repeated in the psalms, as in Psalm 108, where it says: O God, do not keep silent about my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful has been opened against me? This is about one person. Then it continues about many: They have spoken against me with a deceitful tongue, and hatred in return for my love. Then again about one: Set a sinner over him.

In Psalm 108 it seems that one thing refers to the Jewish people and another to Judas the traitor: what is said in the plural refers to the people, what is said in the singular to Judas. Here too we can say that what is said in the plural refers to the saints, and what is said in the singular to our Lord Jesus Christ. For one may suppose that he spoke both on behalf of many through the prophet and also on his own behalf, and that is why he said: My shame is before me, the shame which is called entropē.

Now entropē is when someone wants to strike shame into another in order to bend him from his purpose, as in: Let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusts in God; let God deliver him now. And it is well said, "all day long," because the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ brought light to the world. The incarnation, then, is the day, of which the same Lord says: Walk while you have the light, and: Abraham saw my day. So this shame contains confusion within it, which is why Symmachus says: All day long my confusion is before me.

And what was the confusion of Christ but the cross, in that he hung naked [?]? And "all day long" is well said, because from the time he was fastened to the cross until the ninth hour there was darkness, and after the ninth hour the light shone again until evening. This was the first of the three days. Yet the choir of the saints can also speak of itself in both the plural and the singular. For a choir has, as it were, a single person, but it is made up of a number of many, as in the saying: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.

But what is the confusion that covered the Lord Jesus, since it is sins that produce confusion (for it is they that cover the sinner), and he committed no sin? Just as there is a confusion that brings on sin, so there is a confusion that abolishes sin, such as the confusion of the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which sins are cleansed. Indeed, every confusion that you undergo for the name of Christ is good, and very glorious: if, for example, in a time of persecution there is a law that a Christian is to be beaten, or lose his rank, or be deprived of a privilege, or be led away in chains.

This confusion, even if it carries no privilege, certainly carries the glory of a faithful confession. There is also being ashamed of Christ, as he himself says: Whoever is ashamed of me before men, I too will be ashamed of him before my Father who is in heaven. So confusion is good. Yet to many this kind of confusion over Christ is bitter, that is, to unbelievers, while to believers it is a joy.

So you may understand the confusion of Christ as referring to his cross, which seemed to be a confusion to the Jews who mocked him, as though Christ blushed at the very work by which he was accomplishing the salvation of all. Or you may understand it as the confusion that seemed to be heaped on him by the voice of the reproacher and slanderer, by the face of the enemy and persecutor. For he blushed that his chosen people had fallen so far, and he was put to confusion before the Father on account of those whose end had come. For the Father was present with the Son, from whom the Son can never be separated, and so he heard him saying to the Jews: Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.

There are also those who glory in their own shame, like those of whom the apostle says that their glory is in their shame. Opposed to them is the glory of Christ, who took up the cross and did not shrink from confusion. Neither should we fear it in the least, nor turn away from it out of dread or disdain, lest something that can bring the grace of life should instead bring sin upon us. For there is a glory even in confusion: as when you fall among many pagans or philosophers, and they throw the cross of Christ in your face, and you cannot answer them with a word, and no one will listen to you as you speak words of salvation.

That is confusion, but it comes from the voice of the reproacher and slanderer, from the face of the enemy and persecutor. And so, do not answer a fool according to his folly; be like a man who is mute and silent, as though not hearing the words of those who insult and slander you, not because you cannot answer, but because you ought not to. For there is a time for everything, a time to keep silent and a time to speak. You must keep silent when you find no listener prepared to hear; you must speak when the Lord grants you a learned tongue, so that your words may work upon the hearts of those who hear.

How will someone listen to you who slanders you precisely because he does not want to hear your saving word? Or how will someone agree with you who is a persecutor and wants to take vengeance on you—or, as Aquila or Symmachus put it, to avenge himself and punish in you the fact that Christ's inheritance seems to have been transferred to the nations? This confusion, then, is far from the confusion and reproach of the sinner. For the conscience of the one who has not forgotten his God is enlightened, while the conscience of the others is confounded, for their minds are darkened and the memory of their offenses troubles them.

And so those with a good conscience say: All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, and we have not acted wickedly against your covenant; our heart has not turned back, and you have turned our paths aside from your way. The last verse seems not to agree with what came before. For how could those turn aside who had not been overtaken by any forgetfulness of God, nor by awareness of any wrongdoing, nor by any slackness?

But if you consider that the righteous man is scarcely saved, you will surely understand that even his steps sometimes falter, and that God seems to be the author of their turning aside, because he himself allows the righteous to be tempted often, so that, schooled by temptations, they may be proved all the more. For who is

so strong that he is not shaken at all in temptation, unless the Lord stands by him as his helper? Indeed, even the prophet David himself was troubled, because in his abundance he had said: I shall never be moved. Or who is there whom the place of affliction and the corruption of the earth do not move, since the divine sentence exempted no one from the toil and weariness of this earth, when it was said to him: Cursed is the earth in all your works;

thorns and thistles, it says, it shall bring forth. Indeed Paul himself, the Lord's chosen vessel, though released from the curse of the ancient sentence by the passion of the Lord Jesus, nevertheless lamented most bitterly that he was being led captive under the law of sin, and found no one but Christ to set him free, when the law of his body and the shadow of death pressed hard upon him.

We have given the sense. But it is fitting for us to consider more precisely what the place of affliction is: whether it is this world, which lies in the power of the evil one; or rather our flesh, in which our soul is humbled when it comes down into partnership with this flesh; or the adversities by which we are tried

while placed in this body, in which we groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be stripped but to be clothed over. For it is heavy toil to wait for what is mortal to be swallowed up by life, this of which we ought to strip ourselves; for it is stripped off with less toil than it is swallowed up. And see whether this is not the difference between one who strips himself and one who waits for it to be swallowed up by life: grace strips it off, repentance swallows it up;

loftiness of mind strips it off, diligence swallows it up. And how can you doubt that this is a place of affliction, when it is a body of death, in which the shadow of death also covers us? And so we must always fix our gaze on that lamp which is the word of God, so that we may know how to direct the paths of our soul and the inner footsteps of our mind, that the light of souls may dispel the darkness of the body.

Aquila's translation, too, has beautifully expressed how we ought to understand the place of affliction, when it says: For you have humbled us in the place of the sirens. This means that the fault lies not in the flesh or its nature, but in the things that have made the flesh corruptible. Pagan story tells of the sirens, whom divine Scripture mentions a second and a third time, as certain maidens who by the sweetness of their singing voices lured sailors, eager to hear them, to bring their ships to shore; and ancient story has handed down to later generations that, following the charm of the voice, they were shipwrecked on a rocky spot.

Their meaning is this: the pleasure of the voice and a kind of flattery. So the pleasure of the world delights us with a sort of fleshly flattery, in order to deceive us. Just as there the fault lay not in the shore but in the melodious sweetness that made men fail to beware of the roughness of the shore, so the fault lies not in the flesh but in the things by which this flesh is enticed and tossed about. After all, the sea is calm when there is no storm, but dangerous if a gale rages.

The sense of the Seventy also seems to agree with these, when they say [as it is written]: For you have humbled us [?]. We must fetch testimonies for this translation from the divine Scriptures. For it says in Deuteronomy: If you go out to battle against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hands, and you take their spoils as plunder, and among the plunder you see a woman of beautiful appearance and live with her; and further on:

If you do not want her afterwards, you shall let her go free, because you have humbled her. You see, then, that it is not her own nature that is said to have humbled her, but the man who robbed her of the integrity of her chastity. The humbling, then, comes from the deed by which this flesh has been made a body of sin and a place of affliction. Again elsewhere: If a virgin is betrothed to a husband, and a man finds her in the city and lies with her, both shall be brought out to the gate of their city and stoned; and the girl shall die because she did not cry out in the city or call on anyone to come to her aid, and the man, it says, because he humbled his neighbor's wife.

Here too the reason for the expression is the same: she is said to have been humbled by her violator. You have a third testimony on this matter as well, and more if you look for them. Still, hear from the same book: If anyone finds a virgin who is not betrothed, and lies with her by force, and is found out, the one who lay with her shall give the girl's father fifty denarii, and she shall be his wife, because he humbled her; and he may not send her away all his days, because he humbled her. The same expression is repeated so that you may understand that it is not the condition of the flesh that seems to humble us, but guilt.

Yet we cannot deny that the flesh too is humbled by many things: by its very place, by its very enticements, and also by the frailty through which it lay open to error. Although it was deceived by no mean adversary, the serpent, it nevertheless possessed no mean grace of its own before sin crept in. Adam was in the sight of God, he flourished in paradise, he shone with heavenly grace, he spoke with God. Have you read that he was humbled before his own transgression humbled him?

He has certainly passed on to us the inheritance of this fault, so that, placed in this body, we are unwilling to be away from the body and present with God. And so we humble our soul, which longs to raise itself up to God; but the corruptible body weighs down the soul and the earthly dwelling presses heavily, so that the mind devoted to God is often bent down and cannot submit itself to God, since the wisdom of the flesh, which entangles our affections, knows nothing of submission.

Saying this about ourselves, what do we say about the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ? He certainly took on the reality of this flesh, and so he humbled himself even to death, even death on a cross. Pay careful attention and consider each point. See that he willingly took on this form of our body and the obedience of your servitude, being made in the likeness of men—not in the likeness of flesh, but in the likeness of sinful men; for every man is under sin.

Therefore he was also found in appearance as a man—as it is written of him: He is also a man, and who shall know him? A man according to the flesh, but beyond man in his working—and as a man, it says, he humbled himself, because God came to set free those who had been humbled. So he humbled himself for our sake. His body, then, is not a body of death, since it is a body of life; nor is his flesh the shadow of death, since it is the radiance of glory; nor is there in him a place of affliction, since in that body there is for all the grace

of consolation. He humbled himself so that you might learn what humility is. Listen to him saying: Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart. He humbled himself so that you might be exalted; for whoever humbles himself will be exalted. But not all who are humbled will be exalted, for many are humbled by crime to their ruin. The Lord, however, was humbled even to death, so that he might be exalted from the gates of death.

See, then, the grace of Christ; see his benefits. After Christ came, this flesh which had been the shadow of death began through the Lord's grace to shine and to have a light of its own. Hence it was said: The lamp of your body is your eye. But see which eye he is speaking of: not the outer but the inner. If, he says, your eye

is sound, your whole body will be full of light. It is certainly the inner eye that illuminates the whole body of a person, and it is also the inner eye that brings blindness to the whole body, for it is written: But if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. You see that in one and the same person, light springs from the very place where darkness is born.

So you yourself are your own darkness or light: the darkness of iniquity and the shadows of sin, the light of innocence. You yourself, then, are the author either of your harm or of your grace; the work of God makes no mistake. The light is in yourself, because your infancy is innocence, the pure mind of a person before the slippery ways of adolescence and the errors of youth. It is you, then, who have made what is light become darkness for yourself. Indeed, the same eye, that is, a person's understanding, is dark in the sinner and bright in the innocent.

Nor should we pass over what Symmachus says: You have afflicted us in a desert place. We are afflicted because at times we are left without heavenly protection, and this region lies under a curse, or on the slippery ground of the world. Moreover, our Lord Jesus Christ had not yet blessed his land, and so they toiled, and the gaze of their spiritual eyes was not directed toward the light of his goodness. Then, too, the pleasure and delight of the world often creep in.

Therefore we must not bind and fetter ourselves with the bonds of that man, nor stop our ears with wax, but turn our ears away whenever someone thinks fit to say things foreign to the faith, contrary to it, or opposed to our good, so that the shadow of death may not cover us in such talk. And if anything of the kind is put forward, we must still bring in the word of God, so that it may illuminate the eyes of our mind with the brilliance of its reasoning.

Next comes: If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have spread out our hands to strange gods, will not God search this out? (Aquila: will track this out; Symmachus: will find this out.) For he knows the secrets of the heart. Because for your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for the slaughter. What does it mean when it says "God will search out"? As if, should he not search, he would not know. Rather, God will search out your forgetfulness that has crept in, in order to remove every trace of it. That is why Aquila said: will track out.

For how could he search, who certainly knows the secrets of the heart, to whom even the innermost things are plain? For before God each person's conscience betrays itself, and a person's thought either condemns or clears itself in his presence. Indeed, Aquila said "the visions of the heart," because God sees our heart, and every thought of our heart lies open before God, and the image of our thoughts shines out before him. Aquila also put it well: In you we are put to death, since it is glorious to die in Christ, and the one who has been crowned with a holy passion for his name dies in him.

But why are you surprised that this verse declares God to search out the secrets of the heart, when elsewhere you have read that God is the searcher of the heart? And why are you surprised that the majesty of the divine substance cannot be explained in our words, when the apostle says: Do not pass judgment on anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and reveal the purposes of hearts; and then each one will receive praise from God?

We often read of the darkness of the heart as standing for sin—indeed, almost everywhere. So consider whether the things hidden in darkness are not the hidden things of the heart, and whether they have received the name of darkness because others do not detect them, but they remain hidden. And so the Lord is said to be going to bring to light the things hidden in darkness on the day of judgment, because each person's heart, which was hidden before and known to Christ alone, will be made manifest. Knowing the grace of his judgment, he says: Nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest.

There are many things that we keep down out of modesty and, in order to fulfill the heavenly command, hold within ourselves in silent affection, so that we may not seem to boast of what is ours and, by publishing it, begin to lose its fruit. There are also the hidden things of wisdom, which the apostle Paul heard when he was caught up into paradise, and which he kept covered within himself because it was not lawful for a man to speak them—not because he begrudged others their use or grace, but because what it was not lawful for a man to speak perhaps it also

did not profit a man to hear. These the Lord will bring to light when the time comes for secrets to be brought to light. See whether you may not also find some distinction in the Gospel, where he said: Nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor covered that will not be revealed. Yet this supports the earlier interpretation, so that we may believe both refer to good things, because it is written: The Lord knows those who are his. He knows his own, then, and he knows those who know God, but he does not know those who do not know God; for whoever does not know will not be known. So the Lord recognizes the things that are good: the Lord knows the things that are full of divine knowledge, the hidden things of wisdom, but he turns away from the things that are full of iniquity and sin.

So if you consider the character of these people, whom no forgetfulness of the worship of God separated from him so that they would spread out their hands to a strange god, and who were unwilling to open their souls, you will understand that their hidden things contained no shameful deeds but rather things belonging to innocence, since they were put to death for the worship of God and spent the whole day in the midst of death, as Paul did, who says: I die daily by your glory.

And Paul truly did die daily according to the flesh, in fastings, in shipwrecks, in various dangers, placed amid miseries; but he did not die wholly. His outer man was dying, but his inner man was being renewed, and so he did not lose heart when pressed by so many dangers, because, though his outer man was wasting away, his inner man was being renewed day by day; for each person's faith and the grace of his working light up the day for him.

Hence the apostle Paul did not know night, because whoever is being renewed is always in the light. Or do you not think that one who holds within himself the love of Christ is in the light? And so, secure about being sacrificed, he did not shrink from hardships, and no persecution or famine or sword can separate from Christ the Lord the one whom the bonds of divine love hold fast.

Meanwhile, even in the midst of good works, the human mind is troubled and shaken by temptations. Yet this too is the mark of the righteous: when they see that they are being tempted, they ask for help. So it was with the apostles in the Gospel. When Christ was asleep in the boat, they were terrified by the storm and the waves, and they woke the Lord Jesus so that he would drive their fear away. Do you not think the holy apostles spoke these verses: "Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise, and do not cast us off for ever"?

Certainly, even if the wording seems different, the meaning agrees. Our Lord Jesus Christ, even while he lived in the body, was not so fast asleep that he did not know of the storm at sea, nor did the rising gale of winds escape his knowledge because of the depth [?] of his sleep. He slept in body, but he was awake in power. And this was the plan: the Son of God, the Word of God, would board the boat, and his disciples would board with him. He would not let them become slack and

careless, as though they were safe because the Lord was present and favored them, and so he settled himself into bodily sleep. By this appearance of sleep, then, the Word of God showed the apostles that he was asleep to this world. Yet his power and providence were awake. It was this that stirred up the storm at sea, so that the boat was almost swamped by the rising waves. In this way it would become known whether the disciples, troubled by the storm, would steady themselves with the foresight of sound counsel or would let the remedy slip away [?]. But in those for whom Jesus was not asleep, faith was awake. So they got up and woke the Lord Jesus, saying, "Lord, save us, we are perishing."

See whether what we read about Jonah differs from the Gospel either. He was asleep in the hold of the ship and snoring, and in him a figure of the sacred Passion went before. For just as Jonah slept in the ship and snored without a care, as if he had no fear of being caught, so our Lord Jesus Christ, who fulfilled that figure through the mystery of his death, slept in the boat in the time of the Gospel. And just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, so the Son of Man was three days and three nights in the heart of the earth in the passion of his body.

When he roused himself from death and threw off the sleep of his body, so that he might rise again for the salvation of all, he visited his disciples. This, then, is the true Jonah, who gave his life as a ransom for us. That is why he was taken up and thrown into the sea, to be received and swallowed by the whale, so that once placed inside the whale's belly he might empty out its insides. Hear Job speaking, so that you may know of which whale this is said:

"Who is able," he says, "to take the great whale captive?" You certainly know who this is when you read that our Lord Jesus Christ led captivity captive. For once our adversary and enemy was conquered, we who were captives began to possess freedom through Christ.

Indeed, the prayer of holy Jonah itself shows that these are the mysteries of the Lord's Passion. For he said: "I cried to the Lord my God in my distress, and he heard me from the belly of hell." You see that he said the belly of hell, not of the whale. But the Lord descended not into a whale but into hell, so that those who were in hell might also be loosed from their everlasting chains. And in fact many rose again.

What rivers surrounded Jonah? Or of what abyss did Jonah say: "The deepest abyss surrounded me, it sank my head into the clefts of the mountains; I went down into the earth, whose bars are everlasting restraints"? This certainly does not fit or suit the person of Jonah.

But the Son of God went down into the clefts of the mountains when he went down into the tomb. For, as the Gospel teaches, Joseph laid him in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out of the rock, and he rolled a great stone against the door of the tomb. And in another book it says: "He laid him in a tomb hewn out of rock, in which no one had yet been laid."

And who is it that sacrificed to the Lord with the voice of praise and confession, if not the chief of all priests, who made vows for all and paid them? For he alone had the power to accomplish what he vowed. So just as Jonah was thrown into the sea and the sea ceased from its raging, so our Lord Jesus Christ came into this world

to win the world and by his blood to make peace with all things, whether on earth or in heaven. By his coming, then, he redeemed all people and called them by his works to the worship of God. When he raised the dead and healed the sick, he poured the fear of God into human hearts. He it is who offered to the Lord a saving sacrifice for us and offered to God victims worthy of our conversion. He it is who slept and awoke.

We must take care, therefore, that he does not fall asleep toward us sinners. For he seems to sleep toward those for whom he has not risen and whom he has cast off for ever. And who is cast off, if not the one who is away from the Lord because he is not away from the body? For how can those who are in the flesh please God? So let us not be in the flesh, but let us cling in spirit to the Lord Jesus, who in the eighty-eighth psalm says that he was cast off for our sake: "But you have cast off and rejected as nothing, you have put off your anointed;

you have overturned the covenant of your servant." So, cast off for our sake, he became a reproach to his neighbors. For he took on himself the reproach of the cross so that he might clothe us with the glory of his resurrection. He seems cast off, as one dead, and covered with shame, as one crucified; but blessed for ever is he who took away the curse and won for us the grace of blessing.

Next comes: "Why do you turn your face away?" We think that God turns his face away from us when we are in some affliction, so that darkness is poured over our hearts, and, hindered by it, we cannot take in the brightness of truth with our eyes. For if God attends to our understanding and deigns to visit our mind, we are sure that nothing can draw a cloud over us.

For if a person's face shines more than the other parts of the body, and whoever we look at we either come to know if a stranger or recognize if known, since our gaze does not let him stay hidden, how much more does the face of God enlighten whomever it looks upon! On this, as in his other sayings, there is this splendid word of the holy apostle, who is truly the interpreter of Christ, so that he might pour Christ into our minds with more fitting sense and speech.

So he says: "For God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of the Lord in the face of Christ Jesus." We have heard, then, where Christ shines in us. For he is the eternal radiance of souls, whom the Father sent to earth so that, enlightened in his face, we who were once held in earthly darkness might be able to look upon things eternal and heavenly.

Why should I speak of Christ, when even the apostle Peter said to that man lame from his mother's womb, "Look at us"? He looked at Peter and was enlightened by the grace of faith; for he would not have received the remedy of healing if he had not faithfully believed.

So, when there was such glory in the apostles, Zacchaeus, hearing that the Lord Jesus was passing by, climbed a tree, because he was small and short and could not see him in the crowd. He saw Christ and found light; he saw him, and he who had once seized what belonged to others gave away what was his own. Rightly, then, do these men say: "Why do you turn your face away?"

Or perhaps this is said because the coming of Christ seemed delayed to those who longed for it; for he is the face of the Father, he who is the image and glory of God. Certainly, even if we do not take this as referring to the mystery of his Incarnation, the saints still rightly use the words "Why do you turn your face away?" in this sense: "Even if you turn your face away from us, O Lord, still the light

of your face, O Lord, is sealed upon us." We hold it in our hearts and it shines in our inmost affections. For no one can endure if you turn your face away. "All look to you to give them their food in due season; when you give it to them, they will gather it; when you open your hand, all will be filled with goodness. But when you turn away your face, they will be troubled. You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth."

Do you recognize what the food is that God supplies to people? It is the food on which his only-begotten Son, our Lord, feasts in accordance with the Father's will, as he himself says: "My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven." This food is saving for us, and all the things of God are saving.

You hear of certain members of God; recognize them as powers. His hand is the fullness of goodness; his face is the enlightenment of the mind. So let us always hope in him, direct all our prayers and all our efforts toward him, and not despair, even if we cannot see him with bodily eyes. For Moses did not despair, though he was told: "You cannot see my face; for no one shall see my face and live." And he added: "See, there is a place beside me; you shall stand on the rock; and when my glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with my hand until I pass by; and I will take away my hand and you will see my back, but my face you will not be able to see." So the face of God is not seen by man. Yet there is a place in which God shows himself to man through faith. This place is beside God. Therefore, if we stand on the rock, that is, in the awareness of this flesh and in firmness of faith, then even if we cannot see his fullness, we will still take in, as far as we can, what remains of his light. For Moses did not see the whole fullness of his Godhead, which dwells bodily in Christ, but he saw Christ's back: he saw his splendor as man, he saw the glory of his Passion, through which he opened the heavenly kingdom to us.

Aquila, however, put "Why do you hide your face?", and so did the others too. This seems to agree with the words of Moses, who said, "Show yourself to me," as though he were saying: "Do not hide your face from me, but rather show it to one who longs to see it."

And he added: "Will you forget our poverty and our distress?" What poverty is the holy prophet speaking of when he says it has come to be forgotten by God? Or what is this poverty that he complains has slipped from the mind of our God and Lord? That poverty is no idle thing, unless perhaps it is the kind that has been accustomed to having God as its protector and rewarder.

For if this is the poverty to which the kingdom of heaven lies open, these men rightly thought that their poverty had slipped from God's mind, since they lamented that their soul was brought low to the dust and said that their belly clung to the ground; and those who cling to the ground seem to be deprived of the divine blessing. Hear, then, what this poverty is: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

If, then, the poverty to which heaven lies open is blessed, let us disregard these earthly riches and turn away from bodily abundance. Let us follow the Acts of the Apostles, at whose feet each one laid whatever money he had from the price of his lands, so that it might be distributed to the poor.

These holy men, then, had begun to practice this gospel poverty long before, and so they said: "Will you forget our poverty?" This is like the apostles' saying: "See, we have left everything and followed you." Good, then, is the poverty that comes from piety and is taken up in the practice of virtues.

They lament that not only their poverty but also their distress has come to be forgotten by God. Good too are the distresses proper to the righteous, who endure them not because of their own deserts but for the sake of piety. In them the righteous man is not crushed but enlarged, as the holy prophet declares when he says, "In distress you enlarged me," and the Lord Jesus himself says: "In distress I

called upon the Lord, and he heard me and set me in a broad place." He enlarged the holy apostle Paul when he took away the light of his eyes; for in this way Paul confessed Christ, whom he had denied before. That is why he deserved to be a chosen vessel. And so that you may know that the Lord Jesus enlarged Paul, hear the apostle himself saying: "Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians, our heart is enlarged." So open your mouth and confess Christ, for he is fullness; where there is fullness, there is breadth as well. And like a good teacher who wishes his disciples to be his equals, he urged us too to be enlarged, saying: "You too be enlarged."

When God enlarges someone in distress, then there will be breadth of heart, countless as the sand of the sea. To learn what this breadth is, listen to holy Solomon asking to receive wisdom from God. He asked not for riches, not for nobility, not for power, but for wisdom, and in it he found all the things that

he had not even asked for. That is why Scripture says that the breadth of his heart was like the countless sand of the sea. So that you may grasp this breadth, he says, knowing it from his own experience: "Write it down in the breadth of your heart." Therefore, whoever has wisdom should not keep it hidden, nor only for a moment, but should sing it in the streets and proclaim with authority what he understands everywhere.

Symmachus, however, put "affliction" in place of "distress." But whether it is affliction or distress, we need to remain in the Lord and not depart from him, since with the Lord as our protector and standing by us we can bravely endure every struggle. But if we neglect the Lord and put ourselves far from him, we make our adversary stronger.
EXPOSITION OF PSALM 45

The title of this psalm reads as follows: "To the end; for the sons of Korah; for the hidden things; a psalm of David himself." What does "for the hidden things" mean? In the fiftieth psalm as well, the holy prophet recalls that he had knowledge of hidden things through the revelation of the Lord Jesus, saying: "The uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom you have made known to me." And what those hidden things are we are taught in the holy Gospel, where the Son of God says that the mysteries of wisdom are hidden from the wise and revealed to little children.

These, unless I am mistaken, are the things that eye has not seen nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, which the Lord has prepared for those who love him. Let us, then, hide the hidden things of wisdom in the secret places of our heart and not rashly spread them abroad to anyone except those who share in the sacraments, whom the Lord has called to his grace. He wishes to be asked in secret, since he alone knows what is hidden and secret.

Indeed, the Lord Jesus himself, for the receiving of the Law, wished Moses alone, though not without Joshua, to go up the mountain; and in the Gospel too he revealed the glory of his resurrection to Peter, John and James alone out of the whole number of disciples. So he wished his mystery to be hidden, and he often warned them not to tell anyone lightly what they had seen, so that no weaker person

might stumble, unable with his wavering mind to grasp the power of the mysteries. Indeed, Peter himself did not know what he was saying when he thought three tents should be made for the Lord and his servants. Then he could not bear the radiance of the glory of the Lord as he was transfigured, and he fell to the ground. James and John, the sons of thunder, fell too, and a cloud covered them, and they could not get up until Jesus came and touched them and told them to rise and put away their fear. So they entered the cloud to learn the things that are concealed and hidden, and there they heard the voice of God saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him."

What does "This is my beloved Son" mean? It means: "Do not go astray, Simon, by thinking that the Son of God should be put on a level with servants. This is my Son. Moses is not my son, Elijah is not my son, though the one opened the sea and the other shut the heavens. Each of them, by the word of the Lord, overcame the nature of an element; but they only served, whereas this is he who

made the waters solid, who shut the heavens with drought and, when he willed, released them in rain. Where testimony to the resurrection is called for, let the ministry of servants lend its support; where the glory of the risen Lord is shown, the splendor of servants is hidden. For the rising sun covers even the orbs of the stars, and all their lights fade beneath the sun of this world. How, then, could fleshly stars be seen beneath the eternal Sun of righteousness and that divine radiance? Where now are those lights that shone before your eyes by a kind of miracle? Compared with the eternal light, all things are darkness.

Let others hasten to please God by their service; this one alone is the true and eternal light, in whom the Father is well pleased, or in whom I am well pleased, so that whatever he has done is mine, and whatever I have done may rightly be believed to be the Son's work. Listen to him saying: 'I and the Father are one.' He did not say, 'I and Moses are one'; he did not say that he and Elijah share in any divine glory. Why are you preparing three tents? His tent is not on earth but in heaven." The apostles heard this and fell down, overcome with fear. The Lord came and raised them up and told them not to tell anyone what they had seen.

Keep your hidden things, then, for him to whom David entrusted his own hidden things when he said: "From my hidden faults cleanse me, O Lord"; for the vessels that hold the hidden mysteries of devotion ought to be clean. That is why you are told: "Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your own wells, and let your waters overflow in the streets," so that you may be cleansed by a flowing spring. That is why you are told:

"Let your presses overflow with wine." That is why it says: "In distress you called on me and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction." For in times of distress there is a kind of fierce storm within the heart, when there are battles outside and fears within. There is the water of contradiction when our thoughts toss as if on the swell of the salt sea and are not calmed by any firmness of resolve in the depths of the mind.

Then there is the storm in the hidden place, then the water of contradiction, which can be calmed only by the word of Christ, by which he forgives us our sins, as he himself was pleased to say: "You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you." Speak, Lord Jesus: your word is medicine, your word is light, your word is the washing away of our filth, your word is a spring; you speak, and guilt is washed away.

And since our discourse has turned to the hidden place of the storm and the water of contradiction: the Word of God became all things for us. He became flesh in order to save flesh; he became water in order to temper the water of contradiction by his grace and take away the bitterness of ungodliness. That is why it is written: "A word in a man's heart is deep water"; in one place it says "word," in another "counsel";

for where the word of God is good, there counsel is good. That is why the Law tells you: "Take heed to yourself, lest an evil word arise in your heart," and Jesus says: "Why do you think evil in your hearts?" For God sent his Word to heal man, not to destroy him. This Word is medicine, not punishment. Let this Word be in your heart and in your mouth; let this Word be in the hidden places, where the devil lies in wait. Let the Word enter, let the devil go out. For if the devil creeps in,

Christ departs, just as he departed from Judas after the devil had plunged into his heart. So you too say: "From my hidden faults cleanse me, O Lord," so that the devil may not lie in wait in the hidden places, like a lion in his den. But if you keep the hidden things of Christ devoutly and faithfully, the devil can have no place to lie in wait. That is why David, in the ninth psalm, writing of the hidden mysteries of the Lord—the conversion of sinners, the calling of the Gentiles, the kingdom of God, the preparation of the heart, the judgment of the poor, the refreshment of the needy—first says that the adversary must be driven out of the hidden and secret places of your heart,

so that he may not sit in hiding, eager to kill the innocent. That is why you are told: "Go into your room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret." Let your prayer go down there, where he who searches hidden things may hear it; there let him find your patience, whether in covering over an injury or in avoiding boastfulness; for a wise man conceals the injury done to him. There is the hiding place of wisdom; for "he made darkness his hiding place"; "the wicked will seek me and not find me."

That is why Abraham dug a well, so that whoever sought water might find it; that is why Isaac dug a well; that is why the Lord Jesus sat by a well—and Jacob's spring was there—he sat by the well so that you would seek. Christ was the spring there for you. He is a spring, so that waters may overflow for those who seek them, by which all the sins of the flesh may be washed away or its fires quenched. This, then, is the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God: the wicked do not find it, while the good seek it and devote themselves to the study and meditation of acquiring it. Do you want to know how true this is? Hear the words of Wisdom herself: "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you."

So knock at the door, for Christ is the door; knock at the door of the Word, so that it may be opened to you to declare the mystery of Christ, and so that you may find the treasures of wisdom hidden in Christ. In him our wisdom, in him our life is hidden, as Paul declared, who was caught up as far as the third heaven to hear things that man is not permitted to speak. How great is the discipline of hidden things! Man is permitted to know and not permitted to speak. To know is life; to speak is death.

We know, then, that the purpose of "the hidden things", called [?] in Greek, comes to this: the unworthy do not grasp the teaching of wisdom, while those who long for it, supported by the merits of their life and faith, strive to understand the divine mysteries and toil in daily exercise, and so deserve to gain the fruit of their effort. So let us read the ninth and the forty-fifth psalms with particular care, so that with a faithful mind we may grasp the wisdom hidden in a mystery. For these two alone bear the title "on the hidden things". But now let us take up the psalm.

God is our refuge and strength. What does "our" mean? It means: of us who believe in you. So too elsewhere: Lord, you have become a refuge for us. "For us," he says, that is, for believers, not unbelievers; for us who seek the truth, not for those who flee from it. Only the one who has placed his hope of salvation in the protection of God alone can say this.

So you have become a refuge for us, our refuge and strength, for we come from the peoples of the nations. The Jews denied you, the Jews did not receive you, and so you turned to the Gentiles. You called us, you became our refuge, and you are our strength. Do you want to know how this was said of us who come from the Gentiles? The cross of the Lord is a stumbling block to the Jews and folly to the Greeks, but to us it is the power and wisdom of God. And further on: It is from him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God.

Paul was certainly not speaking of the Jews or of the Gentiles, but of those who had turned to the Lord Jesus and proclaimed him as the author of their salvation. You have taken refuge in Christ, then: do not abandon your foundation, do not forsake the one who makes you firm, so that he who took you up may himself protect you, and the merciful merchant of our souls may recognize his own merchandise.

A helper in the tribulations that have come upon us exceedingly. "Exceedingly" fits both parts well, so that it can be understood both as "in the tribulations that have come upon us exceedingly" and as "a helper exceedingly". For the greater the tribulations, the greater and stronger the help we need. And so it often happens that we are crowned in the heavier and harsher contests, because by tears and groans and more frequent prayers we win for ourselves the aid of the eternal Godhead.

So it is that we do not fear when our earth is troubled and the mountains are moved, for if you are for us, who is against us? We cannot fear the frailties of this flesh, which is broken by fear and dread, inflamed by desires, softened by luxury, enervated by pleasures, burned up by fevers, tormented by pain, and made faint by distress.

Or else, when those mountains are carried into the heart of the sea of which the Savior said: If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, "Be lifted up and thrown into the sea," nothing will be impossible for you. Such a mountain cast itself into the heart of Judas and troubled his mind with a heavy storm, tossing it on the waves of various passions.

For just as a soul fruitful in good works and in the fruits of devotion and faith is compared to the fertility of the land, so that the smell of Jacob is like the smell of a full field, so too the soul of one who does not know how to be at rest, and who stirs up heavy waves with bitter thoughts, is pictured by the restlessness of the stormy sea. In the end not even by his own kiss did the Lord Jesus soften the bitterness of Judas the traitor. The traitor received the kiss, poured in poison, and brought about death; Christ blunted its sting, but the traitor alone did not escape it.

And to show us plainly what kind of mountain this was, elsewhere too, when he had ordered a demon to come out of a man and the apostles asked why they themselves had been unable to cast it out, he said: This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting. And he added: If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, "Move from here to there", indicating with his hand which mountain it was that perfect faith could move. For perfect faith is compared to a grain of mustard seed, as the apostle says: If I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.

There are also some who punctuate it this way: and the mountains will be moved, so that what follows is: in the hearts of the sea its waters roared and were troubled; the mountains were troubled by his might. The waters that roar and are troubled are not good waters, and they cannot give drink. Better are those that pass through, as it is written: Between the mountains the waters will pass, and all the beasts of the field will drink; the wild asses will take them for their thirst.

Indeed, when the legion of demons asked for and received power to enter the swine, it hurled itself into the sea with a great rush, and those waters were troubled by the headlong plunge of the herd. Elsewhere too the same prophet David put it this way: The waters saw you, O God, the waters saw you and were afraid; that is, the good powers, which are calm through knowledge of the heavenly Word, not terrifying with roar and crash. But what does he say of the evil powers? And the depths were troubled;

a multitude of the sound of waters. The depths do not see God, and so they are always subject to turmoil. And he explained what the depths are: a multitude, he says, of the sound of waters. For that beast, the Antichrist, also rises from the abyss to make war against Elijah and Enoch and John, who have been given back to the earth for the sake of their witness to the Lord Jesus, as we read in the Apocalypse of John. To him was given a mouth to speak great things, so that he might sound out against God insults full of fury and sacrilege.

So the waters roared, that is, the unclean spirits, when they were troubled at seeing the works of God, dreading that at the coming of the saving Lord their judgment was drawing near. The waters roared and were troubled at the Lord's passion. Hence it is also said: Why did the nations rage, and the peoples plot vain things?

And elsewhere Scripture says: Their memory perished with a din. The devil seeks noise, Christ seeks silence. Indeed, like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth. And elsewhere: He will not cry out or quarrel, nor will anyone hear his voice in the street, until he brings forth judgment to victory. What victory is this, if not victory over the serpent?

By this might of the Son of God the mountains were troubled, when the devil and his ministers saw the dead rising again. These are the mountains that are troubled; those others are the mountains that are carried into paradise: the one to whom it is said, Today you will be with me in paradise; and another, to whom it is said, If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me; and Enoch, who was taken up so that the wickedness of the world might not change him.

After the Lord's passion, what else had to follow except that a river came forth from the Lord's body, when water and blood flowed from his side? With it he gladdened the souls of all, because with that river he washed away the sin of the whole world. There is also the river that goes out from Eden and encircles the whole earth: the Word of God, by which the spiritual paradise is watered and every soul is called to the grace of Christ, as the Word of God himself says: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.

Whoever I give water to, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water. For from that one Word of God have flowed the streams of the four rivers of prudence and fortitude, of temperance too and justice. For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another the grace of healing by the one Spirit, to another the working of mighty deeds. For one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills. These are the streams of the river, when it pours itself out by free division into the gifts of ministry, of working and of power.

By these channels of the heavenly river, then, that city in which God dwells is watered, and the tabernacle of the Most High is sanctified: every soul in which Christ dwells, or that body which the Virgin brought forth, of which the angel Gabriel said: And the holy one who will be born of you will be called the Son of the living God. A good tabernacle, which no sins could overshadow; a wonderful temple of God and a heavenly palace, which, when it was dissolved, could not

suffer corruption, but rose again within three days, raised by the very one who seemed to be dead. And no wonder, since God was in the midst of his city and was not moved: either because the Son of God was not moved by any lapse into sin, nor did he stumble at the snare of any error or sway under the push of bodily allurement; or because the grace of God did not abandon his soul but remained in it inseparably, since that soul remained unstained by any defilement of sin. Hence the Son of God also said to the Father:

Nor will you abandon my soul in hell. So because it lay within him not to sin even in the flesh, he says, as God: I am in the Father and the Father is in me. And elsewhere: I was handed over and did not go out. Certainly he did not go out from the one to whom he said afterward: I have risen, and I am still with you. But when someone sins more gravely, God is moved in him so as to pass away from him. That is why with the sinning Adam God was seen walking, and with Stephen standing: the one fell in transgression, the other was crowned in martyrdom.

And in the book of Zechariah it is written: The Lord will walk in the commotion of the threat of his wrath. Something similar is said to the Jews in the Gospel: Behold, your house will be left to you desolate. For the Lord abandoned the Jews, and ruin at once followed for the synagogue. Had Christ not deserted it, its final destruction would never have followed. So we have explained what is said: God is in her midst; she will not be moved.

There follows: God will help her at daybreak. This means that the morning resurrection brings us the support of heavenly help, for it drove back the night and poured forth the day again, as Scripture says: Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you. But see the mystery. Christ suffered in the evening; that is why, according to the law, the lamb was also slain toward evening. He rose in the morning, for so it is written: On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb at first light, while it was still dark, and saw the stone rolled away from the entrance.

He is slain toward the evening of the world, as the light was already failing, because this whole world was in darkness, and it would have been wrapped in still greater squalor of darkness had not Christ come to us from heaven as eternal light, to restore to the human race the times of innocence. So the Lord Jesus suffered and by his blood forgave our sins; the light of a purer conscience shone out, and the day of spiritual grace gleamed forth.

That is why the apostle says: The night is far gone, the day is at hand. So we have woken up; let us no longer sleep. We have put on the garment of light; let us not go back to the cloaks and cast-off clothes of a life of darkness. We have said farewell to revelling and pleasures, which belong to the night; we have chosen sobriety, by grace of which Jacob gained the birthright he did not have.

In other manuscripts we also find: God helps her with his face. What this means the prophet himself may teach us, for later on he said: Show your face, and we shall be saved.
