So God's look is our salvation, and in his face lies our help. How great the power of this is, divine Scripture declares, for it was not idly that it added that God looked upon Abel's gifts, but did not look upon Cain's;

and so Cain was grieved, because he knew that his sacrifice had displeased God, while his brother's had pleased him. So too what was sung today in the responsory of the psalm greatly supports our claim: I waited and waited for the Lord, and he looked upon me. Whom the Lord looks upon, he saves. Indeed, at the Lord's passion, when Peter wavered in speech though not in mind (and yet even Peter's wavering speech is more faithful than the teaching of many), Christ looked at him and Peter wept, and so washed away his own error. Thus the one he was seen to deny with his voice, he confessed with his tears.

The nations were troubled, kingdoms were bowed down; the Most High gave forth his voice and the earth was moved. At the coming of the Lord and Savior the hostile powers were troubled together with their legion, when they were ordered to come out of human bodies and begged to be sent into the swine. Once the most wicked powers were troubled, the worshippers of idols had to be troubled too, and the kingdoms of sin bowed down as well. For it was a heavy kingdom, which had subjected the souls of all sinners to itself in heavy slavery; for whoever commits sin is a slave of sin.

And the kingdom of sin is the kingdom of death, which long prevailed over the whole world. Hence the apostle says: But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a type of the one to come. The truth came, and the figure ceased; life came, and the kingdom of death vanished; the forgiveness of sins came, and the chains of sin were loosed. Before, even lighter offences were bound fast by the bonds of death; but after the coming of the saving Lord even graver crimes were forgiven.

So the kingdoms of the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places were bowed down, because the worship of idols and the allure of sin began to diminish through the preaching of the gospel teaching. Unbelief was bowed down, once faith began to reign in the hearts of the nations. The kingdoms of sin are bowed down when it is read: Let not sin reign in your mortal body. The Lord bowed down all the kingdoms of unbelief by his voice, saying: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

This is the voice the Most High gave forth, and all the peoples of the nations followed, fleeing the harsh kingdoms of sin, the cruelty of everlasting death and the unbearable slavery of every vice. For he promised rest to the weary, release to captives, freedom to slaves, and, having shaken off the iron yoke of the king of Babylon, he put his own sweet yoke on the necks of the faithful in its place, so that the enemy might not again bind the empty necks of the Gentiles with the chains of his wickedness. For those whom Christ binds he sets free, and those whom he fastens he releases.

Indeed, whoever was called by the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman, and whoever was called as a free man is Christ's slave. That is why Paul glories in his chains, saying: Paul, prisoner of Jesus. What is a disgrace under others is a glory under Christ. The Lord gave forth his voice in his passion and all the elements trembled, the whole earth was moved, so that the rites of the Gentiles might be dissolved and the earth might become the Lord's, and its fullness, as it is written;

so that the auguries of the unbelievers might cease, and the knowledge of faith and zeal for devotion might abolish the sacrifice of impiety. The Lord gives forth his voice daily, and it echoes in the hearts of each one, so that everything earthly may fall away from the affections of one who believes rightly, and every inner sense of the soul may be moved by devout confession from error to the knowledge of the heavenly mysteries, from the corruption and dissipation of luxury to the pursuit of chastity, from wickedness to virtue.

So he says that those who are on the earth were moved; or else that all men were earth, in whom there was earthly corruption, because they did not know how to lift and raise the eyes of their minds to the heights of heavenly grace, and could not say:

The God of hosts is with us, since there was with them only the instigator of their fall and the author of error. But after the voice of the Lord rang out in the Gospel, the prophet dares to say: The God of hosts is with us. He who believed that a virgin conceived in her womb and gave birth rightly says: The God of hosts is with us. We too dare to say: The God of hosts is with us, now that Emmanuel, that is, God, has begun to be with us. So where Emmanuel is, there the God of hosts is with us.

The God of Jacob is our protector. So let us imitate the patriarch Jacob: his fragrance, his virtue, his labor. For just as we must do the works of Abraham to deserve rightly to be called his sons, so too we must undertake the exercises and contests of holy Jacob, so that the God of Jacob may be believed to be our God. For if he does not recognize in us the works of Jacob, or, since we cannot equal him, at least the zeal for his works and faith, how will he deign to help us as the God of Jacob?

As he says this, behold, through the Holy Spirit a vivid image of things to come is poured into him, and seeing, after the heavy turmoil of wars, peace spread over the whole world at the coming of the saving Lord, he cries out to all, saying: Come and see the works of the Lord, the wonders he has set upon the earth. "Come" refers to gathering together, "see" to attention and the desire to know the truth. See, he says, the works of the Lord, full of miracles, in which are the signs of great powers. Indeed, the Greek word terata means in Latin "things to be wondered at". So do not take the works of the Lord as things of monstrous horror, but as things full of wonder. "He has set upon the earth" is well said, that is, in the earth.

Taking away wars to the ends of the earth, he will break the bow and shatter the weapons and burn the shields with fire. And truly, before the Roman Empire spread, not only did the kings of individual cities fight against one another, but the Romans themselves were frequently worn down by civil wars. Marius fought against Cinna, and Roman blood was shed on both sides. Sulla rose up and again stirred up civil wars against the victorious Marius.

Lepidus and Sertorius showed themselves rebels against Roman rule. Caesar pursued Pompey and roused the fury of the Gauls against Roman arms. After defeating the elder Pompey, he crushed the younger in the regions of Spain. Why should I speak of the triumvirs, who went from enemies to friends and from friends back again to hostile tumults, and of the seas too, stained with Roman blood in the war of Actium? So it came about that, out of weariness with civil wars, the Roman Empire was handed over to Julius Augustus, and in this way the internal conflicts were stilled.

And this served the purpose that the apostles could fittingly be sent throughout the whole world, as the Lord Jesus said: Go and teach all nations. Indeed, even kingdoms shut off by barbarian upheavals were opened to them, India to Thomas, Persia to Matthew. Yet, so that they might travel through more of the earth's expanse, at the birth of the Church he spread the power of the Roman Empire over the whole world, and by granting peace he settled the minds of those at odds and the divisions between lands. All men, living under one empire on earth, learned to confess with faithful speech the empire of the one almighty God.

So he took away wars to the ends of the earth, and there is no doubt that this was done. But consider whether he did not also take away the wars of weakness that are in the hearts of the wavering. For whoever has passed beyond earthly things no longer says: Fighting without, fears within; but he says: Our citizenship is in heaven. So pass beyond the world, so that you may begin to be above the world; for perasai means "to pass over", or, to put it more precisely, "to cross the sea". So the Lord took away the wars that spiritual wickedness waged against us, and having conquered the devil he left us his peace. He broke the bow from which the fiery darts of the adversary were scattered, and he burned the shields of unbelief with fire, so that the shield of faith might remain inviolate.

Be still, he says, and see that I am the Lord. "Be still" is the voice of the Lord after the wars have been stilled, so that the soul may have no preoccupation, lest the overflow of worldly disturbances cloud the inner eye of the mind. Be free, he says, from errors; be free from disturbances; be free from sins, because everyone who sins has not seen God nor known him, as John the evangelist said in his epistle.

So give your leisure to the pursuit of knowing God; do not be taken up with earthly works. That is why the king of the Egyptians ordered the quota of bricks and the other burdens of the Hebrews to be increased, so that they might not know God or have leisure for sacred worship. He was offended by the words of the holy men Moses and Aaron, who said: Let the people of God go, so that we may go and serve the Lord our God.

I will be exalted among the nations, and I will be exalted on the earth. The Lord was lofty in the heights, that is, among the angels and archangels, among the patriarchs and prophets, who thought lofty things of him and did not compare him to earthly images and idols of stone. But he was not lofty among the peoples of the nations, who seemed to seek their god in grottoes and in dwellings in caves. Indeed, Magdalene is rebuked, because she was weeping for Christ as if he were dead and seeking him in the tomb as if he were buried.

That is why Christ says to her: Mary, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking? Surely not one who could be taken away? She heard his voice and recognized him and wanted to touch him, and the Lord said: Do not touch me, whom you think dead; I am going to the Father. Are you surprised that you did not find in the tomb the one whom the heavens await? Or perhaps she is rebuked because only perfect faith touches Christ, as the woman with the flow of blood touched him with full faith. Hence the Lord says: Someone touched me; I perceive that power has gone out from me.

At these words she recognized in herself that she had been healed by the power going out from him, and at once, aware of it, she confessed that she was the one who had touched the Lord. So the Lord says: Your faith has saved you; go in peace. And the Lord was exalted on the earth, according to what he himself says: When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself; or because his will has been done on earth as it is in heaven.

And he repeats it, saying: The God of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector. Repetition is confirmation. Or else it is because God became "with us" not only when he was born of the virgin, but also after the resurrection, when he himself said: Behold, I am with you even to the end of the world. To him be honour and glory, everlasting from ages past, both now and always and for all ages of ages. Amen.
EXPLANATION OF PSALM 47

Its title is this: A psalm of a song for the sons of Korah, on the second of the sabbath. The sons of Korah are good, and were already approved in the earlier psalms, because with fitting thoughts and reflections suited to the pursuit of the virtues they composed within themselves a spiritual

psaltery. Intent on the knowledge of the Godhead from the wakeful watchtower of the mind, they were worthy to draw out the secrets of heavenly mysteries. And so, since they had received the duty and office of the psalms to be sung daily before the ark of the Lord, they seem to have been chosen to receive in a special way the psalm of a song to be sung on the second of the sabbath. For those to whom it was rightly entrusted to sing with their voices the ascension of the Lord rising from the underworld were surely the ones to whom it should be given to celebrate by their office and ministry the very day of the resurrection.

For what is the second of the sabbath but the Lord's day, which followed the sabbath? The sabbath day was later in the order of days but earlier in the sanctification of the law. But when the end of the law came, who is Christ Jesus — for Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes — and by his resurrection sanctified the eighth day, the same day began to be first that is eighth, and eighth that is first, having precedence from the order of number and holiness from the Lord's resurrection.

Hence in the Gospel too we read of the deuteroprōton sabbath, which in Latin is called the "second-first." For when the Lord's day, on which the Lord rose, began to take precedence, the sabbath that had been first began to be counted second after the first; for the first rest ceased and a second succeeded it. Hence the apostle too, writing to the Hebrews, says: Therefore on the following day there remains a rest for the people of God. Let us hasten, then, to enter into that rest.

True rest, then, no longer lies in ceasing from work but in the time of the resurrection. And so those who kept the solemnity of the sabbath according to the law called it "one of the sabbath," as though there were one sabbath and no other. We, who have put on a spiritual observance and long to shape our service after the likeness and rest of God, and to perform our ministry in that heavenly city where there is no copy, no shadow, but the truth, say "the first of the sabbath," as it is written: On the evening of the sabbath, as it was dawning toward the first of the sabbath.

Nothing could be more beautiful, nothing more explicit. Before the resurrection he said "sabbath"; after the resurrection he called it "the first of the sabbath." John the evangelist also says: On the first of the sabbath Mary Magdalene came in the morning, while it was still dark —

darkness referring to the time, morning to grace. But these men spoke more explicitly, in keeping with the Gospel, as though the veil had been drawn back; David, on the other hand, placed under the law, both kept the restraint of due caution and did not suppress the mystery, so that he declared the Lord's day as "the second of the sabbath": in this way he considered that the order of number was preserved for the Jews, while he recognized the spiritual mystery as revealed. Let us hear, then, what he says who sings to God on the second of the sabbath.

Great, he says, is the Lord, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, in his holy place. Is God not, then, great and praiseworthy everywhere? He is indeed great and mighty everywhere, but a narrow mind does not grasp the greatness of his divine power and grace. Yet the nearer our knowledge draws

to God, the more surpassing his majesty appears to us. Thus Thomas, who had earlier said: Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails and put my hand into his side, I will not believe, once he had put in his finger and recognized the clear signs of the resurrection, marvelled within himself at the grace of God

and said: My Lord and my God. It was then, therefore, that he most fully confessed his divinity and lordship, when he no longer doubted that he had risen from the dead. Indeed, a hymn befits God in Zion, and a vow is paid to him in Jerusalem. What wonder, then, if in the heavenly city, in that lofty and ethereal place, his power is proclaimed more mightily?

He added: spreading the exultation of the whole earth. And truly he is called great who has spread exultation through the whole world over this earth, where formerly the shoots of unbearable sins sprang up, where there was sorrow, sadness and groaning. And so the human conscience, which formerly mourned, sunk in the whirlpools of its own crimes, now rejoices, set free from fear through the pardon of Christ and the remission of all sins. It is fitting, then, even if we understand it as we have said.

But since in some old copies we have found εὐρίζω ἀγαλλιάματι πάσης τῆς γῆς, which in Latin means "with the well-rooted exultation of the whole earth," we observe that the sense is indeed the same: the divine gifts in us of God the Father are praised, who has given us an exultation founded on a good root, namely God Jesus, the true and most fruitful vine, from which the heavenly sacraments have flowed, in which there is perpetual and lasting joy, because by them every sin is washed away and the inner conscience cleansed. And we recognize that the expression is fitting, since we who exult in Christ rejoice with a well-rooted exultation. For the joy of the world is temporal, but the joy of one who rejoices in the Lord is everlasting.

Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king. God is known in her steps, when he shall receive her. He has clearly expressed why there is exultation of the whole earth: because the Lord Jesus has gathered to himself a church from among sinners. And so those who were formerly the sides of the north — that is, the companions and adherents of the devil, to whom it is said: Arise, north wind, and let the south wind come — have become faithful to Christ. For they are the ones of whom it is said: Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion.

So they have become Mount Zion through the grace of Christ and the sacrament of baptism. The spiritual north wind, whose heavy blasts stirred up the fiercest storms and tempests in human passions, began to lose his own, he who used to harass others. He had overthrown the whole nation of the Jews; he held all the nations subdued under his rule; they were his sides, that is, they breathed together with him. Just as we call a prince's bodyguards and companions his sides, and just as a woman is the side of a man, because

she is joined to him in a compliant partnership, so those who did the devil's will were his sides. These, then, are now Mount Zion, who contemplate the eternal God and are intent on him night and day. Consider Paul: when he was persecuting the Lord's church, he was a side of the

north; consider him now, when he is read in the church: he is a mountain of watching, through whom we know and see the glory of Christ. And since the Greek said "mountains," that is, ὄρη, see how the servants of Christ are mountains, mountains round about him, among which is the church of the Lord, which is the city of the great king. At the same time, the Lord suffered at the place of the Skull, which according to the tract of the sky was a place on the side of the north. And there is Mount Zion, there is the Jerusalem that is on earth.

See whether this too does not seem to be expressed: that the congregation of God's people, which had been joined to the north through guilt, has become the church of Christ through grace, so that it is now called not the synagogue but the church of Christ. And because the remnant of the Jews has been saved through the election of grace, God is known in them — in Peter, Paul, John and James — who as weighty and lofty men are, as it were, the foundations and summits of the church: weighty foundations, as it were, whom no strong gusts of the north have shaken, but who have kept the foundation of faith unmoved so that the whole church should not totter; very lofty, like summits, who have raised its peak with the towers of their virtue.

For just as a maker is recognized in his works and a builder in his buildings, so that even if you do not hear his name you can still discern the craftsman from the quality of the works — and what wonder is that in human affairs, when even of the eternal Creator himself, who is not seen by us, we nevertheless understand the invisible things through the things that are made? — so in lofty and great houses, which houses we are, if we hold the foundation of freedom and glory firm to the end, God is recognized as the one who dwells there, as the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.

For he is the true God who founded such men by the instruction of his precepts. Therefore, just as he showed himself the eternal God in them, so, he says, when he receives the city of the great king, in her steps [?] they have heard of his reception and thought it must be carried through, so that they may not fall away from the firmness of that house built on the rock.

Seeing this, he says, the kings of the earth were gathered together and passed over into one; seeing, they were then amazed. Good kings are those who can show themselves rulers of their own body, springing from the very origin and teaching of the patriarch Abraham, who taught that sin can be overcome. The true king, then, is the one who did not know how to be enslaved to crimes, in whom the allurement of guilt and error could not reign. Hence it was said to such a man by the sons of Heth: You are a king from God among us.

Such kings of the earth, then, who ruled over the flesh, were gathered together so as to be of one heart and one spirit, as we read that the multitude of believers had one soul and one heart, and there was no division among them. These are the ones who passed over into one — not so much into one place as into the same affection and purpose. For to one who has been approved it is said:

Pass over, recline. For it is no ordinary virtue to pass over from wicked things to honourable ones, from earthly to eternal, to change the habit of carnal life and do away with all its practices, to take on new ways and wrench away the whole state of one's former manner of life. And rightly it is said to such a one: If you pass through water, I am with you. God is with the one who passes over, not with the one who stops.

These, then, who had formerly been at odds within themselves, when they came together into one in mind and zeal, having received the peace that made both one and dissolved the enmities in his flesh by destroying the dividing wall, were amazed either at him who is known in her steps, or that people

had been so converted that those who formerly served the devil were now bound over to the Lord Jesus in the devotion of righteous service. And since, as kings of their own body, they had experienced in themselves no small labour — for it is neither easy nor ordinary to conquer the mind, to cut back desires, to tame the wantonness of the flesh, to root out lust, which fought even against Paul to bind him captive by the law of sin — just as they marvelled at the grace in those who had advanced in virtue, so too were they troubled lest anyone should slip back into vice, cast down from the higher summit of the virtues. For the human condition is prone and changeable in either direction, so that wherever it turns, there it leans and inclines, either toward the pursuit of the virtues or toward the allurement of sins.

And so they were shaken by no slight emotion, so that trembling seized them out of fear, as they considered what is written, that in the places of the ungodly the righteous groan. Consider Peter, for instance, weeping most bitterly because error had crept upon him and had bent the strength of his mind through a lapse of bodily frailty, and rightly reproved by Christ with restraint, because he had dared to claim steadfastness for himself and had not considered how liable his nature was.

He, indeed, corrected his error through grace, but Judas remained in his crime and persisted in groaning. He was righteous when he was joined to the number of the apostles; but because he was tripped up by the devil, he now laments and groans in the places of the ungodly, because he has slipped back from grace into punishment. So when men of this kind fall, such as Judas the traitor, or Saul, who was called to the kingship by the Lord his God, even strong men trembled.

Then, as they considered by how great a struggle one reaches the end — how great the contritions of the righteous, how great the anxieties, what an adversary, how great the striving in long-drawn-out labour, how great the bitternesses of a stricter resolve, what chains of continence, what lashes of conscience — they were greatly disturbed lest anyone should give way either to the great labours of a more austere life or to its pains. For there are pains there, bitter and heavy — that is, in the church; in that city of the great king there are pains as of a woman in labour, until Christ be formed in us.

For Paul was not without pain when he saw the slower progress of his teaching among the foolish Galatians, and so he said: My little children, with whom I am again in labour until Christ be formed in you. The Lord too testifies in the Gospel that the pains of a woman in labour are heavy, when he says: A woman in labour has sorrow, because her day has come; but when she has given birth to a child, she no longer remembers the sorrow, for joy that a human being has been born into this world.

Great, then, is the labour by which someone gains Christ for himself, lest he toss like a ship without a helmsman on the sea of this world. Thus the apostles were sad when Christ told them that he would return to the Father, because they thought they would be left destitute without their guide. Christ is joy; he is also the child whom the one in labour brings forth, the one who has received the spirit of salvation in the womb of his mind. The one who has given birth and nurtured rejoices; the one in labour is shaken and pierced.

It is good that you should both give birth to him and nurture him. Do not boil a lamb in its mother's milk, lest it be said to you: Woe to those who are with child and those who nurse. For Christ was born of Mary in such a way that you might recognize him, as the ox recognized its owner, and know that it was he who created you and he who possessed your forefathers. Do not nurse him as a little child, but know that he is to be worshipped as true and perfect God from true and perfect God.

For this is how the magus worshipped him: he did not boil the lamb in its mother's milk, but venerated him as the eternal God. Indeed, to find him he looked to the sky; so he did not seek on earth the one whom a star shining from heaven pointed out. That is why Mary did not travail with him but bore him, because she knew that one who was both Lord and Saviour was to be born of her, as she herself testifies, saying: My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour. There, then, are pains as of a woman in labour. It is pain to be in labour; it is pain to nurture one whom you ought to possess as perfect from the beginning.

And so many are severely crushed, as the next verse signifies: With a vehement spirit you will shatter the ships of Tarshish. For while the servants of God long to attain perfection of faith, they wear down their body, chastising it more severely and bringing it into subjection, lest those who had already been approved be rejected.

And they do this in the Holy Spirit, strong and vehement. For he is the spirit of counsel and might, so that by great abstinence they dissolve their body and thereby empty out all its pleasures, that it may be said to them: Be strong, you slack hands and loosened knees.

For when someone has been released from this earthly frame, then he rises stronger to eternal life. I am lying, unless Scripture bears me out, which says: To be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better — whoever is dissolved begins to be with Christ — and elsewhere: The time of my dissolution is at hand. Whoever, then, has practised dissolving himself through abstinence cannot fear the day of his passion.

And he aptly said "vehement spirit" when he was about to speak of ships. By ships he meant bodies, which are tossed by the wandering surge of various passions and quickly sink unless they have a helmsman. Hence he says elsewhere: Those who go down to the sea in ships.

And they sail well who carry the cross of Christ before them in their ships like a mast, and from it watch for the blasts of the winds, so as to steer their bodies toward the grace of the Holy Spirit, safe and secure on the wood of the Lord. They do not let their ships drift over the seas on the wandering waves, but by holding a straight course they press on toward the harbour of salvation and the fulfilment of grace, so as to gain a safe anchorage where, though dissolved, they may resume their course in the resurrection, where they can have no fear of shipwreck.

Let us too, then, look about for this grace; let us be its watchmen; let us explore it, so that our bodies may become ships of Tarshish. For the flesh is brought into subjection when we fix our gaze on the grace of God, so that we pursue what is bitter for a time, such as fasting, and not what is sweet and pleasurable. Tarshish, then, is the watchtower of grace, a spiritual city, like the Zion above. It was toward Tarshish that Jonah was hastening. Of it Scripture said that Jehoshaphat allied himself with King Ahaziah, and they agreed to build ships to go to Tarshish.

But because he had joined himself to an ungodly man, a prophet was sent to him to say: The Lord has destroyed your work, and your ships are broken, and they could not go to Tarshish. By this it is signified that the bodies of those who transgress God's commandment cannot reach the fulfilment of grace. But to Solomon, as a wise and peaceable man, ships from Tarshish came with gold and silver and ivory tusks without any

mishap, and he himself sent ships there. For he had with King Hiram a spiritual commerce of sacred trade and an affection of mutual grace in which each vied with the other. These ships, then, those who possess within themselves royal authority to restrain the fierceness of the body celebrate in renowned speech, seeing that they have become incorruptible from corruptible, shining with the highest light of grace from stained, renewed from dissolved and worn out, living from dead, risen from buried.

As we have heard, so also have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God; God has founded it for ever. We heard outside the city; we saw within the city, whose eternal light is God, where day shines without the sun of this world and the moon is not needed; its foundation is not temporal but eternal.

We have received, he says, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple. If this is addressed to the Son of God, we understand the temple in the sense in which he himself spoke of his body: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. Truly the body of Christ is the temple of God, in which is the cleansing of our sins. Truly that flesh is the temple of God, in which no

contagion of sin could exist, but which itself was the sacrifice for the sin of the whole world. Truly that flesh is the temple of God, in which the image of God shone and the fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily, since Christ himself is the fullness. So it is to him that it is said: We have received, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple. What does this mean, if not what he says: There stands in your midst one whom you do not know, that is, he is in your midst and is not seen? But if it refers to the Father, what does "in the midst of your temple" mean, if not that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself?

In that temple, then, he says, we have received your mercy, that is, the Word that was made flesh and dwelt among us. For just as Christ is redemption, so too is he mercy. And what greater mercy is there than that he offered himself to be sacrificed for our crimes, to wash with his blood the world, whose sin could have been abolished in no other way? Indeed, if the apostle said of holy men: You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you, how much more should I call the flesh of the Lord Jesus the temple of God, who, we read, was always full of the Holy Spirit, and who himself testifies, saying: I perceive that power has gone out from me — a power that healed the bitter wounds of all!

It can also be understood that he said he had received, together with the people, the mercy of God in the midst of his temple because he himself founded his church and extended it for ever, because he truly, with his only-begotten Son, conferred this grace on his people. He also showed the Son to be its builder, saying: He shall build me a city — a city that, spread over the whole world, has made the whole earth full of his praise and his name. For just as it is written:

The earth is full of his praise, so too it is written: A name has been given him above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.

Hence the prophet rightly said: According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth; your right hand is full of righteousness. It is no wonder that he who is the right hand of God is full of the righteousness of God. Now the power of God and the righteousness of God are the same. So, because he is full of the righteousness of God, you may know that in him is the same fullness of righteousness that the Father has; and because we read that he is the power and righteousness and wisdom of God the Father, you may understand that nothing of the divine majesty in him is divided. Rather, you may recognize that the Son has received all things from the Father, and that the Son is the radiance of all the Father's glory and the exact imprint of his substance, who so expressed the Father that the whole Father is in him, just as the whole Son is in the Father.

And because the prophet saw in the Spirit that the praises of Christ were to be proclaimed in every land, he rounds off the discourse he had undertaken with a kind of epilogue and exhorts us to joy and to the worship of his name, saying: Let Mount Zion rejoice, that is, those who trust in the Lord, as he himself later explained it when he said:

Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion, and so on. Let the Lord Jesus himself, who is the mountain and the height of his Church, which gazes on its Christ with all its love, rejoice in her faith and devotion, which has pleased God, since the faithless one has been rejected. This can also be understood with reverence: he himself, being higher than all, is also the mountain that the preacher of the faith is commanded to climb, as Scripture says: Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion.

Let the souls that confess you exult, he says. These are the daughters of that Judea in which God is known. For the Judea of the flesh or of the letter did not acknowledge the Lord; had it acknowledged him, it would also have received him. But it did not acknowledge the one it did not receive, and it fled from his judgments,

in which he declared that they sprang not from father Abraham but from the seed of the devil, since every sin is the seed of the enemy. The daughters of confession, however, do not commit sin; they cover it over, and therefore blessed are those whose sins are covered. And rightly will the daughters of confession exult because of the Lord's judgments, when they have come to know his judgments and his ways, which in this age are inscrutable and unsearchable to human beings. But when they begin to behold the truth face to face, then they will grasp what now seems inscrutable and will rejoice in knowing it.

Go around Zion, he says, and embrace her; tell of it in her towers. Those who understand Zion go around her and embrace her with their minds, so as to hold her and not let her go, lest the watchful discipline of virtue be taken from them. That is why the woman in the Song of Songs says: I held him and will not let him go. She was seeking the wisdom of God and embracing the justice of God with the arms of love and, as it were, with the sinews of faith and devotion; for this is the embrace of a devout mind.

Let us too, then, grasp as far as we can the inner mysteries of the truth. Let us write them down and fix them in our minds, together with the power of the heavenly oracle. To attain it Moses, that man learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, climbed the mountain and entered the cloud, so as to learn what was covered and hidden, with his companion Jesus, that is, Joshua, clinging to him, because no one can grasp the uncertain and hidden things of wisdom without the true Jesus. And so, in the figure of Joshua son of Nun, he was shown the inspiring presence of the true Saviour, through whom all would be taught by God, and who would open the Law and reveal the gospel.

So those who have gone around Zion with their prudence and embraced her with their understanding climb her towers and from above tell anyone who has not been able to climb them what must be done and what guarded against. For the city of God is walled, and so the Lord says elsewhere: See, Jerusalem, I have painted your walls. It is set with towers, from which an ambusher can be spotted if he begins to approach.

He has his armies, with which he is accustomed to besiege the souls that belong to God and to bring up siege engines so that he can storm the fortified towers. But you, he says, preach from the towers; for in the towers of Jerusalem there is abundance. Preach justice, urge watchfulness; for wisdom is sung at the gates and proclaimed on the heights of the walls. And elsewhere again he says: On

your walls I have set watchmen day and night; they shall never be silent. Tell of it, then, without pause and without end. The adversary is awake; he prowls about and with the fury of a wild beast seeks whomever he can find to devour. Therefore the Lord must always be sung, who crushes the teeth of lions and shatters their jaws, so that they cannot harm us.

Set your hearts, he says, on his strength, that is, so that you may understand his strength, and distribute his steps, so that you may tell of it to another generation; for this is our God for ever and for ages of ages. He will rule us for ever. The Greek has βάρεις, that is, lofty, towered houses.

So the prophet, speaking of the city of God and those who dwell in it, says: Distribute its steps, that is, its high and lofty mansions in the heavenly places. By this he teaches that the order of merits must be kept, for each is in his own order. That is why the Lord also tells his disciples that he is going to prepare mansions, so that each may obtain a fitting dwelling according to the measure of his merits, in which to enjoy that eternal rest.

There are also sublime and lofty precepts, which contain the hidden mysteries of godliness and the deep truths of the heavenly words. Distribute these, he says, and share them out according to each one's capacity, as much as each can grasp with his own intelligence. For Paul did not discuss the same things with everyone. To some he preached nothing but Christ Jesus and him crucified, not with persuasive words of wisdom but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power; among the perfect, however, he spoke wisdom, because the people as a whole were not able to receive the wisdom that is hidden in a mystery.

Christ hid it so that fools would not understand it, while the prudent would seek it all the more eagerly and tell of it to another generation, one that would be more perfect in the power of the Spirit. For the earlier generation, through weakness of faith, could not know the sacraments of perfect wisdom, and so it sought a sign and rejected the truth, though surely truth is not there for the sake of a sign; the sign is there for the sake of truth.

That is why the Lord answered it: An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. So the example of Jonah is brought in to expose the faithlessness of the Jews. The Ninevites believed a sign and thought they should follow the preaching of Jonah, who had been in the belly of the whale, but the Jews did not believe even after the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, who rose from the heart of the earth after three days, and lives and reigns through all ages. Amen.
EXPLANATION OF PSALM 48
Its title is: To the end; for the sons of Korah, a psalm of David.

Hear these things, all you nations; take them in with your ears, all you who inhabit the world. At the very beginning we recognize the voice of the Lord our Saviour calling the nations to the Church, so that they may renounce error, follow the truth, and acknowledge the gift of true worship. But the hearts of Adam's descendants were infected with the serpent's poison, and the conscience, bound by sins, could not bring itself back while it despaired of pardon. So he promises a remedy and of his own accord, out of the bounty of his goodness, promises forgiveness, so that the guilty need not fear, and the one with a good conscience may rejoice that he serves a good Lord, who knows how to forgive sins and to honour virtues.

Indeed, in the same pattern of calling, the Lord also exhorts us in the gospel, saying: Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart. Then he tells them that his yoke is sweet and his burden light, since anyone who despairs of the medicine cannot be healed. And so gentleness, which heals the wounds of the inner soul, is welcome to all.

So when the physician was about to come to the sick, to heal our grievous sores, he set out his medicines beforehand, so that people might hear and run with faithful eagerness to the remedy of salvation. This is how the woman in the gospel who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years won healing. She heard that the physician had come and hurried to touch him, saying: If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be healed.

She said this within herself, and Christ heard. She touched the fringe, and power went out from the Saviour that healed the sick woman, strengthened the weak, stopped the flow, and approved her devotion. In the same way, here too he calls all nations to the fountain of wisdom and prudence and promises redemption to all, so that no one need tremble and no one despair. No one is excluded; every soul is invited to grace, to be redeemed from guilt without price and to gain the fruit of eternal life.

This is the sense of the psalm, which we will set out in order once we have explained the force and character of the opening words. The nations are commanded to hear, and those who inhabit the world to take it in with their ears. This is surely the world of which he said earlier: The earth is the Lord's and all its fullness, the world and those who dwell in it. He founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers.
This world

the Greeks call the oikoumenē, because it is inhabited by Christ, as he himself said: For I will dwell in them. He dwells in order to fill what seemed empty. What, then, is the oikoumenē but the holy Church, the temple of God and the dwelling place of Christ? And the Latins, using a different word but with the same meaning, have quite fittingly called it the orbis terrae, the circle of the earth, because the life of the saints, who are inhabited by the Spirit, rolls round like a wheel without any check to its course.

So the Church is founded in tribulations, in storms and tempests; it is prepared in anxieties and grief, in adversities and in rivers. What rivers? Hear him say: The rivers have lifted up their voice. Hear also in the gospel: Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly. Now he said this about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were receiving.

It is in these rivers, then, in which the grace of God flows forth, that the Church is prepared. These are the rivers that take in the word of God with their ears and speak, so as to pour the word into each person's heart. That is why Scripture drew a distinction when it said: Hear these things, all you nations; take them in with your ears, all you who inhabit the world. All can hear, but not all take it in with their ears, only the elect of God. That is why the Saviour says: Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.

He means the spiritual ears of the inner man, whose nostrils we also read of when Job says: The divine Spirit that is in my nostrils. Not all people have these ears and these nostrils, for the form of the body is one thing and the form of spiritual grace another. The spiritual man hears all things and judges all things, but the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God; for the one is born of earth, the other is heavenly.

And so he added: Those born of earth and the sons of men, rich and poor together, so as to call everyone. Who is born of earth but a son of man? Who is spiritual but a son of God? The one is formed from blood and begotten of the pleasure of the flesh and of a man; the other is born of God. One is rich in every word

and in knowledge; another is poor, yet rich in grace, for the poor man cried out and the Lord heard him. On the other hand, there is also the rich man in his pride and the poor man in his humility. All are called to the Church, so that all may be redeemed by Christ. The sick man finds a physician, the healthy man acquires wisdom, the captive finds a redeemer, the free man one who rewards him. Divine Scripture builds up everyone;

in it each person finds what will either heal his wounds or strengthen his merits. Moreover, the calling of rich and poor together into one summons us to a kind of humility and equality, so that the rich man does not despise the needy nor the poor man envy the rich, but one grace binds them both together. For the Lord too became poor though he was rich, so that he might be the Saviour of poor and rich alike.

And he went on: My mouth will speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart prudence. All are rightly called, since the fountain of wisdom overflows for all. Wisdom is not to be compared with a treasure of money, for she is declared more precious than all treasures. So the rich man is not turned away nor the poor man shut out, because wisdom discriminates not between people's means but between their wills: the better suited is the one who comes first in love and nearest in discipline. And if the meditation of the heart speaks prudence, how much more does perfect teaching! Next we are warned not to blurt out careless speech, but to weigh what we are going to say through a kind of practised meditation and on the scales of the inner mind, because it is written elsewhere: A false balance is not good.

I will incline my ear to a parable; I will open my proposition on the psaltery. The wise listener pays attention and inclines his ear to understand the figures of parables. The Saviour calls the one who has ears to hear his own ear. The Lord also opens his closed proposition when he has found a fitting instrument and chosen vessel, which he calls a psaltery. Like such a psaltery, Paul rang out the song of sweet grace with all his strings sounding in harmony, striking both the inner and the outer string with the plectrum of the Holy Spirit, so that he prayed both with the tongue and with the mind.

That is why he says: I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also. Christ, then, promises such a man long beforehand, through whom he would make hidden things manifest and open up what was wrapped in the obscurity of prophetic speech. A psaltery is good when life agrees with faith and flesh with soul, and the will is in tune with virtue. That is a sweet psaltery, where the discipline of living is melodious, so that what is written may be fulfilled: The tongue of the mute shall speak clearly.

Then follows: Why should I fear in the evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me. That is: since my mouth speaks wisdom and the meditation of my heart prudence, what can I fear in the day of judgment, unless perhaps the iniquity of my heel has to be washed from me? Our own iniquity is one thing, the iniquity of our heel another. It was in the heel that Adam was wounded by the serpent's tooth, and he left the inheritance of all his human descendants subject to his wound, so that we all limp from that wound.

That is why the Lord washed his disciples' feet, to wash away the serpent's poison, and Peter is rebuked for protesting that the Lord should not wash his feet. So it was said to him: Unless I wash your feet, you will have no part with me. Hearing this, he offered not only his feet but also his hands to be washed. The Lord answered him: Whoever has been washed has no need to wash again except to wash his feet, but he is wholly clean.

So David, who knew that he had been conceived in iniquity and born of his mother in sins, says: My iniquities have gone over my head. But the Lord, who had no sins of his own and knew no iniquities of his own, says: The iniquity of my heel will surround me, that is, the iniquity of Adam, not mine. Yet it cannot terrify me; for in the day of judgment what is punished in us are our own crimes, not the crimes of another's iniquity.

So I think the iniquity of the heel is a slipperiness that leads to sin rather than any guilt for an offence of our own. And rightly the Lord, who took everything upon himself for us, says: Let us wash the feet too, so that we can remove the slipperiness of the heel. Then the virtues can have a firm footing, and no one need slip through his forefather's error; whoever is ready to stand by his own resolve and longs to keep his footing in virtue need not fear the slipperiness he has inherited. The iniquity of our heel, then, is the transgression of Adam, through which he fell into contempt and neglect of the heavenly commandments.

There is also the iniquity of the heel that is the detestable betrayal of Judas. It is called the 'heel' because it is written: He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me. He rightly said 'his' there and 'my' here: 'his,' because Christ is without iniquity and this iniquity belongs to the traitor alone; but Christ calls Judas 'my heel' as being the lowest part of his body, the body whose members we are.

The apostles are the nobler and more active members of Christ; Judas is the heel, the extremity of the body, exposed to the serpent and open to wounding. The first heel, then, is Adam, the second is Judas. The one was the fall of the whole inheritance, the other the fall of the traitor alone, who could not entangle the inheritance, because we are no longer carnal but the inheritance of the Redeemer, as Scripture says: There is an inheritance for those who believe in the Lord.

There is also that iniquity of his heel which surrounded Christ: Surrounding me, he says, they surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them. His heel is the synagogue; the beauty and glory of his face is the Church, as it is written: The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself in beauty.

So they are the heel, of whom he says: Those who trust in their own strength and those who glory in the abundance of their riches; for the rich have been in want and gone hungry. This was said of the Jews; but all who live in luxury and do not hold fast to the head are also the heel of Christ. These, however, are general meanings of broad application; more specifically, he was speaking of Judas the traitor, who thought himself strong and rich in the glory of his apostleship.

Then the discourse moves on to the Lord's passion: A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem. Nor will he give God his propitiation and the price of the redemption of his own soul. That is: Why should I fear in the evil day? For what can harm me, who not only need no redeemer but am myself the redeemer of all? Shall I set others free and then tremble for myself?

See, I make all things new, I who am above even the affection and devotion of brothers. The one whom a brother, brought into the light from the same mother's womb, cannot redeem, because he is held back by the weakness of the same nature, a man will redeem. But it is that man of whom it is written that the Lord will send them a man who will save them, the man who said of himself: You seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth.

But though he is a man, who will know him? Why will no one know him? Because, just as there is one God, so there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. He alone will redeem man, surpassing brothers in devotion, because he shed his own blood for strangers, which no one can offer even for a brother. So he did not spare his own body, in order to redeem us from sin, and he gave himself as a ransom for all, as his true witness the apostle Paul declared, saying:

I speak the truth, I do not lie. But why will he alone redeem? Because no one can equal him in devotion, so as to lay down his life for his lowly servants, and no one can equal him in innocence. For all are under sin, all lie under that fall of Adam; the only one chosen as redeemer is he who could not be liable to the ancient sin. So by 'man' let us understand the Lord Jesus, who took on the human condition in order to crucify the sin of all in his flesh and blot out with his blood the bond that stood against everyone.

But perhaps you will say: 'How can it be denied that a brother will redeem, when he himself said: I will declare your name to my brothers?' Yet it was not as a brother but as the man Christ Jesus, in whom God was, that he forgave us our sins. For it is written: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, in that Christ Jesus of whom alone it was said that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. It was not as a brother, then, but as Lord that he dwelt among us when he dwelt in the flesh. Since, then, he reconciled the world to God, he himself certainly needed no reconciliation. For what sin of his own would he have to appease God, he who knew no sin?

Indeed, when the Jews demanded the didrachma, which under the law was paid for sin, he said to Peter: Simon, from whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax? From their own sons or from strangers? Peter answered: From strangers. The Lord said to him: Then the sons are free. But so that we may not give them offence, cast a hook and take the first fish that comes up; when you open its mouth you will find a stater. Take it and give it for me and for yourself.

He shows that he owed no propitiation for sins on his own behalf, because he was not a slave of sin but the Son of God, free from all error. For the Son sets free, while the slave is held in guilt. So he, free from everything, does not pay the price of redemption for his own soul, though the price of his blood was more than enough to redeem all the sins of the whole world. Rightly, then, does he set others free, since he owes nothing for himself.

I add more. Not only does Christ owe no price for his own redemption, nor any atonement for sin; but even if you take the verse as said of any human being at all, it can be understood to mean that individuals do not owe their own atonement, because Christ is the atonement of all and he himself is the redemption of everyone. For whose blood is now fit to redeem himself, when Christ has poured out his own blood for the redemption of all?

Is there anyone, then, whose blood can be compared with the blood of Christ? Or what man is so powerful that he could offer his own atonement for himself, over and above the atonement that Christ offered in himself, who alone reconciled the world to God through his blood? What greater victim, what more excellent sacrifice, what better advocate is there than he who became the plea for the sins of all and gave his life as a ransom for us?

So no atonement or redemption is sought from individuals, because the price paid for all is the blood of Christ, with which the Lord Jesus redeemed us. He alone reconciled the Father, and he toiled to the end, because he took our toil upon himself, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you.” See him toiling: “I have toiled with crying out; my throat has grown hoarse.” And elsewhere: “Issachar desired what is good, resting between the boundaries”; and further on:

“He put his shoulder to the toil and became a farmer.” So a man will no longer give his own atonement or redemption, since he has been washed once for all from sin by the blood of Christ. Yet he will toil to keep the precepts for living and not to depart from the heavenly commandments. As long as he lives, let him be in toil and persevere in it, so that he may live to the end, lest he too should die by death when he has already been redeemed from death.

Whoever keeps the commandments of life will not see destruction, though he sees those die who seemed to themselves the wisest and most prudent in this world. This refers especially to the scribes and Pharisees, who claim for themselves the chairs in the synagogues as though they held the primacy in wisdom. They truly toil in vain, since they think they are set free by a didrachma, while by some empty interpretation of the law they have despised the spiritual price of their souls and that unique sacrifice of the Lord's body, fleeing from the sacrament of baptism. For the blood of goats and bulls redeems no one; the one blood of Christ sets all free. In Leviticus there is its figure, not its reality. For we are set free not by a didrachma but by the price of his blood alone.

Let us therefore be taught by God, so that none of us may see destruction on that day when the wise of this world, or the leaders of the Jews, will be condemned to everlasting death, when “the senseless and the fool will perish together.” The two are not the same. The fool is one who has no understanding and understands foolish things; the senseless man is one who understands wrongly: “The senseless man has said, There is no God.” In the same way a man is called unjust not because he does not know justice, but because he commits injustice out of the wickedness of his heart; and he is called wicked because he wants to destroy uprightness by his malice, not because he is ignorant of uprightness.

So when the senseless and the fool perish, they leave their riches to strangers, for they cannot find a lawful heir of their own to their folly and wickedness. For the lawful heirs say: “We are children of God. And if children, then heirs; heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.” The senseless, then, have no riches, because they have no inheritance either.

The faithless have no riches and no possession, for to the faithful the whole world is a possession. They have no inheritance, because the inheritance belongs only to those who believe in the Lord. Yet they have riches of their own, and so the greedy man says: “I have nowhere to store my crops”; for money is not true fruit but the fruit of the greedy. And the Lord says to the greedy man: “Go, sell your goods, and come, follow me.” For an estate is not the perfect good; these are the goods of the greedy, which consist in some kind of gain.

Sell, he says, what you think is yours, though it is not yours, since it passes to others like a river, and follow me, so that you may come to know the immortal good. So the wise are led to destruction, those from whom God has hidden what he has revealed to little children. The senseless and the fool will perish together and will be in one and the same place, and they will leave their riches to strangers, because wickedness finds no lawful successor.

“And their tombs are their homes forever, their dwellings from generation to generation; they have called their names upon their own lands.” Everywhere Scripture treats tombs as vile things, to which degenerate people who crave this life are compared: “Their throat is an open tomb.” So for those who live from day to day, tombs serve as homes. For the home of the righteous is not on earth but in heaven, as the Apostle taught when he said:

“But our citizenship is in heaven.” That is our home, which is the home of Christ; hence Scripture says: “And Moses was faithful in all his house as a servant, to testify to what would be spoken, but Christ as a son over his own house.” For the devout, then, the Church is their home and heaven is their homeland; and so the righteous man says:

“I am a stranger with you on earth and a sojourner, like all my fathers.” For the self-indulgent, the tomb is their home. Indeed, they live as if in a tomb who can say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die,” having no resurrection before their eyes. So they cling to their tombs, fastened and buried in them, because they did not believe that they could be raised. Their dwelling is in their own grave, and their tent is in an earthly lineage and generation; they leave worms as heirs to their bodies, so that their memory exists only here and cannot pass into eternity.

Then, “their names on their own lands,” because their works are corruptible and earthly, and so their names are written where they chose to live. But to those who have raised their works on high it is said: “Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” From this, then, let us understand that it was not idly that the Lord rebuked those who built tombs for themselves or monuments for the prophets and adorned them.

For the Jews are condemned, who offered the prophets they had killed earthly consolations, not eternal rewards. And so he forbids his disciple to bury his father, because he must be intent without ceasing on the eternal Father. And in the book of Isaiah it is written: “Why,” he says, “have you built and hewn out a tomb for yourself?” And Mary is rebuked for seeking Christ in the tomb.

Leave the tombs, which were left by those who, hearing the voice of the Lord at his passion, rose from their graves. You who are living, do not dwell among the dead. Hear the voice of Jesus raising you: “Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead,” so that the eternal light of Christ may be poured into you. His light is the Holy Spirit, who shone on the holy apostles like fire when the tongues were distributed.

There follows: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to the beasts that are without sense and has become like them. This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them, and afterward they will take pleasure in their own mouths.” Because man did not understand when he was in honor (and his honor is that he was made in the image of God, made capable of reason), he has been compared to the beasts that have no sense; but whoever has understood is compared to the angels.

So the one is glorious in the brightness of good works, while the other is judged like a neighing horse for the filth of his life, which puts a stumbling block in the way of those who live in shamefulness and obscenity; for “a man's folly defiles his ways.” Such men live according to their appetite, which creates a stumbling block, and after the stumbling block they will take pleasure in their mouth, but not in their heart. For they are not good, those of whom it is said: “With their mouth they blessed, and in their heart they cursed.” This also answers those who have it written in their copies thus: “and afterward with their mouth they will bless.” For let your word be near you, both in your mouth and in your heart.

“Like sheep they will be led down to hell; death will feed on them. And the righteous will rule over them in the morning, and their help will grow old in hell, away from their glory.” Those who did not want Christ to feed them, death will feed on. Who, then, would forsake the good shepherd, who lays down his life for his sheep because the care of his flock belongs to him? Or who would choose death the hireling, which is paid back as the fitting wage for the worst deeds? Recognize at the same time, O man, that Christ is the true shepherd, who feeds his own for life. Death has crept

in, which leads strangers to destruction and devours those over whom it can prevail because of their crimes. Though in this life they were eager for power and riches so as to lord it over others, in the resurrection there will be servitude for them, when the morning splendor has shone on the righteous; a figure of this is that Jacob is set as lord over his brother. Wretched indeed is that servitude, that at the very time when others are called into the glory of splendor and light, their glory should grow old and be consumed in the darkness of hell. Rightly is it said of them: “They have been driven from their honor and from their glory,” because this glory is temporal.

“But God,” he says, “will deliver my soul from the hand of hell, when he receives it.” He says this well, who knew that his soul would not be abandoned in hell. For he went down to set the captives free from the jaws of hell, not to remain a captive among them.

Since, then, the things of this world cannot pass on with us, it is said to you: “Do not be afraid when a man has become rich and when the glory of his house has increased, for when he dies he will not take everything with him, nor will the glory of his house go down with him.” Do not, he says, stand in dread of the riches and power of the rich man or of worldly glory, for these things are perishable and depart more quickly than they came.

This treasure is a dream: you wake up, and it is gone. For whoever has been able to sleep off the drunkenness of this world and take up the sobriety of virtue despises these things and counts money as nothing. Nor should you be afraid when you hear that the glory of some powerful man's house has increased. Look carefully, and it is empty, since it has nothing of the fullness of faith. And why speak of a house? This whole world was empty until Christ filled it with the multitude of believers, and so it is written: “He will judge among the nations, he will fill up the ruins.”

For what else was there in this world before except the ruin of unbelief? What is a ruin? Hear him who says: “Where the fallen body is, there the eagles will be too”; that is, where there is a fall, there is also a resurrection. A ruin is empty of firmness; resurrection is the fullness of life. So the ruin of Adam emptied us, but the grace of Christ filled us again. That is why he emptied himself, to fill us and so that the fullness of power might dwell in human flesh. Learn what a ruin is.

While a man lives, he is filled with breath; when he dies, he is of course empty of this life-giving breath. Much more does the loss of spiritual grace empty the one whom grace used to fill, so that we can say: “For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.” Of another it is said: “I have toiled in vain”; but the righteous man is “like the scent of a full field.”

What is not empty that is worldly and of this age, since he who despised this world with sober virtue rightly said: “Naked I was born, naked I shall also die”? Can anyone take with him what he possesses? Here he leaves everything behind, he enters the tomb alone, and empty is the grave of that rich man whom not even the earth itself could contain. Hence it was said: “Will you alone dwell upon the earth?” Does the glory of his house or his wealth go down into that tomb? See the force of Scripture.

The glory of the world will not go down with the sinner, but the glory of virtue will go up with the innocent; and, to put it more briefly, a man's glory will go up with him if he goes up, and will not go down with him if he goes down. What belongs to grace and virtue will go up. One goes up into paradise; one goes down into hell. “Let them go down,” he says,

“alive into hell.” And so the poor man Lazarus was carried up by angels into Abraham's bosom. The self-indulgent rich man, lifting up his eyes in hell, begs Abraham to send the poor man to touch his tongue with his finger, so that, set in the fiercest heat, he might gain some relief. See that poor man abounding in every good, surrounded by the blessed rest of the holy patriarch; see this one empty, who in this world seemed to himself to abound in everything, whose soul was blessed during his life, but who now lies helpless, tormented by death.

So it fittingly follows: “For his soul will be blessed in his lifetime; he will praise you when you have done well by him.” Foolish men, he says, who consider things present and not things to come, will bless him with an earthly blessing; his hangers-on and parasites will bless him. He too thinks himself blessed if he has seized some field he coveted. He praises God when things go well for him in this world, but when adversity comes he curses with an impious mouth. This is what he means, then: that the worldly man does not give thanks when he is placed in poverty and adversity,

whereas the righteous man blesses the Lord with a more grateful heart in times of distress. Indeed, the devil says to God: “What wonder if Job blesses you? He has plenty of everything. But stretch out your hand,” he says, “and touch what he possesses; let us see whether he blesses you to your face.” And the Lord gave him power to take away what belonged to this world and to cover his flesh with cruel sores. Yet Job blessed him, saying: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

“He will go in to the generation of his fathers; he will never see the light. Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to the beasts that have no sense and has become like them.” So, he says, this man will go in to the generation of his fathers. Who is the father of the wicked the Lord made clear when he said: “You are of your father the devil.”
There are also

those fathers of whom it is said: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead.” That is also why the Moabites were forbidden to enter the assembly of the Lord until the third and fourth generation, so that because of their fathers' sins their sons would enter into the lineage of those whose deeds and ways they imitated. Hence it is also written: “The children of adulterers will not come to maturity.”

So whoever follows not the Father who is in heaven but the one who lives in earthly filth enters into the lineage of the earthly father. For “as was the earthly man, so are those who are earthly,” so that his life is earthly, there is no rest for him after death, and he will never see the light, because he sought what is temporal. But the one who has followed the glory of Christ, who has longed for that light “which enlightens every man coming into this world,” will find and see the eternal light, because Christ has redeemed him from death.

Then, therefore, he will reflect within himself that when he was in honor he did not understand, and so he will be like the beasts, he who ought to have been like the angels through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor, glory and everlasting duration from all ages, now and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.
EXPLANATION OF PSALM 61
(Title: To the end, for Idithun; a psalm of David himself.)

It is the unquestioned habit of all of us to hurry to the end and to want to know the sum of what we have read, seen or heard. So the title itself does not allow us to be idle, or to let an indication of our common desire pass by idle ears. For although the divine oracle shines out in other psalms too, it gleams more brightly in a psalm of this kind than in the rest. So let us consider more carefully what the end is. For “end” means the goal [?] and the sum of the matter we wish to explain. Christ is called the end, because he himself is the end of the law, as it is written:

“For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” He is also called the end because he himself is the beginning and the end. So the psalms entitled “to the end” are either about Christ or Christ's own: about Christ, when he is being proclaimed; Christ's own, when he proclaims himself, promises that he will come to earth, and deigns to reveal to us the passion his own body was to undergo.

And that is why they are inscribed in the title “of David himself,” as though the ministry of the prophetic mouth were assigned to the true David, to the Lord himself, through whom heavenly power thundered by means of a human voice and the divine sentence rang out.

Fittingly, “for Idithun,” who was a prophet and sang psalms with his six sons, serves as a kind of preface, because permission to prophesy belonged to those who, appointed to the ministry of psalm-singing, spoke divine oracles with a human voice. And since the passion of the Lord's body was to be undergone to abolish the error of the whole world, he expressed the more commendable instruction of the people under the name, of course, of the one whose diligence was proven. So let us listen to him speaking.

“Shall not my soul be subject to God?” When our Lord Jesus was about to take on human flesh in order to cleanse it in himself, what did he have to abolish first, if not the contagion of the old sin? For since guilt had crept in through disobedience, when the divine commands were violated, he certainly had to restore obedience before all else, in order to shut out the seedbed of error.

For that was the source from which the fibers of sin had spread, and so, like a good physician, he first had to cut away the roots of the ulcer, so that the edges of the wound might feel the healing remedy of the medicines. It is useless to treat the scar if the infection is creeping inside; indeed the wound grows worse if it is closed on the outside while the poison seethes within. For what good would it have done to forgive sin, if the inclination to sin remained?

That would have been not to heal the scar but to close it. So he wanted to cleanse the wound in order to heal the inclination, so that no trace of disobedience would remain. He took on obedience himself in order to pour it into us. For so it had to be: since through the disobedience of one man very many had been made sinners, through the obedience of one, in turn, many would be made righteous.

So the facts show how greatly those err who say that Christ took on human flesh but deny that he took on human feelings; they also go against the purpose of the Lord Jesus himself, for they take the man away from the man, since a man cannot exist without human feelings. For flesh without feelings is exempt from both reward and guilt. He had to take on and heal that very thing from which

guilt had flowed, in order to close off the source of error and, as it were, the doors through which sin burst forth. How would I recognize the Lord Jesus as man today, when I do not see his flesh but read of his feelings? How, I say, would I recognize him as man, if he had not been hungry, if he had not been thirsty, if he had not wept, if he had not said: “My soul is sorrowful even to death”? Indeed it is written: “He is also a man, and who will know him?”

But he who by his divine works is judged to be above men is recognized as a man through these things. So, although he was God, he wished so much to be believed to be a man that he called himself a man, saying: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth?” And he called himself not only a man but also the Son of Man, as when he says: “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?” Hence that man was declared to hold the sum of the faith who both acknowledged him as the Son of God and did not deny that he was a man.

He himself, then, is both in one: inseparable in number, and to be recognized by the distinction of his works, not by any difference of person. For it is not one who is from the Father and another who is from Mary; rather, he who was from the Father took flesh from the Virgin and took on feelings from his mother, so that he himself might take up our infirmities. Hence the prophet says: “And he grieves for us.” How could he grieve with my grief if he did not bear my feelings? “A man,” he says, “under a blow, and knowing how to bear infirmity.”

So he was made weak as a man, he suffered pain as a man, and we thought him a man in his sufferings. But he was the conqueror of weaknesses, not conquered by them. He suffered for us, not for himself, and was made weak not because of his own sins but because of ours, so that by his bruise he might heal us. What, after all, is "a man under the blow, who knows how to bear weakness," except that he truly felt the blow?

Or how could he know how to bear weakness if he had shut out all feeling of weakness? For what we carry, we bear as a burden. So he took up our sins in order to carry them, and he also took them up in order to cleanse them. Indeed it is written: "And he himself cleansed their sins. Therefore he will possess many as his inheritance and will divide the spoils of the strong." For the greater triumph is where the mind within is made clean. What he carries, then, has to do with forgiveness; what he cleanses has to do with correction.

So he took on our capacity to suffer, and he took on subjection as well. That he subjected all things to himself is his own; that he was subjected is ours. That is why he says: "Shall not my soul be subject to God?" It is the soul, he says, that is subject, not the Godhead; the soul that is subjected, not the power of God. For the power of God is not subject to his authority but united with it, and shares in that authority. What is subjected is the soul, which is often changed by the frailty of the human condition, not that which cannot be changed.

The soul suffers with the flesh and the flesh with the soul, for they are joined together as if sharing one dwelling. The soul that is subjected is the one that is sorrowful, as it is written: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." The soul that is subjected is the one that was taken up, not the one born of God the Father. And yet this subjection is not a mark of weakness but the working of power: it is the servant of a temporary dispensation rather than bound over to perpetual servitude. Hence he says: "Shall not my soul be subject to God?"

Why did he say "shall be" if the subjection is everlasting? Because the Son of God who was speaking is eternal, but he took on a soul in time; so he speaks of his soul's subjection as something still to come. Through that soul, then, came

obedience, and through it humility. Yet these were taken on not out of any weakness in his power, but to teach us discipline. For the Lord Jesus himself, "though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death," as the Apostle says. The Apostle wished to show that this subjection was not continual and perpetual but temporary,

such as was taken on with the flesh and laid aside together with the servitude of that body. So too it is written in the Letter to the Hebrews. For having set out the example, "You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek," Paul goes on: "In the days of his flesh he offered prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard [?] because of his fear.
