Although he was the Son, he learned obedience from the things he suffered; and being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him,
being called by God a priest according to the order

of Melchizedek." Has not the Apostle plainly proclaimed, then, that this obedience and humility belonged not to the Godhead but to the flesh? For what is learned belongs to time. So it was as a man that he learned obedience from what he suffered, in order to be made perfect in the flesh, and, by handing obedience down to us as an inheritance, to become the source of eternal salvation for us, for whom that first Adam had earlier become the source of death through the inheritance of disobedience.

Subjection, then, is a lesson in human virtue, not a diminishing of divine power. For if they call the Son lesser and unequal to the Father because he was subject to God the Father, is he therefore also less than his mother, because he was subject to his mother? For we read of Joseph and Mary: "And he was subject to them." But dutiful devotion is no loss to any of us; it is a gain. Through it the Lord Jesus has poured faith and grace into all of us, so as to make us, by a faithful spirit, subject to God the Father.

And so with a new and profound insight the Apostle says that he himself will be subject to the Father in us, when there is fullness of faith in all, and a kind of unity of devotion. For now, as long as we differ in our opinions, we in some way diminish the kingdom of Christ, since all things are not yet subject to him whose kingdom is unity. But when all things have been made subject to him, then he himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all, as it is written.

For now he is above all by power, but he must be in all by will; and he will so will when he finds everything in us full of himself and empty of sins. He is not yet subject to the Father, then, because Christ is not yet all and in all; but when Christ is all and in all, God will be all and in all. From this we gather that the kingdom of the Father and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit as well, is one, for whoever receives the Son receives the Father and receives the Holy Spirit too, since the power of the Trinity is one, its grace one, its working one.

And rightly the Lord added: "For from him is my salvation," as if to say: "Do not be troubled because I said that my soul will be subject to God. The soul that will be subject is the portion that is yours; but my salvation is from him, that is, I am always from the Father and in the Father. For I came from the Father into this world, and if you see a man, believe that he is the Son of God. But when the Paraclete comes, whom I will send you from my Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from my Father, he will bear witness concerning me."

The Son proceeds from the Father, and the Spirit proceeds from him; there is therefore no doubt at all about the unity of the Godhead. And so David longed for this salvation of God to be given to us, for it is itself eternal life, if we know both the Father as true God and the Son, who certainly came for our salvation, "but did not consider equality with God something to be grasped." He sets aside the assertion of his divinity and takes up the duty of the human dispensation.

And so he immediately added: "For he is my God, my helper, my defender; I shall be moved no more." He certainly says this as a man, since we ought to place our hope in God so as not to slip easily; and yet in saying "I shall be moved no more" he shows that he bears the marks of divine power.

For elsewhere you have him saying: "Yet once more I will move the earth." He moved it by the flood, when all flesh perished except those in Noah's ark; he moved it when Sodom and Gomorrah were consumed by sacred fire. These are signs of heavenly wrath. But since the Lord has chosen to save the human race rather than to destroy it, he who came for mercy will no longer be moved to wrath. He came to redeem us with his blood, not to shed ours; he came to offer himself for us and, like a good merchant, to secure his goods by the suffering of his own body.

And as he said this, he lifted up his eyes and saw his persecutors on one side and the spiritual forces of wickedness on the other, gathering together, and he said: "How long will you rush upon a man, slaying all of you?" That is: "Why are you hurrying to destroy the human race? Do you not know that I came for the redemption of all? I offered myself for all, so that by my offering I might protect everyone." So we take "man" either as the whole multitude of humankind or, if we take it of one man, we understand it as said of him: you rush upon him, but upon a man, since you cannot rush upon God, as you have elsewhere:

"Why do you seek to kill me, a man?" For the Godhead could not be subject to death, but only the humanity he had taken on. "If, then, you rush upon me and want to seize me, why do you want to kill those who are with me? It is enough for you to have the one you seek. I do not look for a partner in my suffering, for I need no helper for the salvation of all. I do not ask for an envoy, I send no messenger ahead; I myself, as messenger, offered myself to those who were not seeking me, I gave myself up to those who were not seizing me, in order to free those who had been seized in the snares of death."

"So you rush upon me as upon a leaning wall and a tottering fence, not knowing that I came not to make the wall lean or push the fence over, but to break it down. For I came as peace, to make the two one, breaking down the dividing wall of the fence" that separated flesh and soul, so that they could not be of one mind. And so the flesh fought against the soul and could not be subject to its rule, for the wall set in between stood in the way and kept it from obeying the soul's guidance.

The law of the flesh, then, was opposed to the law of the mind. The Lord Jesus took away this wall of ancient enmity, as one would a rampart, and opened a way for mind and flesh to meet, so that, coming together into one, they might pursue what was healthful for both. The wall, then, is a kind of towering mass of sins. That is why Paul says to the high priest of the Jews: "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall"; for a wall is built of mud and rubble.

It was with this that the Egyptians built their cities, when the Jews were forced to make bricks. In Egypt mud was worked, and there the people of God labored at sin. That is why they groaned, that is why they were heard and freed from sin; that is why the law was given and grace promised, so that the law might cut away sin in part, and grace forgive it all.

And while he was bestowing these things on us and undergoing these things for us, we were rejecting his price. Hence he says: "Yet they plotted to reject my price," when Judas the betrayer brought back the price and the Jews would not put it into the treasury, saying: "It is not lawful for us to put it into the treasury, because it is the price of blood." Here the betrayer is condemned by his own judgment, since he paid back the price he had received: a weak witness to the sacred gift, but a strong witness to his own crime. For each man is his own harshest accuser and passes on himself a sentence from which there is no excuse.

The rulers of the synagogue condemn themselves by their own judgment, for in finding fault with the one who returned it they admit that what they gave was the price of blood. For if it ought not to be taken back, neither ought it to have been paid. Would that they had either not given it or, having given it, had not taken it back! For they rejected what they would not put into the treasury, and with it they bought a field for the burial of strangers. Rightly, then, the Gentiles, who have gained burial in the field of him who was bought by the death of Christ, are no longer foreigners and strangers, but have become fellow citizens of the saints and members of the household of God, because they are buried with the Son of God. The Jews,

however, who rejected the price of his passion, are strangers to Christ. In this respect even the betrayer is more bearable than they, because he confesses his error, whereas they make their crime worse by excusing it; for confession after a sin shows greater shame. So they shamelessly rebuffed the man who was confessing their shared sacrilege, saying: "What is that to us? See to it yourself." For what was the betrayer saying but this: "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood"? How could what was a crime in the one who handed him over not be a sin in those who received him, when crime was added to crime, so that the one they had wickedly bought they might even more wickedly slaughter?

"I ran in thirst," he says. It is indeed true that our Lord Jesus thirsted. Blessed is the Lord's thirst, for he thirsted for us, and above all in his passion; indeed he said: "I thirst." He was thirsting at the very moment when he was pouring from his side streams of living water to quench the thirst of all. Indeed it is written: "Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly."

But in the Greek the word is ambiguous, since édramon [?] signifies both the singular and the plural. So, since according to the Greek we can understand both "I ran" and "they ran" — and we have said what "I ran" expresses, namely, "I hastened to take on the thirst of all, so that I might satisfy everyone with the abundance of an everlasting spring," for "whoever I give water to will not thirst, either here or in the age to come," as was said to the Samaritan woman — let us now say what "they ran in thirst" means: they hastened, in the heat of their unbelief, to deny the living spring and so to parch their throats with everlasting dryness [?], as the Lord himself says: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have made for themselves broken cisterns."

Nor is it surprising that they thirsted, since they could not hold the water of the eternal spring; it slipped away through the cracks of their unbelief. They thirsted, then, because they deprived themselves of the spiritual drink they had drawn from the rock that followed them. Hence Symmachus too says [?], that is, "they took pleasure in falsehood," when they brought false charges in place of true ones. Every lie brings thirst; truth brings an abundance that lasts for ever.

And how quickly he proved that they ran in falsehood: "With their mouth," he says, "they blessed, and in their heart they cursed." Wretched is the thirst of the faithless, who held one thing in their heart and spoke another with their mouth. But where the abundance of faith overflows, "with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." How they blessed with their mouth and cursed in their heart the course of the passion shows, when they said: "Let him come down from the cross and we will believe him" — fools! He rose from death and they did not believe; how would they have believed if he had come down from the cross? — and "He trusted in the Lord; let him rescue him; let him deliver him now, since he wants him." For they said these things to mock him rather than out of any wish, and they asked whether he was the Son of God, speaking peaceably with their words while plotting in their hearts a charge of sacrilege.

But these are mystical meanings; let us come to the moral sense. For Christ is not attacked only once. He was attacked once in his own body, which he took from the Virgin; he is attacked often in that body which is the Church, for we are the body of Christ and its members; and he is attacked too in each of his saints and in the innocent who have dedicated themselves to the Lord.

Let us recall a man recently attacked by all, abandoned and betrayed by his own. Not long ago he was set on the high seat of empire; suddenly, stripped of everything, he began to be hounded by the very men whose allegiance he had received by inheritance, as they closed in to destroy him and to bring about his death.

He had no helper, no one any longer on his side, no companion. What better could he say than what he had received from the very one to whom he had devoted himself: "Shall not my soul be subject to God?" That is: "Why do you persecute me, why do you rage, why do you insult me? You can kill the flesh; you cannot kill the soul. You can snatch away this life of the body; you cannot extinguish its merit." For it is written: "Do not fear those who can kill the flesh but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell."

The soul, then, that is subject to God is not subject to human power, for from him it hopes for the fruit of eternal life and the help of everlasting salvation. "He, then, to whom I have given myself will protect me though slain, will raise me up though dead, and will avenge me though murdered." The righteous man was taken away lest wickedness should change his heart. So this death is an escape from sin rather than a loss for the one who dies.

"For he is my God, my helper, my defender; I shall be moved no more." Whoever slips is moved, because he slides down from the firm ground, as it were, of his integrity and innocence. For once a man has been set on the rock of Christ, his footing should not slip; he should keep the firm foundation of his own standing.

Hence he is called immovable who keeps an immovable will and carries out his purpose with the resolve of a faithful mind. For we read also of the immovable will of God, as you have in the Letter to the Hebrews: "In this God, wishing to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the immovability of his will, interposed an oath." Rightly, then, the will of God is immovable, since it is moved by the enticements of no sin; human beings are movable, prone to slip into wrongdoing, easily led astray. Indeed it was said of the Jews: "Those who passed by blasphemed him, moving their heads," and the Lord himself says in the psalm: "All who saw me scorned me; they spoke with their lips and moved their heads."

Christ is the head of all; it is better, then, that Christ should remain in us than be moved by some movement of ours. Hence the Jews, moving their heads, said: "Away with such a fellow from the earth"; the Gerasenes begged him to depart from their region; but the Church held him and would not let him go. So she who held him possesses him, while those who moved cannot hold him. And the evangelist says beautifully that those passing by moved their heads — passing by, not standing. We stand in the holy courts; we pass by in the streets. The priest passed by,

the Levite went past; the one who tended the wounds inflicted stood still. And so those who passed along the way did not say: "The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we bless you from the house of the Lord"; for the feet of those who bless are standing feet, not passing ones. Indeed, it is those passing by, not those who stay, who strip the vineyard whose wall has been broken down; it is those passing by who hiss, as we read in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: "All who pass along the way have laid their hands on you; they hissed and wagged their heads at the daughter of Jerusalem."

That is why the priest could not be crowned, nor the Levite, because they passed by and went past like a shadow; but Stephen was crowned with martyrdom, because he saw the Lord standing, [?] immovable, not passing by. Immovable in faith, Stephen saw Christ immovable and was shaken by no fear of death. Stephen did not move, and neither did Christ. It was the sons of the betrayer who were moved, of whom it is said: "Let his sons be moved and driven out, and let them beg"; for whoever is moved needs a physician. The sinner is poor, the righteous man is rich, for he who always seeks the Lord lacks no good thing.

And since our discussion began from his saying "I shall be moved no more," David himself shows that to be moved means to be moved toward sin, when he says: "Who has set my soul in life and has not allowed my feet to be moved." Hence the Lord our God also says to a holy man:

"But you, stand here with me," for whoever is near to God cannot be near to a fall. For every sin, as if with an opponent's thrust, is accustomed to knock the mind from its place and shift it from its proper standing; the image seems drawn either from an enemy or from wrestling. Anger unsettles, lust inflames, envy goads, greed tortures, fear casts down, grief afflicts. And the Lord Jesus said to Peter: "Get behind me." He did not say "Get behind" — for that he said to the devil alone — but "Get behind me";

for whoever is behind Christ is not cast behind. But because Peter was in error, as the Lord himself says to him, "For you do not think the things of God but the things of men," therefore "come behind me, so that you may begin to think not human but divine things." And so this righteous man too, about to be snatched from the earth, says: "I shall be moved no more; for to depart and be with Christ is far better." For whoever has begun to be with Christ cannot slip, since for the righteous death is the end not of nature but of sin.

In the midst of these words he suddenly sees the ranks of his pursuers and, set amid dangers, anxious not for himself but for those he longed to set free, he says: "How long will you rush upon a man, slaying all of you? If it is me you seek, why do you want to kill the others?

I offer myself for many" — for only he who is the author of all could offer himself alone for all. So, as an imitator of the one he followed, he says: "If it is me you seek, let these go," so that the word which Jesus spoke might be fulfilled: "I have not lost any of them" — "except one," for in another book the Lord's saying includes this — "who nevertheless perished by his own will rather than," he says, "being punished by my severity.

And though I offer myself freely, you rush upon me and press down on me as on a leaning wall and a tottering fence." That is: "I, lately the summit of the noble imperial throne, once the mighty wall of an empire spread over the whole Roman world, now collapse like a leaning wall or a tottering fence."

"But be it so: they went after me even to death, they sought to kill me, saying, 'Let us remove the righteous man, let us remove the merciful man, for he is a burden to us even to look at.' Yet they also thought to wound my reputation and my chastity with false accusations." For this is what "they plotted to reject my price" means. Our price is chastity, which separates us from the beasts and joins us to the angels; our price is mercy, which, when given to the needy, redeems us from death; our price is faith, which has won for Christ all those weighed down by pagan error and slavery; our price is a good reputation, by which the course of each one's merits is assessed; our price is purity and simplicity, for it is written: "A pure man is a precious possession"; for nothing is more precious than a simple man.

Hence the Apostle says beautifully: "He abounded in the riches of his simplicity." For what is richer than simplicity, which, like a good head of a household, has abundance enough for itself and, content with its own purity, does not seek or gnaw away at what belongs to others, but pours itself out for others? For the innocent man believes every word and does not keep changing himself into various crafty shapes, as cunning does, which, in order to be cautious, fears everything and does not trust its own counsels, but keeps turning its own opinions over; simplicity, however, knows no fear. In this way, then, they tried to reject the price of the righteous man, though it can also be understood thus: they took his gold in their hands but rejected him in their inmost hearts, keeping the plunder while denying their loyalty.

Hence he also says: “I ran in thirst,” because he was seeking faith and could not find it, abandoned by his companions, deserted by his own. So too we read in the Gospel that the Lord of the laws both hungered and thirsted, since he hungered for our faith and thirsted for our works, and seemed to be seeking what belonged to others. Or, if we take it of bodily thirst, with what indignity he says: “I ran in thirst!” That is: I was thirsting while others belched up my wine, and from that lofty seat of supreme empire and royal opulence I was brought down, like some common man of the people, to the extremity of thirst.

And because the Greek has edramon, which means both “I ran” in the singular and “they ran” in the plural, it can also be understood thus: “They ran in thirst,” those whose throats were parched by their burning eagerness to shed my blood. For just as there is a thirst of faith, so there is also a thirst of faithlessness. The just man thirsts with the first, who says: “My soul has thirsted for you, O God”; the faithless thirst with the second, whose tongue is parched with thirst. With this thirst he thirsted

who, seated among the dishes and cups of a banquet, was plotting the murder of an innocent guest, the Augustus. Did it not seem to you, impious man, as you ate while preparing slaughter, that human bones were cracking beneath your teeth? As you drank wine and contemplated parricide, that you were pouring the blood of an innocent man into yourself from those cups? So utterly estranged were you, not only from imitating the divine word but even from reading it, that there did not come to your mind that little verse of the psalms: “But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance, who took sweet food together with me,” nor that other, which the Lord Jesus himself recalls in the Gospel: “He who ate bread with me has lifted up his heel against me”?

What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah? You have left us many heirs of your betrayal and deceit. For this can also be turned, by apostrophe, against Judas the traitor. You betrayed the Life, the kingdom, the Lord [?]. But the Lord Jesus was betrayed once in himself, and is betrayed often in his little servants: “For what you did to one of the least of these,” he says, “you did to me.” You received the purse entrusted to you and the money of the poor; he received the provinces entrusted to him. You received the honour of an apostle; he the dignity of military command and the insignia of government. I count up his honours in order to magnify his crime.

Each of you violated the fellowship of the table; yet you rose from the banquet to betray, he to murder. That is: you, though steeped in crime, had more shame, for you denied that you had believed death would be inflicted on the Lord you were betraying, and you gave back the price, so that the wages of parricide might not seem to remain with you. He not only kept the reward of betrayal he had received, but even extorted it when it had not been offered. He was not deceived by another's lie; rather, he deceived by his own, and deceived in order to kill.

And when the one refused the banquet, seeing that he was to be put to death, the other offered him a sworn oath, so that no part of the heaping up of his crime might be lost to him. Finally, the money of the earlier traitor served for the burial of strangers; this one denied his own prince a proper burial.

Nor was there lacking one to wash his hands, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this just man.” By this Pilate did not cleanse himself but defiled himself; he did not free himself but entangled himself. For although there is no weight in the judgments of the reprobate, yet there is a stronger bond in their confessions. The just are absolved not by another's sentence but by their own life; the unjust, who cannot bind others, bind themselves the more tightly by their own words. Yet, lest this man too should seem to lack his own confession,

he swore an oath in order to perjure himself; he washed his hands while touching the Gospel, so that nothing might be missing from the precedent; he washed his hands with water so as to defile them more wickedly with innocent blood. Nor was a Herod lacking, whom this second Pilate believed he would please if he sent him the captured prince.

What shall I say of this as well: that he too was clothed in a white garment to be mocked, and afterwards was given a royal garment in which to die, so that he might not seem to have lost the honour due to him? For although he perished by a crime, even in death he retained the right of the power conferred on him, at the hands of the very men by whom it was being denied, whether through their service or their assent.

A funeral procession would have been added to this great crime, had not one who wept bitterly over these things, learning what was being prepared, been moved by just grief to rebuke the proud victor, saying that such things were customarily inflicted on tyrants, not on kings. Thus, stirred by horror at the outrage, he put aside the preparations for that most hideous crime. So neither was one lacking to ask for burial, even if that Joseph who was called just was lacking. But Maximus, far more savage, denied what Pilate himself could not take away. In this the parricide was lacking in humanity, yet grace was not lacking to the innocent; and through patience assumed for a time, vengeance was postponed for a little while.

And therefore he says: “Nevertheless my soul is subject to God, since from him comes my patience. For he is my God and my Saviour, my protector; I shall not be moved away.” That is: has the burial denied to my body taken from me the dwelling of everlasting rest? I have my dwelling

in the Lord's tabernacle, and on his holy mountain I shall rest. I shall not be moved away by human crime, because I have been taken up by the Lord's favour, since neither death nor sword nor tribulation will be able to separate me from the love of Christ. For it is not the innocent but the sinner who is moved out of the tents of the just. The heirs of Judas the traitor are moved away; of them and those like them it is rightly said: “Let his children be shaken and removed and go begging; let them be cast out of their dwellings.”

This also applies well to the Lord Jesus Christ, who, when he had descended to earth and was crucified and buried, did not move away from the Father but remained in the Father: “I was handed over, and I did not go out.” Nor did he lay aside what he was, but kept it; nor did he cease to be in the form of God, but continued in it. The glory of God was not diminished by his taking on a body; rather, abiding, it won a triumph and did not lose its power. Hence he himself says: “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of power.”

Hence he exhorts to faith the peoples of the nations, whom he has called together and won for his Father by his blood, saying: “Hope in him, all the assembly of my people”; that is, not Israel alone, but “all,” he says; not the remnant alone, but also the fullness of the Gentiles; not the Gentiles alone, but Israel too. For when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved. Who can comprehend the divine mysteries?

Their multitude is so great that Paul rightly marvels and justly said: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” The Gentiles were rejected so that Israel might be chosen; afterwards Israel was blinded on account of the calling of the Gentiles, and the remnant of blinded Israel was saved according to the election of grace, after the fullness of the Gentiles had come in. Thus the fault of Israel benefited the Gentiles, and the faith of the Gentiles set free the people of Israel.

“Pour out your hearts before him,” he says. Whoever puts on faith must first put off faithlessness and empty his heart of every stain of malice, so that his heart may become capable of receiving spiritual grace. Therefore the apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind.” For when the old malice is poured out, new grace is taken up, by which each person is renewed.

So the Son of God says, “Pour out your hearts before him,” because he knew that the Father would say: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh.” There is also the common expression by which we are said to pour out our heart when we open all the thoughts and desires of our heart to someone. Let us therefore cast our thoughts upon God and not believe that anything is hidden from him. We pour out our heart before him when we empty ourselves of human disputings.

“But vain are the sons of men; the sons of men are liars in the balances, so as to deceive.” If the sons of men are vain and the sons of men are liars, the sons of God, who were born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man but of God, can be free of vanity. For the sons of men imagine that they weigh out equity and examine justice with the gravity of a stricter judgment: hard on others, lax with themselves, unjust in their deeds, censors in their speech. Hence Solomon says:

“A double weight is an abomination to the Lord, and a false balance is not good.” By this he means those who plot plunder with an insatiable heart while displaying sobriety on their faces. Such are the scribes of the Jews, who lay on others the heavy burdens of a harsher observance, while they have no straight yoke for their own soul but are bent by their leaning toward iniquity, and themselves run from their own precepts. Thus in avarice, as in the root of all vices, is found what is the head and tinder of iniquity; and a man who renounces the world and is buried with Christ through the sacrament of baptism, being dead to the world, ought to turn aside from it and flee it.

“Do not hope in iniquity,” he says, “and do not covet plunder; if riches flow in, do not set your heart on them.” You see that they flow in; do you not see that they flow past? Naked you were born, naked you will die. Why do you seek to take in what you cannot take away with you? What you admire are streams; as they come, so they pass by and ebb away. Only the Jordan, into which you went down, was turned back, and it admonishes you to

return to the very source and origin of nature, which brought you forth naked, not clothed in a garment, so that you may learn not to seek superfluous things. That you blush at being naked was taught you by guilt, not by nature; for there would be no shame about the genitals if there were no guilt. The other animals are neither clothed to be covered nor clothed to be protected; all of them are protected enough by the covering of their own nature.

We, in seeking superfluous things, have lost the covering of nature and forfeited the common right. Therefore a healing teaching is inscribed in this psalm, because he trained either Jeduthun, or himself under Jeduthun's name, through spiritual exercise for undergoing temptations, so that one placed in distress may submit himself to God and, if he has sinned before, may cease to sin and not be swayed by a relapse into error.

“God has spoken once; these two things I have heard.” God spoke once, and many things were heard, because he did not speak through letters and syllables. He spoke through riddles, he spoke through visions, he spoke through the distributions of graces, he spoke through the spirit of individuals; but we speak many things and are scarcely heard. He spoke once in the law; the same things he spoke again in the Gospel.

Or perhaps, as I think, since he spoke in many ways in the prophets but lastly spoke in his Son, he spoke once when he spoke in the Son, and then even those things were heard which had not been heard before by those to whom he had spoken through the prophets. So he spoke once in the New Testament, and the Old Testament, which had not been heard, was heard; for the Lord himself said of the Jewish people: “They will see and not see, they will hear and not hear.” They will hear with the bodily ear, but they will not hear with the hearing of the mind.

So to us, that is, to the Church, he spoke once and two things were heard, because in the Church we have heard and understood what those who read had not understood, and what those who heard had not heard. For Christ alone opened the human ear to know the mysteries; he alone loosed the seal of the book and solved the riddles of the prophets.

“And therefore he will render to each according to his works.” In this he also includes the quality of the works, so that either he restores rewards to the merits of each for many and better works, or, on the contrary, we are weighed down by both the number and the severity of our deserts.
